0.title: If the LORD Is God, Follow Him
0.overview:
The message. First Kings asks one question of every king, and of every reader: will you follow the LORD with your whole heart? Solomon begins with wisdom and builds the temple where God puts his name, but ends with a divided heart; the kingdom splits, and the north turns to golden calves and then to Baal. Yet God does not let go of his people. He keeps a lamp burning in Jerusalem for David’s sake, and sends prophets, above all Elijah, to call Israel back: “If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (18:21). Kings come and go; the word of the LORD comes true to the letter. The book leaves us longing for a king whose heart is wholly true to God, and the New Testament names him: Jesus, “something greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42).

Background: the writer. First and Second Kings were one book in the Hebrew Bible, so 1 Kings carries straight on from 2 Samuel, with David old and dying. The author is not named; Jewish tradition credited Jeremiah, but the book does not say. Its last event is the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon, about 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27–30), so it was finished in the exile. Yet it rests on much older records, which it names: “the Book of the Acts of Solomon” (11:41) and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and of Judah (14:19, 29). Many scholars treat Deuteronomy to Kings as one history compiled in the exile, since Kings measures every reign by Deuteronomy’s law. This commentary takes the writer to be an inspired prophetic historian of the exile, working faithfully from records kept at the time.

When and where. The book covers about 120 years, from Solomon’s accession, about 970 BC, to the death of Ahab, about 853 BC. Solomon reigned forty years (11:42) at a rare moment when Egypt was weak and Assyria had not yet risen, so a small kingdom could grow rich. After his death, about 930 BC, the ten northern tribes broke away. In the north Omri built a new capital at Samaria (16:24), and his son Ahab married Jezebel, daughter of the king of Sidon, and made Baal the state religion. Baal was the Canaanite storm god, thought to send the rain, so when Elijah announces that there will be no rain “except by my word” (17:1), the drought itself is a challenge to Baal.

The first hearers. The book was written for people who had lost the throne of David, the land and the temple, burned by the Babylonians in 586 BC, and they were asking why. God had warned Solomon that the house would become a heap of ruins and passers-by would ask, “Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?” The answer: “Because they abandoned the LORD their God” (9:8–9). The exiles were reading their own story, but also of a God who keeps his word to David and hears his people when they repent in the land of their captivity (8:46–50).

The kind of writing. This is history, but prophetic history: in the Hebrew Bible Kings stands among the Former Prophets. It is selective on purpose. Omri, a powerful king, gets six verses (16:23–28); a widow’s flour jar gets half a chapter. Every king is weighed by one standard: did he do what was right, as David had, or walk “in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin” (22:52)? The narrator often reports without comment, and we are meant to measure events against God’s law: Solomon’s horses, gold and many wives are told as glories, but Deuteronomy 17:16–17 had forbidden all three.

How the book makes its case. The first half belongs to Solomon [1–11]. His throne is secured [1–2], and he asks God for “an understanding mind to govern your people” (3:9) and receives wisdom, wealth and peace [3–4]. He builds the temple, and at its dedication asks, “But will God indeed dwell on the earth?” (8:27) [5–8]. His fame draws the queen of Sheba [9–10]. Then “when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (11:4) [11]. Next the kingdom is torn [12–16]. Rehoboam refuses to lighten the people’s yoke and loses ten tribes; Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan (12:28); the northern throne passes from family to family by murder, while Judah survives only because “for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem” (15:4). Last comes the contest between the LORD and Baal [17–22]. Elijah shuts the sky, is fed by ravens and a foreign widow, and calls down fire on Carmel until the people cry, “The LORD, he is God” (18:39). Fleeing to Horeb in despair, he meets God in “the sound of a low whisper” (19:12). Ahab takes Naboth’s vineyard by judicial murder, and dies in battle “according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken” (22:38).

Can its history be trusted? Some scholars doubt that a book finished in the exile can tell us much about Solomon or Ahab. But where it touches the records of its neighbours it fits them: Pharaoh Shishak’s raid (14:25), listed on his victory inscription at Karnak; Omri, named on the Moabite Stone; and Ahab, recorded with two thousand chariots against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BC. The reign lengths can seem not to add up, but Israel and Judah counted regnal years differently, and sons often reigned alongside their fathers; when this is allowed for, as Edwin Thiele showed, the dates largely fit, though some details are still debated. This commentary’s view is that Kings is true history, its miracles real events, and that numbers differing between Kings and Chronicles are copying slips, not errors in Scripture as first given.

Where it leads: to Christ. First Kings leads to Christ by promise, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The promise is God’s word to David, “You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel” (9:5), and the lamp kept in Jerusalem was kept for the Son of David, who reigns now at the Father’s right hand. Solomon’s wisdom drew a queen from afar, but “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Solomon asked whether God would dwell on the earth; Jesus called his own body the temple: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Jesus pointed to Elijah sent to a widow of Sidon as a sign of grace to the nations (Luke 4:25–26), and Paul saw in the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal “a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5). Above all, the book exposes the need. No king after Solomon had a heart wholly true to the LORD. Micaiah saw Israel “as sheep that have no shepherd” (22:17); Jesus had compassion on the crowds, “because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (Mark 6:34). He is the king whose heart never turned aside, who did not seize a vineyard by murder but laid down his life for his people.

For us. First Kings warns that a divided heart rarely falls in a day. Solomon drifted one compromise at a time after the best start any king ever had. It warns against “limping between two different opinions” (18:21). But it also comforts. When the faithful seem few, God has not lost his people; when his servant is spent, he gives sleep, food and a gentle word before a new task. And the word of God outlasts every throne. Our hope does not rest on our own wholehearted devotion, which fails as Solomon’s did, but on the true Son of David, in whom “all the promises of God find their Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

1.title: Adonijah's Bid and Solomon Anointed
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.<sup>2</sup>Therefore his servants said to him, "Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm."<sup>3</sup>So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.<sup>4</sup>The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not.<sup>5</sup>Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." And he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.<sup>6</sup>His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" He was also a very handsome man, and he was born next after Absalom.<sup>7</sup>He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest. And they followed Adonijah and helped him.<sup>8</sup>But Zadok the priest and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and Nathan the prophet and Shimei and Rei and David's mighty men were not with Adonijah.<sup>9</sup>Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the Serpent's Stone, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials of Judah,<sup>10</sup>but he did not invite Nathan the prophet or Benaiah or the mighty men or Solomon his brother.<sup>11</sup>Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king and David our lord does not know it?<sup>12</sup>Now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.<sup>13</sup>Go in at once to King David, and say to him, 'Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, "Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne"? Why then is Adonijah king?'<sup>14</sup>Then while you are still speaking with the king, I also will come in after you and confirm your words."<sup>15</sup>So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber (now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king).<sup>16</sup>Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, "What do you desire?"<sup>17</sup>She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.'<sup>18</sup>And now, behold, Adonijah is king, although you, my lord the king, do not know it.<sup>19</sup>He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but Solomon your servant he has not invited.<sup>20</sup>And now, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.<sup>21</sup>Otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders."<sup>22</sup>While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.<sup>23</sup>And they told the king, "Here is Nathan the prophet." And when he came in before the king, he bowed before the king, with his face to the ground.<sup>24</sup>And Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'?<sup>25</sup>For he has gone down this day and has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. And behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!'<sup>26</sup>But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon he has not invited.<sup>27</sup>Has this thing been brought about by my lord the king and you have not told your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"<sup>28</sup>Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king.<sup>29</sup>And the king swore, saying, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity,<sup>30</sup>as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,' even so will I do this day."<sup>31</sup>Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"<sup>32</sup>King David said, "Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." So they came before the king.<sup>33</sup>And the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord and have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.<sup>34</sup>And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet there anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!'<sup>35</sup>You shall then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. And I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah."<sup>36</sup>And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.<sup>37</sup>As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David."<sup>38</sup>So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon.<sup>39</sup>There Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!"<sup>40</sup>And all the people went up after him, playing on pipes, and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was split by their noise.<sup>41</sup>Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished feasting. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, "What does this uproar in the city mean?"<sup>42</sup>While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. And Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news."<sup>43</sup>Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king,<sup>44</sup>and the king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And they had him ride on the king's mule.<sup>45</sup>And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have gone up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. This is the noise that you have heard.<sup>46</sup>Solomon sits on the royal throne.<sup>47</sup>Moreover, the king's servants came to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make the name of Solomon more famous than yours, and make his throne greater than your throne.' And the king bowed himself on the bed.<sup>48</sup>And the king also said, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.'"<sup>49</sup>Then all the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose, and each went his own way.<sup>50</sup>And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.<sup>51</sup>Then it was told Solomon, "Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, for behold, he has laid hold of the horns of the altar, saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'"<sup>52</sup>And Solomon said, "If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die."<sup>53</sup>So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and paid homage to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go to your house."
1.overview:
Where we are. First Kings carries straight on from 2 Samuel (see the introduction). David, the giant-killer and king, is old and cannot get warm, and God’s promise of a son on his throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16) is unsettled: no heir has been named in public, and the eldest surviving son moves to fill the gap.

The message. The throne of God’s kingdom is not taken by the man who exalts himself; it is given to the king God has chosen and sworn to. Through an old man’s silence, a court’s planning and a father’s failures, the LORD keeps his word to David: the son who grasped is humbled in an afternoon, and the son who was given the throne is anointed.

Why it was said. The first readers had lost David’s throne altogether (see the introduction). They needed to see how that throne was first secured, not by strength, popularity or the ordinary rules of inheritance, but by God’s promise and choice, and so to keep looking for the son of David whom God would still raise up.

How the chapter makes its case. The king lies cold, and Adonijah, a son his father never once corrected, exalts himself with Absalom’s old props and holds a feast for his supporters (vv. 1–10). Nathan and Bathsheba go to David and make him face his own oath, and the danger his silence has created (vv. 11–27). David rouses himself, swears again by the God who redeemed him, and has Solomon anointed at Gihon and proclaimed with the trumpet (vv. 28–40). The noise ends Adonijah’s feast: his guests desert him, he clings to the altar, and Solomon’s first ruling gives him clear terms (vv. 41–53).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise to David takes its first step here, but Solomon is only the first anointed son (in Hebrew, a messiah), and he will fail. The pattern runs through the whole Bible and ends in Jesus. Adonijah “exalted himself”; Christ “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” but humbled himself, and “therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:6, 9). He is the Anointed Son the Father enthroned, and he stated the rule this chapter acts out: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

For us. God’s promises do not depend on our strength, and they are not hurried by our grasping. We are called to receive from his hand rather than seize, to trust the King he has given, and, like Solomon and unlike David, to say the hard and loving word plainly instead of hiding in silence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With David old and silent about his heir, the son he never corrected helps himself to the throne. The king lies cold under his blankets, and Abishag is brought to warm him, though he does not know her (vv. 1–4). Adonijah exalts himself with Absalom’s old props, chariots and fifty runners, and the narrator explains him in one aside: his father never once asked him why he had done anything (vv. 5–6). Joab and Abiathar back him; Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and the mighty men do not (vv. 7–8). He holds a sacrificial feast at En-rogel and invites everyone except the men loyal to Solomon (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The props are Absalom's, almost exactly: chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him is what Absalom got himself at 2 Samuel 15:1, soon after his father kissed him.
verseByVerse.examples: But verse 6 is not about Adonijah. It is about his father, and it is one of the saddest parentheses in Scripture: David had never once, in the man's whole life, asked him why he had done something.

verseByVerse.quote: Now King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm. Therefore his servants said to him, "Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm." So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king. The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not. Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." And he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" He was also a very handsome man, and he was born next after Absalom. He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest. And they followed Adonijah and helped him. But Zadok the priest and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and Nathan the prophet and Shimei and Rei and David's mighty men were not with Adonijah. Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the Serpent's Stone, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials of Judah, but he did not invite Nathan the prophet or Benaiah or the mighty men or Solomon his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With David old and silent, his eldest surviving son exalts himself and claims the throne, a son his father had never once corrected. The chapter opens on weakness and an empty place: the king can no longer warm himself, no heir has been named in public, and Adonijah steps into the gap with a dead rebel’s props and a feast.

Now King David was old and advanced in years. A deliberate first sentence. The last two books gave us a boy with a sling, a king who danced before his capital and a fugitive who walked up a hill barefoot. Here David lies under a pile of blankets, and the heat will not come.

Abishag the Shunammite. A young woman is fetched from her village and put in a dying man’s bed as a source of warmth, and nobody asks her anything. She has a name and a home town and no recorded word in Scripture. The narrator neither condemns the plan nor commends it; he tells us her name, which is more than the ten concubines of 2 Samuel 20 ever got.

But the king knew her not. The last clause of verse 4 is there for a reason: Abishag is in the household but is not his wife, which explains what Adonijah is really asking for at 2:17, and why Solomon reacts as he does.

Exalted himself. The writer’s own verdict, placed before the quotation (v. 5). Nobody exalted Adonijah: he did it himself, and then said “I will be king”, which nobody had told him. The Bible runs on the contrast between the one who lifts himself up and the one God lifts up, and this chapter acts it out.

Fifty men to run before him. Read verse 5 beside 2 Samuel 15:1: “Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.” The same equipment, the same number of runners, the same king’s son announcing himself before anybody has given him anything. Adonijah was a grown man in the palace when Absalom stood at the gate for four years, stole the hearts of Israel, drove their father barefoot out of Jerusalem, and died hanging in an oak with three javelins in him. He watched it all, and is doing it again, prop for prop.

His father had never at any time displeased him. Verse 6 explains Adonijah, and it is really about his father: one of the saddest parentheses in Scripture. Not once in the man’s life did David rebuke, correct or even question him, and the example given is the mildest question there is. Not a prohibition, not a threat of punishment, just “Why have you done thus and so?” David never asked it.

A pattern in David. Put that beside the previous book. When Amnon raped Tamar, David “was very angry” and did nothing (2 Samuel 13:21). When Absalom murdered Amnon, David mourned, then longed for the murderer and brought him home without a trial and without a pardon. When Absalom sat at the city gate for four years collecting a rebellion, nobody asked him what he was doing. So Adonijah reached his thirties never having been asked to account for anything, and the first large thing he does is help himself to a kingdom.

A warning for parents. Notice which father this describes. It is not the harsh father who produces Adonijah, but the one who cannot bear the discomfort of asking the question. Yet it is a warning, not a verdict on every parent whose child has gone astray. Children make their own choices, and the LORD says of Israel, “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me” (Isaiah 1:2). A parent grieving a wayward son is not thereby a David, and may still bring that son to God in prayer.

The idol behind the indulgent parent. Our culture tends to admire a father like David: love, we assume, means affirming, and correction feels like a failure of love (on that confusion, see the note on Hebrews 12:7–8). But the discomfort David could not bear was his own, not his son’s. Indulgence often looks like love for the child while it is really love for a quiet house, or for being liked, and parents can make an idol of their children’s approval as surely as anyone makes one of money. The child pays for it. The gospel cuts that knot. A parent already approved by the Father in Christ does not need a son’s approval, and so can risk his anger for his good. And it shows what love looks like when it will not indulge: God did not overlook our rebellion to keep the peace; he bore its cost himself, so that he could both correct his children and keep them.

He was also a very handsome man. This history keeps saying that about the wrong men. Saul was the handsomest man in Israel and a head taller than anybody (1 Samuel 9:2); Absalom had no blemish in him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head (2 Samuel 14:25). Over all of them stands the sentence spoken to Samuel in a courtyard at Bethlehem: “the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Born next after Absalom. The succession as the country would have counted it. Amnon and Absalom are dead, and the second son, Chileab (2 Samuel 3:3), is never mentioned again and had presumably died. By every ordinary rule of inheritance the throne is Adonijah’s, which makes this a real contest rather than a squalid grab: he has a case. What he lacks is the one thing that decides it, the oath David had sworn and, behind it, God’s own choice (2:15).

He conferred with Joab. The two names in verse 7 are a shock: both men have been with David since the wilderness. Joab has run his army for more than thirty years. Abiathar is the priest’s son who escaped the massacre at Nob and ran to David, bringing the ephod (the priestly garment used for asking God’s guidance), and to whom David said, “Stay with me; do not be afraid… With me you shall be in safekeeping” (1 Samuel 22:23). Why they go is not stated. Joab has reason to fear a new reign: David has never dealt with his crimes, and Adonijah is the candidate least likely to. Abiathar has watched Zadok rise beside him for a generation. It is the last decision either man makes, and both are ruined by it within two chapters.

Were not with Adonijah. Verse 8 gives the other list, which decides the chapter. Zadok, the other priest. Benaiah, who commands the royal bodyguard and once killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day (2 Samuel 23:20). Nathan, who once walked into this palace and said “You are the man!” And “David’s mighty men”, the thirty-seven whose names are listed near the close of 2 Samuel (23:8–39). Adonijah has the general and one priest; Solomon’s side has the bodyguard, the other priest, the prophet, and the veterans who had followed David since his outlaw days. The Shimei named here is probably not Shimei son of Gera, who cursed David (2:8); the name was common, and nothing more is known of him or of Rei.

Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle. The guest list (vv. 9–10) shows what the feast is for: a sacrificial meal at a spring outside the city, with the king’s sons and the officials of Judah, is a gathering to proclaim him king. The names left off it, Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men and Solomon, show the plan: he knows where he stands with them, and means to present the country with a finished fact before they can react. He is a day too slow.

Uncertain wording. “The Serpent’s Stone” (v. 9) renders a Hebrew name built on a verb used of creatures that crawl or glide; some translate it “the sliding stone”. Why it bore that name, and exactly where it stood, are unknown. It was beside En-rogel, a spring usually placed just south of the city where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet. Nothing in the story depends on it.
verseByVerse.note: 1 and 2 Kings were one book in the Hebrew Bible, tracing the kings from Solomon (about 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC). En-rogel was a spring just south of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promise moves forward through a prophet’s plan and a mother’s plain words. Nathan warns Bathsheba that Adonijah has made himself king without David’s knowledge, and that her life and Solomon’s are now in danger (vv. 11–12). He sends her in to remind the king of his oath that Solomon would reign, and promises to follow and confirm her words (vv. 13–14). She tells the old king the facts and what is at stake: all Israel is waiting for him to speak, and his silence will make criminals of her and her son (vv. 15–21). Nathan arrives as planned and asks whether the king has authorised this (vv. 22–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Bathsheba's argument is not sentiment and it is not a mother's ambition. When a new king takes a throne with rivals alive, the rivals and their households die. She is telling an old man that his failure to say anything will kill two people, and she is right.
verseByVerse.examples: At 2 Samuel 12 Nathan came with a word from God and told the king he was a murderer. Here he plans a sequence and times his own entrance, and the writer records the difference without comment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king and David our lord does not know it? Now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon. Go in at once to King David, and say to him, 'Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, "Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne"? Why then is Adonijah king?' Then while you are still speaking with the king, I also will come in after you and confirm your words." So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber (now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king). Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, "What do you desire?" She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.' And now, behold, Adonijah is king, although you, my lord the king, do not know it. He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but Solomon your servant he has not invited. And now, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him. Otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders." While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in. And they told the king, "Here is Nathan the prophet." And when he came in before the king, he bowed before the king, with his face to the ground. And Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'? For he has gone down this day and has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. And behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!' But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon he has not invited. Has this thing been brought about by my lord the king and you have not told your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathan and Bathsheba make the king face his own oath: his silence is about to hand the throne to the wrong son and cost Solomon and his mother their lives. God’s promise moves forward here not by a vision but through a prophet’s careful planning and a mother’s plain speech.

Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. Nathan moves first, and he goes to the mother. When these two last stood in the same story, Nathan was telling David “you are the man” about her husband’s murder. The child conceived then died; the second is the one this chapter is about, and Nathan brought God’s word of love for him: “the LORD loved him and sent a message by Nathan the prophet”, who named him Jedidiah, which means “beloved of the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:24–25).

That you may save your own life. Not alarmism (v. 12). Everybody in that palace knew that a new king with a live rival does not leave the rival alive, nor the rival’s mother. Bathsheba is being told, correctly, that she and Solomon have hours.

I also will come in after you and confirm your words. Nathan plans the sequence (vv. 13–14), and what kind of thing this is deserves to be said plainly. This is the prophet who told David a story about a lamb and named him a murderer to his face (2 Samuel 12). Yet in this chapter he never once says “thus says the LORD” or claims any word from God. He assesses a political situation, works out a two-stage approach, briefs the person who will go first and times his own entrance. It is a court manoeuvre, and it may well be a righteous one, since there was an oath, Solomon was God’s choice and the alternative was two murders. But it is not the same kind of act as 2 Samuel 12, and the writer lets both stand without explaining the difference. People who serve God are often doing ordinary work with ordinary judgment, and God uses it; pretending that every such decision is a revelation helps nobody.

Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king. The parenthesis in verse 15 is a picture: Bathsheba comes into the room where her husband is dying, and another woman is there looking after him.

You swore to your servant by the LORD your God. She begins with the oath (v. 17), of which neither Kings nor Samuel has told us. But she and Nathan both treat it as known, David does not dispute it, and he confirms it under oath in verse 30. Chronicles reports God’s word to David that a son named Solomon would build the house and that his throne would be established (1 Chronicles 22:9–10), so the promise is not being invented here.

The eyes of all Israel are on you. She reports the facts, guest list included, and lets the omission speak (vv. 18–19). Then the sentence that gets through (v. 20). Not “you owe me”, nor “Adonijah is unworthy”: she tells a king who has been lying under blankets that the country is waiting for him to speak, and is reading his silence as his answer.

Counted offenders. Treated as criminals (v. 21): if Adonijah takes the throne, she and Solomon will not be rivals to be watched but criminals to be dealt with. She is not asking for a crown for her son but not to be executed, and asking it of a man who has never once protected any of his children from the consequences of his own inaction.

Nathan the prophet came in. He arrives while she is still speaking (v. 22), exactly as arranged, and he asks a question (v. 24). He does not accuse Adonijah of treason or tell David what to do; he asks whether the king has authorised this. There are only two possible answers, and one of them requires David to act at once. He ends on the question again (v. 27), now with an edge: if you did authorise it, why were your closest servants not told? Whether that is a courtier’s tact or a prophet’s way of letting a man see what he has allowed, it works either way.

A promise that hangs by a thread and holds. Behind the manoeuvring stands a promise. God had told David, “I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). Here it seems to hang on an old man’s failing attention and a well-timed entrance, and it holds. It will hang by thinner threads later, once on a single royal child hidden in the temple (2 Kings 11:2–3), and hold until an angel tells a young woman of Nazareth that “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). God keeps his word through sleepy kings, and sometimes in spite of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — On the King's Own Mule
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One clear word from the king, sworn before God, puts the chosen son on the throne. David swears again, by the LORD who has redeemed him out of every adversity, that Solomon will reign (vv. 28–31). He gives exact orders: Solomon is to ride the king’s own mule to Gihon, be anointed by Zadok and Nathan, and be proclaimed with the trumpet (vv. 32–35). Benaiah answers with a prayer that the LORD will say the same, and make Solomon’s throne greater than David’s (vv. 36–37). It is done, and the people’s rejoicing is so loud that the earth seems to split (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath he swears, as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity, is almost word for word what he said more than thirty years earlier (2 Samuel 4:9). At the end of his life it still names God as the one who got him out of everything.
verseByVerse.examples: The mule is his own, and everybody watching knows whose animal that is. The last royal son to ride a mule in this history was Absalom.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king. And the king swore, saying, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity, as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,' even so will I do this day." Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!" King David said, "Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." So they came before the king. And the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord and have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet there anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!' You shall then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. And I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah." And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so. As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David." So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon. There Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!" And all the people went up after him, playing on pipes, and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was split by their noise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Roused at last, David swears again by the God who redeemed him and has Solomon publicly anointed and proclaimed, so that the king God chose takes the throne that same day. One clear word from the king, backed by an oath, undoes Adonijah’s whole feast.

Then King David answered. The old man moves, and for this section he is the David of his prime. For twenty-seven verses he has lain in bed while others arranged things around him; now he gives eight orders in a row, every one exact.

As the LORD lives. His last oath in Scripture (v. 29) quotes himself. More than thirty years earlier, to two men who brought him the head of Ish-bosheth expecting thanks, he said, “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity” (2 Samuel 4:9). It answered men who thought he needed help to get a throne, and he swears by it still, arranging a succession from his bed. A lion and a bear, a giant, Saul’s spears, an escape through a window at night, two caves, a burnt town, a forest: God got him out of every one.

Redeemed out of every adversity. To redeem is to buy someone back, to pay what it takes to get him out of a grip he cannot break himself, and David means not one rescue but a lifetime of them. Notice that he is not the hero of his own sentence. We tell our stories with ourselves at the centre, the giant we beat, the trouble we got through; David tells his as a list of times he was bought back. One adversity still lay ahead of him, and no sling would answer it. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Jesus is the true and better David, whose victory becomes his people’s victory though they never lifted a stone themselves. The Son of David went down into death and came out, and so God “gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57). This week, try telling your own story the way David did: as rescues, not achievements. See Redemption in the Theological Dictionary.

Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah. He summons the three loyal names of verse 8 (v. 32), and one of his first orders is about an animal.

My own mule. The king’s personal mount (v. 33), which nobody else rides and everyone in the city can recognise. Putting Solomon on it is a public statement that needs no herald: whatever is happening at En-rogel, this is the king’s own son on the king’s own animal with the king’s own guard around him. And one other royal son in this history rode a mule. He was riding it through a wood when it went under an oak, his head caught in the branches, and “the mule that was under him went on” (2 Samuel 18:9). The writer does not mention Absalom; he has already put the fifty runners in verse 5.

Bring him down to Gihon. As deliberate as the mule. Adonijah feasts at En-rogel, south of the city; Gihon is the spring on the east side, close under the walls and within earshot, probably the spring whose water shaft gave David’s men their way into Jerusalem in the first place (2 Samuel 5:8).

Then blow the trumpet. Priest and prophet, then a trumpet (v. 34). The oil poured on the head marks him as the king God has chosen; the trumpet carries the news. Adonijah has a feast; Solomon has the anointing and a horn heard across the valley.

Anoint him king. The Hebrew for one anointed is mashiach, “messiah”; in Greek, Christos. Every king of David’s line was “the LORD’s anointed”, and Solomon is the first son of David to receive the oil. The title waited for its true bearer. Solomon was anointed from a horn; “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38), the Christ every other anointing pointed towards.

May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so. Better than a cheer (v. 36). The king has spoken, and the soldier says: let God say the same. He neither doubts the order nor flatters it, but asks that what David has arranged prove to be what God has arranged, the only thing that will make it stand. Then, to David’s face, a wish no courtier would risk unless he meant it: may this son’s throne be “greater than the throne of my lord King David” (v. 37). It comes true; the next nine chapters tell how, and chapter 11 tells what it cost.

The Cherethites and the Pelethites. The foreign professionals who had guarded David since early in his reign go with them (v. 38). The bodyguard has chosen.

The horn of oil from the tent. Zadok takes the oil “from the tent” (v. 39), probably the tent David pitched for the ark when he brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17), since the old tabernacle stood at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3).

The earth was split by their noise. The writer enjoying himself (v. 40): a figure of speech, and also the tactical fact of the chapter. Adonijah is half a mile away, and what ends his coronation is a sound.

Is this ride an echo of Palm Sunday? Many Christians hear an echo of the ride to Gihon in the Son of David riding into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt to the crowd’s acclaim (Matthew 21:5–9). Matthew himself points to Zechariah 9:9, not to this chapter, so it is a resonance rather than a fulfilment the Gospels claim; but the likeness is real.

Uncertain wording. “The Cherethites and the Pelethites” (vv. 38, 44) are named, not explained. Cherethites are usually linked with Crete, and Scripture places them beside the Philistines (1 Samuel 30:14; Zephaniah 2:5); “Pelethites” may be a form of “Philistines”. If so, the guard were foreign soldiers loyal to the king himself rather than to any tribe. Likely, but not certain.
verseByVerse.note: Gihon was Jerusalem’s main spring, just below the city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — The Horns of the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who exalted himself is humbled in an afternoon, and the new king begins with clear terms. Adonijah’s feast hears the trumpet, and Jonathan son of Abiathar brings the news: Solomon has been anointed and sits on the throne, and David has blessed God for letting him see it (vv. 41–48). Every guest rises and leaves without a word (v. 49). Adonijah, afraid, clings to the horns of the altar and asks for an oath (vv. 50–51). Solomon gives him a condition instead: if he proves worthy he is safe, but if wickedness is found in him he will die; and he sends him home (vv. 52–53).
verseByVerse.theology: Every guest at that feast worked out the same thing at the same moment and left without speaking to their host. That is what a claim on a throne is worth the instant it fails.
verseByVerse.examples: The altar sheltered a man who had killed without intending it, and the law handed over a wilful murderer even from there (Ex. 21:14). Adonijah has killed nobody, so he gets terms rather than a sentence, and the condition is his own future conduct.

verseByVerse.quote: Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished feasting. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, "What does this uproar in the city mean?" While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. And Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news." Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king, and the king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And they had him ride on the king's mule. And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have gone up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. This is the noise that you have heard. Solomon sits on the royal throne. Moreover, the king's servants came to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make the name of Solomon more famous than yours, and make his throne greater than your throne.' And the king bowed himself on the bed. And the king also said, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.'" Then all the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose, and each went his own way. And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar. Then it was told Solomon, "Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, for behold, he has laid hold of the horns of the altar, saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'" And Solomon said, "If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die." So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and paid homage to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go to your house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One trumpet ends Adonijah’s kingdom: his guests desert him, he runs to the altar for his life, and Solomon’s first ruling gives him not an oath but clear terms. The man who exalted himself is humbled in an afternoon, and the new king shows at once a firmness his father never had.

What does this uproar in the city mean? The old soldier Joab hears a trumpet and knows something is wrong (v. 41). Adonijah greets the messenger with “you are a worthy man and bring good news” (v. 42), a bleak line to a reader of Samuel. David once sat between two gates waiting for word from a forest, saw a runner and said, “He is a good man and comes with good news” (2 Samuel 18:27). He was wrong; the news was that his son was dead.

Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest. He hid in a well at Bahurim under a covering of grain while carrying messages for David in Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 17:17–21). He has been a runner before.

No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king. One word, then the facts, unsoftened (v. 43): the names and then the mule, the order in which news lands on a man who understands the court.

And the king bowed himself on the bed. His last recorded blessing (v. 48). Too weak to rise, he worships where he lies, glad not that the son is his or his enemies outmanoeuvred, but that God let him see it. He had been promised, “your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). He watches the first instalment arrive, and Nathan, who brought the promise, has anointed the son.

My own eyes seeing it. A thousand years later another old man in Jerusalem took the true Son of David in his arms and blessed God in almost the same way: “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). David saw a son who would build a house and then lose his heart; Simeon saw the Son of whose kingdom “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). Believers can die as both did: not with every hope fulfilled, but having seen enough of the promise kept in Christ to trust God for the rest.

All the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose. Verse 49 is devastating. Moments before they were shouting “Long live King Adonijah!” Now every one stands up, without conferring or offering their host a word. “Each went his own way.” That is what a following is worth once its cause stops looking likely. Adonijah had the general, a priest, all his brothers and the royal officials of Judah at his table; not long after a trumpet he is sitting alone at En-rogel with the dishes.

Took hold of the horns of the altar. The horns were projections at the altar’s four corners, and taking hold of them was a recognised plea for protection (v. 50). The law behind it is specific: a man who killed without intending it could flee there, but “if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die” (Exodus 21:14). The altar sheltered the man who did not mean it, and handed over the man who did. Adonijah has killed nobody; he exalted himself, threw a feast, was abandoned, and now clings to an altar expecting his brother to execute him. Hold the picture: Joab runs to the same altar in the next chapter, a wilful murderer twice over, and the law is applied to him exactly as it is written.

A better refuge. The altar could shelter only the man whose guilt was accidental; the deliberate sinner was taken from it. The gospel offers what that altar could not. Christ’s sacrifice was made for the guilty, so that those who “have fled for refuge” to him have a hope that holds (Hebrews 6:18). Adonijah had to bargain for terms at the horns; Jesus says, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

If he will show himself a worthy man. The new king’s first ruling (v. 52) is a good one. Adonijah asked for an oath and gets terms instead. If he proves worthy, “not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth”, a phrase Israel used for total protection (1 Samuel 14:45); if wickedness is found in him, he will die. Solomon neither pardons nor condemns him; he tells him precisely what the rest of his life depends on, in advance, in public, in terms he cannot misunderstand. Set that beside his father with a son in the same position. Absalom came home from Geshur, and David neither tried him nor forgave him, but left him in a house for two years with the door shut and nothing said, and the country burned for it (2 Samuel 14:24, 28). Solomon says it out loud on the first day. Anyone who must hold others to account, a parent, an employer, an elder, can learn from that: the hard thing said plainly and early is kinder than a silence that feels like restraint and lets trouble grow.

Go to your house. That is all (v. 53): no punishment, no exile, no guard. Everything now depends on whether Adonijah can leave it alone, and the first thing he does in chapter 2 is ask for the young woman who nursed the dying king.

1.theology:
The saddest parenthesis in Scripture (v. 6). The example the writer chooses is the mildest question there is: why have you done thus and so? David never asked it, not once, in Adonijah's whole life. The historian has packed the whole family disaster of 2 Samuel 13 to 19 into one clause about a question that was never asked. A father who will not ask it is not being gentle; he is withholding the one thing that tells a child there is a standard and somebody is watching. The verse note sets out what this does and does not say to parents.

Handsome, again (v. 6). This history keeps saying it of the wrong men, and the sentence that stands over all of them is the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Yet Adonijah has a real case: by every ordinary rule of inheritance the throne is his, which makes this a contest rather than a squalid grab.

A court manoeuvre, not a prophetic word (vv. 12-14). Nathan claims no word from God in this chapter. He plans, briefs Bathsheba and times his own entrance. It may well be righteous (there was an oath, and the alternative was two murders), and it is still not the same kind of act as 2 Samuel 12. People who serve God are frequently doing ordinary work with ordinary judgment, and pretending every such decision is a revelation helps nobody.

Two ways to a throne. Adonijah exalted himself and said I will be king; Solomon is set on the throne by his father's oath and anointed by priest and prophet. The Bible runs on that contrast and it ends in Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but humbled himself, and whom God therefore highly exalted (Philippians 2:6-9). He is the Anointed Son whom the Father enthroned, and he stated the rule this chapter acts out: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled (Luke 14:11). Many Christians have also heard an echo of the ride to Gihon when the Son of David rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt to the crowd's acclaim (Matthew 21:5-9), though Matthew himself points to Zechariah 9:9 rather than to this chapter.

Terms, stated out loud on the first day (v. 52). Adonijah asked for an oath and gets a condition instead. He is neither pardoned nor condemned; he is told in advance and in public exactly what the rest of his life depends on, which is the very thing his father never did.
1.examples:
Then: A king's son who had never once in his life been asked why he had done something helped himself to a throne, hired fifty men to run in front of him exactly as his dead brother had, threw a coronation feast for the whole court, and not long after hearing a trumpet half a mile away, every guest at his table stood up and left without speaking to him.

Now: Two things. Verse 6 is the one that lands hardest, and it lands on parents: the failure recorded there is not harshness but the refusal to ask an uncomfortable question, and the child it produced reached his thirties having never accounted to anybody for anything. And Solomon's first ruling is the contrast worth keeping. His father managed a dangerous son by leaving everything unsaid, which felt like restraint and was in fact the only course that could not work. Solomon says the terms out loud, on the first day, in public, so that the man knows exactly where he stands. Clarity is kinder than silence, even when what it has to say is hard. And a parent who recognises David's silence in himself is not shut out: the God who forgave David forgives, and his Spirit gives the courage to ask the hard question in love.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.
keyVerse.note: David’s last blessing names the real actor in the chapter. Adonijah exalted himself (v. 5), and Nathan and Bathsheba planned, but it is the LORD who has “granted” a son to sit on the throne, keeping his promise of 2 Samuel 7. The throne of David is God’s gift, not a prize to be seized, and it looks on to the Son of David whom Simeon blessed God for letting him see (Luke 2:30).

1.reflection:
Adonijah “exalted himself” (v. 5), while Solomon was given the throne by his father’s oath and anointed by priest and prophet. Where are you tempted to grasp at position, recognition or control instead of receiving what God gives? How does Christ, who humbled himself and was exalted by God (Philippians 2:6–9), reshape that?

Verse 6 says David never once asked his son, “Why have you done thus and so?” Why is it so tempting to avoid hard conversations in families, churches and workplaces, and what does it cost? How does the gospel give us courage to speak plainly and in love?

Nathan acts in this chapter through careful planning and good timing, not through a vision (vv. 11–14), and God keeps his promise through it. How does God use ordinary wisdom and courage? Is there somewhere he may be calling you to act rather than wait?

At the end of his life David names God as the one “who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity” (v. 29). If you told your own story that way, what rescues would you list? What does it mean that Christ has redeemed you from the last adversity, death itself?

2.title: David's Charge and the Kingdom Established
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When David's time to die drew near, he commanded Solomon his son, saying,<sup>2</sup>"I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man,<sup>3</sup>and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn,<sup>4</sup>that the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me in faithfulness with all their heart and with all their soul, you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'<sup>5</sup>"Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war, and putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet.<sup>6</sup>Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.<sup>7</sup>But deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother.<sup>8</sup>And there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.'<sup>9</sup>Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol."<sup>10</sup>Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David.<sup>11</sup>And the time that David reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>So Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.<sup>13</sup>Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully."<sup>14</sup>Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak."<sup>15</sup>He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign. However, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."<sup>17</sup>And he said, "Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."<sup>18</sup>Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak for you to the king."<sup>19</sup>So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. And the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right.<sup>20</sup>Then she said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." And the king said to her, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you."<sup>21</sup>She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as his wife."<sup>22</sup>King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother, and on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah."<sup>23</sup>Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "God do so to me and more also if this word does not cost Adonijah his life!<sup>24</sup>Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and placed me on the throne of David my father, and who has made me a house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death today."<sup>25</sup>So King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.<sup>26</sup>And to Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your estate, for you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction."<sup>27</sup>So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.<sup>28</sup>When the news came to Joab—for Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom—Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar.<sup>29</sup>And when it was told King Solomon, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and behold, he is beside the altar," Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."<sup>30</sup>So Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king commands, 'Come out.'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Then Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, "Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me."<sup>31</sup>The king replied to him, "Do as he has said, strike him down and bury him, and thus take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause.<sup>32</sup>The LORD will bring back his bloody deeds on his own head, because, without the knowledge of my father David, he attacked and killed with the sword two men more righteous and better than himself, Abner the son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah.<sup>33</sup>So shall their blood come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever. But for David and for his descendants and for his house and for his throne there shall be peace from the LORD forevermore."<sup>34</sup>Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and put him to death. And he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.<sup>35</sup>The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in place of Joab, and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.<sup>36</sup>Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever.<sup>37</sup>For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head."<sup>38</sup>And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.<sup>39</sup>But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath,"<sup>40</sup>Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath.<sup>41</sup>And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned,<sup>42</sup>the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.'<sup>43</sup>Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?"<sup>44</sup>The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head.<sup>45</sup>But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever."<sup>46</sup>Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
2.overview:
Where we are. Solomon has been anointed and Adonijah given terms (chapter 1). Now David dies, and the chapter tells how “the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon” (v. 46).

The message. God establishes the throne he promised David, and the chapter shows what that involves: a king placed under God’s written word, and a reckoning in which old wrongs come home and God’s spoken word comes true. It is told without flattery: David’s last words join the finest charge in the book to the settling of old scores, and Solomon’s justice is firm and hard.

Why it was said. The exiles were asking why David’s house had fallen (see the introduction). Here they read that its kings were bound from the start to walk in the Law of Moses, and that the promise had a half about conduct (v. 4). And they read that what God says comes true, even a century later (v. 27): warning and comfort at once.

How the chapter makes its case. Dying, David charges Solomon to keep the LORD’s law as it is written, then names Joab and Shimei to be dealt with and the sons of Barzillai to be honoured; he dies, and the kingdom is established (vv. 1–12). Adonijah asks for Abishag, a claim on the throne, and is executed (vv. 13–25). Abiathar is banished, fulfilling God’s word against the house of Eli, and Joab, a deliberate murderer, is struck down even at the altar (vv. 26–35). Shimei is confined to Jerusalem under oath, breaks it for two runaway slaves and dies, and the kingdom is established (vv. 36–46).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need the chapter exposes. No son of David kept his father’s charge whole except one: Jesus obeyed perfectly in the place of those who do not. God promised “a faithful priest” to replace Eli’s house (1 Samuel 2:35), given first in Zadok and finally in Jesus, “a merciful and faithful high priest” whose priesthood never passes to another (Hebrews 2:17; 7:24). And the contrast is plain: Solomon secured his kingdom by removing his enemies, but Christ secures his by dying for his, so that “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).

For us. Live under God’s written word, not your own, and walk his way one ordinary step at a time. Take seriously that God’s words come true and that small crossings of his lines matter. And come to the King whose terms are stated in public now, and who, unlike Solomon’s court, pardons all who come to him confessing what they have done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Be Strong, and Show Yourself a Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom passes to Solomon with a charge to live under God’s written word, and with old accounts still to settle. Dying, David tells Solomon to be strong and keep the LORD’s commands as written in the Law of Moses, so that God will keep his word about the throne (vv. 1–4). Then he names Joab, who murdered two commanders in peacetime, and says he must not die in peace (vv. 5–6); asks kindness for the sons of Barzillai, who fed him in his flight (v. 7); and tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless, though David had sworn to spare him (vv. 8–9). David dies and is buried, and Solomon’s kingdom is firmly established (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The first half of this speech is as good as anything in the book. The second half is a list of two men to kill, and the writer runs the two halves together with no break between them.
verseByVerse.examples: The Shimei instruction is the hard one, because David names the oath he swore at the Jordan (2 Sam. 19:23) while telling his son to get round it. Between the two death sentences sits Barzillai, and that instruction is pure gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: When David's time to die drew near, he commanded Solomon his son, saying, "I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn, that the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me in faithfulness with all their heart and with all their soul, you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.' "Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war, and putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet. Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace. But deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother. And there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.' Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol." Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David. And the time that David reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. So Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dying, David charges Solomon to walk in God’s written law so that God’s promise to his house will stand, then names men to be dealt with and one family to be rewarded; and the kingdom passes to Solomon. The finest charge in the book and the settling of old scores sit side by side, and the writer leaves both in plain view.

I am about to go the way of all the earth. David’s last charge begins as well as it could (v. 2): no self-pity, no evasion. He is dying and names it, in the words Joshua used at the end of his own life (Joshua 23:14).

Be strong, and show yourself a man. The first command is the one Moses gave Joshua and God repeated to him at the Jordan (Deuteronomy 31:7; Joshua 1:6–7). And “a man” is at once defined by what follows: not toughness or conquest, but keeping the charge of the LORD. In David’s last words, manhood is obedience.

As it is written in the Law of Moses. Read what he does not say: nothing about alliances, the army or the treasury. He tells his son to keep the law, as it is written (v. 3): not according to your own judgment or what I did, but written, already available, and the same for a king as for anybody. And the charge rests on what God has already done: it is the charge of “the LORD your God”, and the next verse quotes a promise already sworn. Solomon is not told to earn a throne he has been given, but to live as the son of a covenant God has made.

The king under the book. How strange this was is easy to miss. In much of the ancient world the king stood above the law, or claimed descent from the gods who gave it. Israel’s king was to copy out for himself a law he had not written and read in it “all the days of his life” (Deuteronomy 17:18–19), as bound by it as the shepherd at his gate. When the Scottish minister Samuel Rutherford argued in 1644 that even a king is under law, he called his book Lex, Rex, the law is king, and drew on passages like this. We think the rule of law a modern achievement, yet we have kept the old royal instinct and spread it around: each of us would like to write the rules for our own life. David hands his son a book and says, in effect, you are not its author. That is humbling, and it is also freedom, because a king under God’s word is protected from his own worst self. And the story runs on to the one King who kept that book perfectly, “born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5).

Walking in his ways. The picture is a road: walking is what you do over and over, one ordinary step after another, and it takes you somewhere. So Scripture asks of a life not whether it ever stumbled, for David’s did, badly, but which way it was going and with whom. Verse 4 adds “before me”: the walk is done in God’s sight, as a child walks ahead of a father who is watching. Most of us would rather have one great moment with God than a long road with him; Solomon had his great day in chapter 8 and drifted on the road afterwards. The gospel puts the walk the right way round. We do not walk in order to be received: “as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (Colossians 2:6). He walked the whole road first, and walks it with us. The next step is usually small: the prayer before work, the honest answer, the apology you owe tonight.

If your sons pay close attention to their way. In verse 4 David quotes God’s covenant of 2 Samuel 7, and notice which half. It had two sides. God said the throne would be established forever and that his steadfast love would not depart from David’s son “as I took it from Saul” (2 Samuel 7:15): the unconditional half. And he said, “When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men” (2 Samuel 7:14): the half about conduct. David passes on only the second. That is no distortion but what a father tells a son about to inherit: the covenant holds whatever the house does, and what happens to the house depends greatly on what it does. Solomon is told his part, and chapter 11 records how he handled it.

The one Son who kept the charge. No son of David kept this charge whole but one, Jesus Christ, who walked before his Father with all his heart and soul and obeyed in the place of those who do not. For a believer, failure here is met by Christ’s obedience counted as ours and by the way back God has promised (1 John 1:9), and what the written law could not produce in a king, the Spirit now works in God’s people (Romans 8:4).

Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me. Then, with no transition (v. 5), the speech turns into a list of people to deal with. The writer sets the halves side by side with no seam, and the effect is deliberate and uncomfortable. One breath: walk in the ways of the LORD as it is written in the Law of Moses. Next breath: you know what Joab did.

Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether. The charge against Joab is the stronger of the two, and everything in it is true and specific. Joab killed Abner at the gate of Hebron under pretence of a private word, in a city of refuge, in peacetime, when Abner had come under safe conduct (2 Samuel 3:27). He killed Amasa on the road at Gibeon with the same greeting and the same wound, when Amasa was the king’s own appointed commander (2 Samuel 20:10). Both were “in time of peace”: unlawful killings by a serving officer.

Thirty years too late. What is uncomfortable is not the verdict but the timing. David had more than thirty years to act himself. After Abner’s murder he said publicly, “These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I” (2 Samuel 3:39), a confession that he could not touch the man. He could not touch him after Absalom either, when Joab disobeyed a public order and killed the king’s son. And every time, he needed him. So the charge is true, and the man who should have acted on it is handing it to somebody else.

Deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite. Verse 7, in the middle of the list, changes the shape of the speech. Barzillai, eighty years old and very rich, fed David’s army at Mahanaim when the king arrived across the Jordan with nothing: beds, basins, wheat, honey, curds and cheese, at his own expense and at an age when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it (2 Samuel 17:27–29). He declined a place at court because he could no longer taste food or enjoy music, asked only to die in his own town near his parents’ grave, and sent Chimham instead (2 Samuel 19:31–40). Years later, dying, David has not forgotten the bedding. A place at the king’s table, as Mephibosheth had (2 Samuel 9:7), was the highest thing an Israelite king had to give. So the last instructions hold two death sentences and one remembered kindness, set between them; the writer arranged it so, and did not comment.

Shimei the son of Gera. David states his oath to Shimei accurately, quotes his own words and names the God he swore by (vv. 8–9). Go back to that day. Shimei walked along a hillside throwing stones and dust at a barefoot king and shouting, “Get out, get out, you man of blood”, and when Abishai offered to take his head off, David refused with one of the finest answers in Scripture: “Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me” (2 Samuel 16:7–12). When the man came grovelling to the Jordan with a thousand Benjaminites and Abishai asked again, David said, “Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?” And he swore it (2 Samuel 19:22–23).

The letter and the substance. Set beside those days, no reading makes this instruction admirable, and none should be attempted. But the defences should be stated, for they are not worthless. The oath was David’s own and personal (“I will not put you to death”) and did not bind the crown after him. A king has a duty to justice as well as to his word, and Shimei had cursed the LORD’s anointed, which Abishai had called a capital matter (2 Samuel 19:21). And Shimei may well have remained dangerous: a Benjaminite of Saul’s house who could bring a thousand men with him (2 Samuel 19:17), when the north had already broken away twice.
