All of that is arguable, and it amounts to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for its substance to be broken by somebody who did not swear it.

Both are David. The book records the mercy at the Jordan and this, and reconciles neither. The man who would not touch Saul in a cave, who wrote a lament for the king who hunted him, who fed Mephibosheth at his table and remembered Barzillai’s bedding to the end, also said this on his deathbed. Scripture does not flatter its heroes; even the best of them needed a better King. In fairness, when Shimei dies (v. 46) it is not for the cursing but for breaking a fresh oath he swore himself, three years later, of his own free will; Solomon does not simply carry out the sentence he was given.

Then David slept with his fathers. Fourteen words for the death of David (v. 10): no lament, no funeral, no oration. The man who wrote the elegies for Saul and Jonathan and for Abner gets the set form of words that will be used of king after king. A thousand years later Peter stood in Jerusalem and pointed to that grave: David “both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day” (Acts 2:29). He did it to show that David’s words about not being abandoned to the grave were spoken of the Christ, whose tomb was empty (Acts 2:30–32).

His kingdom was firmly established. The chapter ends with this clause again (v. 46), and everything between is what it took.

Uncertain wording. “Putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet” (v. 5) is compressed. It may be literal, Amasa’s blood running onto the belt where Joab’s sword hung (2 Samuel 20:8–10), or figurative, Joab wearing the guilt of wartime killing in peacetime as though it were honourable. Either way it marks him as stained with blood he had no right to shed.
verseByVerse.note: David reigned forty years: seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Ask for Him the Kingdom Also
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A request that sounds like a wish for a wife is a bid for the throne, and it costs Adonijah his life. Adonijah comes to Bathsheba peaceably, admits that the kingdom became his brother’s “from the LORD”, and asks her to win him Abishag as his wife (vv. 13–18). Solomon honours his mother with a seat at his right hand and promises to grant her request (vv. 19–20). But when he hears it, he sees at once a renewed claim backed by Abiathar and Joab: “Ask for him the kingdom also” (vv. 21–22). He swears by the LORD who has established him, and Benaiah executes Adonijah that day (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Asking for a dead king's woman is a claim on his throne, and everybody in that world knew it. Abner took Saul's concubine and Ish-bosheth read it as a bid; Ahithophel told Absalom to take his father's concubines publicly for exactly this reason (2 Sam. 3:7; 16:21-22).
verseByVerse.examples: Whether Bathsheba understood what she was carrying, the text does not say. What is certain is that Solomon understood it before she finished, and that Adonijah had been told in public on the first day precisely what would end his terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully." Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak." He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign. However, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD. And now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak." And he said, "Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife." Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak for you to the king." So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. And the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right. Then she said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." And the king said to her, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you." She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as his wife." King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother, and on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah." Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "God do so to me and more also if this word does not cost Adonijah his life! Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and placed me on the throne of David my father, and who has made me a house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death today." So King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adonijah asks for Abishag, the young woman of his dead father’s household, and Solomon reads it as a renewed claim on the throne and has him executed: the terms of 1:52 have been broken. A request that sounds like a disappointed man’s wish for a wife was, in that world, a bid for a crown.

Do you come peacefully? Bathsheba’s first question (v. 13) tells you the atmosphere in that palace.

You know that the kingdom was mine. The first half of verse 15 is a grievance, and not a baseless one: by every ordinary rule the throne was his, and the country expected it. The second half is sound, what a man who had accepted God’s decision would say: “it was his from the LORD.” He concedes not merely that he lost but that God gave it to Solomon; and then he asks for something, which is why he said it.

To give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife. Consider what he asks (v. 17). Abishag was brought to keep an old man warm, and “the king knew her not” (1:4). So she is not David’s widow in the ordinary sense but a young, unmarried woman of the royal household. Yet in that world she was also part of a dead king’s household, and taking a dead king’s woman is how a man announced that he had taken his place. This history has shown it twice. When Ish-bosheth accused Abner over Rizpah, Saul’s concubine, the charge was political: it meant Abner was reaching for the throne, and the quarrel cost Ish-bosheth his kingdom (2 Samuel 3:7–11). And when Ahithophel wanted to make Absalom’s rebellion irreversible, he told him to take his father’s concubines publicly, on the roof, in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:21–22). The request is not romantic but political.

Did Adonijah understand it? He is not a clever man: he announced himself with fifty runners and lost a kingdom to a trumpet, and he may simply have wanted the girl. Or a man told in public that his life depended on his conduct may have been testing how far the terms extended. The text does not say, and the outcome does not depend on it.

Very well; I will speak for you to the king. Did Bathsheba know? Two readings are possible, and the text settles neither. On one, she does not follow the politics, hears a modest-sounding request from a defeated man and carries it in good faith. On the other, she has lived in that palace since before Absalom’s rebellion, knows precisely what taking a king’s woman means, and carries the request because she can see what her son will do with it. What can be observed is that she says “very well” (v. 18) without a word of warning to Adonijah, and that she must have known what Absalom did on that roof. Better to leave it open than to decide it by preference.

She sat on his right. The king rises, bows to his mother and seats her on a throne at his right hand (v. 19), the place of honour. In Judah the king’s mother held a recognised position at court, and the writer will introduce king after king with his mother’s name (for example 14:21). Keep the picture: the woman David first saw from a roof, whose first child died, whose husband was told by a prophet that he was a murderer, now sits beside the king of Israel while the court watches.

I have one small request to make of you. She presents it as modestly as Adonijah had (v. 20), and Solomon promises to grant it before he hears it, the one careless thing he does in this chapter.

Ask for him the kingdom also. Solomon’s reaction (v. 22) is instant, and not paranoia. He names what makes the request dangerous. “He is my older brother” is the claim by birth, which Adonijah stated himself seven verses earlier. “On his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab” names a priest and the commander of the army. That is not a disappointed man asking for a wife but a faction with a candidate and a claim, testing the ground. Solomon is right about the facts. Whether the sentence he passes is proportionate to them, the writer does not say.

Who has made me a house, as he promised. In his oath (v. 24) Solomon quotes the covenant: “made me a house” echoes 2 Samuel 7:11, the promise God gave his father in a night vision. He knows whose throne he sits on, and invokes it while ordering an execution. Whether the covenant authorised that particular order is a different question, one the writer leaves alone. The house God promised was finally built in a Son who rules not by removing his rivals but by laying down his life, and “Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house” (Hebrews 3:6).

And he struck him down, and he died. One sentence (v. 25), and Adonijah is gone. He had been given terms in public on the first day of the reign: “If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die” (1:52). He had one thing to do, to keep away from anything that looked like a claim, and within a chapter he had asked for the dead king’s companion through the king’s own mother.

Was executing Adonijah for asking for Abishag too harsh? To take a king’s concubine was to claim his throne (2 Samuel 16:21–22), and Adonijah had already tried to seize it once (1:5). Solomon read the request as a renewed bid and acted as kings then did to secure a kingdom. The narrator records it without praising it, and Scripture’s recording an act is not the same as its approving it.

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 22 is compressed in Hebrew, which reads literally “and for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah”. The ESV takes it as “on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab”; older versions continue the sarcasm, “ask for him the kingdom… even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab”. Either way Solomon sees the request as the move of a faction, not of one man.
verseByVerse.note: Abishag was the young woman of 1:1-4, brought in to care for David in his last illness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Take Him from My Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word comes true and his law is kept: an old prophecy is fulfilled, and blood shed by cunning finds no shelter. Abiathar deserves death but is spared for his service to David and sent home to Anathoth (v. 26), fulfilling the LORD’s word against the house of Eli (v. 27). Joab flees to the altar and refuses to come out (vv. 28–30). Solomon orders him struck down there, to take from David’s house the guilt of the innocent blood Joab shed when he murdered Abner and Amasa, men better than himself (vv. 31–34). Benaiah replaces Joab over the army, and Zadok replaces Abiathar (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 closes a thread opened in the first chapters of 1 Samuel, where a man of God told Eli that his house would be cut off and that God would raise up for myself a faithful priest (1 Sam. 2:31-35).
verseByVerse.examples: The altar does exactly what the law says it does. Adonijah held these horns in chapter 1 and was given terms, because he had killed nobody; Joab, a wilful murderer, is not sheltered by them.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your estate, for you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction." So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. When the news came to Joab—for Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom—Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar. And when it was told King Solomon, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and behold, he is beside the altar," Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down." So Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king commands, 'Come out.'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Then Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, "Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me." The king replied to him, "Do as he has said, strike him down and bury him, and thus take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause. The LORD will bring back his bloody deeds on his own head, because, without the knowledge of my father David, he attacked and killed with the sword two men more righteous and better than himself, Abner the son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah. So shall their blood come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever. But for David and for his descendants and for his house and for his throne there shall be peace from the LORD forevermore." Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and put him to death. And he was buried in his own house in the wilderness. The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in place of Joab, and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abiathar is spared but removed from the priesthood, fulfilling God’s old word against the house of Eli, and Joab, a deliberate murderer, is struck down even at the altar, as the law required. Old words and old sins both come home: what God said at Shiloh comes true, and blood shed by cunning finds no shelter.

Because you shared in all my father’s affliction. Abiathar is spared (v. 26) for two reasons, both about the past: he carried the ark, and he shared David’s hardships in the caves. He fled to David after Doeg killed eighty-five priests at Nob, and David told him then, “With me you shall be in safekeeping” (1 Samuel 22:23). More than forty years of that, and it ends with a man sent to a village to farm.

Thus fulfilling the word of the LORD. In verse 27 the writer halts the story, and the thread runs back more than a century. An unnamed man of God came to Eli at Shiloh, when Israel had judges and no king, and said: “Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that there will not be an old man in your house… and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men.” Then came the promise beneath it: “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever” (1 Samuel 2:31–35).

How the word unfolded. Hophni and Phinehas died on one day at Aphek; Eli fell backward from his seat when he heard it, and his daughter-in-law named her son Ichabod. Eli’s great-grandson Ahimelech was slaughtered at Nob on Saul’s order with the other priests, and one son escaped with the ephod, the survivor the prophecy had foretold: “The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out” (1 Samuel 2:33). That son was Abiathar. He served David for more than forty years, backed the wrong brother in a single day, and here the line ends, in a field at Anathoth, with Zadok in his place (v. 35).

Not court politics. The writer will not let it pass as court politics. A word spoken at Shiloh before Israel had a king has been completed, not by plague or execution: a man made a bad political judgment at a feast, and God’s word about his great-great-grandfather’s house came true through it. God works his purposes through ordinary choices, even wrong ones, without making the chooser any less responsible for them.

A faithful priest. The promise of a faithful priest was fulfilled first in Zadok’s line, which served at the temple for centuries. Yet no priest of that line served for ever, and Christians have long seen the promise’s final answer in Jesus, “a merciful and faithful high priest” (Hebrews 2:17), who “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). Abiathar was removed for backing the wrong king; our High Priest can never be removed, and “he always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

Jeremiah of Anathoth. More than three centuries later a boy is born in that village to a priestly family, and his book opens: “The words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin” (Jeremiah 1:1). It may well be that the line put out of the priesthood here produced Jeremiah, the prophet of the exile.

Although he had not supported Absalom. Verse 28 explains Joab’s flight. Decades of loyalty to David through a civil war, a rebellion and every crisis of the reign, and at the very end, with nothing left to gain, he backed the losing son.

No, I will die here. Entirely in character (v. 30): no pleading, no repentance. He is a dead man either way, and has decided where. Whether he thought the altar would protect him is doubtful; he knew the law as well as anybody. More likely this is the last calculation of a long career: make them kill me at the sanctuary, before the priests, so that the blood is on the new king’s reign.

Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me. Benaiah, to his credit, goes back and asks. Solomon’s answer (v. 31) stands on the law, which is explicit about this very case: “if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die” (Exodus 21:14). By cunning is exactly how Joab killed. He took Abner aside at the gate as though to speak with him privately; he took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. Both times a friendly gesture hid the weapon. The altar does not cover that, and the writer expects us to remember that Adonijah held these same horns a chapter ago and was sent home alive.

Without the knowledge of my father David. Solomon says two things worth noticing (v. 32). First, Joab acted “without the knowledge of my father David”. A king is answerable for what his officers do in his name, and Solomon establishes that these were not royal acts. Hence “take away from me and from my father’s house the guilt” (v. 31): blood shed without cause was a guilt on the land and on those responsible for justice until it was answered, for “no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (Numbers 35:33).

More righteous and better than himself. Abner led a rebellion against David for years and killed Asahel; Amasa commanded the army that lost twenty thousand men in the forest of Ephraim. Neither was a saint, and the comparison is not about their careers. They were killed by cunning, in peacetime, by a man they trusted enough to stand still for.

Blood that speaks a better word. Innocent blood cried out for justice, and the law allowed Joab no other answer. The gospel does not lower that standard; it meets it. Christians have come “to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). The guilt Solomon removed from his house by Joab’s death, Christ removes from his people by his own.

Both posts change hands. In verse 35 Benaiah takes the army and Zadok the priesthood, both posts held until now by men who had gone to Adonijah’s feast.
verseByVerse.note: Anathoth lay about three miles north-east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–46 — You Shall Know for Certain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man who kept his word for years throws his life away over something small, and the kingdom is secured. Solomon lets Shimei build a house in Jerusalem on one sworn condition: if he ever leaves the city, he will die (vv. 36–38). Three years later two of his slaves run off to Gath, and Shimei rides after them and brings them back (vv. 39–41). Solomon charges him with breaking his oath to the LORD, adds the harm he did to David, and has him executed (vv. 42–46). The chapter closes as its first section did: the kingdom is established in Solomon’s hand (v. 46).
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are exact and public and generous: a house in the capital and a boundary he chose to swear to. He kept it for three years and then crossed it for two runaway slaves.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on the sentence its first section ended with: verse 12 said the kingdom was firmly established in his hand, and verse 46 says it again, after three deaths and a banishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever. For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head." And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days. But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath," Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath. And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned, the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.' Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?" The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head. But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever." Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon confines Shimei to Jerusalem under a sworn condition; three years later Shimei crosses it to fetch two runaway slaves and dies for it, and the kingdom is established. A man who kept his boundary for years lost everything over something small, because the line had never been about the size of what lay beyond it.

Build yourself a house in Jerusalem. The terms are generous (v. 36). David said to bring the man’s grey head down with blood; Solomon lets him build a house in the capital, with one restriction: do not leave the city. House arrest in a comfortable form, far less than a man who cursed and stoned the LORD’s anointed could have expected.

The brook Kidron. “Know for certain” and “your blood shall be on your own head” (v. 37) leave no ambiguity, and no discretion to anybody. The line is a named brook on the east side of the city, the one David crossed weeping on the day Shimei came out to curse him (2 Samuel 15:23, 30), and the road home to Shimei’s town of Bahurim. Gath lies the other way, so Shimei may never have crossed the Kidron itself; but the condition was not to go “to any place whatever” (vv. 36, 42), and the brook simply named the likeliest way out. For the second time in two chapters Solomon states terms in public, before anything happens. His father, faced with a dangerous man, said nothing for two years and let a rebellion grow.

What you say is good. Shimei accepts (v. 38), and verse 42 shows he did more: Solomon made him “swear by the LORD”, so there is now an oath of Shimei’s own on the arrangement.

Two of Shimei’s servants ran away. Three years later two slaves run (v. 39). (Servitude in Israel was often a form of debt service, hedged by protections the surrounding nations lacked, as in Exodus 21:2, 26–27 and Deuteronomy 15:12–15; it was still servitude, and the gospel would later work against it from within, Philemon 16.)

Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath. Look how small the thing is (v. 40): not a conspiracy or a plot with the house of Saul, but two runaway slaves he wanted back. He saddles a donkey, fetches them and rides home. He kept a sworn boundary for three years and crossed it for a loss he could have written off. Gath matters too: Philistine territory, Goliath’s town, where David twice took refuge, and Achish is the name of the king David dealt with there. Shimei has gone out of Israel altogether.

Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD? The charge (vv. 42–43) is not the cursing but the oath: Solomon quotes the terms, the warning and Shimei’s own answer back to him. That puts the chapter in line with everything the books of Samuel have said about promises made in God’s name. Saul broke Israel’s oath to the Gibeonites and there was a famine (2 Samuel 21:1–2). David kept his oath to a dead friend and fed his lame son at his own table (2 Samuel 9). Shimei swore one, and rode to Gath for two slaves.

All the harm that you did to David my father. Then the old matter is added (vv. 44–45). It is not the ground of the sentence, but it is not pretended away either.

So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon. The chapter ends (v. 46) with the clause of verse 12. Everything between shows what establishing it involved: a deathbed list, a request for a young woman, an old priest sent to a village, a soldier at the altar, and a man who rode to Gath for two slaves. The writer states it twice without a word of approval or regret, and turns the page to Gibeon.

A kingdom established another way. Solomon’s kingdom was made secure by removing his enemies. Christ’s is made secure by dying for his: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). He too states his terms in advance and in public. God “commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:30–31). Shimei had three years; we are given today. And unlike Solomon’s terms, Christ’s come with a pardon for every boundary already crossed.

The ordinary way ruin comes. Few talk themselves into the large disobedience. They keep the line for years and step over it for something that seemed too minor to count. The help is not more grit but staying near the God who drew the line in kindness, whose Spirit is given to keep us, and who, unlike Solomon’s court, receives back those who confess they have crossed it: “I acknowledged my sin to you… and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

What troubles the reader. Four men are dealt with in forty-six verses; two were on David’s deathbed list, one under David’s own oath, and that is genuinely troubling (see the note on vv. 1–12). But Solomon does not simply execute the list. Abiathar is on nobody’s list and is spared, with reasons given. Adonijah dies for breaking terms he was given in public. Joab dies under a written law that covers his case exactly. Shimei dies for breaking an oath he swore himself, not for the cursing, which is mentioned second and is not the charge. None of that makes the chapter comfortable, and the writer does not soften it. But the new king is not merely settling his father’s scores. He is doing what his father could not, stating a rule, applying it, and being seen to apply it the same way twice.

Uncertain wording. The king of Gath is “Achish, son of Maacah” (v. 39); the king David served in 1 Samuel 27:2 was “Achish the son of Maoch”. The two names may be forms of one, in which case this is the same man, very old after some forty years on the throne, or a grandson who bore the family name. Which is meant cannot now be known; the story does not depend on it.

2.theology:
What he tells him to do (v. 3). Not statecraft, not alliances, not the army, but to walk as it is written in the Law of Moses: written, available, and the same for a king as for anybody, which is what Deuteronomy 17:18-19 had required of Israel's kings in the first place. And the charge rests on what God has already done: it is the charge of the LORD your God, and the next verse quotes a promise already sworn. Solomon is not told to earn a throne he has been given, but to live as the son of a covenant God has made.

Which half of the covenant he quotes (v. 4). The promise had two sides: a throne established forever, and discipline with the rod of men for iniquity. David gives Solomon the conduct half, which is what a father says to a son about to inherit. The covenant holds whatever the house does, and a great deal depends on what the house does. Chapter 11 records how Solomon handled it. No son of David kept this charge whole but one, Jesus Christ, who obeyed in the place of those who do not. For a believer, failure here is met by Christ’s obedience counted as ours and by the way back God promised (1 John 1:9), and what the written law could not produce in a king, the Spirit now works in God's people (Romans 8:4).

The seam that is not there (vv. 5-9). One breath: walk in the ways of the LORD as it is written. Next breath: you know what Joab did. The verse notes set out both charges. Joab's guilt is real, and the discomfort is that David never acted on it himself. The Shimei instruction keeps the letter of David's oath while arranging for someone who did not swear it to break its substance. The book records the mercy at the Jordan and this, and reconciles neither. Both are David.

A word from Shiloh, completed (v. 27). Abiathar's banishment ends the line of Eli, as a man of God had foretold at Shiloh (1 Sam. 2:31-35), and Zadok stands in his place. The promise of a faithful priest is fulfilled first in Zadok's line, yet no priest of that line served for ever; Christians have long seen the promise's final answer in Jesus, whom Hebrews calls a merciful and faithful high priest whose priesthood never passes to another (Hebrews 2:17; 7:23-25).

The honest reckoning. Three men are dead and a fourth banished at the start of a reign, and the chapter does not soften it. Yet Solomon does not simply execute his father's list: each man is dealt with on stated grounds, and the new king has stated a rule, applied it, and been seen to apply it the same way twice, which his father, faced with a dangerous son, could not do.

The same clause at both ends (vv. 12, 46). The kingdom is said to be established at the start and again at the end, and everything between is what filled the space. Set beside the Son of David who is greater than Solomon, the contrast is plain. Solomon's kingdom was secured by removing his enemies; Christ's is secured by dying for his, who are reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). And Christ too states his terms in advance and in public: God now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day of judgment by the man he has appointed (Acts 17:30-31).
2.examples:
Then: A man was given a house in the capital and one condition, not to cross the brook, and he swore to it in the name of the LORD and kept it for three years. Then two of his slaves ran off to a Philistine town, and he saddled a donkey and went and fetched them back, and it cost him his life.

Now: Three things. Shimei is the study in how boundaries actually get broken: not by defiance, and not over anything large. He held the line for three years and stepped over it for a piece of property, because the thing on the other side looked too small to count, and the line had never been about the size of it. The help is not more grit but staying near the God who drew the line in kindness, whose Spirit is given to keep us, and who, unlike Solomon's court, receives back those who confess they have crossed it (Psalm 32:5). Second, David's speech, which should be read whole rather than in the half that flatters him: the finest charge in the book about walking in God's written word, an accurate account of a murderer he had never been willing to touch, an oath he named while arranging for someone else to break it, and in the middle of all of it a years-old debt of kindness he had not forgotten. And third, Solomon's method, which is the contrast the chapter is built on: terms stated out loud, in advance, in public, and then applied. His father managed dangerous men by leaving everything unsaid, and it cost him a kingdom and a son.

keyVerse.quote: Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn.
keyVerse.note: David’s dying charge sets the standard by which the books of Kings will weigh every king: not power or wealth, but whether he walked in God’s ways as they are written. Solomon is not told to earn his throne but to live as the son of a covenant already made (v. 4). No son of David kept the charge whole but Jesus, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him.

2.reflection:
David’s last charge is to walk in God’s ways “as it is written in the Law of Moses” (v. 3). What difference does it make to live under a written word you did not author? In which part of your life would you most like to write your own rules?

David’s deathbed speech holds a noble charge, a just verdict delayed for thirty years, a kindness remembered and an oath evaded (vv. 2–9). Why do you think Scripture tells even its heroes’ lives without flattery? Is there unfinished business you are leaving for others to deal with?

The writer stops to say that God’s word against Eli’s house has been fulfilled (v. 27), more than a century after it was spoken. How does God’s faithfulness to his word, in warning and in promise, make you both more sober and more confident?

Shimei kept his boundary for three years and crossed it for two runaway slaves (vv. 39–40). Where are you tempted to think that a small step over a line God has drawn does not count? How does Christ, who forgives those who confess, help you both to keep the line and to come back when you have crossed it?

3.title: Wisdom at Gibeon and the Two Mothers
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.<sup>4</sup>And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.<sup>5</sup>At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you."<sup>6</sup>And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day.<sup>7</sup>And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in.<sup>8</sup>And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude.<sup>9</sup>Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?"<sup>10</sup>It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.<sup>11</sup>And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right,<sup>12</sup>behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you.<sup>13</sup>I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days.<sup>14</sup>And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days."<sup>15</sup>And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.<sup>16</sup>Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.<sup>17</sup>The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house.<sup>18</sup>Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house.<sup>19</sup>And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him.<sup>20</sup>And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast.<sup>21</sup>When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne."<sup>22</sup>But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king.<sup>23</sup>Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king.<sup>25</sup>And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other."<sup>26</sup>Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."<sup>27</sup>Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."<sup>28</sup>And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
3.overview:
Where we are. The executions and banishment of chapter 2 are over, and “the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon” (2:46). Chapter 3 opens his reign proper with the gift on which all of it will rest.

The message. Wisdom to rule God’s people is God’s gift, given to the one who knows he cannot do the job and asks. A young king with a nation too great for him asks not for long life, wealth or victory but for “an understanding mind to govern your people”, and God gives it, with riches and honour besides. The proof follows at once: the wisdom of God shows itself as justice for two women nobody else would have heard. Yet even this bright beginning carries warnings: an Egyptian wife, the high places, and an if.

Why it was said. The exiles who first read Kings were asking why they had lost king, land and temple (see the introduction). Here they see the reign that began best of all, and learn that a king’s greatness was always God’s gift, measured by whether he walked in God’s ways and did justice for the least. The seeds of the later ruin are already in the first three verses.

How the chapter makes its case. Three verses of mixed promise come first: a marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter, worship at the high places, and a king who loved the LORD, only (vv. 1–3). At Gibeon God says, “Ask what I shall give you”; Solomon asks for a hearing heart to govern God’s great people, and God gives wisdom, riches and honour outright, and long life on condition of obedience (vv. 4–15). Then the gift is tested in the smallest and hardest case in the land, two prostitutes and one living child, and the king’s sword brings out the true mother, so that all Israel sees “that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice” (vv. 16–28).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Solomon is the son of David given wisdom to judge, a picture of the promised shoot of Jesse on whom “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” would rest and who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:1–4). But Solomon did not keep wanting what he asked for at Gibeon. Jesus is the King in whom are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), who needed no sword to know what was in a person (John 2:25), and who said of himself, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42).

For us. Ask God for wisdom: he “gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5), and delights to be asked for what will serve others. Let your own requests show you your heart, and bring it to him. And measure wisdom, in a parent, a leader or a church, by how it treats the people with no standing at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Only at the High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reign opens with three verses that read like praise and each carry a warning. Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter, a diplomatic triumph that the law about kings and the end of his own story both call into question (v. 1). The people sacrifice at local high places, and the writer himself supplies the excuse: there is no temple yet (v. 2). Then comes the warmest thing Kings says of any king, “Solomon loved the LORD”, followed at once by the word “only”, which the writer will attach to almost every good reign that follows (v. 3). Real love for God and divided loyalties sit side by side from the start.
verseByVerse.theology: The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a foreign marriage, and to Egypt of all places. The writer states it and adds nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 has a sting in it: Solomon loved the LORD, only he sacrificed at the high places. The high places are the thing that will still be standing at the end of both books.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem. The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD. Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign opens with a dazzling alliance, scattered worship and real love for God, and the writer quietly marks each with a warning that the rest of Solomon’s story will bring back.

Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. Once the executions of chapter 2 are over, the first thing recorded about the reign is a wedding to Egypt. Politically it was a triumph, and everyone at the time would have read it so. Egypt had long refused to give its daughters to foreign kings; in the Amarna letters (Egyptian royal correspondence of the fourteenth century BC) a pharaoh says flatly that a daughter of Egypt is given to nobody. That Solomon got one measures how large Israel had suddenly become.

The law about kings. Two things stand against it. The first is the law about Israel’s kings, by which this history quietly measures everyone: “Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses… And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Egypt and wives, in consecutive clauses, and this verse has both. Behind it stands the older command about the nations of the land: “You shall not intermarry with them… for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The reason the law gives is never race; it is what happens to worship in a household.

He took Pharaoh’s daughter. The second is what chapter 11 says happened: “Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh… For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (11:1, 4). Pharaoh’s daughter heads that list, and she arrives here, before the temple is built and before Gibeon. This writer does not stop to comment. He plants a detail and waits.

The people were sacrificing at the high places. High places were open-air sanctuaries, often on hilltops, and they will be the running problem of both books, because the law required sacrifice at the one place the LORD would choose (Deuteronomy 12:5–14), and local shrines easily drew in the worship of other gods. The writer gives the excuse himself, which is unusually generous of him: “no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.” The tabernacle was at Gibeon and the ark in a tent in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17), so worship was scattered.

Solomon loved the LORD. Kings says this of no other king: not of Asa or Jehoshaphat, nor of Hezekiah or Josiah, who receive its highest praise. And it is love shown in obedience, “walking in the statutes of David his father”.

Only he sacrificed. Then comes only, the first of the reservations this writer will attach to almost every good reign in both books: king after king did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet “the high places were not taken away” (2 Kings 12:3; 15:4). Here it appears for the first time, attached to Solomon on the page before he asks for wisdom. So three verses that a quick reader takes as a glowing introduction, a magnificent alliance, a fair excuse for irregular worship and the finest compliment in the book, each hold something the history will come back for.

A love with no “only” in it. A king who loved the LORD with a divided heart leaves the reader waiting for a Son whose love has no reservation attached. Jesus could say of his Father, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and that wholehearted obedience is now counted to all who trust him.

The small compromise. Real love for God and a quiet compromise can sit side by side for years, and the compromise is usually the thing that looks most sensible at the time: a good alliance, a convenient arrangement, a habit everyone else shares. The question to put to them is not whether they are respectable but where they lead a heart.

Why is Gibeon a fault when the tabernacle was there (2 Chronicles 1:3)? It is not. The fault is the many high places (v. 2), not Gibeon itself, which was “the great high place”, where the tabernacle and its altar stood until the temple was built.
verseByVerse.note: “High places” were local hilltop shrines; they were later condemned because the law required sacrifice at the one place the LORD chose (Deut 12), and because they easily drew in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom to rule God’s people is God’s gift, freely given to the one who knows he cannot do the job. At Gibeon, after a thousand burnt offerings, God appears to Solomon in a dream: “Ask what I shall give you” (vv. 4–5). Solomon begins with God’s steadfast love to David, confesses that he is “but a little child”, and asks for “an understanding mind to govern your people” (vv. 6–9). God is pleased, names the three things he did not ask for, and gives him wisdom beyond any king, with riches and honour besides (vv. 10–13). Only long life carries a condition: “if you will walk in my ways” (v. 14). Solomon wakes and worships before the ark in Jerusalem (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: What he asks for in verse 9 is an understanding mind, to discern between good and evil: a mind that listens, which is what a judge needs before anything else, and what his father had lost.
verseByVerse.examples: And the gifts are not given on the same terms. Wisdom and riches are given outright; length of days has an if attached to it. Chapter 11 is where that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day. And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in. And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude. Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?" It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this. And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right, behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you. I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days. And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days." And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offers Solomon anything he wants; Solomon, knowing the job is beyond him, asks for a listening heart to govern God’s people justly, and God, pleased, gives him that and more, attaching a condition only to long life.

For that was the great high place. Gibeon (v. 4) held the tabernacle Moses made, with its bronze altar (2 Chronicles 1:3–5). So this is not one of the irregular hilltop shrines but the national sanctuary, at the town whose people once tricked Joshua into a treaty and were spared for the sake of an oath (Joshua 9).

A thousand burnt offerings. An enormous act of worship. A burnt offering was wholly consumed on the altar, with nothing kept back for the worshipper to eat.

Ask what I shall give you. A startling offer (v. 5), put to one man, open, with no terms attached and no hint of what a good answer would be. It is a test, because nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything. The request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside.

Great and steadfast love. Solomon begins not with his request but with what God has already done (v. 6), and the word he uses twice is hesed, the covenant love that keeps its promises after the reasons for keeping them are gone. His picture of David walking “in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart” may be hard to take for a reader who has just finished 2 Samuel. It is a son’s account and not a full one, but it is not false: David never served another god, he repented when confronted, and the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 rested on God’s character rather than David’s. Solomon describes the direction of a life, not a list of its failures.

I am but a little child. He is not literally a child (v. 7); he is a grown man who has just had three men executed and married a princess of Egypt. Josephus’s figures would make him fourteen, and many estimates put him nearer twenty. Whatever his age, the phrase confesses inexperience. I do not know how to go out or come in is a soldier’s idiom for leading an army out and bringing it home, and it is what the tribes said of David when they made him king: “it was you who led out and brought in Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2). Solomon is saying: I cannot do what my father did.

Your people whom you have chosen. New on the throne, he already knows that the nation is not his (v. 8). And there is a quiet irony in “too many to be numbered or counted for multitude”, since the last thing his father did before the plague was count them (2 Samuel 24).

An understanding mind. In Hebrew, lev shomea, a hearing heart (v. 9). The heart in Hebrew is not chiefly the seat of the feelings, as in English, but where a person thinks and decides. So he asks not for a large memory, a quick answer or the gift of out-arguing people, but for a mind that listens before it decides: exactly what a judge needs, and exactly what his father had stopped having. Two men came to David with stories. He heard Ziba and handed over an estate in a sentence, then heard Mephibosheth and split the land rather than admit he had judged carelessly (2 Samuel 16:1–4; 19:24–30).

To govern your people. He says what the gift is for: “that I may discern between good and evil”. It is a tool for a job, and the job is other people. That makes it a prayer anyone can borrow who has been put in charge of others, as a parent, an employer or an elder: ask God for a heart that listens, and then do what such a heart does, hearing both sides before deciding, since “The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him” (Proverbs 18:17).

Who is able to govern this your great people? Not modesty but a real question with an implied answer: nobody. He has looked at what is in front of him, concluded that it cannot be done, and asked for the one thing that would let him try.

Have not asked for yourself long life or riches. God names what Solomon did not ask for (v. 11), and it is the most revealing verse in the chapter. These are the three things every king in the ancient world wanted: long life, to enjoy what he had; riches, the measure of a reign then as now; and “the life of your enemies”, to have the men who threatened him dead. Solomon had reason to want the third, after dealing with a brother, a general, a priest and a Benjaminite, with more where they came from. He asked for none of them, and nothing prompted his answer: there was no hint and no list of approved requests. That is why “It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this” (v. 10): not the eloquence of it, but that when a man could have had anything at all, this is what was in him.

I give you also what you have not asked. He gets what he asked for, more of it than anyone before or since (v. 12), and riches and honour besides (v. 13). Jesus states the principle a few sentences after naming “Solomon in all his glory” (Matthew 6:29): “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). The order is the point. Solomon did not win riches by cleverly not asking for them; the man who asks for an understanding mind is the man it is safe to give them to. Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10’s question.

And if you will walk in my ways. Verse 14 differs deliberately from the two before it, and Solomon’s life turns on the difference. Wisdom, riches and honour are given outright, with no condition: “I give you… I give you also”. Long life alone comes with an if, and the standard named is his father. The writer will come back for that if: “Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you” (11:11). The gifts were never withdrawn, for he died the wisest and richest man in the world; it was the conditional side that came due.

And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. This is not scepticism, for the writer has just said that God appeared to him; it is precision (v. 15). Solomon had no vision to point to and no stone to show anyone, only a conversation in his head as he woke in the dark at Gibeon. His first act was to go to Jerusalem, stand before the ark, and offer burnt offerings, which keep nothing back, and peace offerings, which were shared and eaten, and then to feast all his servants. Given the greatest promise of his life, he went first to worship and then fed the people who worked for him.

A greater Son of David. Solomon wanted the right thing for one night, and did not keep wanting it. Jesus, offered all the kingdoms of the world, refused them (Matthew 4:8–10), and in Gethsemane prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He is the King whose heart never divided, and in him the wisdom Solomon was given is found in full (1 Corinthians 1:24).

What would you ask for? Put God’s question to a modern heart and the three things Solomon passed over come back in new clothes. Long life is the wellness culture, health pursued as if it were salvation. Riches are the career, the house, the security of enough. And the life of your enemies, for most of us, is not a death but a defeat: to be proved right, to see the people who hurt us exposed, to win. Those are the requests that rise unbidden, and they show what we worship. Kierkegaard called one of his books Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing, arguing that a divided heart, wanting God and everything else as much, cannot be at rest. We do not keep wanting the right thing either, which is why the story does not end at Gibeon. Jesus promises that the Father will “give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11:13), the one gift that slowly changes what we want.

Can I ask God for anything and get it? This was a unique offer to a king at the start of his reign. But God does promise wisdom to all who ask: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). The riches and honour were God’s added gift to Solomon, not a promise to every believer.
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay about 6 miles north-west of Jerusalem; the tabernacle stood there at the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–28 — Give Her the Living Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisdom God gave is proved at once in the smallest and hardest case in the kingdom, and it is proved as justice. Two prostitutes share a house; their babies are born three days apart; one dies in the night, and there is no witness at all (vv. 16–22). The king states the deadlock fairly, then calls for a sword and orders the living child divided (vv. 23–25). The true mother, “because her heart yearned for her son”, gives him up to save his life, while the other says, “divide him” (v. 26). Love has shown itself, and the king gives the child to his mother (v. 27). All Israel stands in awe, seeing “that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice” (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who gets a hearing: two prostitutes with no husbands, no witnesses, no standing and nothing to offer, and the case goes to the king in person.
verseByVerse.examples: He does not detect a liar. He makes a situation in which love has to show itself, because love will act against its own interest and a false claim will not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him. The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house. Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house. And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him. And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast. When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne." But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king. Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'" And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king. And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other." Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother." And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom God gave at Gibeon is proved at once as justice for two women nobody else would have heard: with no witness to decide the case, Solomon makes a situation in which a mother’s love has to show itself.

Then two prostitutes came to the king. The placing is the point. The previous paragraph had a thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God and a promise that no king would compare with him; the very next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room. They had no husbands or male relatives to speak for them, no standing in any court, nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and their trade put them at the bottom of society. It is the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person. The writer set the two paragraphs side by side so that we would see where the wisdom promised in a dream shows up first: in a hearing nobody powerful cared about.

There was no one else with us in the house. The first woman states the problem of proof herself (v. 18): there are no witnesses. She knows it, says it, and comes anyway. Verse 21 has the detail that makes the story real: “when I looked at him closely in the morning”. She woke to feed her baby and found him dead, and in the half-light she did not know at first. It took looking properly.

The king states the deadlock. He repeats both claims exactly (v. 23), and that is the first thing an understanding mind does. He has listened closely enough to state each position without favouring either, and has established aloud that nothing in the evidence separates them. No amount of further questioning will settle it.

Bring me a sword. It is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it (vv. 24–25). A sword is fetched; the order is given in plain words. Neither woman knows it is a test. Would he have gone through with it? Surely not, but she does not know that. Nor is it a trick, or cleverness for its own sake. Nobody could tell which woman was lying, so he stopped trying to detect a liar and made a situation in which love would have to show itself. Love acts against its own interest, and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give him up; a woman who loves a baby will give up anything, even the baby, to keep him alive. So the sword does not test their honesty. It tests what each of them wants more: the child, or winning.

Because her heart yearned for her son. The narrator gives the reason before her words (v. 26). The Hebrew is physical: her compassion grew warm. It is the deep, tender love of a parent felt in the body, the churn a person feels when someone they love is in danger. Joseph felt it on seeing his brother Benjamin: “his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep” (Genesis 43:30).

Give her the living child. She loses, and that should not be hurried past. To keep her son alive she must hand him to the woman who stole him, go home without him, and live the rest of her life knowing where he is and unable to say a word about it. She does it in one sentence, and its second half is all she cares about: “and by no means put him to death.”

He shall be neither mine nor yours. The coldest sentence in the chapter. She is not choosing the child, for the king has ruled that neither of them gets him whole; she is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either. This is what her grief has become. She lost her own son in the night and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby but that the woman across the room should not be happy. Anyone who has watched a bitter dispute go past the point where either side can gain anything has heard this sentence: if I cannot have it, destroy it.

She is his mother. The verdict gives back the true mother’s own words, “by no means put him to death”, and then four more: “she is his mother” (v. 27). The last verse is careful about what it praises. Not the king’s cleverness: “they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice” (v. 28). The wisdom is God’s, given a page earlier, and it is known by what it produced: a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever. Solomon had asked for an understanding mind to govern God’s people, and the first thing it did was find a baby’s mother. This is David’s reign at its best put into practice, for “David administered justice and equity to all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15), and all was always the test: the courts of that world were judged by how they treated the people nobody had to be fair to.

Something greater than Solomon is here. The scene points beyond this courtroom. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse on whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest, who would not judge by what his eyes see or decide by what his ears hear, but would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:1–4). Solomon needed a sword to bring out the truth. The Son of David needed no one to tell him what was in a person, “for he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:25), and Paul calls him the wisdom of God, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3). When Jesus said that something greater than Solomon was here (Matthew 12:42), this was part of what he meant.

Grief is not the sin. The second woman’s sin was the theft and the cruelty, not the grief. A mother who loses a baby has lost something real, and Scripture never treats that sorrow lightly: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18), and Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). What she shows is what grief can become when it is nursed into envy, and that is a warning held out gently, not a judgment on anyone who mourns.

3.theology:
The plant in verse 1. The first fact recorded after the executions is a wedding to Egypt, stated flatly and left there. The law had warned Israel's king against both Egypt and many wives, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17), and chapter 11 names the daughter of Pharaoh first among the women who turned Solomon's heart. This writer does not stop to comment; he plants a detail and waits.

The word only (v. 3). Solomon loved the LORD is said of no other king in Kings. Yet the qualification attached to him on the page before he asks for wisdom is the one this writer will attach to almost every good reign that follows: the high places were not taken away.

An understanding mind (v. 9). What he asks for is a hearing heart. In Hebrew the heart is where a person thinks and decides, so this is a mind that listens and discerns before it rules, which is what a judge needs before anything else. And it is a tool for a job, and the job is other people.

Given outright, and given with an if (vv. 12-14). Wisdom, riches and honour are given with no condition; long life alone is hedged with if you will walk in my ways. The riches come on the principle Jesus states in the Sermon on the Mount: the one who seeks God's kingdom first is the one to whom other things can safely be added. The gifts were never withdrawn, for Solomon died the wisest and richest man alive; it was the conditional side that came due in chapter 11.

Who gets a hearing (v. 16). The wisdom promised at Gibeon shows up first in a case nobody powerful cared about, for two women with no standing at all. That is justice and equity to all his people in practice, and all was always the test.

What the last verse praises (v. 28). Not that the king was clever: they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice. The wisdom is God's, given a page earlier, and it is identified by what it produced. Many Christians have also heard an echo here, and it is no more than an echo: a mother gave up her claim so that her son might live, and God did not spare his own Son so that people with no standing might live (Romans 8:32).
3.examples:
Then: God appeared to a young king in his sleep and told him to ask for anything at all, with no hint of what a good answer would be, and he asked for a heart that could listen, so that he could do the job properly for people who were not his. The first case it was used on was two prostitutes and a baby, with no witnesses and nothing to decide it by.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is the test that never stops being a test: what you would ask for if you could have anything is a photograph of you, and nobody is going to tell you the right answer beforehand. Yet the God who asks is the one who gives: he promises wisdom generously to any who ask him (James 1:5), and it is his Spirit who changes what we want. Second, what he asked for was a tool for a job, and the job was other people, which is the difference between wanting wisdom and wanting to be thought wise. And third, the sword. He could not tell who was lying, so he stopped trying and made a situation in which love had to declare itself, because love will act against its own interest and nothing else will. Know that about other people, and know it about yourself: the question is never what you claim to care about but what you will give up to keep it.

keyVerse.quote: Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?
keyVerse.note: Solomon’s request holds the chapter together: wisdom asked for as a gift, for the sake of people who belong to God, by a man who knows he is not able. Everything that follows, from the two mothers to the queen of Sheba, flows from God’s answer, and the question it ends with is answered fully only in Christ, the King in whom all wisdom dwells.

3.reflection:
God said to Solomon, “Ask what I shall give you” (v. 5). If God put that question to you today, what would you honestly ask for, and what does your answer show about your heart?

Solomon asked for “an understanding mind” to serve people who were God’s, not his (vv. 8–9). Where has God put you in charge of others, at home, at work or in the church, and what would a listening heart look like there?

“Solomon loved the LORD”, yet he had married Pharaoh’s daughter and sacrificed at the high places (vv. 1–3). What small compromises sit alongside real love for God in our lives, and why are they so easy to overlook?

The first case Solomon judged was for two women with no standing at all (vv. 16–28). How should the wisdom of Christ, who is greater than Solomon, shape the way we treat people who can do nothing for us?

4.title: Solomon's Officials and His Wisdom
4.text: <sup>1</sup>King Solomon was king over all Israel,<sup>2</sup>and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest;<sup>3</sup>Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;<sup>4</sup>Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;<sup>5</sup>Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend;<sup>6</sup>Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.<sup>7</sup>Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year.<sup>8</sup>These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;<sup>9</sup>Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan;<sup>10</sup>Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher);<sup>11</sup>Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);<sup>12</sup>Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam;<sup>13</sup>Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars);<sup>14</sup>Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;<sup>15</sup>Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);<sup>16</sup>Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;<sup>17</sup>Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar;<sup>18</sup>Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin;<sup>19</sup>Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.<sup>20</sup>Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy.<sup>21</sup>Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.<sup>22</sup>Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal,<sup>23</sup>ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.<sup>24</sup>For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him.<sup>25</sup>And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon.<sup>26</sup>Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen.<sup>27</sup>And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking.<sup>28</sup>Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.<sup>29</sup>And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore,<sup>30</sup>so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.<sup>31</sup>For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations.<sup>32</sup>He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005.<sup>33</sup>He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish.<sup>34</sup>And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
4.overview:
Where we are. Solomon has received wisdom at Gibeon and proved it in the case of the two mothers (chapter 3). Chapter 4 steps back to show the kingdom that wisdom ran, before the temple building begins in chapter 5.

The message. God kept his word. In Solomon’s reign the promises to Abraham come as near to fulfilment as they ever will in the Old Testament: a people “as many as the sand by the sea”, borders from the Euphrates to Egypt, peace on every side, every family safe under its own vine and fig tree, and a king whose God-given wisdom draws the nations. Yet beneath the glory the writer lets us see its cost and its danger: forced labour, a heavy royal table, and forty thousand stalls of horses.

Why it was said. The exiles had lost the land promised to Abraham (see the introduction). This chapter reminded them that God had once kept that promise to the letter, which was their ground for hoping he would keep his word again; its quiet warnings showed how the slide began, at the top, in the best of times.

How the chapter makes its case. First a full cabinet, ending with the officer over forced labour, and twelve districts drawn partly across the old tribal lands to feed the court a month at a time (vv. 1–19). Then the promise to Abraham fulfilled in numbers, borders, daily provision and peace, every man under his vine and fig tree, with horses and chariots listed among the glories (vv. 20–28). Last, God’s gift of wisdom beyond all the sages of the east and Egypt, and the nations coming to hear it (vv. 29–34).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. Solomon’s kingdom previews the peace the prophets promised, when “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (Micah 4:4). But it rested on a king who multiplied horses and laid a heavy yoke on his people. Jesus is the King whose “yoke is easy” and whose “burden is light” (Matthew 11:30), in whom Abraham’s offspring become “a great multitude that no one could number” from every nation (Revelation 7:9). The nations came to hear Solomon, but “something greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 11:31).

For us. Thank God that he keeps his promises to the letter, and rest your security in him rather than in your own horses, whatever they are. Let wisdom show itself as attention to God’s word and to his world. And if you lead anything, a home, a church or a business, remember that people are not resources to be organised for the comfort of the centre.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Officials and the Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s kingdom is now a full government, and its order already carries the seeds of later trouble. The cabinet (vv. 1–6) is larger than David’s: priests, secretaries, a recorder, the army commander, an officer over the district officers, the king’s friend, a palace steward and, last of all, Adoniram over the forced labour, the man the north will stone when the kingdom splits.
