Twelve officers each feed the court for one month a year (v. 7), and their districts (vv. 8–19) are drawn partly across the old tribal inheritances, reorganising God’s gift of the land to supply the capital. Loyal families are rewarded, and Judah seems to stand apart.
verseByVerse.theology: The new offices make this a state rather than a court, and the last name on the list matters most.
verseByVerse.examples: The twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than by tribe, and the old boundaries are cut across to make a map for collecting supplies. It is efficient, and chapter 12 shows what it cost.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend; Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor. Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year. These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan; Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam; Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s kingdom has become a full government, larger and more organised than David’s, and the writer quietly includes the officer and the system that will one day tear it apart.

Another cabinet list. We have seen two before, at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and 20, each time to show the kingdom in working order. This one is longer, and the difference is the point: Solomon runs a full government, not a royal household. There are two secretaries where David had one. Jehoshaphat the recorder held the same post under David. Abiathar is still listed, although he was banished to Anathoth in chapter 2, which suggests the writer is giving the offices of the reign rather than a snapshot of one afternoon.

The sons of Nathan. Azariah the son of Nathan is “over the officers”, a layer of administration that did not exist under David, and Zabud the son of Nathan holds the title Hushai once held, “king’s friend”, the king’s trusted adviser. If this is Nathan the prophet, who confronted David and then secured Solomon’s succession, his family is now inside the government.

Adoniram the son of Abda. He stands at the bottom of the list, where nobody looks, and he is the name to keep. His office appeared once before, in the last cabinet list of 2 Samuel, and it was new even then: “and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor” (2 Samuel 20:24), probably the same man under a fuller form of his name. Follow him forward. Under Solomon the forced labour becomes enormous: thirty thousand men conscripted in shifts, seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters (5:13–15). When Solomon dies, the northern tribes bring his son one request: “Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you” (12:4). Rehoboam refuses, threatening scorpions in place of his father’s whips, and then “King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones” (12:18). The kingdom splits over this man’s department, and the writer puts him last on the list and says nothing.

Each man had to make provision for one month in the year. An elegant arrangement: the burden is spread, the supply never fails, and the whole country is now organised around keeping the capital fed.

Not the twelve tribes. Read the district list as a whole, because the pattern is what matters. Some districts carry a tribal name: Naphtali, Asher, Issachar, Benjamin, Gilead. Others are defined by towns and regions that cut straight across the old inheritances: the hill country of Ephraim, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, Arubboth, Naphath-dor, Taanach and Megiddo and Beth-shean. The tribal boundaries were not administrative conveniences. They were allotments given by lot under Joshua, each family’s portion of the land God promised Abraham, and the law made them almost impossible to sell away for good: “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine” (Leviticus 25:23). A man’s field was his tribe’s, and his tribe’s was God’s gift. The new map is drawn over the top of them to collect food. It is more efficient, and it begins to wear away what made Israel a covenant people rather than just a country. When the north finally walks out in chapter 12, its slogan is about inheritance: “What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse” (12:16).

Loyalty repaid. Mahanaim, one of the district seats, is where David fled across the Jordan from Absalom and where three men brought him beds and cheese (2 Samuel 17:27–29). Baana the son of Hushai probably belongs to the family of the friend in the torn coat who walked into a captured Jerusalem and deceived Absalom to save David’s life (2 Samuel 15:32–37). And two of Solomon’s daughters are married to district officers (vv. 11, 15). The families that stood by the father are provided for by the son.

A missing tribe. A reader who counts will notice something the writer does not mention: Judah, the king’s own tribe, is not among the districts. Was Judah exempt from the monthly provision? The text does not say outright. But the ten tribes will say something in chapter 12 that sounds very much as though they thought so.

A different kind of King. There is nothing wrong with officials and districts, but this list shows how quickly a kingdom comes to exist for the comfort of its centre, as Samuel warned that a king would “take” sons, daughters, fields and harvests (1 Samuel 8:11–17). Jesus turned that order upside down: “even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The heavy yoke that split Solomon’s kingdom is the one he came to lift: “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

People are not resources. Efficient systems are good, in a business, a church or a household, but ask whom they serve and who carries their cost. A leader who never looks at the bottom of the list will one day hear from it.

Uncertain wording. The last clause of verse 19, “And there was one governor who was over the land”, is terse in Hebrew and its meaning is not certain. It may refer to an officer over Judah, a district not otherwise listed, which would answer the question of the missing tribe; to one official over all twelve, perhaps Azariah the son of Nathan (v. 5); or simply to Geber as the only governor of his large territory. What is not in doubt is that the districts named lie outside Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Every Man Under His Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For one generation God’s promise to Abraham is kept to the letter. Judah and Israel are as many as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking and happy (v. 20), and Solomon rules from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (v. 21). His court’s provision for a single day is enormous (vv. 22–23). He has peace on every side, and every family lives safely under its own vine and fig tree, the picture the prophets will borrow for the age to come (vv. 24–25). But among the glories stand forty thousand stalls of horses, which the law for kings forbade (v. 26), and the officers keep all of it supplied (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The writer tells the high-water mark of the Old Testament in the words of the promise to Abraham.
verseByVerse.examples: In the middle of the plenty stand forty thousand stalls of horses, which the law told Israel's king not to gather (Deut. 17:16). His father had hamstrung captured chariot horses in obedience to that command; the son builds stables.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl. For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him. And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking. Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For one generation God’s promise to Abraham is kept to the letter, with a people beyond counting, borders from the Euphrates to Egypt and every family at peace under its own vine; yet the writer sets the cost and the danger, a heavy royal table and forty thousand stalls of horses, right beside the glory.

As many as the sand by the sea. This is the high-water mark of the Old Testament. The phrase is not a loose word for a crowd but the promise God swore to Abraham on the mountain in the land of Moriah, after the ram was found in the thicket: “I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore” (Genesis 22:17). And here it is, in a sentence about ordinary people having dinner: “They ate and drank and were happy.” Not conquering, building or fighting, but eating, drinking and content.

From the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines. The borders are Abraham’s too: “To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18). Nothing before this and nothing after it comes as close. Joshua took the land, David subdued the neighbours, and here, for one generation, the map matches the promise. The book’s first readers had lost that land (2 Kings 25:21), and the writer sets this moment down for them: God had once kept his word to Abraham to the letter, which was their ground for hoping he would keep it again.

Solomon’s provision for one day. A cor was something like six bushels, so this is several tons of flour and meal daily, thirty head of cattle and a hundred sheep, with game and poultry besides, enough by most estimates to feed thousands. It is splendour, and it is also an invoice. Somebody grew that grain and raised those animals, and the twelve districts of the previous section exist precisely to deliver it, one month each. Read from the other end, the king’s glory is the country’s tax burden, and the writer has put the two paragraphs in that order. The prosperity is real, and the machinery beneath it is what the north will complain of on the day Solomon dies.

And he had peace on all sides around him. His name sounds like shalom, the Hebrew for peace, and the promise tied the two together: “his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days” (1 Chronicles 22:9). God had told David he would not build the temple because “You have shed much blood and have waged great wars” (1 Chronicles 22:8), and promised instead a son who would be “a man of rest”. This verse is that promise kept: the father fought the wars so that the son could build.

Every man under his vine and under his fig tree. The power of the picture is that it is so homely: not an empire, a temple or an army, but a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been in one place long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait. The prophets take it up for the age to come. Micah sees the day when the nations beat their swords into ploughshares and “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (Micah 4:4), and Zechariah uses it of the day God removes the iniquity of the land in a single day (Zechariah 3:9–10). Peace, in Scripture, does not look like a throne. It looks like an ordinary person, unafraid, in the shade of his own fig tree.

Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses. Then, in the middle of it, comes this, stated as one more item of glory. The law for Israel’s kings begins its three prohibitions: “Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, ‘You shall never return that way again’” (Deuteronomy 17:16). We have watched somebody obey this, recently and at cost. When David captured Hadadezer’s chariot force he hamstrung the horses, keeping enough for a hundred chariots: the finest military asset in the region, deliberately ruined because of one clause in a book (2 Samuel 8:4). The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables. Chapter 10 completes it: “Solomon’s import of horses was from Egypt” (10:28), the other half of the same prohibition.

Why the law forbids horses. The reason is never economic. A chariot corps is what a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so directly: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). The writer records the forty thousand stalls between men sitting under their fig trees and officers who “let nothing be lacking” (v. 27), and does not say one word about them. The system works perfectly, and the last verse of the section is about feeding the horses.

The peace that lasts. Solomon’s peace was real, and it lasted one reign. The peace Micah saw is secured by a greater Son of David, the Prince of Peace, who “himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and the promise of offspring like the sand reaches its goal in “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9). He needs no stables: he won his kingdom on a cross.

What are your horses? Every life has its stables. A chariot corps was the ancient king’s guarantee of safety; ours are quieter: a pension, a house, a qualification, a good name, a body that still works. None of them is wicked, but the law’s question lies beneath them all: what do you lean on when you lie awake at three in the morning? Security idols always ask for more, because the fear was never about money or horses. It is the fear of being finally unprotected, and nothing in a stable reaches it. The gospel does not answer it by saying there is nothing to fear. It points to a God “who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). A God who has done that can be leaned on, and a heart that knows it is held can own a stable without living in one.

Why do the numbers differ from Chronicles? Kings has 40,000 stalls and Chronicles 4,000 (2 Chronicles 9:25); most likely the larger figure was miscopied. Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and parallel accounts sometimes count different things, such as a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches, and those who hold Scripture to be without error have always meant what was first written, not every later copy (see the introduction).

Where Christians differ. Solomon’s rule reached the borders promised to Abraham (v. 21; Genesis 15:18), so the land promise was fulfilled in its Old Testament sense, and the New Testament looks for its fuller fulfilment in the whole earth inherited by Christ’s people: Abraham’s offspring were promised that they “would be heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). Christians differ over whether a further fulfilment in the land itself still awaits the Jewish people. Some, dispensationalists especially, read the promises that way; others read them as widened in Christ to the renewed earth (Hebrews 11:10–16). Both rejoice that God keeps his word to Abraham.

This commentary’s view. The land promise was fulfilled in the days of Joshua and Solomon and points beyond itself to the whole new earth, which Christ will give to all Abraham’s children by faith, Jewish and Gentile alike.

Uncertain wording. Two rare words make some details uncertain. “Fattened fowl” (v. 23) translates a Hebrew word found only here; it may mean geese, guinea fowl or some other fattened bird, and no one knows for sure. “Swift steeds” (v. 28) renders a rare word for a fast horse, perhaps of the kind used by royal couriers. Neither affects the picture of a lavishly supplied court.
verseByVerse.note: “The Euphrates” is “the River” in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — Wisdom Like the Sand on the Seashore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisdom God promised at Gibeon is now reported as fact, and the nations come to hear it. God gives Solomon understanding beyond measure and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore, surpassing the famed wisdom of the east and of Egypt and the best-known sages of Israel (vv. 29–31). He speaks thousands of proverbs and songs (v. 32) and studies the whole created order: trees from the cedar to the hyssop, then beasts, birds, reptiles and fish (v. 33). His wisdom is close, careful attention to what God has made, and people of all nations come to hear it (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon's wisdom is God's gift, and verse 33 shows what it was: sustained attention to what God has made.
verseByVerse.examples: Heman and Ethan, two of the men Solomon is measured against, have psalms in the psalter with their names in the headings. And the nations who come to hear him prepare for the Queen of Sheba in chapter 10, whom the Lord Jesus will hold up as an example (Matthew 12:42).

verseByVerse.quote: And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore, so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations. He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005. He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish. And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Solomon a wisdom wider than any in the ancient world, a wisdom of close attention to everything God had made, and the nations came to hear it.

Like the sand on the seashore. The promise of Gibeon is now reported as fact, in the same picture the writer has just used of the population. Breadth of mind is literally largeness of heart. It is not a moral phrase here but one of range: the capacity to hold a great many things at once and see how they fit.

All the wisdom of Egypt. The east and Egypt were the two great wisdom traditions of the ancient world, Egypt with centuries of written wisdom teaching, and Solomon is placed above both.

Wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman. The four men named were famous enough to need no explanation, and two of the names turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88, a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, is the darkest psalm in the book, ending “my companions have become darkness”. Psalm 89, a maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite, is the long meditation on the covenant with David which asks, when the crown has been cast to the ground, “Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?” So the men Solomon is measured against wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom meant in Israel: not a stock of good advice, but the ability to look steadily at troubles that have no easy answer.

He also spoke 3,000 proverbs. Of three thousand proverbs, the book of Proverbs holds a few hundred; of a thousand and five songs, the Song of Songs is one, and two psalms carry his name (Psalms 72 and 127). Almost all of it is lost.

From the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop. Verse 33 shows what kind of wisdom this was. Trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish: that is the order of the created world as Genesis 1 sets it out, and Solomon went through it and paid attention. The range within the first category is the point. The cedar was the largest and most valuable tree in the region, the timber kings imported for palaces and temples. Hyssop is a small bushy plant that grows in cracks in masonry; the Israelites used it to daub blood on their doorposts in Egypt (Exodus 12:22), and on a hyssop branch a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on the cross (John 19:29). Solomon looked at both, the greatest tree and the weed in the wall.

Wisdom as attention. So the wisdom God gave was not a mystical faculty or a stock of clever rulings but sustained, curious, unembarrassed attention to what God had made, from the cedars down to whatever grows out of the brickwork. Proverbs does the same on every page: go to the ant; consider the rock badgers, the locusts and the lizard; look at the field of the sluggard, overgrown with thorns (Proverbs 6:6; 30:24–28; 24:30–31). Israel’s wisdom believed the world was made by a consistent God, so that whoever watches it carefully, in the fear of the LORD, will learn how to live.

Something greater than Solomon is here. One of the visitors, the queen of Sheba, has chapter 10 to herself and says the half was not told her. Jesus spoke of her to a generation that wanted a sign: “The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 11:31; compare Matthew 12:42). A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour, and the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.

Ask, then pay attention. For a believer the pattern still holds. Ask God for wisdom, since it is still his gift (James 1:5), and then pay attention: to his word first, and then to his world, to how work, money, households and friendships actually go, and to the people in front of you. Above all, come to the one in whom all its treasures are hidden (Colossians 2:3), as the nations came to Solomon, with far more reason.

Uncertain wording. Who exactly the four sages were is not certain. “The sons of Mahol” may be a family name, or the word may mean dance, making them members of a guild of musicians. An Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara appear among the descendants of Judah’s son Zerah (1 Chronicles 2:6), and “Ezrahite” may mean a descendant of Zerah; yet Heman and Ethan are also named among David’s Levite singers (1 Chronicles 15:19). Whether these are the same men, and whether they wrote Psalms 88 and 89, cannot be settled. The point is plain either way: they were the wisest names Israel knew.
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible, 4:21-34 is numbered 5:1-14.

4.theology:
A state, not a court (vv. 2-6). Two secretaries, an officer set over the officers, a palace manager, and a department of forced labour: layers David never had. The forced labour is the office to watch. It was new when it first appeared at 2 Samuel 20:24, under Solomon it becomes enormous (5:13-15), and when he dies the north asks his son for one thing only, to lighten the yoke (12:4). Samuel had warned that a king would take Israel's sons for his chariots and his fields (1 Samuel 8:11-17), and this list is that warning beginning to come true.

A revenue map over an inheritance (vv. 7-19). The tribal boundaries were each family's portion of what was promised to Abraham. Drawing a food-collection map over them is efficient, and it begins to dissolve what made Israel a covenant people rather than a country. When the north finally walks out, its slogan is about inheritance (12:16).

The promise kept, and the bill (vv. 20-23). For one generation the people are as many as the sand and the borders reach the Euphrates, as God swore to Abraham (Gen. 22:17; 15:18), and the sentence that says so is about ordinary people eating dinner. The writer then sets the king's daily table beside it, so that what reads from one end as glory reads from the other as the country's tax burden. Both are true, and the reader is meant to hold both.

Peace, and the King who gives it (vv. 24-25). The son of peace, a man of rest, builds what the warrior father could not (1 Chron. 22:8-9). The man under his own vine and fig tree becomes the prophets' picture of what God intends to give the world (Mic. 4:4; Zech. 3:10). But Solomon's peace lasted all the days of Solomon and no longer. Isaiah promised a son on David's throne of whose government and peace there would be no end (Isaiah 9:6-7), and Paul says of Christ that he himself is our peace, having broken down the wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The fig tree Micah saw is his to give.

What the horses mean (v. 26). The law forbade the king many horses not for economic reasons but because a chariot corps is what a nation leans on instead of God. The writer records the stables without comment, between the fig trees and the full storehouses, and chapter 10 will show where the horses came from.

Wisdom as a gift and as attention (vv. 29-34). God gave Solomon wisdom: it begins as a gift. Its range is the order of Genesis 1, from the cedar to the hyssop, and it is measured against men who wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant (Pss. 88, 89). Wisdom in Israel was never a stock of clever answers; it was the capacity to look steadily at the world God made, including what has no easy answer. And the one who gives it is greater than Solomon (Matt. 12:42).
4.examples:
Then: a king whose court ate thirty head of cattle and a hundred sheep a day reorganised the whole country into twelve supply districts drawn straight across the tribal inheritances, and the minister he put in charge of the conscripted labour that built it all was stoned to death by ten of the tribes on the day the kingdom broke in half.

Now: two things. First, verse 33 is what wisdom looks like when the Bible describes it, and it is more ordinary and more demanding than most people expect: sustained attention to what God has actually made. And it is a gift before it is a discipline: God gave Solomon wisdom (v. 29), and he still gives it generously to those who ask (James 1:5). Solomon was the wisest man alive and he used that wisdom to look at fish and lizards. Second, notice how the chapter is built. Everything in it is a genuine good (peace, plenty, safety, a man under his own fig tree, a promise to Abraham arriving), and the writer lays the machinery that pays for it right alongside. Prosperity is not neutral. It has a bill attached and somebody is paying it, and a prosperous people quietly gathers the very things God told it not to.

keyVerse.quote: And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon.
keyVerse.note: This verse captures the reign at its height: the promise to Abraham kept, and peace measured not by a throne but by ordinary families safe at home. The prophets took it up as their picture of the age to come (Micah 4:4), a peace that only the Prince of Peace can bring and keep.

4.reflection:
Verses 20–21 show God keeping his promise to Abraham to the letter, centuries after he made it. How does his faithfulness in the past help you trust him with promises not yet fulfilled?

The officer over forced labour and the enormous daily provision show the cost of Solomon’s splendour (vv. 6, 22–23, 27). Where might the systems in your home, church or workplace serve the comfort of a few at the expense of others, and how does Jesus’ easy yoke challenge that?

David hamstrung the chariot horses; Solomon built forty thousand stalls (v. 26). What are the “horses” you are tempted to lean on for security, and what would it look like to trust in the name of the LORD instead?

Solomon’s wisdom showed itself as careful attention to God’s world, from the cedar to the hyssop (v. 33). How could you grow in that kind of wisdom, and what does it mean for you that Jesus is “something greater than Solomon”?

5.title: Preparations for the Temple
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon sent word to Hiram,<sup>3</sup>"You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet.<sup>4</sup>But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune.<sup>5</sup>And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.'<sup>6</sup>Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."<sup>7</sup>As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people."<sup>8</sup>And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber.<sup>9</sup>My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household."<sup>10</sup>So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired,<sup>11</sup>while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.<sup>13</sup>King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men.<sup>14</sup>And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft.<sup>15</sup>Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country,<sup>16</sup>besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work.<sup>17</sup>At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones.<sup>18</sup>So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.
5.overview:
Where we are. Solomon’s kingdom is at peace and his wisdom famous (chapter 4). Now, for the first time, he turns to the work God promised David that his son would do: building a house for the name of the LORD.

The message. The temple is built on a promise, in a rest God gave. Solomon builds not because a great king ought to have a great temple but “as the LORD said to David my father”, in a peace God gave. God’s promised wisdom shows itself in an honest treaty with a foreign king, and the forests and craftsmen of the nations serve the house of Israel’s God. But the work is also paid for with a levy of Israel’s own men, a burden the kingdom will one day break over.

Why it was said. The exiles who first read this had seen the temple burned (see the introduction). They needed to remember that it had been built on God’s promise to David, not on Solomon’s greatness, and that the promise still stood when the building was gone, and to see in the levy one root of the division that followed.

How the chapter makes its case. Hiram of Tyre, David’s old ally, sends an embassy, and Solomon replies that his father could not build because of war, but God has given rest, so he will build as God promised; he asks for cedar and skilled woodcutters at Hiram’s price (vv. 1–6). Hiram blesses the LORD for David’s wise son and agrees to raft timber down the coast in return for wheat and oil year by year, and the writer credits the treaty to the wisdom God promised (vv. 7–12). Then the levy: thirty thousand Israelites in monthly shifts under Adoniram, with carriers and stonecutters quarrying costly stones for foundations no one would see (vv. 13–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The son of David who builds God’s house in a time of rest points to the greater Son of David, who said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), and called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21). The nations bringing their timber anticipate Isaiah’s vision, “The glory of Lebanon shall come to you… to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isaiah 60:13), fulfilled as people from every nation are built into God’s house. And where Solomon built with conscripted labour, Christ builds with “living stones” who come to him freely (1 Peter 2:5), and is himself the costly cornerstone.

For us. The church stands, like the temple, on what God has promised, not on our greatness. Enjoy the rest you were given rather than won, and serve gladly in building what God builds. And let those who lead God’s work never let a project’s glory hide its cost to the people doing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Now the LORD My God Has Given Me Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon begins the temple on the strength of God’s promise and in the rest God has given. Hiram of Tyre, who always loved David, sends envoys on his own initiative (v. 1). Solomon replies that his father could not build because of constant war, but now the LORD has given rest on every side, with neither adversary nor misfortune (vv. 2–4). So he will build a house for the name of the LORD, exactly as God told David his son would (v. 5). He asks for cedars of Lebanon and offers to pay Hiram’s servants whatever wages he sets, admitting that no one in Israel can cut timber like the Sidonians (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon gives the wars as the reason his father could not build; God gave another reason, the blood David had shed (1 Chron. 22:8). The verse note explains why both are true, and why a son would give the first in a letter to a foreign king.
verseByVerse.examples: Rest on every side is the condition that makes building possible, and the word that opened the covenant chapter (2 Sam. 7:1). The father fought so that the son could build.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David. And Solomon sent word to Hiram, "You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet. But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune. And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.' Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon begins the temple because God promised David that his son would build it, and because God has now given the rest in which to do it; he asks a foreign king for help, honestly and at a fair price.

For Hiram always loved David. The first embassy of the reign arrives unasked, and the reason given is personal. Loved is the ordinary word, which in treaty language also meant loyal alliance. Hiram had sent cedar and craftsmen to build David a house years earlier (2 Samuel 5:11), and that cedar made David uneasy enough to say, “I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent” (2 Samuel 7:2). The remark led to the greatest promise in the Old Testament, God’s covenant with David. So the man who supplied the timber that started the conversation now supplies the timber for the building.

David my father could not build a house. Solomon’s explanation is true but not the whole truth. He says his father was prevented by the wars. David himself, in Chronicles, gives God’s reason: “You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth” (1 Chronicles 22:8; compare 28:3). Not too busy, but too bloody. Solomon is not lying, since the same wars are where the blood was shed, but his account reflects better on his father. It is also, in fairness, a letter to a foreign king about a timber contract, not the place to explain that God refused his father a building permit on account of bloodshed. The writer records what was said and lets a reader who knows Chronicles supply the other half.

Rest on every side. This is the word the whole thing turns on. The covenant chapter opened, “when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies” (2 Samuel 7:1); rest first prompted David to think about the tent. And rest is what Solomon has been given rather than won. He has fought nobody. His father broke the Philistines, twice destroyed Syrian armies and subdued Moab, Edom and Ammon, and the son inherits a country with “neither adversary nor misfortune” and builds in the quiet. Twice now he says the LORD my God (vv. 4–5), where he spoke of the LORD his God for David (v. 3): his father’s God is his own.

As the LORD said to David my father. His whole authority for the project is a quotation. He builds not because a king ought to have a temple, but because God told his father through Nathan, before Solomon was born: “He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). David wanted to build God a house and was told instead that God would build him one, a dynasty, and that his son would build the temple. Every stone that goes up in the next three chapters goes up on the strength of that sentence.

No one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians. He asks for the timber and the men, and concedes the point that makes the request necessary: Israel had no forests of that kind and no tradition of felling, hauling and rafting great timber. The Phoenicians did it for the whole eastern Mediterranean. So the temple of the LORD will be built of foreign wood, cut by foreign hands, by an arrangement in which Israel admits it cannot do this part. And he offers to pay “such wages as you set”, neither asking a gift nor naming his own price: God’s work may use the help of those outside, but on honest terms.

A Son who builds. The promise Solomon quotes reached beyond him: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.” Solomon’s throne and temple both fell. The Son of David in whom the promise holds said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), and he builds it in a rest he won himself, in the battle against sin and death fought at the cross. His people do not build in order to earn that rest; they build because they have entered it (Hebrews 4:9–10).
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was the great Phoenician port on the coast north of Israel. Lebanon’s cedars were prized timber.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Blessed Be the LORD This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A foreign king blesses the LORD, and God’s promised wisdom shows itself in an honest treaty. Hiram rejoices at Solomon’s words and blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son (v. 7). He agrees to send cedar and cypress down from Lebanon, raft it along the coast and break it up wherever Solomon directs, asking in return for food for his household (vv. 8–9). So timber flows south, and wheat and fine oil flow north, year by year (vv. 10–11). The writer’s comment is that the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised, and the two kings make a treaty of peace (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name and credits him with Solomon's wisdom. It should not be overclaimed, since Hiram's own gods were Baal and Astarte, and Jezebel comes from next door in Sidon a century later; but it should not be skipped either. The writer records a foreigner getting the credit right.
verseByVerse.examples: Read the agreement as a business agreement. Tyre had the finest timber and craftsmen in the region and almost no farmland; Israel had grain and oil and no cedar. This is not charity in either direction but two kings each supplying what the other could not grow.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people." And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber. My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household." So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired, while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year. And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A foreign king blesses the LORD for David’s wise son, and the honest, mutually useful treaty that follows is credited not to Solomon’s shrewdness but to the wisdom God had promised him.

Blessed be the LORD this day. A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name, and it should be neither overstated nor dismissed. What he says is right in every particular: he uses God’s covenant name, not a general word for a god; he gives the credit to God rather than Solomon; and he names what has actually happened, a wise son given to David. That is better theology than many Israelites managed. But it is not a conversion. Tyre’s gods were Baal and Astarte, kings of that world habitually honoured a neighbour’s god as a courtesy, and a century later a princess of Sidon called Jezebel will marry a king of Israel and bring a worship that burns through the northern kingdom for three generations.

A good word from a foreigner. Still, the writer of Kings, merciless about Israel’s own kings, gives a foreigner an unqualified good line and lets it stand. The reader has met the pattern before, in Uriah the Hittite, Ittai the Gittite, Obed-edom and the Ammonite who brought bedding to Mahanaim, and will meet it again in a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general.

I will make it into rafts. Cedar was felled in the mountains, dragged to the coast, lashed into rafts and floated down the coast to a landing point (Chronicles names Joppa, 2 Chronicles 2:16), then hauled some thirty-five miles overland up to Jerusalem. Every beam in the house of God came that way.

Providing food for my household. Hiram’s price is food. Tyre was a trading city on a rocky coast with little farmland behind it, and it fed itself by importing; what Israel had that Tyre needed was grain and oil. The payment is a standing obligation, year by year for as long as the work goes on, and the wheat and oil must come from somewhere, which is what the twelve districts of chapter 4 are for. Beaten oil was the best grade, from olives crushed rather than pressed, the quality the law required for the lamps of the sanctuary (Exodus 27:20).

And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. Notice where verse 12 stands. The writer has just described a shrewd and favourable trade agreement, at market rates, with the one supplier in the world who had what Israel needed, and his comment is not that Solomon negotiated well but that the LORD gave him wisdom. The wisdom in a timber contract is the wisdom given in a dream at Gibeon, and as he promised him marks the promise as kept. So a believer may ask God for wisdom over a contract, a budget or a hard negotiation as readily as over a question of faith, and thank him, not his own shrewdness, when it turns out well.

The nations bring their glory. A Gentile king blesses Israel’s God and sends the best of his forests for God’s house. Isaiah saw this become the pattern of the last days: “The glory of Lebanon shall come to you, the cypress, the plane, and the pine, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isaiah 60:13). In Christ it comes true more deeply still, as people from every nation become “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God”, built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:19–22).

Uncertain wording. The second timber (v. 8), berosh, is translated cypress, fir, pine or juniper in different versions. It was clearly a tall, valuable conifer of the Lebanon range, but which tree is meant is not certain.

Textual note. In verse 11 the Hebrew text reads twenty cors of beaten oil, which older translations such as the KJV follow; the ESV follows the ancient Greek translation in reading 20,000 cors. Twenty cors of the finest oil, perhaps for Hiram’s own household, is not impossible, and Chronicles records the payment differently, in wheat, barley, wine and oil for the workmen (2 Chronicles 2:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The temple is built at great cost, and part of that cost falls on Israel’s own people. Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelites as forced labour and sends them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of ten thousand, a month away and two at home, under Adoniram (vv. 13–14). Seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters work in the hill country under 3,300 officers (vv. 15–16). At the king’s command they quarry great, costly stones for foundations no one will see (v. 17), and Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders and the men of Gebal prepare timber and stone side by side (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the department the kingdom eventually breaks over. The one thing the northern tribes ask of Solomon's son is to lighten his father's yoke (12:4), and when he refuses they stone the man named in verse 14 (12:18). The work it served was glorious, and the cost was real.
verseByVerse.examples: A tension should be stated rather than smoothed: 9:22 says Solomon made no slaves of the people of Israel, and this section says he drafted forced labour out of all Israel. The usual answer, set out in the note below, is plausible; the men of chapter 12 evidently did not feel the distinction as a large one.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men. And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft. Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work. At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones. So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of God is built with a vast levy of Israelite labour, humane by the standards of its day and glorious in its purpose, yet heavy enough that the kingdom will one day break over it.

King Solomon drafted forced labor. Verse 13 describes what will eventually break the kingdom apart. The word is mas, compulsory unpaid labour owed to the crown, and Israel had met it before. In Egypt “they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens” (Exodus 1:11), and the word for those taskmasters is built on this one.

A month in Lebanon and two months at home. The terms are humane by the standards of the age, and that should be said. It is a third of a man’s time, not all of it, so a farmer could still get his crop in: a call-up by turns, not slavery. But the man in charge is Adoniram from the cabinet list (4:6), and when the northern tribes are refused relief after Solomon’s death they stone “Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor” (12:18). The kingdom split over this department and never came back together.

Of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. There is a tension here that should be named rather than smoothed over. Four chapters on, the writer says, “But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves” (9:22), and that the permanent labour gangs came from the surviving Canaanite peoples (9:20–21). Yet this chapter says that he “drafted forced labor out of all Israel”. The usual reconciliation is probably right: two arrangements are described. The Canaanites were in permanent bondage; the Israelite levy was rotational, temporary, and for the temple in particular. The distinction is real and legal, and it is also the kind that looks much smaller to the men carrying the loads. The men who came to Rehoboam did not say ‘your father enslaved us’. They said, “Your father made our yoke heavy” (12:4), of a system its own records called fair.

Glory and cost. The work is glorious: these men are building the place where Israel will meet God for nearly four centuries, and each could tell his grandchildren what he had a hand in. And it is paid for by conscripted labour on a scale the country had never seen, run by a department that did not exist under David, and the bill arrives at the end of Solomon’s life and is presented to his son. The writer states the numbers and does not comment, as he has from the start (the Egyptian wedding of 3:1, the forty thousand stalls of 4:26, the levy here), laying things down in order and trusting the reader still to be holding them in chapter 11.

Great, costly stones. The foundation, which no one would ever see, gets the best material. That says something about how this building was made, and for whom: the part only God would see was built as carefully as the rest.

And the men of Gebal. The last verse lists three workforces, and two are foreign: Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders, and the men of Gebal, which is Byblos, another Phoenician port up the coast, famous for its craftsmen. So the house of the LORD is quarried, dressed, felled and rafted by Israelites and Phoenicians side by side, from a foreign king’s timber, to a plan God gave David (1 Chronicles 28:11–19), on ground David bought from Araunah the Jebusite (2 Samuel 24:24).

A better foundation, and a lighter yoke. Solomon laid costly stones that no one would see. God laid in Zion “a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation” (Isaiah 28:16), and that stone is Christ (1 Peter 2:6). His house is built not by conscripts but by people who come to him freely, “like living stones” (1 Peter 2:5), and its builder invites the weary to take a yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:28–30). The burden of Solomon’s house was laid on the people; the burden of Christ’s house was laid on the King.

Counting the cost to others. Church leaders, like kings, can mistake a worthy project for permission to overload the willing. Ask who is carrying the loads, and whether they would describe the yoke as you do.

Why does Chronicles give 3,600 officers? Kings has 3,300 chief officers, Chronicles 3,600 (2 Chronicles 2:18). The two books seem to divide the ranks differently, for the totals agree: the 3,300 here plus the 550 senior officers of 9:23 make 3,850, and so do Chronicles’ 3,600 plus 250 (2 Chronicles 8:10).

5.theology:
Two true reasons that are not the same (v. 3). Solomon says the wars prevented his father; God said the blood disqualified him (1 Chron. 22:8; 28:3). The accounts touch, because the same wars produced the bloodshed, but they are not interchangeable. A son writing to a Phoenician about a timber contract is not going to say that his father was refused a building permit by God, and the writer trusts the reader to hold the other half.

Rest is given, not won (v. 4). The word that opened the covenant chapter (2 Sam. 7:1), the rest that first set David thinking about the tent, is now Solomon's inheritance. He has fought nobody. His father broke the Philistines and subdued the neighbours, and the son inherits neither adversary nor misfortune and builds in the quiet. Much of what any of us enjoy was won by people before us.

The warrant is a quotation (v. 5). Solomon builds because of 2 Samuel 7:13, spoken in a night vision before he existed. David wanted to build and was told no, and told instead that God would build him a house. The temple is not a good idea being carried out; it is a promise being kept. And the promise looked past Solomon. The prophets spoke of a man called the Branch who would build the temple of the LORD and rule as priest and king (Zechariah 6:12-13); Jesus, David's greater Son, spoke of the temple of his body raised in three days, and of the church he would build (John 2:19-21; Matthew 16:18). Solomon's house was burned. The house the Son builds is still going up.

Help from outside (vv. 6-12). Israel admits it cannot cut timber like the Sidonians, and Solomon offers the going rate rather than asking for a gift or naming his own price. Then a Phoenician king blesses the LORD by the covenant name. It is not a conversion: Tyre's gods were Baal and Astarte, and a courtesy to a neighbour's god was common practice. But this writer, who is merciless about Israelite kings, lets a foreigner's good line stand, as he does elsewhere with Uriah, Ittai, a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general. And he credits the shrewd trade agreement to the wisdom God promised at Gibeon, not to Solomon's bargaining: as he promised him is the historian checking the account against the promise.

The levy, held both ways (vv. 13-18). Israel remembered taskmasters from Egypt (Ex. 1:11), and this levy, though rotational and humane by the standards of the age, is felt as a yoke by the men who carry it (12:4). The reconciliation with 9:22 is real, and it is also the kind of distinction that looks smaller to the men carrying the loads. Yet the work is glorious. The men quarrying in the hill country are building the place where Israel will meet God for nearly four centuries, on a foundation of costly stones nobody would ever see. The writer states the numbers and comments on none of it, trusting the reader to still be holding them in chapter 11.

Built by Israel and the nations together (v. 18). Solomon's men, Hiram's men and the men of Byblos work side by side, on a foreign king's timber, to a promise given to David, on ground bought from a Jebusite. Isaiah saw the picture enlarged: foreigners building up Zion's walls, and the glory of Lebanon brought to beautify God's sanctuary (Isaiah 60:10, 13). Paul sees it fulfilled when Gentiles once far off are built together with Israel into a holy temple, with Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19-22), the chosen and precious stone of 1 Peter 2:4-6.
5.examples:
Then: every cedar beam was cut by Phoenician woodcutters, rafted down the coast and hauled thirty-five miles inland, and paid for with wheat and the finest hand-crushed oil, every year, for as long as the building took.

Now: two things. First, Solomon's version of why his father was excluded is worth thinking about honestly: it was true, it was kinder than the truth God had given, and it was told to somebody who was never going to check. Most of the half-accounts people give of their families are exactly like that: not lies, just the version that reflects better, offered where the fuller one would cost something. Second, the levy. Everything about that project was good; the thing being built was the house of God, and the arrangement was legal and by the standards of the age humane. And the people carrying it experienced it as a yoke, and said so the moment the man who imposed it was dead. Those who lead anything, a church building project included, do well to ask the people carrying the load how it feels while there is still time to change it. It is possible to build something genuinely magnificent on terms the builders would not have chosen, and to find out what they thought only when it is too late to ask. The king the prophets promised lays a different yoke on those who come to him: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt. 11:30).

keyVerse.quote: And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, ‘Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.’
keyVerse.note: Solomon’s whole reason for building is a promise God made before he was born. The temple rests on God’s word to David, not on a great king’s ambition, and that word reached further than Solomon: it is kept in Christ, the Son of David who builds a house that will never fall.

5.reflection:
Solomon’s whole reason for building was “as the LORD said to David my father” (v. 5). How does knowing that God’s work rests on his promises, not on our greatness, change the way you serve in your church?

Solomon built in a rest he had been given rather than won (vv. 3–4). How does Christ’s finished work give you rest, and how should that rest shape the way you work for him?

Hiram blessed the LORD and sent the best of his forests for God’s house (vv. 7–10). What does this foreshadow about the nations and God’s people, and how should it shape the way we see those outside the church?

The temple was glorious, but the levy laid a heavy yoke on Israel (vv. 13–14; 12:4). Where might good work for God place unfair burdens on others, and how does Jesus’ easy yoke guide us?

6.title: Solomon Builds the House
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.<sup>3</sup>The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.<sup>4</sup>And he made for the house windows with recessed frames.<sup>5</sup>He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around.<sup>6</sup>The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.<sup>7</sup>When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built.<sup>8</sup>The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.<sup>9</sup>So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar.<sup>10</sup>He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.<sup>11</sup>Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon,<sup>12</sup>"Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father.<sup>13</sup>And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."<sup>14</sup>So Solomon built the house and finished it.<sup>15</sup>He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress.<sup>16</sup>He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place.<sup>17</sup>The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long.<sup>18</sup>The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen.<sup>19</sup>The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar.<sup>21</sup>And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold.<sup>22</sup>And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold.<sup>23</sup>In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high.<sup>24</sup>Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.<sup>25</sup>The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form.<sup>26</sup>The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub.<sup>27</sup>He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house.<sup>28</sup>And he overlaid the cherubim with gold.<sup>29</sup>Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>30</sup>The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>31</sup>For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided.<sup>32</sup>He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.<sup>33</sup>So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square,<sup>34</sup>and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding.<sup>35</sup>On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work.<sup>36</sup>He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams.<sup>37</sup>In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.<sup>38</sup>And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
6.overview:
Where we are. The timber and stone are gathered and the workforce raised (chapter 5). Now, in the fourth year of his reign, Solomon begins the house of the LORD, and this chapter takes it from foundation to completion seven years later.

The message. God’s house is built to his plan and for his presence, and God makes plain that the building itself secures nothing. In the middle of the specifications he speaks: what matters is walking in his ways, and his promise is not a magnificent house but that he will dwell among his people and never forsake them. The house itself, carved with cherubim, palm trees and flowers around a golden room for the ark, is Eden remembered and a sign of God living with his people.

Why it was said. The first readers had watched this house burn (see the introduction). They needed to hear that God had never tied his faithfulness to a building, that he warned against trusting it from the day it went up, and that his promise outlasted the stones.

How the chapter makes its case. First the date, counted from the exodus, and the plan: the tabernacle doubled, with porch, windows and side chambers, its stone finished at the quarry so that no iron tool was heard on the site (vv. 1–10). Then God’s word in the middle of the work: obey, and I will keep my word to David and dwell among my people (vv. 11–13). Then the interior: cedar everywhere, a cube-shaped inner sanctuary overlaid with gold for the ark, two great cherubim, and cherubim, palms and flowers carved on every wall (vv. 14–30). Last, the carved and gilded doors, the inner court and the dates: seven years, finished to every specification (vv. 31–38).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. The temple was where God dwelt among his people; in Christ “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Jesus called his body the temple (John 2:19–21). The inner room, entered once a year with blood, waited for the one who entered “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12), and at his death the curtain before it was torn. The golden cube becomes the shape of the new Jerusalem, which has no temple, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). And the obedience God required of Solomon, which no son of David gave, Christ gave in full.

For us. Trust no building, tradition or record of service to secure God’s favour; walk with him inside his promise. God is shaping his people now as living stones, often out of sight and by hard cutting, for a place already prepared. And the way into his presence that the cherubim once guarded is open through Christ, so draw near.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — No Hammer or Axe Was Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The temple is the next chapter of the exodus story, built on the tabernacle’s pattern and with deep reverence. The writer dates it from Israel’s rescue from Egypt, 480 years before, in Solomon’s fourth year (v. 1). The house is sixty cubits by twenty by thirty, exactly double the tabernacle on the ground, with a porch across the front, narrow windows, and three storeys of side chambers resting on ledges so that no beam pierces the temple wall (vv. 2–6, 8–10). Every stone was finished at the quarry, so that no hammer, axe or iron tool was heard on the site while the house went up (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The date is given from the exodus, not from a dynasty or a foreign king's reign, which says what the building is for before a single dimension is given.
verseByVerse.examples: Every stone was finished at the quarry so that no iron tool would be heard on the site: not efficiency but reverence, as the verse note explains.

verseByVerse.quote: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house. And he made for the house windows with recessed frames. He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around. The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house. When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built. The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third. So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar. He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple is begun as the next chapter of the exodus story: the tabernacle rebuilt at twice its size in stone and cedar, raised with such reverence that every stone was finished away from the site and no iron tool was heard where God would be met.

In the four hundred and eightieth year. The writer could have dated this by the monarchy or by a foreign king’s reign, as the ancient world usually did. He dates it from the exodus. No other date in the historical books is reckoned this way. It says what the building is for before a single dimension is given: Israel’s calendar runs from the night God brought them out of a country where they were slaves, and the temple is a chapter in that story, built for the God who did that.

In the month of Ziv, which is the second month. The month is named twice because Ziv was an old Canaanite month-name that had gone out of use, and the writer explains it for readers who no longer knew it (see the Jewish calendar). That habit of explaining suggests the account was written down long after the event, from records.

Sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. Roughly ninety feet by thirty by forty-five (a cubit was about eighteen inches). Beside the great temples of Egypt and Mesopotamia it was modest. It was never meant to hold a congregation; Israel worshipped in the courts, and the building itself was the dwelling. Nor are the proportions invented. The tabernacle was thirty cubits by ten, with walls ten cubits high; this is exactly double on the ground and three times as high. So what goes up is not a new idea but the tent Israel carried through the wilderness and set up at Shiloh, rebuilt at twice the size, in stone and cedar and gold, and no longer portable. That last change is the significant one. God had never asked for a house of cedar (2 Samuel 7:6–7), and he speaks about it in the middle of this chapter.

He made side chambers all around. The windows were probably narrow openings high in the wall, letting in light while keeping out weather and eyes (v. 4). Round the outside of the temple stood three storeys of storerooms and service rooms, and the builders went to deliberate trouble so that not one of their beams was set into the wall of the house itself. Instead the temple wall was stepped, narrowing as it rose, so that each floor rested on a ledge (v. 6). It would have been far easier to socket the beams straight in. They designed the building to avoid it, and the walls of God’s house have no holes cut into them.

Stone prepared at the quarry. Every stone was cut, squared and finished in the hill country, then carried to the site and set in place, so the whole enormous structure went up in something close to silence (v. 7). Every block had to be measured exactly before it left the quarries where the stonecutters of 5:15 worked. Why go to such trouble? The law for altars shows the thinking: “If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it” (Exodus 20:25). Whatever the full reason, the effect is that the noise and violence of manufacture are kept away from the place where God will be met. The work is done elsewhere; what arrives at the site is finished.

Living stones. Peter takes the picture further: “As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:4–5). Christ is the chosen stone, and his people are stones shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the place already fitted for where they go. That is what God is doing with his people now: the cutting and shaping happen in this life, often painfully and unseen, away from the finished house. None of the blows is wasted, and none of them will be heard in the house.

Where Christians differ. Does the 480 years fix the date of the exodus? Faithful readers take it two ways. Read as a plain count, it puts the exodus about 1446 BC, since Solomon’s fourth year was about 966 BC; those who hold this early date point to the plain sense of the figure and to Jephthah’s 300 years in the land (Judges 11:26). Others hold a later date, about 1260 BC: Exodus 1:11 names a store city Raamses, which fits the reign of Ramesses II, and much of the archaeology of Canaan seems to fit the thirteenth century better; they read 480 as twelve generations of forty years, a round figure, with real generations nearer twenty-five. Early-daters reply that the name Raamses may have been updated for later readers, as in Genesis 47:11. Both take the verse as true; they differ over what kind of number it is. Paul’s “about 450 years” (Acts 13:20) covers a different span.

This commentary’s view. The question is still debated, and this commentary leaves it open, as in the introduction to Exodus, since nothing in the message of either book hangs on it.

Uncertain wording. Several building terms in verses 4–6 are rare. The “windows with recessed frames” (v. 4) may be windows that narrow inwards, latticed openings, or windows with fixed frames that could not be opened; the Hebrew phrase is obscure. The general picture is clear even where the details of the architecture are not.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads 440 years here.
verseByVerse.note: The 480th year after the exodus: about 966 BC. The temple was about 90 feet long, 30 wide and 45 high (60 × 20 × 30 cubits).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Concerning This House That You Are Building
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the building work God speaks, and nothing he says is about the building. Concerning the house Solomon is building, the condition is that he walk in God’s statutes, obey his rules and keep his commandments (vv. 11–12). Then God will establish the word he spoke to David, the covenant promise of a lasting throne. And the promise is not a magnificent house but God himself: “I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel” (v. 13). The building is a sign; walking with the God who made the promise is the reality it points to.
verseByVerse.theology: The placement is the message. God interrupts a building account to say that the house secures nothing; the if is about walking in his statutes, not the quality of the stonework.
verseByVerse.examples: The promise at the end is what the whole building exists for: God will dwell among his people and not forsake them. The temple was always the sign of that and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon, "Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father. And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the building work God reminds Solomon that the house secures nothing: what matters is walking in God’s ways inside the promise he has already made, and the promise itself is that God will dwell among his people and never forsake them.

Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon. The writer is in the middle of a building specification, and he breaks off to record that God spoke. Nothing prepares for it, nothing in the building account follows from it, and the narrative goes straight back to cedar boards in verse 15. The three verses sit in the middle of the masonry like a hand laid on someone’s arm, and that placing is the message.

Concerning this house that you are building. God names the very thing Solomon is standing in the middle of, the project that has consumed a hundred and fifty thousand men, the finest timber in the world and the wealth of a kingdom, and then says something about it that has nothing to do with building. There are four clauses, walk, obey, keep, walk, and every one is about conduct; there is no ‘if you build it well’. The condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel’s history is entirely about whether the man building it keeps the commandments.

Then I will establish my word with you. What is promised is not a good building but the word “which I spoke to David your father”: the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, already given by grace, with its throne and its “house” that means a line of kings, not a temple. The commands are not the price of God’s favour; they are the way of life inside a promise God made first.

The temptation it guards against. A man watching a magnificent thing that God himself asked for rise out of the ground is in real danger of thinking that the building is the relationship, that a house this good must guarantee something. God says otherwise in the middle of the scaffolding, before the roof is on. Israel forgot it completely.
