Three centuries later Jeremiah had to stand in the gate of this very building and rebuke people chanting “The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” as though the words were a charm, and tell them to go and look at Shiloh, where God first made his name dwell, and see what he did to it (Jeremiah 7:4, 12).

And I will dwell among the children of Israel. The promise at the end is the sentence the whole building exists to serve: God will dwell, not in this house, but among the people. He has been saying so since Sinai: “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8). The tabernacle was never a residence; it was a sign that God had come to live in the middle of a camp, and the temple is the same sign in stone.

And will not forsake my people Israel. This is the promise that outlasts the building. The house Solomon is standing in will be looted by Shishak within a generation (14:25–26), stripped by later kings to pay tribute, defiled, and finally burned by Nebuchadnezzar’s men (2 Kings 25:9). And God does not forsake his people. He goes into exile with them: Ezekiel sees his glory by a canal in Babylon (Ezekiel 1), and hears him say of the scattered exiles, “yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone” (Ezekiel 11:16).

The temple of his body. Solomon did not keep these four clauses (11:4–6), and no son of David did until the one who could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). His obedience is counted to those who trust him, and his Spirit now writes these statutes on their hearts, as God promised: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). In him, too, the promise to dwell among his people is kept in person. Standing in the courts of the temple that later replaced this one, Jesus said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, and John adds, “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”, literally pitched his tent among us, “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). And the line runs out to the end of the Bible: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3). God dwelling with people is the reality; every building between is a sign, and the signs are destroyed while the reality is not.

Our own temples. The same reflex is still with us. A church building, a tradition, a baptism or a long record of service can quietly be treated as though it secured God’s favour, when what God asks is that we walk with him inside the promise he made first. These are good gifts and real signs; they were never meant to be charms.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–30 — The Inner Sanctuary He Overlaid with Pure Gold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heart of the house is a golden room made for God’s presence, and everything around it recalls Eden. The walls are lined with cedar and the floor with cypress, so that no stone is seen, and the carvings are gourds and open flowers (vv. 14–18). The rear twenty cubits form the inner sanctuary, a perfect cube overlaid with pure gold and prepared for the ark of the covenant, and gold covers the whole house and its altar (vv. 19–22). Two olivewood cherubim, ten cubits high and overlaid with gold, spread their wings from wall to wall over the ark’s place (vv. 23–28). Cherubim, palm trees and open flowers are carved on every wall, and gold covers the floor (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: The house is the tabernacle at double scale, built in stone and cedar and gold, and no longer moved from place to place; and its heart is the room for the ark.
verseByVerse.examples: The cherubim over the ark recall the guardians of Eden, and the carvings of palm trees and flowers on every wall make the whole house a remembered garden.

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon built the house and finished it. He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress. He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place. The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long. The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen. The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD. The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar. And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold. And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold. In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high. Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form. The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub. He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house. And he overlaid the cherubim with gold. Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms. The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of the temple is a golden room made for the ark, where God promised to meet his people, guarded by great cherubim and surrounded by carvings of a garden: Eden remembered in cedar and gold, and a room still closed to all but one man once a year.

All was cedar; no stone was seen. The whole interior is lined, so that not an inch of masonry shows, and every surface a person could look at is worked wood carved with gourds and open flowers, with cypress on the floor. The stonecutters in the hill country finished those stones so exactly that the building could go up without a hammer being heard, and then the stones were covered over and nobody ever saw them again. The care was not for an audience but for the God who would be in the room, and so is all faithfulness that no one else will ever see (Matthew 6:4).

As the Most Holy Place. The rear third of the building is partitioned off, and this is the room the whole structure exists for. Nothing about it is designed to be seen. It has no windows, and no one enters except the high priest, once a year on the Day of Atonement, with blood (Leviticus 16).

To set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD. Here is what all of it is for: a box. The gold and the cedar, the seven years and the hundred and fifty thousand men, are to make a room for the ark: the chest Moses made in the wilderness, with the tablets of the covenant inside and the mercy seat, its gold cover, on top, between the cherubim where God said, “There I will meet with you” (Exodus 25:22). It is the same chest the Philistines captured and sent home on a cart, that stood for years in a house at Kiriath-jearim, struck down Uzzah and came into Jerusalem with a king dancing before it. It has been in a tent since David pitched one for it. Now it gets a room.

Twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. A perfect cube, and it looks deliberate. The only other place where Scripture says that length, width and height are equal is at the far end of the Bible. When John is shown the holy city coming down out of heaven, the angel measures it: “The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width… Its length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16). The new Jerusalem is shaped like the Most Holy Place, and what John notices about it is what is missing: “And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The room where one man went once a year becomes the shape of a city where everybody lives.

And he overlaid the whole house with gold. The writer repeats the word until the reader can see nothing else: gold on the inner room, on the altar before it, on the chains across its front, on the whole house, on the cherubim and on the floor.

Two cherubim of olivewood. Each stands ten cubits, fifteen feet, high, with a wingspan to match, and their four wings span the whole room from wall to wall, meeting in the centre over the place where the ark will stand. We first met cherubim at the end of Genesis 3. A man and a woman are driven out of a garden, and “at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). Cherubim are what stand between people and the presence of God, to keep them out. Here are two of them, standing over the very place where God has promised to meet his people. The guards are still there. The sword is not mentioned.

Cherubim and palm trees and open flowers. The same three things are carved on every wall: guardians and growing things. Whoever designed this room wanted a person standing in it to be reminded of a garden with something watching over it. It is Eden, remembered in cedar and gold, in a building whose innermost room no one may enter.

The way opened. Hebrews reads this room as a copy of the true one. Christ “entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12; compare 9:24). Cherubim were also woven into the curtain that hung before it (2 Chronicles 3:14), and when Jesus died, the curtain of the temple of his day “was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38). Believers now enter the holy places “by the blood of Jesus… through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). The way to the tree of life that the cherubim guarded is opened by him.

Did the carved cherubim break the second commandment? No. God himself commanded them (Exodus 25:18); they represented the angels around his throne, not God, and they were never worshipped. The commandment forbids images of God and images made for worship, not all art.

Uncertain wording. Verses 20–21 are compressed in Hebrew. The “altar of cedar” overlaid with gold is probably the altar of incense that stood before the inner sanctuary (compare 7:48), and the “chains of gold” drawn across in front of the inner sanctuary may have barred its entrance or hung beside a curtain; exactly how they were arranged is not known.
verseByVerse.note: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), the length of a forearm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house is finished to God’s plan, in seven years. The doors of the inner sanctuary are olivewood, carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers and overlaid with gold (vv. 31–32), and the doors of the nave are folding doors of cypress, carved and gilded in the same way (vv. 33–35). The inner court is built of cut stone and cedar beams (v. 36). The foundation was laid in Ziv of the fourth year, and the house was finished in Bul of the eleventh, “in all its parts, and according to all its specifications” (vv. 37–38). Solomon built to a pattern God had given, and he took seven years over it.
verseByVerse.theology: The doors carry the same garden carvings as the walls, and the chapter closes with a date and a number worth remembering: seven years.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep the seven years in mind for one verse, because the next chapter opens with the time he spent on his own house.

verseByVerse.quote: For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided. He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees. So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square, and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding. On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work. He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams. In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv. And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house is finished to every detail of the plan God gave, after seven years, with the garden carvings carried onto its gilded doors.

Cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. The same three designs appear again, on the doors of the Most Holy Place and of the nave, overlaid with gold. Olivewood is used for the inner doors and the cherubim, cedar for the walls, cypress for the floor and the outer folding doors: all of it once living trees that grew and were cut down for this house.

According to all its specifications. Chronicles tells us where they came from. David gave Solomon the pattern for all of it, porch, houses, treasuries, courts and chambers, and said, “All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 28:11–19). That is what Moses was told about the tabernacle: “see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain” (Exodus 25:40). Solomon did not design this building; he built to a plan he was given, and God’s house is still built to a pattern its builders did not design.

He was seven years in building it. From Ziv of the fourth year to Bul of the eleventh is seven and a half years by our counting. Some see in the seven a hint of completeness; the writer does not say so, and the figure is simply the time it took. And the next sentence in the book is this: “Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house” (7:1). Seven years for the house of God, and thirteen for his own. The writer sets them in consecutive verses, does not remark on the difference, and goes straight on to describe the palace. That is not by itself a rebuke, for the palace was a complex of several buildings, and David had gathered much of the temple’s material in advance. But the reader is allowed to notice.

The true house. The tabernacle and the temple were built to a heavenly pattern and were copies of it (Hebrews 8:5). Christ “has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). Solomon’s house, finished in seven years, stood for less than four centuries; the house Christ is building, his people, he will present finished in every part, and it will never fall.

Uncertain wording. “Five-sided” (v. 31) and “in the form of a square” (v. 33) translate Hebrew expressions that mean literally “a fifth” and “a fourth”. They may describe the shape of the doorframes, a pointed or stepped frame for the inner doors and a square one for the outer, or their size in proportion to the wall; the exact sense is uncertain.
verseByVerse.note: Ziv (v. 1) falls around April and May; Bul (v. 38) around October and November.

6.theology:
Dated from the exodus (v. 1). The house is for the God who brought slaves out of Egypt, and the date says so before a single dimension is given. (What the 480 years means for the date of the exodus, about 1446 BC or about 1260 BC, is debated among faithful scholars; the commentary on verses 1–10 sets out both views.)

The tent made permanent (vv. 2-10). The tabernacle Israel carried through the wilderness is built again at double scale, not large by the standards of Thebes or Babylon, and never meant to hold a congregation: the building was the dwelling, and Israel worshipped in the courts. Even the side chambers are designed so that no beam is set into the wall of the house.

Silence on the mountain (v. 7). Iron is kept away from the place where God will be met, as the law kept it from altars. Peter takes the picture further than any reader of this chapter could have predicted: Christians are living stones being built into a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:4-5), shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the site already fitted for their place.

The house secures nothing (vv. 11-13). In the middle of the scaffolding God speaks, and no clause is about the building. What is promised is his word to David, already given by grace. The temptation guarded against never goes away: to mistake the thing we build for God for our standing with God. Solomon did not keep these clauses, and no son of David did until Christ, whose obedience is counted to those who trust him. Israel forgot the lesson, and Jeremiah stood in this gate rebuking those who chanted the temple of the LORD as a charm (Jer. 7:4).

Among, not in (v. 13). God promised to dwell among his people, not in a house, and that promise outlasts the building. This house is looted, stripped and finally burned, and God goes into exile with his people. The line runs out to John, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), to Jesus speaking of the temple of his body (John 2:21), to a church that is itself God’s temple by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16), and to the city where the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev. 21:3). Every building in between is a sign; the signs are destroyed, and the thing they signify is not.

The room for the ark (vv. 16-20). All the gold and cedar and labour is for a windowless cube that held the ark, where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22), and which one man entered once a year with blood. Its shape returns at the end of the Bible in a city with no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple (Rev. 21:22). The covered stones and hidden gold say that the care was not for an audience but for the God who would be in the room.

The guards are still there (vv. 23-29). Cherubim first appear guarding the way back to Eden with a sword (Gen. 3:24). Here they stand over the place where God meets his people, and the sword is not mentioned; and the walls all round are carved with palm trees and open flowers. Eden is remembered in cedar and gold, but the innermost room is still closed. When Jesus died, the curtain before it was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the way in is now through him (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Built to God's pattern, in seven years (vv. 37-38). Solomon did not design this house; he built to the drawing God gave David (1 Chron. 28:11-19), as Moses built the tabernacle to the pattern shown on the mountain (Ex. 25:40). The next verse gives thirteen years for his own house. As the note on verses 31-38 says, that is not by itself a rebuke, since the palace was several buildings and the temple's materials were gathered in advance, but the writer lets the reader notice.
6.examples:
Then: A building the size of a large barn went up on a hilltop over seven years without one blow of an iron tool being heard on the site: every stone measured, cut and finished miles away in the hill country and carried up already fitted, and when it was done, every one of those stones was panelled over in cedar so that nobody ever saw them again.

Now: three things. God's interruption in verses 11-13 is the one to remember, because the confusion it guards against never goes away: the condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel's history had nothing whatever to do with the building. It is very easy to mistake the thing you are doing for God for your standing with God, and the more magnificent the thing, the easier it gets. Our standing rests on the obedience of Christ, and what God asks of us is a walk with him that his Spirit makes possible. Second, the covered stones. Work done to a standard nobody will ever inspect, for an audience of one, is not wasted: it is most of what the Christian life actually consists of. And third, Peter's use of the quarry: the shaping happens off-site, out of sight, before the stone is set in place. If your life feels like being worked on in a noisy place a long way from anything that looks finished, that is where the cutting is supposed to happen, and the one doing it knows the place he is fitting you for.

keyVerse.quote: And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of the building, God names what the house was for: not a residence for God, but a sign that he lives among his people. The temple fell; this promise did not. It is kept in Christ, the Word who “dwelt among us”, and completed when “the dwelling place of God is with man” for ever (Revelation 21:3).

6.reflection:
God interrupted the building work to say that obedience mattered more than the house (vv. 11–13). What good things, a church building, a tradition, a record of service, are we tempted to treat as though they secured God’s favour?

Every stone was shaped at the quarry, away from the site (v. 7), and Peter calls believers “living stones” (1 Peter 2:5). How does it help to see God’s hard shaping of your life now as preparation for a place already prepared?

The cherubim that once guarded the way to the tree of life stand over the place where God meets his people, and at Jesus’ death the curtain was torn (vv. 23–29; Mark 15:38). What does it mean for your prayer and worship that the way into God’s presence is now open?

The finest stonework was covered with cedar and gold and never seen again (v. 18). Where is God calling you to faithful work that no one else may ever notice, and why does it matter to him?

7.title: The Palace and the Temple Furnishings
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house.<sup>2</sup>He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.<sup>3</sup>And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row.<sup>4</sup>There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers.<sup>5</sup>All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers.<sup>6</sup>And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them.<sup>7</sup>And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters.<sup>8</sup>His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage.<sup>9</sup>All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court.<sup>10</sup>The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits.<sup>11</sup>And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar.<sup>12</sup>The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.<sup>13</sup>And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.<sup>14</sup>He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.<sup>15</sup>He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same.<sup>16</sup>He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.<sup>17</sup>There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital.<sup>18</sup>Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital.<sup>19</sup>Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits.<sup>20</sup>The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital.<sup>21</sup>He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz.<sup>22</sup>And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.<sup>23</sup>Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.<sup>24</sup>Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.<sup>25</sup>It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.<sup>26</sup>Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.<sup>27</sup>He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.<sup>28</sup>This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames,<sup>29</sup>and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work.<sup>30</sup>Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each.<sup>31</sup>Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round.<sup>32</sup>And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half.<sup>33</sup>The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast.<sup>34</sup>There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands.<sup>35</sup>And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it.<sup>36</sup>And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around.<sup>37</sup>After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form.<sup>38</sup>And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands.<sup>39</sup>And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.<sup>40</sup>Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD:<sup>41</sup>the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;<sup>42</sup>and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;<sup>43</sup>the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands;<sup>44</sup>and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea.<sup>45</sup>Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze.<sup>46</sup>In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.<sup>47</sup>And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained.<sup>48</sup>So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence,<sup>49</sup>the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;<sup>50</sup>the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple.<sup>51</sup>Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 raised the temple in seven years, with God’s reminder that what mattered was not the house but Solomon’s obedience (6:11–13). Chapter 7 turns to the king’s own buildings, then back to the temple’s bronze and gold furnishings, so that all is ready for the ark (chapter 8).

The message. The chapter sets two houses side by side, the king’s and God’s, and quietly asks which will come first. Solomon spends thirteen years on his own, larger house. Yet God’s house is furnished with things that preach: a pillar at the door named “he will establish”, because the throne rests on God’s promise to David, not on Solomon’s splendour; and a sea and ten basins for washing, because sinners may come near a holy God only when they are cleansed.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen these pillars, stands and sea broken up and carried to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). They needed to see how the fall began, with a king’s heart slowly divided, and that the promise the pillars announced had not gone to Babylon with the bronze (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Thirteen years for the palace, with its great halls and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter, are set beside the seven years of 6:38 without comment (vv. 1–12). Then Hiram, a widow’s son gifted like Bezalel, casts the pillars Jachin and Boaz (vv. 13–22), the great sea on twelve oxen and ten wheeled stands with their basins (vv. 23–39), and the smaller bronze, too much to weigh (vv. 40–47). Solomon makes the gold furnishings of the holy place (vv. 48–50), and the chapter ends by carrying in the gifts of David, who was not allowed to build (v. 51).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The pillar named “he will establish” points to the throne God gives Mary’s son, whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32–33), and Christ promises to make everyone who conquers “a pillar in the temple of my God” (Revelation 3:12). The washing pictures the cleansing his blood gives, so that we draw near with “our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). And a king who built more for himself than for God shows our need of the Son of David who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Set your own seven and thirteen side by side honestly, knowing that the God who sees misplaced loves also forgives and reorders them. Use every skill he gives in his service. And come to God washed, not by anything you bring but by Christ, whose promise stands when everything else is carried away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon builds his own house for thirteen years, and the writer sets it beside the seven spent on God’s house without a word of comment. The palace complex is described at length and with admiration: the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a hall four times the temple’s floor area, standing on rows of cedar pillars (vv. 2–5); the Hall of Pillars and the cedar-panelled Hall of Judgment, where the king who asked for wisdom would hear cases (vv. 6–7); his own house, and one for Pharaoh’s daughter (v. 8); all of huge, costly, sawn stone (vv. 9–11). The great court matches the temple’s inner court (v. 12): the king’s house and God’s house rise together, and the reader is left to weigh which comes first.
verseByVerse.theology: Seven years for the house of the LORD; thirteen for his own. The writer puts the two figures in consecutive sentences, describes the palace at greater length than the temple, and lets the reader weigh it.
verseByVerse.examples: The daughter of Pharaoh gets a house of her own, named as such. She entered the story in 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple, and she is named first among the women who turn his heart in 11:1. The writer keeps mentioning her and never comments.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house. He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars. And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row. There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers. All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers. And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them. And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters. His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage. All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court. The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits. And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar. The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon spends thirteen years on his own house after seven on God’s, and builds it larger; the writer accuses no one, but sets the figures side by side and lets the reader weigh where a king’s heart is going.

Solomon was building his own house thirteen years. The sentence before this gave seven years for the house of the LORD (6:38). The writer sets the two figures in consecutive verses without comment, then describes the palace at greater length and in more admiring detail than the temple. In fairness, the palace was several buildings (an armoury, a colonnade, a courtroom and two residences) where the temple was one modest structure; the projects overlapped, the twenty years of 9:10 covering both; and probably nobody in Israel thought thirteen years unreasonable for a royal quarter. But the figures are still seven and thirteen, and the writer still put them side by side.

The House of the Forest of Lebanon. A hundred cubits by fifty by thirty, about a hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five by forty-five, more than four times the floor area of the temple. It is named for the forty-five cedar pillars standing in rows inside it: to walk through it was to walk through trees. Chapter 10 tells us its use: three hundred shields of beaten gold were kept there (10:17), and Isaiah later rebukes Judah because “you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest” (Isaiah 22:8). It is an armoury, a treasury and a statement.

The Hall of Judgment. One room deserves a moment: a purpose-built courtroom, “finished with cedar from floor to rafters”. The man who asked at Gibeon for “an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (3:9) has built a room to do it in, and rightly: David “administered justice and equity to all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15), and now that work has a building. But a hall is not a hearing. Two prostitutes with no standing got a verdict from this king in chapter 3 without any cedar panelling, and what Absalom exploited at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of rooms but that “there is no man designated by the king to hear you” (2 Samuel 15:3). God had made the same point one chapter ago, while the temple was going up: what mattered was not the building but whether Solomon obeyed him (6:11–13).

A house like this hall for Pharaoh’s daughter. She arrived in 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple; now she has a house built to the standard of the Hall of Judgment. She moved into it from the city of David (9:24), and Chronicles gives Solomon’s reason: “for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy” (2 Chronicles 8:11). She is mentioned five times in nine chapters (3:1; 7:8; 9:16, 24; 11:1), each time flatly, with no comment, until chapter 11 opens: “Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh” (11:1). The writer puts things down in order and trusts the reader to remember them when the reckoning comes.

The great court. The last verse quietly joins the two projects. The palace court is built to the same specification as the temple’s inner court, three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams (compare 6:36). The house of God and the house of the king go up on the same hill, from the same quarry, to the same standard: the king was to reign under God, beside his house. Whether the two stay in that order is the question the rest of the book answers.

A different King. Solomon built himself a palace greater than God’s house. The greater Son of David came the other way. He was laid where there was no room, said “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He did not build himself a house first; he spent himself to build God’s house out of people.

Seven and thirteen in our own lives. We can set the same two figures side by side: how much of our time and money goes to God, and how much to ourselves. It is safe to look, before a God who forgives misplaced loves and reorders them. This does not make good homes or fine buildings wrong; the Hall of Judgment was a right thing to build. The question is which house comes first in the heart (Matthew 6:33).

Uncertain wording. The layout of the palace buildings cannot be reconstructed with confidence. Several building terms are rare, such as the “window frames” of v. 4 and the “canopy” of v. 6, and the pillar numbers of vv. 2–3 are hard to fit together: four rows of cedar pillars, yet forty-five pillars “fifteen in each row”, which suggests three. It is also unclear how Solomon’s own house and the house for Pharaoh’s daughter (v. 8) stood in relation to the halls. The overall picture is clear: a group of great cedar-and-stone halls for the king, beside the house of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is furnished through a gift God gives, and its door is flanked by a promise. Solomon brings Hiram from Tyre, a widow’s son of Naphtali with a Tyrian father, described in the words once used of Bezalel, the Spirit-filled maker of the tabernacle (vv. 13–14). He casts two hollow bronze pillars twenty-seven feet high, with capitals of lattice, lily-work and pomegranates (vv. 15–20), and sets them free-standing at the vestibule, holding up nothing. Their names say why they are there: Jachin, “he will establish”, and Boaz (vv. 21–22). Every worshipper entered between them, past God’s promise to establish David’s throne.
verseByVerse.theology: The craftsman is half-Israelite, a widow's son from Naphtali by a Tyrian father, and he is described in the words used of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit to build the tabernacle (Ex. 31:1-5).
verseByVerse.examples: The two pillars stand at the door, twenty-seven feet high, free of the building. They hold nothing up; their whole function is to say something as a person walks in.

verseByVerse.quote: And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre. He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work. He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same. He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits. There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital. Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital. Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits. The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital. He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz. And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A half-Israelite craftsman, gifted like Bezalel who made the tabernacle, casts two great bronze pillars that hold nothing up and names one of them for what God had promised: “he will establish”.

Hiram from Tyre. This is a different man from the king of 5:1. He is “the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali”, and his father was a Tyrian bronze-worker. Chronicles calls his mother “a woman of the daughters of Dan” (2 Chronicles 2:14); probably she was a Danite by birth who lived in, or married into, Naphtali, so the two notes need not conflict. So the man who casts every piece of bronze in the house of the LORD is half a foreigner from a Phoenician port, the son of a woman with no husband. The timber was foreign, the stonemasons of Gebal were foreign (5:18), and now the metalwork: the nations are already serving the house of Israel’s God.

Full of wisdom, understanding, and skill. A reader of the Pentateuch hears the words God used of the tabernacle’s maker: “I have called by name Bezalel… and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze” (Exodus 31:2–4). The echo is deliberate: skill in a craft is a gift of God, not a natural talent he tolerates, nor a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying. So a believer who builds, repairs, cooks, nurses, designs or makes things can do it as service to God, ask him for skill and thank him for it, without thinking it second-rate (Colossians 3:23).

He cast two pillars of bronze. Each was eighteen cubits high and twelve round, about twenty-seven feet tall and six across, hollow, with walls four fingers (about three inches) thick, under capitals another five cubits high. Casting objects that size in the tenth century before Christ was a serious achievement. The capitals carried lattices, chains, lily-work and two hundred pomegranates each. The temple walls were carved with palm trees and open flowers (6:29), the sea has a brim like a lily (v. 26), and here are lilies and pomegranates in cast metal: everything decorative in this house is a growing thing, and many see in it a memory of Eden, the first garden where God walked with man.

Jachin and Boaz. The pillars stand free in front of the vestibule, one each side of the door, holding up no roof and carrying no beam. Columns that carry nothing are there to say something. Jachin means “he will establish”, from the verb God used to David: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). Every priest going in to serve, and every Israelite coming up to the courts, walked between them, past a promise cast in bronze.

Stripped and broken. About two and a half centuries later Hezekiah stripped the gold from the temple doors to pay the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:16), and about a century after that the Babylonians came: “the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD… the Chaldeans broke in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon” (2 Kings 25:13). The first readers knew where the pillars had gone.

The promise outlived the bronze. What they stood for was still true. An angel said of Mary’s son, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). The bronze went to Babylon; the throne the pillars spoke of went to Christ. And he makes the picture personal: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it” (Revelation 3:12). Solomon’s pillars were broken up and carried off; the pillars of Christ’s temple are his people, established by him, and they are never removed.

Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar. Chronicles gives thirty-five cubits (2 Chronicles 3:15), most likely the two pillars’ combined length, or a copying difference in a numeral; Jeremiah 52:21 agrees with Kings.

Uncertain wording. Jachin almost certainly means “he will establish”. Boaz is less clear. It is the name of David’s ancestor (Ruth 4:21), and many take it to mean “in him is strength”, but that is a guess, and it is wiser not to build on it; some suggest the two names were the opening words of inscriptions or prayers, and no one knows. The capitals are also hard to picture: “the rounded projection” (v. 20) translates a word meaning “belly”, and exactly how the bowls, lattices, chains and lily-work fitted together (vv. 16–22) is uncertain, as differing reconstructions show. The overall picture is plain: two great decorated columns at the door of God’s house, one of them named for his promise.
verseByVerse.note: Jachin probably means “he will establish”; the meaning of Boaz is uncertain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — The Sea of Cast Metal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Water stands all around the altar, because no one may come near a holy God unwashed. Hiram casts “the sea”, a bronze basin fifteen feet across with a brim like a lily, holding two thousand baths and set on twelve oxen facing the four directions (vv. 23–26); Chronicles explains that it was for the priests to wash in. Then come ten bronze stands on chariot-style wheels, panelled with lions, oxen, cherubim and palm trees and described in loving engineering detail (vv. 27–37), each carrying a basin of forty baths for rinsing the offerings (vv. 38–39). Five stands go on each side of the house and the sea at the south-east corner. The tabernacle’s little laver has become a sea.
verseByVerse.theology: The sea is the tabernacle’s laver, its washing basin, at enormous scale, and Chronicles says plainly what it was for: the sea was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6).
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve oxen carry it, three to each point of the compass: probably the tribes, facing the whole earth, holding up water for washing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast. It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths. He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high. This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames, and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work. Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each. Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round. And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half. The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast. There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands. And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it. And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around. After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form. And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands. And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vast bronze basin and ten wheeled stands supply water for washing, because no one, neither priest nor offering, may come near the holy God as they are.

The sea of cast metal. A bronze basin ten cubits across and five deep, about fifteen feet by seven and a half, cast in one piece. “The sea” describes the impression it made: nobody had seen so much standing water in a vessel. It held two thousand baths, something like forty thousand litres (see bath and hin), and stood on twelve bronze oxen facing outward, three to each point of the compass. The twelve probably recall the tribes, and the four directions the whole earth.

A line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Thirty round for ten across has prompted much needless argument. The figures are round numbers describing a physical object; the brim flared “like the flower of a lily”, and the walls were a handbreadth thick, so a diameter across the outer brim and a circumference measured below it or inside would not give the ratio of a perfect circle. There is no error here to explain away.

For the priests to wash in. So Chronicles says (2 Chronicles 4:6), which sends the reader back to a small basin and a hard sentence. God told Moses to set a bronze laver between the tent of meeting and the altar, and Aaron and his sons were to wash their hands and feet before they ministered, “so that they may not die” (Exodus 30:17–21). A man who is going to handle holy things does not simply walk up; he washes first. In the permanent house the little laver has become a sea standing on twelve oxen.

The ten stands. These are wheeled bronze carts about six feet square, their panels showing lions, oxen and cherubim, each carrying a basin of forty baths, so that water could be moved about the court. The writer gives them more mechanical detail than anything in the temple itself. Chronicles supplies their use: “in these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in” (2 Chronicles 4:6). The sea is for the men; the ten basins are for what is offered. With five stands on each side and the sea at the south-east corner, there was water all around the altar.

Blood and water. There is a great deal of blood in this building and a great deal of water, and both are there because people cannot come near God as they are. The New Testament takes up both. Because Jesus has opened the way through his own blood, believers may “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). What a sea of water could only picture, he does: he makes unclean people fit to come in, and keeps them clean, as he showed when he washed his disciples’ feet and said, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me” (John 13:8).

Come and be washed. No priest walked up to the altar unwashed, and no one need come to God unwashed now. The washing is not something we bring but something he gives, so however soiled the week has left you, come, and come through him.

It held two thousand baths. Chronicles says three thousand (2 Chronicles 4:5): either Chronicles gives the full capacity and Kings the usual filling, or a numeral was miscopied.

Uncertain wording. The description of the stands (vv. 27–37) uses several technical words found almost nowhere else, translated here as “panels”, “frames”, “stays” and “wreaths of beveled work”, and the account of the round opening within its “crown” (v. 31) is very hard to picture; translations and drawings differ. The “gourds” under the brim of the sea (v. 24) were probably gourd-shaped ornaments. The general picture is clear: ten decorated bronze carts on chariot-style wheels, each holding a basin.
verseByVerse.note: A bath was a liquid measure of roughly 22 litres (about 5 gallons), though estimates vary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–51 — The Weight of the Bronze Was Not Ascertained
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house is finished, in bronze too heavy to weigh and gold down to the door sockets, and the last gift brought in is David’s. Hiram completes the smaller bronze, the pots, shovels and basins, and the writer lists them alongside the pillars and the sea (vv. 40–45). All of it was cast in the clay of the Jordan valley, and there was so much that no one weighed it (vv. 46–47), the first thing in Solomon’s reign too great to count. Solomon makes the golden altar, the table and ten lampstands with their utensils (vv. 48–50). Finally he brings in the silver, gold and vessels his father had dedicated (v. 51), the treasure of a king who was not allowed to build.
verseByVerse.theology: One measurement was never taken: the bronze was simply too much to weigh.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by bringing in what David dedicated: the tribute of Edom and Moab and Ammon and Amalek and Hadadezer, set apart for the LORD by a man who was told he could not build (2 Sam. 8:11-12). He funded it for years and never saw a stone laid.

verseByVerse.quote: Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD: the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars; and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars; the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands; and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea. Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained. So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold; the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple. Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bronze and gold furnishings are finished, with more bronze than anyone could weigh, and the last thing carried into the completed house is what David, who was forbidden to build it, had given.

Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. The craftsman who cast the pillars and the sea also made pots for carrying ash and shovels for clearing the altar, and the writer lists them in the same sentence as the pillars. Somebody had to shovel out a fire that was never allowed to go out (Leviticus 6:13). Ordinary service in God’s house is counted with the grand.

In the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. The casting was done some forty miles away in the Jordan valley, where the clay was right for the moulds. Everything in these chapters was made somewhere else and brought: the stone dressed at the quarry (6:7), the cedar rafted down the coast from Lebanon, the bronze cast in the mud of the Jordan plain.

Solomon left all the vessels unweighed. Everything else in these chapters has been measured, down to four hundred pomegranates counted; the bronze alone was not weighed, because there was too much of it. Read plainly, it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends; but it is also the first thing in this reign too big to count, and not the last. Within four chapters the gold coming in yearly is six hundred and sixty-six talents (10:14), silver is “as common in Jerusalem as stone” (10:27), and there are seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (11:3). A reign that began by measuring everything to the cubit ends with quantities nobody bothers to total.

All the vessels that were in the house of the LORD. The golden altar of incense, the table for the bread of the Presence and ten lampstands of pure gold are the tabernacle’s furniture at scale: Moses had one lampstand, Solomon has ten. Even the door sockets, the hinge-pivots in the floor that no one would ever see, are gold. Nothing in the house of the King is common.

The things that David his father had dedicated. The dedicated things are listed in 2 Samuel 8: the tribute of Toi of Hamath, and the spoil of Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek and Hadadezer of Zobah: “These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued” (2 Samuel 8:11). David could not build, and was told plainly why: “You have shed much blood and have waged great wars” (1 Chronicles 22:8). So he handed the spoils of his wars to a project he was forbidden to work on, laid up gold, silver, bronze and iron beyond weighing, gave his own fortune to it at the end, and died before the foundations went in (1 Chronicles 22:14; 29:2–5). The house is finished, and the last thing carried into it is his, a man dead for more than a decade.

Builders who never see the building. Some of the best work God gives his people is finished by someone else: “One sows and another reaps” (John 4:37). David gave towards a house he never saw, and the house he truly longed for was not finished by Solomon either. Its builder is David’s greater Son, who said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), and in his hands nothing given in faith is lost.

7.theology:
Seven and thirteen (vv. 1-12). The writer accuses no one. He sets the two figures side by side, gives the palace a longer and warmer description than the temple, and lets the reader weigh it, along with what can fairly be said in Solomon’s defence. The great court of the palace is even built to the pattern of the temple's inner court: the house of God and the house of the king go up on the same hill, from the same quarry, to the same standard.

A hall is not a hearing (v. 7). The man who asked at Gibeon for an understanding mind builds a courtroom, cedar from floor to rafters. It is right that justice should have a proper place, and David before him had administered justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15). But what makes justice is a king who listens, as Solomon did to two prostitutes in chapter 3; what Absalom exploited at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of rooms but the lack of anyone to hear. A fine room does not make justice, just as God said one chapter ago, while the temple was going up, that what mattered was whether Solomon obeyed him (6:11-13).

Pharaoh's daughter (v. 8). Five flat, factual mentions in nine chapters (3:1; 7:8; 9:16, 24; 11:1), with no comment attached to any of them, until 11:1 names her among the women who turned his heart. The writer puts things down in order and trusts the reader to remember them when the reckoning comes.

Skill as a gift of the Spirit (vv. 13-14). Hiram is described as Bezalel was, the man God filled with his Spirit to work in gold, silver and bronze for the tabernacle (Ex. 31:2-4). Scripture says this in very few places and means it every time: skill in a craft is a gift of God, not a natural talent he tolerates and not a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying. And the man who had it most here was half a foreigner and a widow's son.

Pillars that hold nothing up (vv. 15-22). Their whole function is to stand at the door of the house of the God who had promised to establish David's throne forever (2 Sam. 7:13). Nearly four centuries later the Chaldeans broke them in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). The promise was still true: it is kept in Mary’s son, to whom God gives the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32).

So that they may not die (vv. 23-39). The law told the priests to wash before they came near the altar, and said plainly that the penalty for not washing was death (Ex. 30:18-21); here the little laver, the washing basin of the wilderness, becomes a sea. There is a great deal of blood in this building and a great deal of water, and both are there because people cannot come near God as they are. The washing the sea pictured is given in Christ: through his blood we draw near with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22).

Too much to count (vv. 40-50). Everything is measured to the cubit except the bronze. Read plainly it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends; but it is the first thing in this reign too big to count, and by chapter 11 the gold, the silver and the wives are past counting too. Alongside the splendour stand the pots and shovels: somebody had to shovel out a fire that never went out.

The last thing carried in (v. 51). David could not build, because he had shed much blood (1 Chron. 22:8). He spent the rest of his life handing the spoils of his wars to a project he was forbidden to work on, and died before the foundations went in (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5). Some of the best work God gives his people is finished by someone else. The house is complete, and the last thing carried into it is his.
7.examples:
Then: Two hollow bronze columns twenty-seven feet high were cast in the mud of the Jordan valley, hauled forty miles up to Jerusalem, and stood one on either side of the temple door holding up absolutely nothing, because their entire purpose was to stand at the door of the house of the God who had promised to establish David's throne forever.

Now: three things. Verse 1 is the writer's method at its purest: he does not accuse Solomon of anything, he puts a seven and a thirteen in consecutive sentences, and anybody honest can set the same two figures side by side for their own life: how much goes to God, and how much to ourselves. It is safe to do, before a God who forgives misplaced loves and whose Spirit reorders them. Second, Hiram the craftsman, because the skill to make something beautiful out of metal is described here in the words used of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit for the work of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3). Skill in a trade is a gift, and the man who had it most was half a foreigner and a widow's son. And third, the pillars. They carried no weight and were broken up and carted to Babylon in the end, and the promise they stood beside was true the whole time and stayed true after they were gone.

keyVerse.quote: He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz.
keyVerse.note: The two great pillars hold nothing up; they stand at the door to say something. Jachin means “he will establish”, the word God used when he promised to establish David’s throne forever (2 Samuel 7:13). The bronze was later broken up and carried to Babylon, but the promise it announced stood, and it is kept in Christ, whose kingdom will have no end.

7.reflection:
The writer sets Solomon’s seven years on God’s house beside thirteen on his own, without comment (6:38; 7:1). Why do you think he lets the facts speak rather than condemning? If you set side by side what goes to God and what goes to yourself, what would you see, and why is it safe to look honestly?

Hiram’s skill is described in the words used of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit (vv. 13–14; Exodus 31:2–5). How does this change the way you think about practical and creative work, your own and other people’s?

The pillar Jachin, “he will establish”, was broken up and carried to Babylon, but the promise it announced came true in Christ (Luke 1:32–33; Revelation 3:12). What do you lean on that could be carried away, and what does it mean to rest on what God has promised instead?

The sea and the basins were for washing, “so that they may not die” (Exodus 30:21). How does Hebrews 10:19–22 show what Christ has done about our uncleanness, and how should that shape the way we come to God in prayer and worship?

8.title: The Glory Fills the House: Solomon's Prayer
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.<sup>2</sup>And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month.<sup>3</sup>And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark.<sup>4</sup>And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.<sup>5</sup>And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.<sup>6</sup>Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim.<sup>7</sup>For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.<sup>8</sup>And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.<sup>9</sup>There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD,<sup>11</sup>so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.<sup>13</sup>I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."<sup>14</sup>Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying,<sup>16</sup>'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.'<sup>17</sup>Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>18</sup>But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.'<sup>20</sup>Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>21</sup>And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt."<sup>22</sup>Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven,<sup>23</sup>and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart;<sup>24</sup>you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.'<sup>26</sup>Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father.<sup>27</sup>"But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!<sup>28</sup>Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day,<sup>29</sup>that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place.<sup>30</sup>And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.<sup>31</sup>"If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house,<sup>32</sup>then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.<sup>33</sup>"When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house,<sup>34</sup>then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers.<sup>35</sup>"When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them,<sup>36</sup>then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an Israel with a loud voice, saying,<sup>56</sup>"Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant.<sup>57</sup>The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us,<sup>58</sup>that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers.<sup>59</sup>Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires,<sup>60</sup>that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other.<sup>61</sup>Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day."<sup>62</sup>Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD.<sup>63</sup>Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD.<sup>64</sup>The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings.<sup>65</sup>So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days.<sup>66</sup>On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
8.overview:
Where we are. The temple and its furnishings are finished (chapters 6–7), and at the feast of Booths the house is dedicated. This is the high point of Solomon’s reign and of the whole book, before the decline that begins in chapter 11.

The message. God comes to dwell among his people, and he is far greater than the house that receives him: his glory fills the temple, yet its builder confesses, “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (v. 27). The temple is not a box for God but the place where he has put his name, so that sinners, foreigners and exiles know where to turn, and its dedication prayer asks again and again, “hear in heaven… and forgive”, and rests everything on a God who keeps his promises: “Not one word has failed” (v. 56).

Why it was said. The first readers had watched this house burn and were praying in Babylon (see the introduction). Here they found that Solomon had already prayed for them: sinners carried captive who would turn back to God in the land of their enemies (vv. 46–50). The way back depended not on the building but on the God who hears.

How the chapter makes its case. The ark, holding only the tablets of the covenant, is set beneath the cherubim, and the cloud of glory fills the house (vv. 1–13). Solomon praises God for keeping his word to David (vv. 14–21), prays the promise back to him, and asks whether God will indeed dwell on the earth (vv. 22–30). Seven petitions follow, for justice, defeat, drought, plague and the troubled heart, the foreigner, war and exile, most of them asking God to forgive (vv. 31–53). Rising from his knees, Solomon blesses God that not one word has failed, prays that God will incline their hearts and calls them to be wholly true (vv. 54–61), and a great feast sends the people home glad (vv. 62–66).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, by promise and by the need the chapter exposes. The answer to the question of verse 27 is yes: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), and Jesus called his body the temple (John 2:21). Prayer is now made through him, not towards a building. The forgiveness this prayer keeps asking for, because “there is no one who does not sin” (v. 46), was won by his sacrifice; the foreigner is welcomed in him; the new heart Solomon prayed for is given by his Spirit; and where Solomon’s heart was not wholly true, his was.

For us. Come to God through Christ, the true temple, with any trouble and any sin, from near or far: he hears and forgives. Begin your prayers with a God who keeps his word, and ask him for the heart he commands, wholly true to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Glory of the LORD Filled the House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself comes to the house built for his name. Solomon gathers all Israel at the feast of Booths in the seventh month, and the priests carry the ark, with the old tent of meeting and its vessels, up from the city of David amid sacrifices beyond counting (vv. 1–5). The ark is set beneath the cherubim in the Most Holy Place, its carrying poles left in (vv. 6–8), and it holds nothing but the two stone tablets of the covenant made at Horeb (v. 9). Then the cloud fills the house, as it once filled the tabernacle, and the priests cannot stand to minister because of the glory of the LORD (vv. 10–11).
