Solomon speaks of the God who dwells in thick darkness, and of the house he has built for him (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The cloud fills the house as it filled the tabernacle when Moses finished it (Ex. 40:35). The priests have to walk out of the building because God has come into it.
verseByVerse.examples: Inside the ark are two stone tablets and nothing else: a copy of the covenant God made with slaves he had brought out of Egypt. That is what the whole house was built to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month. And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark. And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up. And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered. Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles. And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day. There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt. And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD. Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark, holding only the tablets of the covenant, is carried into the inner room at the feast of Booths, and God himself fills the house with the cloud of his glory, as he once filled the tabernacle.

To bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD. Everything in the last three chapters has been building towards moving one object about half a mile uphill, from the tent David pitched for it (2 Samuel 6) to the temple. David’s first attempt to bring it to Jerusalem, on a cart, ended when Uzzah took hold of it and God struck him down; the second time it was carried properly, on poles on the Levites’ shoulders.

At the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month. The seventh month was later called Tishri, and the feast is Booths, the week when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember that their fathers had no houses at all and God travelled with them. That is the week Solomon chooses to give the ark a permanent house.

The tent of meeting. This is the end of something. The tabernacle that Moses made at Sinai to the pattern God showed him, carried through forty years of wilderness, set up at Shiloh and standing at Gibeon in Solomon’s own day, is brought up and stored. Nearly five centuries of portable worship end in this verse.

Underneath the wings of the cherubim. The two great olivewood cherubim of chapter 6, their wings meeting in the middle of the room, now stand over the ark. So the room holds two sets: Solomon’s, and the small gold ones on the mercy seat that Moses made, where God had said, “There I will meet with you” (Exodus 25:22).

The poles were so long. The carrying poles stay in, as the law required: “The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it” (Exodus 25:15), so that the ark could always be lifted and never handled. That was the law broken when the ark was put on a cart, and Uzzah died at a threshing floor because of it. Now the ark has reached the place where it will stay for nearly four centuries, and still the poles stay in, their ends visible from the Holy Place. A priest in the outer room could see them: God was settling into a stone house, but he was not tied to it.

Nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone. Here is what all of it was for. Seven years of building, a hundred and fifty thousand labourers, cedar rafted down a coast, gold over every surface, bronze pillars and a sea on twelve oxen: all to make a room, for a box, containing two pieces of stone. And the writer says what they are: the tablets Moses put there at Horeb, from the covenant made as Israel came out of Egypt. At the centre of the most expensive building in Israel’s history lies a copy of the terms on which God bound himself to a company of runaway slaves.

A cloud filled the house of the LORD. And God comes. The priests come out, and the building fills with cloud. Nearly five centuries earlier, when Moses finished the tabernacle, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting” (Exodus 40:34–35). The same thing happens, in the same words, at the completion of the same design at twice the scale. And the professionals cannot work. They have spent their lives learning a liturgy, and the moment the glory arrives the liturgy stops and trained men walk out into the courtyard. Nobody plans a dedication like that.

The glory of the LORD. We use “glory” of a fine sunset or a cup final. In the Old Testament the glory of the LORD is God himself, present and showing himself, so weighty (the Hebrew kabod carries that sense) that trained priests cannot stand in it. Moses once asked, “Please show me your glory,” and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:18, 20). The God we most need is the God sinners cannot come near.

The glory in a face. The New Testament answers with a face: God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The glory that drove priests out of this room came near in a man who ate with sinners, and by his cross it draws them in. So when you long to see God’s glory, do not wait for a cloud or a feeling: open a Gospel and look at Jesus. See also Glory in the Theological Dictionary.

The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. The room has no windows, the cloud is in it, and the king says the darkness is the point. God said at Sinai, “I am coming to you in a thick cloud” (Exodus 19:9), and Moses “drew near to the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). The dark is not the absence of God in that room; it is where he is. That is worth remembering in our own dark places: God’s hiddenness is not his absence.

I have indeed built you an exalted house. Solomon’s first sentence about his own work is a proud one: “a place for you to dwell in forever.” He will correct it himself fourteen verses later (v. 27).

And they are there to this day. A reader may ask how the poles can be there “to this day” when the temple was burned before the book was finished. The phrase most likely comes from the earlier record the writer used, written while the temple stood, and he kept its wording.

What else was in the ark? Hebrews describes the ark as holding “a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant” (Hebrews 9:4). Exodus and Numbers record the jar and the staff being placed “before the testimony” (Exodus 16:34; Numbers 17:10), which may mean in front of the ark rather than inside it, and in any case this verse describes the situation four centuries later. What is certain is what Kings says: by Solomon’s day there were two stone tablets in the ark and nothing else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–27 — Will God Indeed Dwell on the Earth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything Solomon has done rests on what God promised and has now kept. Turning to the assembly, he blesses the LORD, who has fulfilled with his hand what he spoke with his mouth: he chose David, honoured David’s wish to build, and gave the work to his son (vv. 14–21). Then, standing before the altar with his hands spread towards heaven, he praises the God who has no equal because he keeps covenant and steadfast love (vv. 22–24), and asks him to keep the rest of his word to David (vv. 25–26). And the builder asks the question at the heart of the book: will God indeed dwell on the earth, when heaven itself cannot contain him (v. 27)?
verseByVerse.theology: He has just spent seven years and the wealth of a kingdom on this building, and on the day he dedicates it he says out loud that it cannot possibly do what it was built for. Nobody made him say that.
verseByVerse.examples: He prays before the altar in the courtyard with his hands open toward heaven, and verse 54 reveals that he had been kneeling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood. And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying, 'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon turns to bless the people, and begins by blessing God, who has done with his hand what he promised with his mouth, and who chose first not a city but a man, David.

The king turned around and blessed all the assembly. Solomon has been facing the house, where the cloud has just filled the inner room; now he turns to the people, who stand to receive the blessing, as David blessed the people when the ark first came to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:18). But before he blesses the people he blesses God, because everything he is about to say is about what God has done.

Who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth. He begins with a promise kept, and the phrasing is exact: spoken with the mouth, done with the hand. God’s words and his deeds never come apart.

But I chose David. Look at what God says he chose. For nearly five hundred years, from the exodus to this morning, he picked no city and no site for a house; what he chose was a man. It is the point God made in chapter 6 (6:11–13), seen from the other side: his interest was never chiefly in a site. He chose a shepherd out of a field near Bethlehem and made promises to him, and the building exists only because of those promises. The promise ran on past Solomon to another son of David from Bethlehem, who is “faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house” (Hebrews 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.' Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told David that his longing to build was good even though he would not be allowed to build, and Solomon now stands as proof that God has kept both halves of his promise: a son on the throne, and a house for his name.

You did well that it was in your heart. This is one of the kindest sentences in the Old Testament, and it is easy to read past. David wanted to build the temple and was refused; he never laid a stone of it, was told why, and died more than a decade before this day. Yet God says it was good that he wanted to. The desire is commended though the project was denied, and that is neither a consolation prize nor politeness: God saw the wanting and valued it.

When God says no. Anyone who has had a genuine desire to do something for God and been prevented, by health, by circumstances, by other people’s decisions or simply by being the wrong person for it, is looking at the verse that speaks to it. The thing was refused; the wanting was not wasted. “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10).

I have risen in the place of David my father. Nathan’s promise had two halves: a son on David’s throne, and that son building a house for God’s name (2 Samuel 7:12–13). Solomon points to both as done. He presents himself not as a founder but as evidence that God keeps his word. Twice in these verses (vv. 16, 21) he grounds it all in the exodus: the covenant in the ark was made with people coming out of Egypt, and the building exists to house it.

A fuller fulfilment. Solomon was a real but partial fulfilment. Within a generation the kingdom was torn in two, and four centuries later the house was burned. The promise of a throne established “forever” (2 Samuel 7:13) waited for a Son of David who would not fail, and it is kept in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven, and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart; you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing before the altar with open hands, Solomon begins his prayer with who God is: there is no God like him, because he keeps covenant and steadfast love, as this very day has proved.

Before the altar of the LORD. Notice where he stands: not on a throne, not in the building, but before the altar in the courtyard, in front of everybody, with his hands open and lifted. Verse 54 will add something this verse does not: he was on his knees.

There is no God like you. The prayer opens where every good prayer in Scripture opens, with who God is. And what Solomon singles out is not power or majesty but “keeping covenant and showing steadfast love”. Steadfast love (hesed) is loyal love, the love that keeps its promises. God’s distinguishing mark, on the lips of a man dedicating a temple, is that he keeps his word.

To your servants who walk before you with all their heart. God’s steadfast love is not wages, but it is enjoyed by those who walk with him wholeheartedly; the phrase looks ahead to the heart “wholly true” of verse 61 (see the note on vv. 59–61). Verse 24 gives the proof from that very day, “You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day”, the same pairing of mouth and hand as verse 15.

Every promise kept. The God who kept his word to David has kept it supremely in Christ, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). So we may begin where Solomon began: not with our need, but with a God who has never broken his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.' Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon prays God’s promise back to him, asking him to do what he has said, without leaving out what the promise asks of David’s sons.

Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David. He prays the promise back, exactly as his father did. When Nathan brought the covenant, David sat before the LORD and said, “do as you have spoken”, and gave his reason: “you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant… Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you” (2 Samuel 7:25–27). Solomon does the same: “let your word be confirmed.” He is not telling God anything new; he is asking God, to his face, to do what he has said. It is the boldest kind of prayer, and the safest, and Christians may pray the same way, holding God to what he has promised in Christ.

If only your sons pay close attention to their way. Solomon quotes the promise with its condition and does not leave the condition out. The throne is promised, but each son must walk before God as David did; God will repeat the terms to Solomon in person (9:4–5), and chapter 11 will show what happens when a son does not. To pray a promise back to God is not to forget what it asks of us. Only one Son of David ever met that condition perfectly, and in him the promise is secure (see the note on vv. 59–61).

verseByVerse.quote: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day his temple is finished and filled with glory, its builder says that it cannot contain God, since heaven itself cannot, and asks the question the whole Bible answers: will God indeed dwell on the earth?

But will God indeed dwell on the earth? What matters first is who says it, and when: the man who has just finished seven years of work with the finest timber in the world and gold over every surface, standing before it on the day of its dedication, with the glory of God inside it and the nation watching. And the question is not whether God will dwell in this building, but whether he will dwell on the earth at all. Is such a thing even possible?

Heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you. Neither the sky nor the sky beyond the sky will hold him; there is no space anywhere large enough. God is not a very large being inside the universe. He made it, and he is present everywhere in it without being contained by it: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24).

How much less this house that I have built! Then come the words that make the sentence what it is: that I have built. He names it as his own work and says it is not adequate to its purpose, on the day it was finished. No prophet stood there to correct him; the assembly would have been satisfied with verse 13, and he corrects it himself, aloud, in public. That is what an understanding mind looks like when it has been used for seven years: the more magnificent the building became, the clearer it was that it could not do the one thing it was for. It is easy to be humble about somebody else’s achievement.

The sentence has a long life. Isaiah gives it as God’s own words: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me… But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:1–2). Stephen, before the council that was about to stone him for speaking against the temple, said that “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands” (Acts 7:48), and Paul told a city full of temples that God “does not live in temples made by man” (Acts 17:24). But it was said first by the man who built the finest religious building of his age, on the day he opened it.

Where God dwells now. Solomon’s question has an answer he could not have guessed. God did dwell on the earth: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), and the word John uses for “dwelt” means pitched his tent, the language of the tabernacle. Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21), and by his Spirit his people are now God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). Worship is no longer bound to a place but offered “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23), and we no longer pray towards a building but come to the Father through the Son. The eternal Son, without ceasing to be the God whom heaven cannot contain, lay in a womb, in a manger and in a tomb: not because God became small, but because he loved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — Hear in Heaven, and Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because no house can contain God, Solomon asks him to hear from heaven every prayer made towards the place where he has put his name, and to forgive. He asks that God’s eyes be open night and day towards the house (vv. 28–30). Then come the petitions: for the oath sworn at the altar when human justice fails (vv. 31–32), for defeat brought on by sin (vv. 33–34), for drought sent to teach the good way (vv. 35–36), and for every famine, plague and siege, and every person who knows the affliction of his own heart (vv. 37–40). God alone knows every heart, and his forgiveness is meant to lead his people to fear him.
verseByVerse.theology: Most of the petitions are about sin and its consequences, and none asks for prosperity, victory or a secure throne. The refrain is hear in heaven... and forgive.
verseByVerse.examples: In a national dedication, the prayer stops for the one man who knows the affliction of his own heart (v. 38).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day, that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place. And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though no house can contain God, Solomon asks him to keep watch over this one, where he has put his name, to hear from heaven every prayer made towards it, and to forgive.

Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant. The single word yet is the turn. He has just said the building cannot contain God, and now he asks God to attend to it anyway. That is not inconsistency. He holds two things that both need holding: God is not contained by any building, and God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot go up to heaven.

My name shall be there. This is what the temple is, in the phrase Solomon keeps returning to. He does not say “I shall be there”, as though God lived in a room like a householder, but “my name”: his revealed character, the way he has made himself known so that he can be found. The house is where God has put his name so that people know where to turn. And Solomon, who has just built God a house, does not call it God’s dwelling place: “listen in heaven your dwelling place” (v. 30). The house on the hill is where you face when you speak.

Night and day toward this house. There is to be no hour when a prayer made towards it goes unheard. And every petition that follows is about praying toward this place, not in it: almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles of verse 46 will not be able to get there at all. Daniel took this at its word in Babylon, kneeling three times a day at a window open towards Jerusalem, long after the house had been burned (Daniel 6:10).

And when you hear, forgive. Then, for the first time, comes the word the whole prayer runs on. Solomon expects that most of the prayers made towards this house will come from people who have sinned.

A God everywhere in general is found nowhere in particular. Many people today agree with verse 27 and draw the opposite conclusion: God, if there is one, is too big for buildings, books or creeds; I feel nearer to him on a hillside than in a church. Solomon said the first half before any of us, but he did not conclude that God could be met anywhere on our terms. A God spread thinly over everything is very easy to live with: he never says anything, never meets you anywhere, never asks for anything, and tends to agree with us. C. S. Lewis observed in Miracles that people are comfortable with an impersonal God, a force or a feeling inside our own heads, and grow uneasy only when he turns out to be alive, “pulling at the other end of the cord”. The name in this house was God’s answer: he made himself findable, and told sinners, foreigners and exiles where to turn and what he was like. Then he went further than a place. The God whom heaven cannot contain has a face and a name, and the way to him is not a mood but a person who says, “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where human courts cannot reach the truth, Solomon asks God to be the judge of last resort, condemning the guilty and clearing the innocent.

If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath. The first petition concerns a dispute with no evidence, one man’s word against another’s, so the accused is put on oath at the altar. Solomon knows such cases: two women once stood before him with a baby and no witnesses (3:16–28). The procedure is in the law. Where property was in dispute and there was no proof either way, “an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor’s property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution” (Exodus 22:11). The oath ends the case, because there is nothing else to end it with, and so everything rests on the man who swears believing that God is listening. Take that away and the oath is an empty form of words, and the guilty man says them and walks off with his neighbour’s ox.

Condemning the guilty… and vindicating the righteous. This petition has no “forgive” in it. Solomon asks God to act, and both halves matter. There is a man in this scenario who has been wronged and cannot prove it, and the prayer is that he be publicly cleared. Every court in the world produces people who were right and could not show it, and the first thing Solomon asks of the new temple is that God be the place where that is finally put right.

The Judge who sees. God will do this fully on the last day, when he “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). Until then, those wrongly accused can do what Christ did under false charges, and keep entrusting themselves “to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 31 is compressed, something like “and he lays on him an oath to make him swear, and the oath comes before your altar”. It is not certain who imposes the oath, the wronged neighbour or the judges. The sense is clear enough: the accused swears at the altar, calling down a curse on himself if he is lying.

verseByVerse.quote: "When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel is defeated because of its sin, Solomon asks that confession and prayer may open a way back, to forgiveness and to the land.

Because they have sinned against you. The second petition sets the pattern for most of the rest: a disaster, caused by sin; then turning and prayer; then “hear in heaven and forgive”. Solomon is not asking God to keep trouble away from Israel. He assumes trouble, assumes that much of it will be deserved, and asks for a way back from it. That is a striking thing to build into a dedication: not that the nation should prosper, but a road back from disasters that have not yet happened and will be their own fault.

If they turn again to you and acknowledge your name. The Hebrew for “turn” (shuv) is the Old Testament’s ordinary word for repentance: a change of direction, not only of feeling. To “acknowledge your name” is to confess that God is who he says he is and that he was just in what has happened (compare Nehemiah 9:33). The defeat is not explained away as bad luck or a stronger enemy; it is owned.

Bring them again to the land. In the ancient world defeat meant deportation: populations moved, land lost, families scattered across an empire. Solomon asks that losing the land need not be final, which is the ground the seventh petition will stand on (vv. 46–50) when the loss is total.

The road back is open. The way back Solomon asked for is open wide in Christ. The God who disciplines his children does it to bring them home, not to drive them off (Hebrews 12:10–11), and no defeat we have brought on ourselves is beyond his forgiveness when we turn.

verseByVerse.quote: "When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God shuts the sky because of sin, Solomon asks that the drought do its work, teaching the people the good way, and that God then forgive and send rain.

When heaven is shut up and there is no rain. Rain in that land was not just weather; God had tied it to the covenant. “If you will indeed obey my commandments… he will give the rain for your land in its season”, with the warning attached: “then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain” (Deuteronomy 11:13–17). So a dry sky was a sermon. A nation that went after other gods because they were thought to control the weather would find the weather stopped. Elijah will stand before a king in chapter 17 and shut the sky for three and a half years, and this petition explains why: God withholds rain because of sin, to bring his people back.

When you teach them the good way in which they should walk. This clause, slipped into the middle, lifts the petition above a bargain. The drought is not simply a penalty but instruction, and Solomon asks that it actually teach what it was sent to teach.

In a dry season of your own. Anyone in a long dry season can pray verse 36 as it stands: not “take this away” first, but “teach me the good way”, and then the rain. The Father disciplines his children “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). Not every dry season is a punishment, but every one can be a school, and the God who teaches in it is the same God who sends the rain.

What it does not mean. This does not license us to read every drought, illness or hardship, our own or anyone else’s, as punishment for a particular sin. Jesus refused that conclusion (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3), and the book of Job shows suffering serving purposes hidden in God. Solomon speaks of droughts that come “because they have sinned”; he does not say that every drought does.

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is, whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house, then hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind), that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever disaster comes, and whatever any one person knows to be wrong in his own heart, Solomon asks God, who alone knows every heart, to hear, forgive and deal rightly with each, so that his people may fear him.

Whatever plague, whatever sickness there is. In the fourth petition Solomon lists everything that can go wrong, famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, caterpillar and siege, and then, because no list is complete, adds “whatever plague, whatever sickness there is”.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart. This is the most personal clause in the whole prayer. On the greatest public occasion of his reign, Solomon stops to ask God to hear the individual who knows what is wrong with him. The Hebrew word behind affliction is the one just translated plague: after the blight and the locusts the prayer turns inward, for a man’s own heart can have its plague. This one is for “any man”, alone, who knows something about himself that nobody else in that crowd knows, and stretches out his hands. Whatever else the temple was for, it was for him.

For you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind. The words in brackets are why such a prayer can be heard, and why it can be made without words that anyone else hears. They are also why the judgment asked for is exact: “render to each whose heart you know”. God deals with each person as the one he knows, not as part of a crowd. A believer can pray this way today, no longer towards a building but to the Father through the Son (see the note on v. 27): naming the particular sin or sorrow he knows in his own heart, and trusting that the one who knows it fully is the one who forgives (1 John 1:9).

That they may fear you. Verse 40 gives the purpose of every answer asked for so far: not that Israel may feel safe, but that they may fear God all their days in the land. Forgiveness does not make God smaller in the eyes of the forgiven; it makes him more to be revered: “with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — The Foreigner, and the Far Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer reaches beyond Israel’s borders and beyond Israel’s worst future. A foreigner who comes from far away because he has heard of God’s great name is to be heard without conditions, so that all the peoples of the earth may know and fear the LORD (vv. 41–43). Israel, sent out to war by God, is to have its cause upheld (vv. 44–45). And if Israel sins, as everyone does, and is carried captive, then if they repent in the land of their enemies and pray towards the house, God is asked to forgive and to move their captors to compassion (vv. 46–50), because they are his own people, brought out of Egypt’s iron furnace (vv. 51–53).
verseByVerse.theology: The foreigner's petition carries no condition, unlike Israel's, and the reason given is missionary: that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name.
verseByVerse.examples: The seventh petition foresees the exile centuries before it happened, and the book's first readers were captives reading a prayer that had already asked God to hear them there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake (for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house, hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon asks God to answer the foreigner who comes because he has heard of God’s great name, freely and in full, so that all the peoples of the earth may know and fear him.

When a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel. The fifth petition concerns someone with no covenant, no claim, no inheritance in the land, and no business being there at all. What draws him is a reputation: “your great name and your mighty hand, and… your outstretched arm” are exodus words, the phrases Deuteronomy uses again and again for what God did in Egypt. What reaches a foreigner in a far country is the story of God rescuing slaves.

Do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you. Read that against the other petitions, because the difference is startling. For Israel the asking has conditions: “if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name”, “if they… turn from their sin”, “if they repent with all their heart”. For the foreigner there is no condition attached, no repentance specified and no requirement that he become an Israelite first. His coming, for the sake of God’s name, is itself his faith. Solomon asks God to give him everything he asks for, and not as a footnote about hospitality: on the day the house became the one place on earth where God had put his name, the king asks God to answer foreigners generously so that the whole world will hear of him.

Comes from a far country. The petition begins to be answered within Solomon’s own reign. Two chapters on, the queen of Sheba comes from far to the south, having heard of Solomon’s fame “concerning the name of the LORD” (10:1), and goes home blessing the LORD (see the note on 10:1–13).

A house of prayer for all peoples. The temple was never meant to be a wall. Isaiah says so, quoting God about foreigners who join themselves to the LORD: “these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer… for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7). A thousand years later Jesus found the court of the Gentiles in the rebuilt temple, the one place a foreigner could pray, full of money-changers and animals, drove them out and said, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17). They had filled the only room a foreigner could pray in with livestock, and Solomon had asked God to hear that foreigner on the day the building opened.

The foreigner is us. In Christ this prayer is answered beyond anything Solomon asked. Gentiles who “were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13) and now belong to God’s own household. Most readers of this commentary are the foreigner of verse 41.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel goes to a war God has sent them to, Solomon asks God to hear and uphold their cause: not to bless any war Israel chooses, but to see that right is done.

If your people go out to battle. The sixth petition is the shortest, and like the foreigner’s it does not mention sin. There is no suggestion that the war is a judgment or that anybody has done wrong: sometimes trouble is simply trouble.

By whatever way you shall send them. The qualification matters. He is not asking God to bless whatever war Israel decides to fight; the petition covers armies God has sent and quietly excludes the rest. That is more restraint than most national prayers show, from a king with twelve thousand horsemen (4:26).

Maintain their cause. The request is not simply for victory but for judgment: take up their case and see that right is done. It is the phrase he uses again for the exiles (v. 49), and it is what someone asks who trusts the judge more than the verdict he wants. Christians may pray so for their own nation, but must never confuse any nation’s wars with the cause of Christ, whose kingdom “is not of this world” (John 18:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,' if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions that they have committed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foreseeing that Israel will sin and be carried into exile, Solomon asks that if they repent in the land of their captors and pray towards this house, God will hear, forgive and make their captors kind to them.

For there is no one who does not sin. This parenthesis should not be hurried. Solomon puts it in as a matter of course, in the middle of a sentence, as a fact so obvious it needs no argument: nobody is excepted. Paul builds a chapter of Romans on that proposition, and then gives the answer this prayer could only ask for: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:23–25), a sacrifice that turns away God’s anger at sin. “Hear in heaven… and forgive” is answered at the cross.

Carried away captive to the land of the enemy. Think who first read this. Kings was completed in the exile, and its last scene is a king of Judah eating at a Babylonian table (2 Kings 25:27–30); its first readers had watched this temple burn. What they found, in the record of the day it opened, was a prayer that had already asked God to hear them where they were. Solomon names the land of their captors three times, nearly four centuries before it happened. A man in Babylon could put his finger on the sentence and know that on the greatest day in Israel’s history someone had prayed for him, far from a ruined city, with nothing left to bring.

If they turn their heart. Literally, “if they bring it back to their heart”: if, far from home, they come to their senses, as the younger son in Jesus’ parable “came to himself” in the far country (Luke 15:17). The words come from Moses, who foresaw this very thing: Israel scattered among the nations would “call them to mind” and return “with all your heart and with all your soul”, and God would restore them (Deuteronomy 30:1–3). Solomon even supplies the confession they will need, “We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly”, and the exiles later prayed in very similar words (Daniel 9:5).

Grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive. Notice what the prayer asks first: not a return, but that their captors be kind to them. That smaller, humbler request is the one answered first: Daniel in a Babylonian court, Nehemiah as cupbearer to a Persian king, Esther. Each was a case of God granting his people compassion in the sight of those who held them, as a psalm says: “He caused them to be pitied by all those who held them captive” (Psalm 106:46).

Never too far to turn back. No one is too far away to come home. Whether the distance is a place or a road of sin we chose ourselves, the way back is the same: come to ourselves, confess, and pray, and the Father runs to meet us (Luke 15:20).

verseByVerse.quote: (for they are your people, and your heritage, which you brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace). Let your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, giving ear to them whenever they call to you. For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage, as you declared through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s final plea rests not on Israel’s worth but on God’s own choice: they are his people, whom he brought out of the iron furnace of Egypt and set apart as his heritage.

From the midst of the iron furnace. The prayer ends where the whole day has kept returning, in Egypt. “The iron furnace” is Deuteronomy’s phrase for the slavery (Deuteronomy 4:20). Standing in the most beautiful building in the world, in the richest reign in Israel’s history, the king’s final argument for why God should hear his people is that he once brought them out of a smelting furnace. Israel never claims to deserve a hearing; the claim is always what God has done.

Let your eyes be open. The prayer closes as it began (v. 29), asking God to keep his eyes open and his ear turned to his people. Its last ground is God’s own choice: he “separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage”, as he said at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6). Solomon rests the whole prayer not on Israel’s worth but on what God chose and what God said.

Our plea too. Christians pray on the same ground, only greater: not our worth but God’s choice and God’s rescue. We are “a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), redeemed not from a furnace in Egypt but from sin and death, by the blood of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–66 — Not One Word Has Failed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day ends in praise, a call to wholehearted faithfulness and a great feast of joy. Solomon rises from his knees and blesses the LORD, who has given rest to Israel: not one word of all his good promise has failed (vv. 54–56). He prays that God will stay with them and incline their hearts to obey him, so that all nations may know that the LORD is God, and charges the people to be wholly true to him (vv. 57–61), a word the end of his own life will test. Then come peace offerings on a vast scale, shared as a meal (vv. 62–64), and a feast for the whole land, after which the people go home glad for the LORD’s goodness (vv. 65–66).
verseByVerse.theology: Not one word has failed of all his good promise is Joshua's claim (Josh. 21:45; 23:14) restated at the high-water mark of the whole story, by a man standing in a finished temple with the glory of God inside it.
verseByVerse.examples: The benediction ends with a call to hearts wholly true, and chapter 11 will measure Solomon by that very word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven. And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying, "Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rising from his knees, Solomon blesses God for the rest he has given and pronounces the verdict on Israel’s whole history: not one word of all God’s good promise has failed.

Where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven. Only now are we told what he had been doing for the last twenty-six verses: he was on his knees. Verse 22 said he stood before the altar and spread out his hands; the writer holds back the kneeling until the prayer is over, and mentions it in passing as the king gets up. The wealthiest king of his age, on the day of his greatest achievement, prayed on his knees in a courtyard, before the whole nation, with his hands open and empty.

Who has given rest to his people Israel. Moses had promised that when God gave Israel “rest from all your enemies around”, he would choose a place “to make his name dwell there” (Deuteronomy 12:10–11). Rest has come and the place is chosen; Solomon himself had been promised to David as “a man of rest” (1 Chronicles 22:9). Yet this rest was not the last word: Hebrews says that “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), and the land’s rest pointed beyond itself.

Not one word has failed. This is the verdict on the whole story so far. Joshua said it twice at the end of the conquest: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (Joshua 21:45), and in his farewell, “not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you” (Joshua 23:14). Now Solomon says it again, from a finished temple, at the widest borders Israel ever held, with the glory of God in the building behind him.

What lies behind it. Count what is behind that sentence. A promise to childless Abraham about offspring like the stars and the sand. A land promised to a man who owned one field in it, and that a grave. Four hundred years of slavery, a bush that did not burn up, blood on the doorposts. Forty years with a tent in the wilderness. The judges. David, a boy with a sling and then a hunted man in a cave. A promise in a night vision about a son who would build a house. Through all of it, God kept every word, and the same God holds every promise he has made to us in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us, that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon prays that God will stay with his people and, deeper still, bend their hearts towards himself, because the law in the ark cannot make them love it.

May he not leave us or forsake us. The words echo Moses’ promise to Israel and God’s to Joshua on the edge of the land: “he will not leave you or forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:6; Joshua 1:5). Solomon turns the promise into a prayer, and Hebrews gives it to Christians as God’s own word to them, a reason to be content (Hebrews 13:5).

That he may incline our hearts to him. This is the request that sees deepest in the chapter. He does not ask God to help them keep the commandments; he asks God to bend their hearts towards himself in the first place. Solomon has understood something easily missed on a day like this. The problem is not information: they have the law, and the tablets are in the ark inside the house. The problem is that the heart does not lean the right way on its own, and if God does not tilt it, nothing else will help.

The new covenant. He asks for what God would promise in Jeremiah’s new covenant some three centuries later, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), and through Ezekiel: “I will give you a new heart… And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:26–27). That promise is kept in Christ, whose blood is the blood of the new covenant (Luke 22:20) and whose Spirit now writes God’s law on believers’ hearts. When we pray for a heart that loves God, we pray Solomon’s prayer with the promise already given.

His own heart. He asked for the one thing he needed most, and chapter 11 will record that his own heart was turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires, that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other. Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon asks God to uphold Israel day by day so that all nations may know that the LORD is God, and calls the people to hearts wholly true to him, the very words by which he himself will later be found wanting.

As each day requires. Literally, “the matter of a day in its day”. Solomon asks God to keep the words of this prayer before him and to take up Israel’s cause day by day, as each day’s need arises: the same daily dependence Jesus teaches in “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

That all the peoples of the earth may know. The nations appear again, the second time on this day that Solomon looks out to the whole world, and the phrase is Deuteronomy’s great confession: “the LORD is God; there is no other” (Deuteronomy 4:35, 39).

Let your heart therefore be wholly true. The last word of the benediction is the word he will be measured by. It is shalem: whole, complete, undivided, at peace, and it shares a root with his own name. He calls the nation to hearts wholly true towards God, not partly or mostly but undivided, on the ground of the promise he has just praised as kept (v. 56). And here is what the writer records at the end of his life: “For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father” (11:4). These are the words of his own blessing, with a “not” added, applied to him. The writer does not point it out; he never points anything out. He puts the word in Solomon’s mouth in chapter 8, takes it from him in chapter 11, and leaves the reader to lay the two verses side by side.

God must incline the heart he commands. That is why the command of verse 61 rests on the prayer of verse 58. No son of David kept his heart undivided until Jesus did. His obedience is counted to those who trust him, and when they fail, the way back is the confession and forgiveness this whole prayer has asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD. Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD. The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house is dedicated with peace offerings on a vast scale, sacrifices shared as a meal, so that the whole nation feasts in the presence of God.

Peace offerings. The numbers are enormous, and the kind of offering matters. A burnt offering is entirely consumed; a peace offering is shared, with a portion burned and the rest given back to the worshippers as a meal. So a hundred and forty-two thousand animals means a national feast on a scale no one there had ever seen. This is not slaughter for its own sake; it is dinner, for two weeks, for everybody in the country who came.

A meal in God’s presence. The peace offering pictured fellowship with God restored: sinners eating in his presence because a sacrifice had been made. Christ is the sacrifice that makes that peace real, for “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and his people eat together at his table in remembrance of him.

Can the numbers be real? A hundred and forty-two thousand animals over the days of the feast is roughly ten thousand a day. With thousands of priests and Levites, the whole nation present and many altars in a consecrated court, it is enormous but not impossible, and verse 64 says that the bronze altar was too small, so the middle of the court was consecrated as well. Some think the Hebrew word for a thousand could also mean a smaller group, and others that the figures were copied in round form; Chronicles gives the same totals (2 Chronicles 7:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days. On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole nation, from the far north to the far south, keeps the feast and goes home glad, not for the building or the king, but for all the goodness the LORD had shown to David and to Israel.

From Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. The full extent of the land, north to south: the whole country is there.

Joyful and glad of heart. This is the last verse of the high-water mark, and little in the rest of the Old Testament is like it. The whole nation goes home joyful, and the writer says why: not the building, the king, the empire or the wealth, but “all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people”. The ark is in its place, the glory has filled the house, not one word of God’s promise has failed, and every man sits under his own vine and fig tree (4:25). This is as good as it ever gets.

But not yet. Three chapters from now the same writer will record that Solomon’s heart was not whole, that God raised up adversaries against him, and that a prophet met a young official on a road outside Jerusalem and tore a new cloak into twelve pieces (11:29–31). But on this day the people went home glad.

A joy no one can take. That gladness did not last, because the king could not keep it. The joy Jesus gives rests on a King who cannot fail: “no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22). And the feast kept here points to a greater one, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

Textual note. The Hebrew text reads “seven days and seven days, fourteen days”; the ESV follows the Greek Old Testament here and reads seven. Chronicles explains the two weeks: seven days dedicating the altar, then the seven days of the feast, with the people sent home after the closing assembly (2 Chronicles 7:8–10).

Uncertain wording. “Lebo-hamath” may be the name of a town, Lebo, in the valley between the Lebanon ranges, or it may mean “the entrance of Hamath”, as older translations have it; either way it marks the far northern frontier. “The Brook of Egypt” is probably the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai, not the Nile.

8.theology:
God is not tied to the building (vv. 1-11). The ark comes up in the week when Israel remembered that God had travelled with them in tents. Its carrying poles are left in, as though it might yet be moved. At the heart of the costliest building in Israel's history are two stones, the covenant made when they came out of the land of Egypt. And when the glory comes, the trained priests can do nothing but walk out, as Moses could not enter the finished tabernacle (Ex. 40:34-35).

God chose a man, not a place (vv. 16-18). The building exists only because of a promise to David, and the son of David who finally builds God’s house is Christ, faithful over God's house as a son. And we are his house (Hebrews 3:6). David himself was refused the work and told that the wanting was good: a refused desire to serve God is not wasted. Solomon then prays the promise back, let your word be confirmed, as his father had done (2 Sam. 7:25-27): not telling God anything new, but asking him to his face to do what he has said.

Will God indeed dwell on the earth? (v. 27). The builder says, on the day his work is finished, that it cannot hold God. Seven years of labour, the finest timber in the world, gold over every surface, the glory visibly inside and the nation watching, and he names it as his own work, this house that I have built, and says it is not adequate to its purpose. Nobody required it of him. That is what an understanding mind looks like after seven years of use: the more magnificent the work became, the clearer it was that it could not do the one thing it was for. Isaiah gives the thought back as God's own words and adds where God does look: to the humble and contrite (Isa. 66:1-2). Stephen and Paul repeat it to those who trusted in temples (Acts 7:48; 17:24). And the question was answered beyond anything Solomon could ask: God did dwell on the earth, in the flesh, and Jesus called his own body the temple (John 1:14; 2:19–21). The place to turn to God is now a person.

His name, and praying toward it (vv. 28-30). The building cannot contain God, yet God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot come to heaven. Both are true. The house is where God has put his name, the way he has made himself known, so that people far away know where to turn; almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles could not get there at all. Heaven remains his dwelling place, and the prayer asks him to hear from there.

A prayer about sin, with a way back (vv. 31-53). The petitions assume trouble, much of it deserved, and ask that there be a road home from it: hear in heaven, and forgive. They make room for the single man who knows the affliction of his own heart, for the foreigner who has heard of the exodus, and for exiles in a land not yet lost. Solomon says in passing that there is no one who does not sin, the conviction Paul will build a chapter of Romans on.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart (v. 38). In the middle of a national occasion the prayer stops for the one man who knows something about himself that nobody else in the crowd knows. Such a prayer can be answered because of the words in brackets in verse 39: God alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind. So the prayer needs no words anyone else hears, and God answers each person as the one he knows.

The foreigner, with no conditions (vv. 41-43). Israel's petitions all carry a condition, that the people repent. The foreigner's carries none: Solomon asks God to do all the foreigner asks, so that all the peoples of the earth may know his name. The temple was never meant to be a wall: Isaiah called it a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa. 56:7), and Jesus cleared the one court a foreigner could stand in with that verse on his lips (Mark 11:17).

Prayed for in advance (vv. 46-50). Kings was completed in the exile; its first readers had watched this temple burn, and they found in the record of its opening a prayer that had already asked God to hear them in the land of their captors. The first answer was the humbler request, that their captors would show them compassion: Daniel in a Babylonian court, Nehemiah at a Persian king's table, Esther.

Hear and forgive, but on what ground? (vv. 30-50). Seven times the prayer asks God to forgive, and never says how a holy God can. The answer was in the building: blood on the altar outside, blood carried once a year into the room behind the curtain. Those sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); they pointed to the one who could. Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12), and now he is the one we turn toward when we pray. Every repentant Israelite who faced Jerusalem and asked for mercy was, without knowing his name, leaning on him.

Never merit, always the exodus (vv. 51-53). In the most beautiful building in the world, the king's last argument for why God should hear is that he brought his people out of the iron furnace. That is the ground of every appeal to God: not what we have built, but what he has done.

Not one word has failed (vv. 54-61). The writer holds back until now that the king prayed all this on his knees, hands open and empty, in front of the nation. He rises to say what Joshua said at the end of the conquest (Josh. 21:45; 23:14): the promises to Abraham, to Moses and to David have all come true. Then he asks God to incline their hearts, to bend them toward himself. That is what God later promised in the new covenant through Jeremiah and Ezekiel (Jer. 31:33; Ezek. 36:26-27). And he calls for hearts wholly true. Chapter 11 measures him by that word, and he falls short. The command (v. 61) depends on the prayer (v. 58): God must give the heart he commands.

As good as it ever gets (vv. 62-66). The great peace offerings are a shared meal for the whole nation, a portion burned and the rest eaten, so many that the bronze altar could not take them and the middle of the court had to be consecrated as an overflow; and the people go home glad, not about the building or the king, but about all the goodness that the LORD had shown. Three chapters on, the decline begins; but not yet.
8.examples:
Then: The richest king on earth finished the most expensive building in his nation's history, watched the glory of God fill it so completely that the priests had to walk out of the room, and then knelt down in the courtyard in front of the whole country and said out loud that the thing he had just spent seven years building could not possibly hold the God it was built for.

Now: three things. Verse 27 is the one to take away, and its power is who said it and when. It is easy to be humble about somebody else's achievement; Solomon said his own finest work was inadequate on the day it was finished, with everyone watching and nobody requiring it of him. Second, verse 38: in the middle of a national occasion with a hundred and forty thousand animals being offered, the prayer stops for the one man who knows the affliction of his own heart and cannot say it to anybody. If you are that person, the temple was for you, and such a prayer can be heard because of the words in brackets in verse 39: God alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind. And third, verse 58, which is the honest request. He did not ask for help obeying. He asked God to incline their hearts, because the heart does not lean the right way on its own, and the man who prayed it had his own heart turned away in the end, which is why it is the prayer to keep praying. God has answered it in his Son, whose heart was wholly true in our place, and in the Spirit he now gives to incline ours (Ezek. 36:27; Gal. 5:16).

keyVerse.quote: But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
keyVerse.note: The builder of the finest house of his age says, on the day it opens and fills with glory, that it cannot contain God. His question is the one the whole Bible answers: God did dwell on the earth when the Word became flesh (John 1:14), and by his Spirit he now makes his people his temple.

8.reflection:
At the centre of the temple were only the two tablets of the covenant, and when the glory came the trained priests could not stand to minister (vv. 9–11). What does this teach about what matters most in worship, and about our efforts to impress God?

Solomon said on the day of dedication that the house he had built could not contain God (v. 27). How does John 1:14 answer his question, and what difference does it make that we now come to God through Christ rather than towards a place?

Most of Solomon’s petitions assume that God’s people will sin and ask for a way back (vv. 33–50). Why is it striking to build that into a dedication prayer? Which petition best fits a situation you or your church face now?

Solomon prayed “that he may incline our hearts to him” (v. 58) and urged, “Let your heart therefore be wholly true” (v. 61), yet his own heart turned away (11:4). Why do we need God to change our hearts, and not only to tell us what to do? How does the new covenant in Christ answer that need?

9.title: The LORD Appears a Second Time
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build,<sup>2</sup>the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.<sup>4</sup>And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules,<sup>5</sup>then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'<sup>6</sup>But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,<sup>7</sup>then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.<sup>8</sup>And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'<sup>9</sup>Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"<sup>10</sup>At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house,<sup>11</sup>and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.<sup>12</sup>But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him.<sup>13</sup>Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day.<sup>14</sup>Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold.<sup>15</sup>And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer<sup>16</sup>(Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife;<sup>17</sup>so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon<sup>18</sup>and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah,<sup>19</sup>and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.<sup>20</sup>All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel—<sup>21</sup>their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day.<sup>22</sup>But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen.<sup>23</sup>These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work.<sup>24</sup>But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo.<sup>25</sup>Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house.<sup>26</sup>King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.<sup>27</sup>And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon.<sup>28</sup>And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
9.overview:
Where we are. The temple and palace are finished and the great dedication prayer of chapter 8 has been prayed. At the height of the reign’s glory, the LORD appears to Solomon a second time.

The message. God answers Solomon’s prayer and more than answers it: his name, his eyes and his heart will be on the house for all time. But the house is no guarantee. The throne stands on a son of David who walks before God with a whole heart, and if Israel turns to other gods, the house that bears God’s name will become a heap of ruins, and the world will know why. The rest of the chapter, set beside that warning, quietly shows a king whose attention is drifting towards “whatever Solomon desired to build”.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen the ruins (see the introduction). Verses 8–9 put their own question into the mouth of passers-by and answer it: not that God had failed or that Babylon’s gods had won, but that Israel had abandoned the LORD. A God who judged them for a stated reason was a God to whom they could return.

How the chapter makes its case. God appears a second time, grants the prayer and consecrates the house (vv. 1–3). He sets the condition for the throne, walking as David did (vv. 4–5), and the threat if Israel serves other gods: exile, a house cast out of his sight, and ruins that explain themselves (vv. 6–9). Then come the reign’s accounts, told without comment: twenty Galilean towns that sour Hiram’s friendship, the levy for Solomon’s building, and Gezer, Pharaoh’s dowry for his daughter (vv. 10–19); Canaanites in permanent bondage, Pharaoh’s daughter moved to her own house, the feasts kept, and gold from Ophir (vv. 20–28). God’s appearing and the gold stand side by side, and chapter 11 will show which held the king’s heart.

Where it leads. To Christ by covenant and by the need it exposes. The condition of verse 4, “integrity of heart and uprightness”, was never fully met by Solomon or any king after him. It was met by Jesus, who walked before his Father with a whole heart to the cross, and to whom God gave “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). And the temple whose ruin is foretold here pointed beyond itself to his own body, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21), where God’s name and heart now dwell for good.

For us. Privilege is not protection. Solomon heard God speak twice and still drifted, and no heritage or past blessing will keep a heart that goes after other gods. But this chapter also shows that God’s judgments have reasons, so they can be repented of, and in Christ we have a King whose wholehearted obedience stands in the place of ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — My Eyes and My Heart Will Be There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Solomon’s dedication prayer, and in the same speech tells him that the temple is no guarantee. When the building work is done the LORD appears a second time, as at Gibeon (vv. 1–2). He has heard the prayer and consecrated the house by putting his name there for ever, and he promises not only his eyes, as Solomon asked, but his heart (v. 3). The throne will stand if Solomon walks as David did, with integrity of heart (vv. 4–5). But if Solomon or his sons turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land and the house cast out of God’s sight (vv. 6–7), and its ruins will tell passers-by exactly why (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the answer to chapter 8: Solomon asked for God's eyes on the house (8:29), and God adds his heart, which nobody asked for.
verseByVerse.examples: In the same breath God says the building may become a heap of ruins. Verse 8 asks the question the first readers were asking in Babylon, and verse 9 is the answer that the whole of Kings works out.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build, the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the building is finished, God appears to Solomon a second time and answers his prayer beyond what he asked: the house is holy because God has put his name there, and God’s eyes and heart will be on it for all time.

All that Solomon desired to build. The writer keeps a running account of the building and adds to it without comment; the phrase returns in verse 19 (see the note on vv. 10–19).

A second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. The writer points back to Gibeon on purpose. Few people in Scripture are visited by God more than once (Abraham, Jacob and Moses among them), and this man was visited twice: once as a young king who asked for an understanding mind, and once here, at the summit of his reign. Two chapters on, when the reign is judged, this is the fact that makes the charge so heavy: “the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice” (11:9).

I have heard your prayer and your plea. This is the answer to chapter 8, and it should be read with that prayer open beside it. Solomon asked “that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, ‘My name shall be there’” (8:29). God grants it in the words it was asked in, and then adds what nobody asked for: Solomon asked for the eyes, and God adds the heart.

I have consecrated this house. Solomon built and dedicated the house, but only God can make it holy, and he has done it “by putting my name there forever.” Its holiness is God’s gift, not the builder’s achievement.

My eyes and my heart will be there for all time. It is a remarkable thing to say about a building, and it should not be softened into a figure of speech. The word for heart is lev, the word Solomon used when he asked for an understanding heart (3:9), and the word that will be used against him in chapter 11. God is saying that both his attention and his affection are fixed on that place. So when the building is looted by Shishak within a generation (14:25–26), stripped by Ahaz and Hezekiah to pay tribute, defiled by Manasseh, and finally burned by Nebuchadnezzar’s men, God’s heart is in it the whole time. He is not indifferent to the destruction of his own house, and he says so before he threatens it.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
