The throne promised to David’s line will stand for the son who walks before God as David did, with a whole and upright heart. The promise is God’s; enjoying it depends on faithfulness.

As David your father walked. The standard is David, and these are the terms of the covenant that depend on obedience: the throne is promised “if you will walk before me”. David quoted that same condition to Solomon on his deathbed (2:4).

With integrity of heart and uprightness. Integrity is tom: wholeness, undividedness. It is very close to the “wholly true” heart Solomon called for in his own benediction (8:61), and it is exactly what 11:4 will say his own heart was not.

You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel. God answers in the words of the promise Solomon prayed back to him at the dedication (8:25; see the note on 8:25–26), with its condition stated just as Solomon stated it.

Was the Davidic covenant conditional? In different respects, both. The promise of a throne for ever was unconditional (2 Samuel 7:16); whether each son of David enjoyed it depended on his faithfulness (2 Samuel 7:14). So the condition here does not cancel the promise. It decides whether each generation sits under its blessing or under its rod. The line could be judged, but not ended.

A whole heart at last. Every king after David failed the test of verse 4. Jesus alone walked before his Father with a whole heart, “obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), and God raised him to sit on David’s throne (Acts 2:30–36). He also wept over the next temple on this hill and foretold its fall (Luke 19:41–44), because the house that mattered was his own body, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21).

verseByVerse.quote: But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Solomon or his sons turn to other gods, Israel will lose the land and the house will be cast out of God’s sight: the building that bears his name is no guarantee against judgment.

You or your children. In verse 6 the Hebrew “you” becomes plural: the warning reaches past Solomon to his sons and to the whole nation.

Go and serve other gods and worship them. The sin is named in advance, and it is exactly the one Solomon will commit: not injustice, cruelty or pride, but serving other gods. Chapter 11 opens with seven hundred wives, and within five verses “Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (11:5). He was told the precise thing to avoid, twice, by God in person.

A proverb and a byword among all peoples. This is the very curse Moses set before Israel (Deuteronomy 28:37). The people meant to make God’s name known to the nations (8:43, 60) would become a warning told among them.

I will cast out of my sight. Read the two sayings together, four verses apart, because between them they hold the whole theology of the temple: God’s eyes and heart will be there for all time, and the house consecrated for his name may be cast out of his sight. The building is not the guarantee. God said so in the middle of the scaffolding (6:11–13); Solomon said as much on dedication day, praying for a people carried captive for their sin (8:46–50); and here God says it a third time, in the harshest form: a house with his name on it and his heart in it will go if Israel goes after other gods.

Not the building. Christians are tempted the same way: to trust the building, the heritage, the name over the door or the memory of past blessing. God’s presence is a gift to be treasured, never a possession that shelters a people whose hearts have gone elsewhere (Jeremiah 7:4; Revelation 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?' Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruined temple will itself preach a sermon: passers-by will ask why, and the answer will be that Israel abandoned the LORD who brought them out of Egypt. That answer rules out defeat and leaves room for repentance.

And this house will become a heap of ruins. The first readers had seen it happen: the house of the LORD and every great house in Jerusalem burned, the bronze pillars broken up and carried away, the men of Judah marched off in chains (2 Kings 25:9–13). Their whole national theology said that God had chosen Zion and put his name there, so when it burned the question was not Is God angry? but Is God finished, or has he been defeated?

Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house? Verse 8 puts that question into the mouth of a passer-by, nearly four centuries before it was asked, in a word spoken to the man who laid the foundations. The exiles found their own question in the middle of the account of the temple, and found it already answered.

Because they abandoned the LORD their God. This is the main point of both books of Kings, and everything to the end of 2 Kings works it out: kings who did evil in the sight of the LORD, prophets ignored, high places not taken away, and at last the armies from the north. The answer matters as much for what it rules out. God did not fail, and Babylon’s gods were not stronger, which any other ancient nation would have concluded from the same evidence; so the writer puts the answer in the mouth of foreign passers-by.

Who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt. The exodus appears in the answer, as Solomon kept returning to it in chapter 8. The charge is not that Israel broke rules but that they walked away from the God who had come and brought them out of the iron furnace (8:51).

Mercy inside the judgment. There is a mercy here that is easy to miss. A God who has been defeated cannot help you; a God who has judged you can. If the ruin is God’s own doing and for a stated reason, then repentance is possible and there is someone to repent to, which is exactly what Solomon asked for in the seventh petition of his prayer (8:46–50), and exactly what a man in Babylon needed to know.

The curse borne. The ruin of the house was the curse of the broken covenant falling on God’s people (Deuteronomy 28:37). At the cross that curse fell on the King himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). So for those who return to God through him, the ruins are not the last word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The glory of the reign has a ledger, and some of its entries are sour. After twenty years of building, Solomon settles his account with Hiram by handing over twenty towns in Galilee, land that was not the crown’s to sell, and his old ally scorns them (vv. 10–14). Then comes the account of the levy for Solomon’s works: the temple and palace, Jerusalem’s defences, the fortress cities of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, the store cities and the chariot cities (vv. 15–19). A parenthesis records that Gezer came as the dowry of Pharaoh’s daughter, after an Egyptian army had burned it. The writer comments on none of it, but twice sums up the programme as what Solomon desired to build (vv. 1, 19).
verseByVerse.theology: A sour note with Hiram, the best friend Israel had, is recorded and left there, and the name it gave a district stuck.
verseByVerse.examples: Gezer arrives as a wedding present from Pharaoh: the marriage of 3:1 delivering territory, and with it the dealings with Egypt the law warned about.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house, and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him. Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day. Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold. And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer (Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife; so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reign’s accounts show strain beneath the glory: Solomon pays his debt to Hiram with Israelite land his friend despises, and builds fortress after fortress, including a town that came as the dowry of Pharaoh’s daughter.

At the end of twenty years. Seven years on the temple and thirteen on the palace (6:38; 7:1), and the writer adds them up. Hiram had supplied cedar, cypress and gold “as much as he desired”, and the settlement is paid in territory rather than money.

Twenty cities in the land of Galilee. The land of Israel was not the crown’s to sell. It had been allotted by lot under Joshua, tribe by tribe and family by family, as each household’s share of what God had promised Abraham, and the law made permanent sale nearly impossible: “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). Solomon hands over twenty towns of it to pay a bill.

What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother? Hiram had been the best friend Israel had. He loved David and sent him cedar unasked, blessed the LORD by name for Solomon’s wisdom, supplied every beam in the house of God, sent his own craftsmen, and added 120 talents of gold. Now he inspects his payment and asks a pointed question. Brother is treaty language between allied kings, here with the edge such a word has when a business relationship has soured. It is a small sour scene in the middle of the glory, and the writer leaves it there.

The land of Cabul to this day. The district was named from Hiram’s displeasure, and the name stuck: people were still calling that stretch of Galilee by a Phoenician king’s rude remark long afterwards. Chronicles records the transaction the other way round, with Hiram giving cities to Solomon (2 Chronicles 8:2); the likeliest explanation is that Hiram handed them back and Solomon rebuilt them.

The account of the forced labor. The building list keeps growing. It began with the house of the LORD and now includes the Millo, the city wall, and three great fortress cities: Hazor in the north, Megiddo above the Jezreel valley, and Gezer on the approach from the coast.

Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer. Verse 16 is a parenthesis with a great deal in it. An Egyptian army came up into the land, took a Canaanite town inside Israel’s borders, burned it and killed its people, then gave the site to Pharaoh’s daughter as a wedding present, and she brought it to Solomon. Gezer lay in the territory allotted to Ephraim (Joshua 16:3) but had never been taken; the Canaanites lived on in it (Judges 1:29). So a standing failure of the conquest is solved for Israel by a foreign power. The writer states it flatly, but two things lie underneath. Egypt has conducted a military operation inside the land of promise and been thanked for it. And this is what the marriage alliance of 3:1 actually produced: territory, a burned town and an obligation. The law’s warnings about a king and Egypt (Deuteronomy 17:16) were not superstition about a country; dealings with Egypt always cost Israel more than they brought.

The cities for his chariots. The forty thousand stalls of 4:26 have to be somewhere, and here are the towns built to hold them. Archaeologists have found what may be stabling at Megiddo, though many date those buildings a century or so later.

Whatever Solomon desired to build. The phrase from verse 1 returns, and the writer never comments on it. Twice now the account of a reign that began by asking God for an understanding mind has been summed up as a list of what the king wanted.

What we desire to build. Ambition for good work is no sin, and Solomon’s building served his people. But a life can be summed up by its desires, and the question is whose desires sit at its centre. Only one Son of David could say without reserve, “I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30).

Uncertain wording. Two words here are not fully understood. The Millo (v. 15) comes from a root meaning “fill”, and probably refers to an earthwork or stepped terracing on the Jerusalem ridge, but what exactly it was is not known. And the name Cabul (v. 13) was probably heard by Hebrew ears as something like “as good as nothing”, which is the point of the story, though the precise origin of the name is uncertain.
verseByVerse.note: Gezer, Hazor and Megiddo guarded the main routes through the land: Megiddo the pass on the coastal road, Hazor the road north to Damascus, Gezer the approach to Jerusalem from the coast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with how the kingdom was run and where its wealth came from. The surviving Canaanite peoples, whom Israel never drove out, are put to permanent forced labour, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers (vv. 20–23). Pharaoh’s daughter is moved out of the city of David into a house of her own, a real scruple that leaves the marriage itself untouched (v. 24). Solomon keeps the three yearly feasts at the LORD’s altar (v. 25). And a fleet built at Ezion-geber and crewed with Hiram’s seamen brings 420 talents of gold from Ophir (vv. 26–28). The chapter that opened with God’s heart closes with a shipment of gold.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 says Solomon made no slaves of Israelites, yet 5:13 records forced labour drafted from all Israel. The note on verses 20-28 sets out how the two fit.
verseByVerse.examples: Pharaoh's daughter is moved out of the city of David out of a genuine scruple about holiness, carefully applied; and it does not touch the marriage, which is where the danger lay.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel— their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day. But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen. These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work. But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo. Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house. King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon. And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom’s order and wealth are set out without comment: Canaanites in permanent bondage, Pharaoh’s daughter moved but not given up, the feasts faithfully kept, and gold arriving by the ton. Each item is real, and each will look different by chapter 11.

Whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction. The permanent labour force is drawn from the peoples Israel never drove out. To devote to destruction (herem) was to hand a people over wholly to God in judgment, and the phrase reaches back to Joshua and Judges. The conquest was never completed: Judges opens with a long list of what each tribe failed to take, and God said at Bochim, “they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you” (Judges 2:3). Two chapters from now, Solomon is worshipping their gods.

But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. This seems to contradict 5:13, where “King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel”. The two fit honestly: Canaanites were in permanent bondage, while Israelites were drafted in turns for a particular project and otherwise served as soldiers, officials and commanders. In law the distinction holds. But the men who came to Rehoboam three chapters later did not feel it as a large one. Their word for it was yoke (12:4).

Pharaoh’s daughter went up from the city of David to her own house. This is a genuine scruple, carefully applied, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Chronicles gives Solomon’s reason in his own words: “My wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy” (2 Chronicles 8:11). The ark had come into the city of David, the ground it touched was holy, and a woman who worshipped the gods of Egypt should not live on it. That is neither hypocrisy nor nothing. But it does not touch the marriage: he saw that a foreign wife and the holiness of God did not fit together, and solved it by moving her to another address. The law’s concern was never the address: “You shall not intermarry with them… for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The danger was in the house, not in the neighbourhood.

Care aimed to one side. It is a recognisable kind of care: real, sincerely costly, and aimed slightly to one side of the actual problem. We still rearrange the furniture around a sin rather than give it up. Chapter 11 shows where Solomon’s arrangement led.

Three times a year. The law required all Israel’s males to appear before the LORD at the three pilgrim feasts, Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths (Deuteronomy 16:16), and Solomon keeps them. His outward worship never lapses, which is part of what makes chapter 11 so sobering.

King Solomon built a fleet of ships. Israel builds ships and has to borrow sailors, as it borrowed woodcutters. The fleet is Solomon’s and the port lies in Edomite territory his father conquered, but the seamen come from Tyre: the Phoenicians were the great sailors of the ancient world, and Israel was not. Hiram, having just complained about his twenty cities, sends his crews anyway. The alliance survives the argument.

And they went to Ophir. Ophir lay somewhere down the Red Sea, in Arabia or Africa or further; nobody knows, and it became a byword for the finest gold (Job 22:24; Psalm 45:9). Four hundred and twenty talents is something in the order of fourteen tons. The chapter that began with God saying “My eyes and my heart will be there for all time” ends with a shipment of gold, and the next chapter is about what came in every year.

Not slaves but heirs. Solomon made the Canaanites who remained in the land his permanent labour force. The greater Son of David once met a Canaanite woman and granted her plea for her daughter, praising her faith (Matthew 15:22–28), and through the gospel he brings people of every nation not into bondage but into his family, “fellow heirs, members of the same body” (Ephesians 3:6).

Was it right to make the Canaanites forced labourers? It was what Israel did instead of driving them out (Judges 1:28), and Scripture records it without approving it. The law did allow a distant city that surrendered to be put to forced labour (Deuteronomy 20:10–11), but the same law forbade oppressing the foreigner (Exodus 22:21), and in Christ, Paul says, there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

Numbers in Kings and Chronicles. The officers number 550 here and 250 in 2 Chronicles 8:10; the two lists probably count different ranks (see the note on 5:13–18). The gold from Ophir, 420 talents here and 450 in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 8:18), may differ by the cost of the voyage, or by a copying slip.
verseByVerse.note: A talent weighed roughly 30 kilograms (about 75 pounds).

9.theology:
Eyes, heart, and a warning (vv. 1-7). God appears to Solomon a second time, and 11:9 will say that this made his fall worse. He grants the prayer of chapter 8 and promises that his heart, as well as his eyes, will be on the house: he is not indifferent to the house he will later judge. Then he names in advance the one sin to avoid, other gods, and holds up David's integrity of heart, the undivided heart Solomon himself called for in his benediction. For the third time (chapters 6, 8 and here), we are told that the building guarantees nothing by itself.

The exiles' question, answered (vv. 8-9). For the first readers, who had seen the house burned (2 Kings 25:9-13), the question was whether God was finished or defeated. The answer rules out both: the ruin is his judgment on a people who walked away from the God who brought them out of Egypt. And there is a mercy in that answer. A God who has been defeated cannot help you; a God who has judged you can, and there is somebody to repent to. The condition of verse 4 is finally met by one King only. Jesus kept it, and bore the judgment the faithless deserved, so that the throne promised here is his and the way back is open (Acts 2:30–36).

The accounts of a reign (vv. 10-28). The rest of the chapter reads like a ledger, and the writer lets each entry speak. Land that was God's gift, not the crown's to sell (Lev. 25:23), pays a bill and disappoints the friend who receives it: Hiram, who loved David, blessed the LORD and supplied every beam of the temple, ends his recorded dealings asking what kind of cities these are. The most generous friendship of the reign closes on a sour note, and the writer does nothing with it. A failure of the conquest four centuries old is solved by Pharaoh and received as a dowry: the deal with Egypt costs more than the goods. The peoples Israel never drove out become a labour force, as Judges warned they would become thorns and their gods a snare (Judg. 2:3). Israelites are spared that permanent bondage. Their own forced labour (5:13) was different in law, a turn of duty on a set project; but the men who came to Rehoboam had one word for it, and the word was yoke. A real scruple about holiness moves Pharaoh's daughter to another house but leaves the marriage itself untouched, and that was where the danger lay (Deut. 7:3-4). The feasts are kept, the alliance with Tyre survives, and the gold arrives.

Whatever Solomon desired to build (vv. 1, 19). Twice in one chapter the list grows: the house of the LORD, the king's house, the Millo, the wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, store cities, and the cities for his chariots and horsemen. A reign that began by asking God for an understanding mind is now summarised as a list of what the king wanted.
9.examples:
Then: When the building was finished, twenty years in, God appeared to the man who had built it and said that his eyes and his heart would be in that house for all time, and four verses later that if Israel went after other gods he would cast it out of his sight and leave it a heap of ruins that passers-by would ask questions about. Nearly four centuries later, people standing in the ash of it read that paragraph and found their own question written down in it.

Now: three things. Verse 3 and verse 7 belong together, and neither should be read without the other: God is not detached about the things he gives, and he will not be held hostage by them either. Second, verse 9 is the answer to the hardest question anybody asks in a national catastrophe, and notice the mercy hidden in it. (It is not a verdict on every private grief: Jesus refused to read every disaster as a judgment on the sufferer, Luke 13:1-5.) A God who has been defeated cannot help you. A God who has judged you can, and there is somebody to go back to. And third, verse 24, which is the uncomfortable one: Solomon took holiness seriously enough to move his wife out of a whole district over it, and the danger was never the district. It was a real scruple at real cost, aimed just to one side of the actual problem, which was the marriage itself, and chapter 11 records what came of it. The remedy is not sharper scruples but the undivided heart God himself gives by his Spirit, the very thing Solomon prayed for (8:58; Ezek. 36:26-27).

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD said to him, “I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.
keyVerse.note: God answers Solomon’s prayer and gives more than was asked: not only his eyes on the house but his heart. Yet four verses later the same God warns that this house can be cast out of his sight. Both sayings find their rest in Christ, in whom God’s name and heart have come to dwell among us in a temple that can never be destroyed for good (John 2:19–21).

9.reflection:
God appeared to Solomon twice, and still his heart drifted (vv. 2; 11:9). What spiritual privileges have you been given, and why do privileges on their own not keep a heart faithful?

God says his eyes and heart will be on the temple, then warns that he will cast it out of his sight if Israel turns to other gods (vv. 3, 7). What might Christians and churches be tempted to trust in place of a whole heart for God?

The answer to “Why has the LORD done thus?” is that Israel abandoned him (vv. 8–9). Why is it a mercy that God’s judgments have reasons? How does the cross show both his judgment and his mercy?

Solomon moved Pharaoh’s daughter to another house but kept the marriage (v. 24). Where are we tempted to rearrange things around a sin instead of dealing with it, and what would it look like to bring it honestly to Christ?

10.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Wealth
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions.<sup>2</sup>She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her.<sup>4</sup>And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,<sup>5</sup>the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.<sup>6</sup>And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom,<sup>7</sup>but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard.<sup>8</sup>Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!<sup>9</sup>Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness."<sup>10</sup>Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones.<sup>12</sup>And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day.<sup>13</sup>And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.<sup>14</sup>Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold,<sup>15</sup>besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land.<sup>16</sup>King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield.<sup>17</sup>And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.<sup>18</sup>The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold.<sup>19</sup>The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests,<sup>20</sup>while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom.<sup>21</sup>All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon.<sup>22</sup>For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.<sup>23</sup>Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.<sup>24</sup>And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind.<sup>25</sup>Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.<sup>26</sup>And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>28</sup>And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price.<sup>29</sup>A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with gold arriving from Ophir. Chapter 10 shows Solomon’s reign at its summit: his fame reaches the ends of the earth, and wealth pours into Jerusalem.

The message. God kept his promise to give Solomon wisdom, riches and honour, and through Solomon’s fame the name of the LORD reached the nations, as Solomon had prayed it would (8:41–43). A pagan queen came to test the reports, found that “the half was not told me”, and blessed the LORD for giving Israel a king to do justice. But the same glory, told in tones of wonder, quietly breaks the law for Israel’s kings. Splendour that God gave can still become the thing that draws a heart away from him.

Why it was said. The exiles who first read this had lost the gold, the throne and the temple (see the introduction). They needed to see both how high God had raised David’s son and why the summit was where the slide began: the law had warned of exactly these things.

How the chapter makes its case. The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame “concerning the name of the LORD”, comes with hard questions, and sees his wisdom, his house and his worship; she confesses that the reports fell short, blesses the LORD who loved Israel, exchanges gifts and goes home (vv. 1–13). Then comes the inventory: gold by the ton, golden shields, an ivory throne, curiosities from the Tarshish fleet, and the whole earth seeking Solomon’s wisdom (vv. 14–25). Last come chariots and horsemen, silver as common as stone, and a horse trade with Egypt (vv. 26–29). Two of the three things Deuteronomy 17 forbade a king to multiply are here told as achievements; the third opens chapter 11.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Jesus named this queen himself: she “came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 11:31). All she praised in Solomon is true of Christ without the shadow that follows. He is the wisdom of God; his throne does justice and righteousness for ever (Isaiah 9:7); and the nations bring him their gifts, from the wise men’s gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11) to the glory of the kings of the earth (Revelation 21:24). And where Solomon piled up gold and horses, the true King became poor for our sakes and rode into Jerusalem on a donkey.

For us. Come to Christ as the queen came to Solomon, with your hardest questions, and expect to find more than you were told. And hold God’s good gifts with open hands: they are given to be received with thanks and used for others, and they make poor masters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Half Was Not Told Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fame of Solomon’s God draws a pagan queen across the desert, and she goes home having blessed the LORD. She comes because of Solomon’s fame “concerning the name of the LORD”, with a great caravan and hard questions, and Solomon answers them all (vv. 1–3). She sees his wisdom, his house, his court and the burnt offerings at the temple, and it leaves her breathless (vv. 4–5). She admits she had not believed the reports, but the half was not told her, and she blesses the LORD who loved Israel and made Solomon king to do justice and righteousness (vv. 6–9). Gifts are exchanged, Hiram’s fleet brings almug wood for the temple and for harps, and she returns home (vv. 10–13).
verseByVerse.theology: She came a very long way on a rumour, and the rumour was not about the gold. What reached the ends of the earth was something about God. When God's people live under his blessing and worship him openly, others notice, and some come asking hard questions. That was always the purpose of Israel's blessing: that the nations might know his name.
verseByVerse.examples: She did not take the reports on trust; she came to see for herself, and was honest about how much she had doubted. Faith is not afraid of that kind of testing, and Christ invites it: come and see was Philip's answer to a doubting Nathanael (John 1:46). Those who come to see him honestly find more than they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her. And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her. And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard. Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness." Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones. And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day. And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A pagan queen, drawn by what she has heard of the LORD’s name, tests Solomon’s wisdom, finds it greater than every report, and blesses the LORD for giving Israel a king to do justice. The nations are beginning to come, as Solomon had prayed they would.

Concerning the name of the LORD. What drew her was not his wealth in the first place, nor even his wisdom on its own, but “the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD”. What travelled to the ends of the earth was something about God. That is exactly what Solomon asked for at the dedication, that God would hear the foreigner “in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name” (8:43), and here is a foreigner arriving because she has heard the name.

The queen of Sheba. Sheba is most probably in south-west Arabia, in the region of modern Yemen; Ethiopian tradition places her across the Red Sea in Africa, but the kingdom of Saba in Arabia is the better fit. That is a journey of some fifteen hundred miles across desert each way by camel: months of travel at enormous expense, on the strength of a report. Sheba grew rich on the incense and spice trade carried north by caravan, and Solomon’s new fleet on the Red Sea (9:26–28) reached into that trade, so the visit probably had commercial business in it too. The writer, though, names only what drew her: the name of the LORD.

To test him with hard questions. She is not a tourist. The word is the one for riddles, used of Samson’s riddle at his wedding feast (Judges 14:12), and testing a foreign king’s wisdom with hard questions seems to have been a recognised diplomatic contest. She has come to find out whether the reports are true. And she “told him all that was on her mind”, in Hebrew all that was in her heart: she brought hard questions and ended up telling him everything she was carrying. That is what happens when someone turns out to be worth talking to.

His burnt offerings… there was no more breath in her. Read the list of what she saw in its order: wisdom, house, table, officials, servants, cupbearers, and last “his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD”. What overwhelmed her in the end was the worship. The writer’s phrase for the effect is physical: it knocked the breath out of her.

The half was not told me. She is honest about her own scepticism, which is why her testimony counts. She did not take the reports on trust; she came to check, and found more than she had refused to believe. And she envies not the king but his servants, the men who stand before him every day and listen. She has had one visit, and she can see what a lifetime of it would be worth.

Blessed be the LORD your God. Verse 9 gets three things right that Israel keeps forgetting. First, she does not congratulate Solomon on his achievements but credits God, with a warm word: he “has delighted in you”. Second, “because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king”. She has seen that the king is a gift to the nation and not the other way round, as David knew at his best: “the LORD had established him king over Israel, and… he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:12). Third, and hardest: “that you may execute justice and righteousness.” She names the purpose of the throne. Not glory, building, wealth or empire, but right done for people, as when David “administered justice and equity to all his people” (2 Samuel 8:15).

The visitor sees the point. There is something uncomfortable here, and it is meant to be felt. A foreigner, only visiting, looks at the gold, the table and the servants in their livery and names the point of it all better than the people living in it. Keep verse 9 in mind for two chapters: when the north comes to Rehoboam asking for relief from a yoke, what they get is the threat of scorpions (12:14).

So she turned and went back to her own land. The writer does not tell us what she did with any of it. There is no record of her worshipping the LORD, or of Sheba turning to him. She came, she saw, she blessed God, and she went back across the desert.

Something greater than Solomon. A thousand years later, when scribes and Pharisees demanded a sign, Jesus brought her up: “The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Luke 11:31; compare Matthew 12:42). She had no Scriptures, no covenant, no prophets and no invitation, only a rumour about the name of a God she did not worship, and she crossed a desert to find out whether it was true. They stood in front of the wisdom of God himself, come in a human body, and asked him for a miracle first.

All she praised, without the shadow. Everything the queen praised in Solomon is true of Christ without the shadow that falls across chapter 11. He is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). His is the throne that truly does justice and righteousness for ever (Isaiah 9:7), and happy indeed are the servants who stand before him and hear his words. A psalm of Solomon pictured kings of Sheba bringing gifts to the king’s son (Psalm 72:10, 15), and Isaiah saw those from Sheba bringing gold and frankincense to Zion (Isaiah 60:6); many Christians have heard an echo of that when wise men from the east laid gold and frankincense before the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11).

The sceptic who crossed a desert. Our culture tends to treat religion as a private preference, inherited like an accent or chosen like a hobby, and so not the sort of thing anyone would cross a desert to check. The queen did not believe the reports, and she was right not to take them on trust; but she thought the question mattered enough to spend months finding out. Pascal divided people into those who have found God and serve him, those who have not found him and are seeking, and those who neither seek nor find; the first two, he said, are reasonable, the third foolish. The great modern obstacle to faith is often not doubt but a shrug. Honest doubt goes and looks, and Scripture makes room for it: “You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). And here is the surprise. Most of us suspect that if we looked closely, God would turn out smaller than we had been told. The queen found the opposite, and so do those who bring their hard questions to Christ: the half was not told them.

Uncertain wording. Almug wood (vv. 11–12; “algum” in 2 Chronicles 9:10–11) has not been identified. It was a rare, fine timber brought from Ophir and used for the temple and for musical instruments; red sandalwood and a kind of juniper are among the guesses, but no one knows. The writer’s own comment is that none like it was ever seen again.
verseByVerse.note: Sheba was probably in south-west Arabia (modern Yemen).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–25 — Silver Was Not Considered as Anything
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s wealth is described at its height, with wonder, and with small signs that riches are beginning to outrank wisdom. Gold comes in at 666 talents a year, besides trade and tribute (vv. 14–15). Five hundred shields of beaten gold hang in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (vv. 16–17); a great ivory throne overlaid with gold and lined with lions has no equal in any kingdom (vv. 18–20); every drinking vessel is gold, and silver counts for nothing (v. 21). The Tarshish fleet brings gold, ivory and curiosities every three years (v. 22). Solomon excels all kings “in riches and in wisdom”, and the whole earth comes to hear the wisdom God gave him, bringing gifts year by year (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything here is stated as glory and the writer stages it beautifully. Yet the law about Israel's kings had said nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17), the last of its three prohibitions, and here it is described in a tone of wonder.
verseByVerse.examples: Abundance changes what we notice. When enough comes in, things that once cost something stop registering at all, and gratitude goes quiet. David once refused to offer God what cost him nothing; a generation later silver was not counted. The remedy is not to despise God's gifts but to keep counting them as gifts, and to give in a way that still costs something.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield. And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests, while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom. All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom. And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind. Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s wealth reaches its height, and every item is told with wonder; but riches now stand before wisdom, and the gold of this chapter will be carried off within a generation.

666 talents of gold. The yearly gold was something over twenty tons, and that was only the first item: the trade, the tolls, the tribute and the revenue of the provinces all came on top of it (v. 15).

Shields of beaten gold. Five hundred shields of beaten gold (some 600 shekels in each of the large ones) hung in the great pillared hall. Gold is soft, so these were not for fighting but for ceremony, carried in procession and displayed on the walls. Keep them in mind, because the writer comes back for them. Five years after Solomon dies, Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem: “He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made” (14:26). Rehoboam replaces them with bronze and has the guard carry them before him into the house of the LORD and back to the guardroom afterwards (14:27–28): the same ceremony, in cheaper metal, with everyone pretending not to notice.

A great ivory throne. Six steps, twelve lions, a rounded back, ivory and gold. The lion is the emblem of Judah: “Judah is a lion’s cub… he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9), and twelve of them, probably for the tribes, line the way up. It is a magnificent object, and it is also, precisely, a chair for judging in, the seat in the Hall of Judgment (7:7). The man on it had asked for an understanding mind to judge God’s people (3:9).

Silver was not considered as anything. This is more than an exchange rate. It says what happens to a scale of value when enough comes in: the second most precious metal in the world stopped registering. Fifty shekels of silver once bought David the threshing floor where the temple now stands, and he insisted on paying rather than take it free: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). That was a real price to a real man once. Now the metal is not counted.

Ivory, apes, and peacocks. The apes and peacocks give the game away. Gold, silver and ivory are wealth; these are curiosities, fetched on three-year voyages because they are interesting to have. “Ships of Tarshish” were large ocean-going trading ships, named after a far western port.

In riches and in wisdom. At Gibeon the order was the other way round: Solomon asked for wisdom and not for riches, and God said, “I give you also what you have not asked” (3:13). Riches came second, as an addition. Here the summary reads “in riches and in wisdom”. It may be nothing, but it is the sort of small thing this writer does.

His wisdom, which God had put into his mind. The credit is still given correctly: the writer will not let the wisdom become the man’s own property. And horses are now arriving as tribute year by year (v. 25); the next verses say where the rest came from.

Treasure that cannot be carried off. Solomon’s gold did not outlast his son’s fifth year. The Son of David who was greater than Solomon told his followers, “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal” (Matthew 6:19), and he himself is the treasure no Shishak can take: an inheritance “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).

Is this the 666 of Revelation? The number turns up again at the end of the Bible: “let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666” (Revelation 13:18). Some readers connect the two, and there is a grim aptness to it, since this chapter is the inventory of a man’s accumulation. But honesty requires saying that the writer of Kings makes nothing of the number; he records it as an annual revenue figure and moves straight on to shields. Nor does Revelation cite this verse or allude to Solomon anywhere in the passage. A reader may notice the figure; nothing should be built on it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “peacocks” (v. 22) is uncertain, and some versions translate it baboons; the cargo’s other items are clear. Where Tarshish lay is also not certain, though a port in Spain is the most common view, and Ophir, the source of gold, has been placed in Arabia, East Africa and India.
verseByVerse.note: 666 talents of gold is roughly 20 to 25 tons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–29 — And Horses Were Imported from Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with chariots, silver and horses, the very things the law told Israel’s king not to pile up. Solomon gathers 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen in his chariot cities and in Jerusalem (v. 26). Silver becomes as common as stone, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore (v. 27). His traders import horses and chariots from Egypt and Kue and sell them on to the kings of the Hittites and of Syria (vv. 28–29). The writer makes no comment, but a reader who knows Deuteronomy 17 hears the warning, and the next verse names the third thing the law forbade.
verseByVerse.theology: Four verses, and they complete the breaking of the law for kings. The law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, and nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:16-17). Horses, Egypt, and silver like stones, in the space of one paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples: Only one prohibition is left, and its reason is the king's heart: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. The very next verse in the book shows what became of it. Outward success and inward drift can run side by side for years, which is why the heart needs guarding most when things go well.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price. A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with chariots, horses from Egypt and silver as common as stone: two of the three things the law forbade Israel’s king to multiply, told as achievements, with the third waiting in the next verse.

And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. Fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, in cities built to house them, which chapter 9 listed. (Chapter 4:26 gives forty thousand stalls, where Chronicles has four thousand (2 Chronicles 9:25); the smaller figure fits fourteen hundred chariots, and most think a numeral was miscopied in Kings.)

The law about kings. The law about Israel’s kings is a short paragraph with three prohibitions in it, and this is the first: “Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, ‘You shall never return that way again’” (Deuteronomy 17:16). Silver as common as stone breaks the third, two clauses later: “nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold” (Deuteronomy 17:17).

Solomon’s import of horses was from Egypt and Kue. Kue is Cilicia, in the south-east of modern Turkey. And the text says outright that the horses came from Egypt. The law’s concern was not economic. Israel came out of Egypt: that was the founding act, the event the calendar was reckoned from, the event Solomon’s own prayer went back to again and again. The danger was that a king with a taste for cavalry would open a road back to the country God had brought them out of, with trade running the wrong way down it. That is exactly what has happened: a standing commercial relationship with Egypt for military horses, run by the king’s own traders.

Exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria. The last verse makes Solomon the middleman, the broker in the arms trade of the region, buying chariots and horses from Egypt and selling them on to the Hittites and the Syrians at a margin. Within a century or so the Syrians will besiege Samaria, and a king of Israel will hear of his people eating their own children (2 Kings 6:24–29). Syria’s kings are being supplied with cavalry by the king of Israel, out of Egypt, for cash.

Wonder and warning. Every item in these twenty-nine verses is glorious. The queen is genuinely awestruck and her praise is good theology; the wisdom is real and God gave it; the throne is magnificent and the trade skilful; and the reputation reaches the ends of the earth, as verse 1 says, “concerning the name of the LORD”. Yet two of the law’s three prohibitions are here, told as achievements: horses from Egypt (vv. 26, 28), and silver and gold beyond counting (vv. 14–27). The remaining one sits between the other two in the same law, and its reason is the king’s heart: “And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). The next verse in the book is “Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh” (11:1). The writer does not say so. He puts chapter 10 beside chapter 11 and lets the reader make the connection.

The King who kept the law. The law about kings ends with what a king should do instead: write out a copy of the law, read it all his life, and not lift up his heart above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Only one son of David has kept that paragraph whole. He had nowhere to lay his head; though he was rich, he became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9), and he rode into Jerusalem on a donkey rather than a war horse (Matthew 21:5). The glory of chapter 10 is real, and it fades; his does not.

Good gifts, piled up. Nothing in this chapter is evil in itself: wealth, skill, trade and fame were all God’s gifts. The danger lay in the piling up, which slowly changes what a heart trusts and loves. Ask what you are quietly accumulating, and whether it is still serving God and others or has begun to serve you.

10.theology:
The name of the LORD reaching the nations (vv. 1-9). The chapter opens with the answer to Solomon's prayer for the foreigner (8:43). What crossed the desert was not the wealth but a report about God, and what the queen found most breathtaking was the worship at his house. Her blessing in verse 9 is a small summary of what kingship in Israel was for: God's delight, God's love for his people, and a throne that exists for justice and righteousness. It is good theology from an outsider, and it quietly judges the insiders, as Jesus' use of her judges his own generation (Matt. 12:42).

Glory that the law forbade (vv. 14-29). The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 named three dangers: many horses (and the road back to Egypt), many wives, and excessive silver and gold. This chapter describes two of them with wonder, and the writer adds no criticism. He lets the arrangement speak, and the next verse names the third. Scripture often works like this: a thing can look like blessing at the time and be the beginning of a fall. Success is not proof of faithfulness, and the reckoning does not always come at once.

Why the road to Egypt mattered (v. 28). The law's worry about horses was not mainly military or economic. Egypt was the house of slavery God had brought his people out of, and the exodus was the founding act of the nation, the event its calendar and its worship looked back to. A king who opened a standing trade route back there for cavalry was undoing, by way of trade, the rescue that had made Israel a nation. The commandment had given the reason in God's own words: You shall never return that way again. Solomon did not go back to Egypt as a slave. He went back as a customer, which is harder to notice and in some ways more dangerous. Many of the drifts that take God's people back to what he rescued them from look like this: not a dramatic return, but a profitable arrangement.

Gold and bronze. The golden shields of verses 16-17 quietly point to what is coming. Within five years of Solomon's death they are gone to Egypt, and Rehoboam's bronze copies are carried in the same procession as if nothing had happened (14:26-28). Glory that rests on piled-up wealth can be carried off; the outward form of religion can continue after the reality has gone. That is a warning for churches as well as kings.

Gifts that slip out of their place. Wisdom was God's gift, and the writer says so even at the height of the display (v. 24). But the order of verse 23, riches before wisdom, and the silver that no longer counted, hint at what abundance does to a heart. The gifts are not evil; the danger is that they stop being received as gifts.

The greater Solomon. Israel had to wait for a King who would keep the whole law for kings (Deut. 17:14-20) and, though rich, become poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is the wisdom of God in person (1 Corinthians 1:24), the King whose throne truly does justice and righteousness (Isaiah 9:7), and the one Solomon’s glory could only point toward. The number in verse 14, 666 talents of gold, sometimes gets linked to the number of the beast (Rev. 13:18), but the real contrast in this chapter is simpler: the glory of a man who accumulated, against the glory of the Son who gave himself away.
10.examples:
Then: A queen crossed fifteen hundred miles of desert on the strength of a rumour about the name of a God who was not hers, because she wanted to find out. What took her breath in the end was not the gold or the throne but the king's burnt offerings at the house of the LORD.

Now: Three things. Verse 9 stings: the outsider on a single visit named the purpose of the whole institution more plainly than anybody inside it, and people at a distance often see what a thing is for more clearly than those running it. Second, silver was not considered as anything is a warning about what abundance does to our sense of what things are worth. And third, the shape of the chapter: nothing in it is condemned and much of it is against the law. Remember that in seasons when everything is going extremely well. Our safety then is not our own record but the Son of David who kept the law whole for us, and whose Spirit keeps our hearts from turning.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness.
keyVerse.note: A pagan queen names what the whole chapter’s glory was for: a king given out of God’s love for his people, to do justice and righteousness. The gold, the throne and the horses that follow drift from that purpose. Only Christ, the Son of David greater than Solomon, fills it perfectly, reigning for ever “with justice and with righteousness” (Isaiah 9:7).

10.reflection:
The queen of Sheba came because she heard of Solomon’s fame “concerning the name of the LORD” (v. 1). What do people around you hear about God through his people? What would make that report more true?

She did not believe the reports until she came and saw, and then said, “the half was not told me” (v. 7). How might her honest searching encourage someone with hard questions about Christ, and how did Jesus use her example (Luke 11:31)?

The queen saw that God made Solomon king to “execute justice and righteousness” (v. 9). Where has God placed you to serve others, and how might the good things he has given you pull you away from that purpose?

Gold, silver and horses are told as glories, yet the law had forbidden a king to pile them up (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). What blessings in your life could slowly turn your heart, and how does Christ, who became poor for our sakes, set us free from them?

11.title: Solomon's Heart Turned Away
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women,<sup>2</sup>from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love.<sup>3</sup>He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart.<sup>4</sup>For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.<sup>5</sup>For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.<sup>6</sup>So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done.<sup>7</sup>Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice<sup>10</sup>and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded.<sup>11</sup>Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant.<sup>12</sup>Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son.<sup>13</sup>However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom.<sup>15</sup>For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom<sup>16</sup>(for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom).<sup>17</sup>But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad still being a little child.<sup>18</sup>They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land.<sup>19</sup>And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.<sup>20</sup>And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh.<sup>21</sup>But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country."<sup>22</sup>But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me depart."<sup>23</sup>God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah.<sup>24</sup>And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus.<sup>25</sup>He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.<sup>26</sup>Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king.<sup>27</sup>And this was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father.<sup>28</sup>The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.<sup>29</sup>And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country.<sup>30</sup>Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces.<sup>31</sup>And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes<sup>32</sup>(but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel),<sup>33</sup>because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did.<sup>34</sup>Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes.<sup>35</sup>But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes.<sup>36</sup>Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name.<sup>37</sup>And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel.<sup>38</sup>And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.<sup>39</sup>And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'"<sup>40</sup>Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.<sup>41</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?<sup>42</sup>And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.<sup>43</sup>And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 ended with gold, silver and horses, two of the three things the law forbade Israel’s king to multiply (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Chapter 11 opens with the third, many wives, and closes Solomon’s story.

The message. A heart can be lost without one dramatic decision. Solomon, warned twice by God in person, let his foreign wives turn his heart to their gods one courtesy at a time, until the wisest king who ever lived was building shrines on the hill facing the temple. God’s judgment is real: the kingdom will be torn, and adversaries rise on every side. But God’s promise is stronger than Solomon’s failure: for David’s sake one tribe is kept, and a lamp is left burning in Jerusalem.

Why it was said. The exiles were asking how the kingdom had come apart, and whether the house of David still mattered (see the introduction). Here they saw where the ruin began, in a divided heart at the very top, and that God’s promise to David had outlived it.

How the chapter makes its case. First the sin: in his old age Solomon’s foreign wives turn his heart after their gods, and he builds them high places (vv. 1–8). Then the verdict: the LORD, who had appeared to him twice, will tear the kingdom from him, yet not in his days and not all of it, for David’s sake (vv. 9–13). Then the adversaries raised up from David’s old wars, Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus (vv. 14–25). Then the servant: the prophet Ahijah tears a new garment into twelve and gives Jeroboam ten pieces; Solomon tries to kill him, and he flees to Egypt (vv. 26–40). Last, the closing formula (vv. 41–43).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the need it exposes. Solomon proves that wisdom, privilege and even God’s own appearing cannot keep a human heart wholly true; the need is for a King whose heart never turns. Jesus is that Son of David, “something greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42), wholly true to his Father all the way to the cross. The lamp God kept burning for David’s sake (v. 36) burned low through exile to a carpenter’s family, and the angel said of Mary’s son, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). And where Solomon’s marriages to the nations drew him after their gods, Christ gave himself for a bride gathered from every nation (Ephesians 5:25; Revelation 5:9), and draws her to the one true God.

For us. No one is past drifting: Solomon fell when he was old, after the best start any king ever had. Watch the small concessions, keep coming back to the Lord, and do not trust knowledge to hold your heart. But take heart as well: God’s faithfulness to his promise outlasts our failures, and those who belong to Christ are kept by his wholehearted obedience, not by their own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Now King Solomon Loved Many Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s heart is turned away from the LORD, not in a moment of open rebellion but through his love for many foreign wives and his courtesy to their gods. He loves women from the very nations the law said would turn Israel’s heart after their gods, and clings to them (vv. 1–2). With seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines, his heart is turned in his old age, and it is no longer wholly true to the LORD as David’s was (vv. 3–4). He goes after Ashtoreth and Milcom and does what is evil in the LORD’s sight (vv. 5–6). He builds high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem, and does the same for all his foreign wives (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the last of the three prohibitions in the law about Israel's kings, and its reason is the king's heart: lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Chapter 10 broke the other two.
verseByVerse.examples: Hearts are rarely lost in one decision. They are lost in accommodations, each reasonable on its own, made for people we love or need. It is worth asking, gently and with the gospel in view, what has quietly been given a place beside God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love. He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart. For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done. Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem. And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s foreign marriages did exactly what the law said they would: in his old age his wives turned his heart after their gods, and the wisest king who ever lived built shrines for idols facing the temple.

Along with the daughter of Pharaoh. She is named first, and the writer has been preparing for this. She has been in the account since 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple; she was given a house of her own (7:8) and moved out of the city of David for reasons of holiness (9:24): four flat mentions with no comment attached. Here is the comment.

You shall not enter into marriage with them. The writer quotes the law from Deuteronomy 7:3–4, including its reason, and the reason is never about blood or nationality: “surely they will turn away your heart after their gods.” It is a warning about worship, and the danger comes through the home. The passage has been misused, so it should be said plainly: Rahab of Jericho married into Israel and stands in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:5); Ruth was a Moabite, from one of the nations named in verse 1, and became David’s great-grandmother; Uriah was a Hittite and one of David’s mighty men. What made the difference was not ancestry but which God they had come to.

Solomon clung to these in love. To cling, or hold fast, is what Deuteronomy asks of Israel towards God: “You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him” (Deuteronomy 10:20). The devotion that belonged to God went to these women.

He had 700 wives, who were princesses. Seven hundred princesses are not seven hundred romances. Each is a treaty sealing an alliance with a neighbouring royal house, as the daughter of Pharaoh was: the many wives are his foreign policy. That makes it worse, not better, for a man who marries a princess to secure an alliance must let her worship her own gods, or the alliance is insulted. Every one of those marriages carried that obligation, and verse 8 shows Solomon meeting it.

And his wives turned away his heart. The writer reports the outcome in the law’s own words. Deuteronomy said of the king, “lest his heart turn away” (17:17); this verse says “his wives turned away his heart”. The law said how it would happen, and the history records it happening.

When Solomon was old. Verse 4 holds three things, and each matters. The first is when. Not in the reckless years, but at the end: after Gibeon, the temple, the dedication prayer and a second appearing of God. He had every advantage a man could have, for decades, and went wrong at the end. There is no age at which a person is past this, and the drift can begin in the part of life that looks safest. That is a warning, not a sentence hanging over every believer who fears growing cold. The same Scriptures promise that “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), and that God is “able to keep you from stumbling” (Jude 24). The way to be kept is not to lean on past advantages but to keep coming back to him, and a heart troubled by its own coldness is already being drawn near.

His heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God. The second is the phrase itself. The word is shalem: whole, complete, undivided, sharing its root with Solomon’s own name. He used it himself on the greatest day of his life, standing before the finished temple with the glory of God inside it: “Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments” (8:61). The writer waits three chapters and then takes the word off him. He does not call Solomon false or apostate. Solomon kept the feasts, the temple stood and the sacrifices went up. What he lost was the undividedness: his heart had more than one thing in it, and he had told the nation that would not do.

As was the heart of David his father. The third is the comparison, and a reader fresh from 2 Samuel may find it hard: David committed adultery, arranged a murder and failed to act when his daughter was raped. So what is being compared?
