Not sinlessness. The measure in this book is single: whether a king served the LORD alone or went after other gods. On that measure the difference is total. David never worshipped another god or built a shrine to one. Everything he did wrong he did as a man who belonged to the LORD, and when he was confronted he broke and said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13), and wrote Psalm 51. Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech facing the temple. This is not a whitewash of David but the distinction the whole book runs on: every king who follows is measured against an adulterer and a murderer, because whatever else he was, he had one God.

Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and… Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. Ashtoreth (Astarte) was the Canaanite goddess of fertility and war, the goddess of Sidon. Milcom was the national god of Ammon; verse 7 calls him Molech, the name the law links with the offering of children: “Any one of the people of Israel… who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death” (Leviticus 20:2). Chemosh was the god of Moab. The writer calls them abominations and does not soften it.

Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. The phrase appears here for the first time in Kings. From here to the end of 2 Kings it will be stamped on king after king until it becomes the drumbeat of the whole history, and the first king it is used of in these books is the wisest king who ever lived, who built the temple.

On the mountain east of Jerusalem. A high place was an open-air shrine, usually on raised ground, with an altar and often a standing stone or sacred pole. The mountain east of Jerusalem is the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley: from the temple courts a worshipper could look up and see them. They were still there three hundred years later, when Josiah destroyed them: “And the king defiled the high places that were east of Jerusalem, to the south of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites” (2 Kings 23:13). Still standing, and still called Solomon’s.

And so he did for all his foreign wives. How it happened should be stated exactly, because it is not what most people imagine. There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD, abolishes the priesthood or declares for Ashtoreth. He builds his wives their shrines, and each is a courtesy. A princess arrives from Moab as part of a treaty and needs somewhere to worship; refusing would insult her father. So a high place goes up, then another for the Ammonite, and verse 8 says he did it “for all his foreign wives”. One reasonable concession at a time, each defensible on its own, and at the end the hill facing the house of God is covered in altars and the king is going up to them. That is how a heart stops being wholly true: not by a decision, but by a series of arrangements nobody would have called a decision.

The Bridegroom whose heart did not turn. Solomon loved brides from the nations, and they drew him after their gods. Christ also loves a bride from every nation, “ransomed… from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9), but the drawing runs the other way: he “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25) to bring her home to God, and his heart was never divided for a moment, not in the wilderness, not in Gethsemane, not on the cross.

Wasn’t Solomon simply being tolerant? To modern eyes this can look like the most attractive thing he ever did: a husband respecting his wife’s faith, a capital becoming plural and hospitable. The writer calls it evil. Not because Solomon let others worship, but because he went after their gods himself (v. 5), and a heart pledged to one God came, for good reasons each time, to belong to several. Nor were the gods on that hill harmless symbols of diversity: Molech, as the law knew him, was offered children. Every age has a respectable pantheon whose gods ask for sacrifices: success takes the evenings that belonged to the family, comfort takes the courage to speak, approval takes the truth. Tolerance between neighbours is a real good, and Christians should defend it; a heart with room for every god is a divided one. The God who in Christ gave himself wholly for us may rightly ask for a whole heart in return, and gives the Spirit who makes it whole.

Does the Bible approve of Solomon’s many wives? No. Scripture records polygamy without commending it. God’s pattern from the beginning is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus goes back to that beginning (Matthew 19:4–6); the law for kings forbade exactly this multiplying of wives (Deuteronomy 17:17); and almost every household with several wives in the Old Testament, from Jacob’s to David’s, is shown full of rivalry and grief. Ancient royal harems could be very large, and the writer gives the numbers to show how far the king had gone.

Does the ban on foreign wives apply to Christians? The danger named is that “surely they will turn away your heart after their gods” (v. 2), and the principle carries over: a believer is free to marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39; compare 2 Corinthians 6:14). It is about faith, not race. And a believer already married to an unbeliever is not told to leave, but to stay and live faithfully if the unbelieving spouse is willing (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

Was Solomon saved? Scripture does not say whether he repented. Some take Ecclesiastes as the reflection of an old king who came back to God, and the Lord had loved him from birth (2 Samuel 12:24–25); others see in his end a warning of how far a gifted man can fall. The text gives no verdict on his soul, and we should not claim more than it says. Its plain lesson is that his heart was turned away (v. 4), and that even wisdom does not keep a heart that will not stay near God.

Why does Chronicles say nothing about this? Its account of Solomon (2 Chronicles 1–9) leaves out the foreign wives and the high places altogether. That is not a denial: Chronicles was written later, for readers who already had Kings, and concentrates on the temple and David’s line, which the returned exiles needed in order to rebuild. Nehemiah, from the same period, names Solomon’s sin outright: “foreign women made even him to sin” (Nehemiah 13:26). The two books choose different things to tell; they do not disagree about what happened.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 names Milcom as the god of the Ammonites, and verse 7 names Molech; both names seem to come from the Hebrew word for king (melek). Here the writer appears to use them for the same Ammonite god, but scholars debate whether the two names always mean the same deity elsewhere in the Old Testament.
verseByVerse.note: Chemosh was the god of Moab; Molech (Milcom) the god of Ammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–25 — Because He Had Appeared to Him Twice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD answers Solomon’s unfaithfulness with judgment tempered by mercy. He is angry, because Solomon had been warned twice in person (vv. 9–10). He will tear the kingdom from him and give it to his servant, yet not in his days and not all of it, “for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem” (vv. 11–13). Then the judgment begins, through adversaries raised up out of David’s old wars: Hadad the Edomite, a royal survivor who grew up at Pharaoh’s court and went home once David and Joab were dead (vv. 14–22), and Rezon, who seized Damascus and loathed Israel all Solomon’s days (vv. 23–25). The rest Solomon once spoke of is gone.
verseByVerse.theology: Who had appeared to him twice. God did not only send a prophet; he appeared to Solomon himself, twice, and told him the exact thing to avoid. The more light we are given, the more seriously our turning from it is taken.
verseByVerse.examples: Judgment here does not come out of nowhere. Old wars, old grievances and men who had waited a lifetime become the instruments God uses. Sin's consequences often travel a long road before they arrive, and that is a reason to deal with it early, while the way back is open.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is angry with Solomon, and his anger is all the heavier because he had appeared to him twice and had warned him against this very sin.

Because his heart had turned away. The verb is the one used three times just before: the wives “turned away his heart” (vv. 2–4). God’s anger is not a flash of temper. It is the jealousy of covenant love towards a man who has given his heart elsewhere, the anger Moses warned of if Israel’s sons were turned away to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:4).

Who had appeared to him twice. Now we see why chapter 9 bothered to say “a second time” (9:2): the writer laid that fact down so that it would make the charge heavier here. God did not leave this man to work it out for himself. He came in person, once at Gibeon to a young king who asked for an understanding mind, and once when the building was finished, and both times he said the same thing.

And had commanded him concerning this thing. This was not a general exhortation to godliness. God had named the specific sin in advance, and Solomon committed that one: “But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children… but go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land” (9:6–7). The more light a person has been given, the heavier the account (Luke 12:48).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant. Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son. However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will tear the kingdom from Solomon and give it to his servant, yet even in judgment he keeps his promise to David: not in Solomon’s days, and not all of it.

Since this has been your practice. This describes a settled state of affairs, not an incident: the high places had been there for years. And “my covenant” names what Solomon has broken: not a rule of etiquette but the bond on which his throne stood (9:4–7). The kingdom goes “to your servant”: not to a rival dynasty or a foreign power, but to one of his own officials, named in verse 26, the overseer of Solomon’s forced labour.

I will surely tear the kingdom from you. The Hebrew doubles the verb for certainty: tearing, I will tear. The word will be acted out with a torn cloak a few verses on (see the note on vv. 29–31).

For the sake of David your father. Then the mercy, and it is inside the judgment rather than instead of it, three times over: not in your days, not all of it, and one tribe kept. Solomon is spared the sight of it, and the reason has nothing to do with Solomon. God is honouring a promise made to a man, dead now some forty years, who wanted to build him a temple and was told no. One tribe out of twelve is a kindness, not a right. And God names the city he chose: the promise now hangs on a man and a place, both chosen by God.

Kept for another’s sake. That is the shape of the gospel too. Sinners are kept on account of another, the Son of David whose obedience is counted for them: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

Is it fair that the kingdom is torn from Solomon’s son? It was a judgment on Solomon’s house, softened for David’s sake, and Rehoboam lost the north by his own folly (12:13–15).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom. For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom (for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom).
verseByVerse.commentary:
God begins his judgment by raising up an adversary, a survivor of the royal house of Edom, whose hatred grew out of David’s war there.

The LORD raised up an adversary. The word is satan, in the ordinary Hebrew sense of an opponent, and the writer uses it three times in this section (vv. 14, 23, 25). What follows is a piece of history not recorded in 2 Samuel, whose consequences took a generation to arrive.

He was of the royal house in Edom. Hadad is a prince, so when he returns he has a claim Edomites would follow. Edom lay across the route to Ezion-geber, Solomon’s port on the Red Sea “in the land of Edom” (9:26), so a hostile prince there probably threatened the trade on which the wealth of chapter 10 depended.

Joab and all Israel remained there six months. Joab spent six months in Edom killing every male he could find. Second Samuel mentions the campaign in a verse about eighteen thousand Edomites struck down in the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13–14); here is what the occupation was like. It is recorded as fact, not commended, and it explains why Hadad hated Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad still being a little child. They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land. And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen. And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hadad, carried as a child out of the massacre, grows up honoured at Pharaoh’s court, a reminder that the Egypt Solomon married into kept friends on both sides.

Hadad still being a little child. A small boy is carried out of the slaughter by his father’s servants. The escape runs south through Midian and the wilderness of Paran to Egypt, the old refuge of fugitives. There he finds great favour: Pharaoh gives him a house, an allowance and land, and later his own wife’s sister in marriage, and Hadad’s son Genubath is raised among the sons of Pharaoh. Tahpenes the queen has not been identified in Egyptian records.

To Pharaoh king of Egypt. Egypt gave a daughter to Solomon (3:1) and a royal bride to Solomon’s enemy. The great power kept friends on both sides, and the alliance Solomon trusted was never as firm as it looked.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country." But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me depart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Comfort in Egypt cannot hold Hadad once David and Joab are dead: he goes home to trouble Israel.

What have you lacked with me? Pharaoh’s question is fair: Hadad had everything Egypt could give. But a homeland, a people and an old grievance are stronger than comfort. He waits until David and Joab are dead, and the writer gives him no speech about vengeance and no plan, only “Only let me depart.” How far Hadad succeeded is not said. Verse 25 says he did Israel harm, probably as a raider on the southern border; Edom did not throw off the rule of Judah until the days of King Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22).

verseByVerse.quote: God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah. And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus. He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second adversary, Rezon, seizes Damascus and becomes Israel’s enemy for the rest of Solomon’s reign: the rest God once gave on every side has come undone.

Rezon the son of Eliada. Rezon comes out of David’s Syrian campaign (2 Samuel 8:3–8) the way Hadad came out of the Edomite one. Damascus will be the great northern enemy for two centuries: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria in chapter 20, Naaman commands the army of Syria, and the Syrian wars run through the whole of 2 Kings. It starts here, with a man who escaped from David’s victory.

God also raised up as an adversary to him. Both adversaries come out of David’s wars; they were fugitives while Solomon built his temple, and they have been waiting all his life. The writer says twice that God raised them up: the judgment comes through real men whose causes go a long way back. God did not manufacture Solomon’s adversaries; he raised up the ones who were already there.

He loathed Israel and reigned over Syria. Early in the reign Solomon told Hiram, “the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune” (5:4). The word for adversary there is satan, the word used of Hadad and Rezon here. The peace he spoke of has quietly come undone: now there are adversaries to the south and to the north, and Rezon’s hatred lasts “all the days of Solomon”. Peace was God’s gift, and when the heart turned from the Giver, the gift went with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the servant who will take ten tribes, and Solomon’s answer is to try to kill him. Jeroboam, a capable Ephraimite whom Solomon set over the forced labour of the northern tribes, lifts up his hand against the king (vv. 26–28). The prophet Ahijah meets him alone in the open country, tears his own new garment into twelve pieces and gives him ten, a sign that God is tearing the kingdom (vv. 29–31). One tribe is kept for David’s sake, so that David may always have a lamp in Jerusalem (vv. 32–36). Jeroboam is offered a sure house like David’s, if he will walk as David did (vv. 37–39). Solomon seeks his life, and Jeroboam flees to Shishak in Egypt (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet tears a new cloak into twelve pieces on an empty road. A torn garment has stood for a torn kingdom before in this history, when Saul lost his throne (1 Sam. 15:27-28), and the sign is meant to be remembered.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam is offered David's own covenant terms. The offer is genuine and it is conditional, and chapter 12 records what he did with it. God's gifts come with his word attached, and they are kept by keeping close to that word.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king. And this was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father. The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third adversary comes from inside: Jeroboam, a gifted Ephraimite whom Solomon himself set over the forced labour of the northern tribes.

Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite. This adversary, Jeroboam, is an Israelite and a servant of the household. Ephraim was the leading tribe of the north, the tribe of Joshua, and had never been comfortable under a king from Judah. And his mother was “Zeruah, a widow”: a widow’s son from the north, as the writer said of Hiram the craftsman (7:14).

This was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. To lift up the hand against the king is to rebel. The writer does not describe the revolt; he tells how it began, in Solomon’s building works. While the king “closed up the breach of the city of David”, repairing the gaps in his capital’s defences, a breach was opening in his kingdom, and the young man he set to work there would lead the north through it.

He gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph. In hindsight the appointment is almost unbelievable. The man who will take ten tribes from Solomon’s son spent his formative years running the very thing they will break away over: the conscripted work gangs of the north. He knew the men, the quotas, what the levy cost a farming family, and what was said about the king when nobody from Jerusalem was listening. Solomon gave him that education himself, because he was good at his job.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country. Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces. And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet Ahijah tears his new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten: God himself is tearing the kingdom, and giving most of it to Solomon’s servant.

The prophet Ahijah the Shilonite. He is from Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood for centuries, where Hannah prayed and Samuel was called, and which God later destroyed as a warning to Judah (Jeremiah 7:12). He has put on a new garment for this, because he is about to destroy it. And the two of them are “alone in the open country”: the most dangerous conversation in the kingdom, about taking it from the king’s house, with no witnesses.

Tore it into twelve pieces. He rips his own new coat into twelve. Prophets in Israel acted their messages out, and this sign has a history. When Samuel turned to leave Saul, Saul caught at the hem of his robe and it tore, and Samuel said: “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you” (1 Samuel 15:27–28). That tear was an accident and this one is deliberate, and the sentence that follows is nearly the same sentence.

Take for yourself ten pieces. Jeroboam must stretch out his hands and take them, but the words that follow make clear who is giving: “Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes.” The kingdom is not Jeroboam’s to seize; it is God’s to give, and the giver sets the terms for keeping it (v. 38).

verseByVerse.quote: (but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel), because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One tribe is kept for David and for Jerusalem, and the reason for the tearing is stated: the people have forsaken the LORD for the gods of the nations.

But he shall have one tribe. The one tribe is kept again, for the same reasons again: David, and the city God chose. Twelve pieces, ten given and one kept, leaves one unaccounted for. The likeliest answer is that the one tribe is Judah with little Benjamin bound to it (12:21), while Simeon’s land had long lain inside Judah’s (Joshua 19:1); the numbers describe the map, not a count of tribes.

Because they have forsaken me. Notice that it is “they”. It is not only Solomon. The high places were public and had been there for years, and the nation had grown used to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes. But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes. Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David’s sake Solomon keeps the throne for life and his son keeps one tribe, so that David may always have a lamp before God in Jerusalem.

David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments. Even in judgment God speaks warmly of David. David was not sinless, and Kings itself remembers “the matter of Uriah the Hittite” (15:5). But he never went after other gods, and when he sinned he repented, so God counts him as one who kept his commandments (see the note on vv. 1–8). Solomon keeps the throne for his lifetime, and his son keeps a tribe, on David’s account.

That David my servant may always have a lamp. The word goes back a long way. David’s men used it of him on a battlefield when he grew weary and a giant nearly killed him: “You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel” (2 Samuel 21:17). Here God takes the word up as his own. He uses it again when Abijam reigns badly, “for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem” (15:4), and again when Judah deserves destruction: “the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (2 Kings 8:19).

A small light that does not go out. A lamp is a small thing: not a blaze, not a guarantee of prosperity, just a light God undertakes not to let go out. And it does not go out. It burns down to almost nothing, a king in a Babylonian prison at the end of 2 Kings, and then to a carpenter’s family in a village, where a child was born of whom the angel said, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). However low God’s cause seems to burn in a church or a life, the light he has promised to keep is kept.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel. And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offers Jeroboam a lasting dynasty on David’s own terms, if he will listen and walk as David did, and promises that David’s line will be humbled, but not for ever.

And I will take you. God chooses Jeroboam as he once chose David, and offers him more than he could have seized: to reign “over all that your soul desires.” The best of it is in verse 38, “I will be with you”, the presence promised to Joshua (Joshua 1:5) that made David what he was (2 Samuel 7:9). Everything is given to Jeroboam except what cannot be handed over: a heart that listens.

A sure house, as I built for David. This is the language of 2 Samuel 7: an enduring dynasty in the north on David’s own footing. It is not a consolation prize but everything, on the one condition that governs everything in this book: listen, walk in my ways, keep my statutes, “as David my servant did”. Hold it for one chapter: the first substantial thing Jeroboam does with his kingdom is make two golden calves (12:28).

But not forever. Even the sentence on David’s line has a limit written into it. The humbling would last through division and exile, but the prophets saw its end: one shepherd over a reunited people, “my servant David” (Ezekiel 37:22–24). It ended in Jesus, the Son of David who gathers the scattered into one flock (John 10:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s last recorded act is an attempt to kill the man God had named, and Jeroboam escapes to Egypt.

Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. Told that the kingdom will be torn from his son, he does not repent, remove the high places or speak to God. He orders a killing. He is doing what Saul did: told by a prophet that the kingdom was going to a neighbour, Saul spent the rest of his life trying to kill that neighbour, David. You cannot kill your way out of a word from God. Solomon of all people knew it, and he tried anyway.

To Shishak king of Egypt. Jeroboam goes where Hadad went as a boy and where the daughter of Pharaoh came from. Egypt has now sheltered two of Solomon’s three adversaries, and five years after his death Shishak comes up and takes everything in Jerusalem that is not nailed down (14:25–26). Shishak is the Pharaoh known from Egyptian records as Sheshonq I, who founded a new dynasty around 945 BC, which probably explains why Egypt, once bound to Solomon by marriage, now shelters his enemy. His victory inscription at Karnak lists towns in the land that he took on that later campaign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — So Solomon Slept with His Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon’s reign is closed with the formula that will mark every king to come. The rest of his acts, and his wisdom, are written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon (v. 41). He reigned forty years over all Israel, as David had (v. 42). He slept with his fathers, was buried in the city of David, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place (v. 43). The writer adds no verdict here, because the whole story has already given it: a reign that began with a request for wisdom and ended with a divided heart.
verseByVerse.theology: The formula arrives, and from here to the end of both books it will be repeated over king after king: the rest of his acts, the source, the years, the burial, the successor. Solomon is the first to receive it in full.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer, who has told us about the wisdom and the temple and the gold and the seven hundred wives, closes the account by pointing at a book we do not have and telling us there was more. Every life is larger than its record, and only God holds the full one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon’s reign is filed and closed like every reign to come, and the account it leaves is of a man given everything, whose heart at the end was not wholly true.

Are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? Here the closing pattern appears for the first time: the rest of his acts, the source, the length of the reign, the burial, the successor. It will be applied to some forty kings, most in a few lines, and gives Kings its relentless quality: a whole life summed up, filed and closed, and then the next one. The writer also cites a source we do not have. He is not writing an exhaustive account but showing what God was doing, and he selects: four chapters on the temple, one on the wives, almost nothing on the running of a forty-year empire.

Forty years. Solomon reigned forty years, like David, and like Saul (Saul’s forty is given in Acts 13:21; the numbers in the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 are damaged). Three kings, forty years each, and then the kingdom breaks.

The whole man. Stand back from the whole account. He began by asking God for an understanding mind and was given more than he asked. He judged two prostitutes rightly, built the house of God and confessed that heaven itself cannot contain God. He prayed for the foreigner and the exile, and a queen crossed a desert on a rumour about the name of his God. He also acquired horses, traded with Egypt, made silver as common as stone, married seven hundred princesses, built shrines for them on the hill facing the temple, and tried to kill the man God had chosen. All of it is the same man, and the writer records all of it without resolving it. What he does instead is put two words in Solomon’s mouth in chapter 8 and take them away in chapter 11: wholly true. He told the nation their hearts must be that towards God. At the end, with every advantage a man has ever had, his was not.

Isn’t education what makes people good? It is one of the oldest hopes of the West. Socrates, as Plato tells it, held that wrongdoing is at bottom ignorance; the Enlightenment hoped schools and science would do what sermons had not; and we still assume that the right information will make people better. Solomon is the Bible’s answer to that hope. Nobody ever knew more. He had wisdom from God himself, and he still built shrines on the hill facing the temple. Augustine, looking back in his Confessions on the years before his conversion, found that his trouble was not a lack of knowledge but a will divided against itself, and Paul says the same: “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). Knowledge is a gift, but it cannot hold a heart, because the heart is not merely uninformed; it loves the wrong things. That is why the gospel is not first advice but rescue: not information about how to be wholly true, but a Son of David who was wholly true in our place, and a Spirit who changes what we love.

11.theology:
The heart is the issue. The law's ban on marrying into the nations of Canaan was never about blood or nationality (Rahab and Ruth are in the line of Christ); it was about worship: they will turn away your heart after their gods. Kings shows the warning coming true in the household of the wisest man alive. The undivided heart that Solomon urged on the nation (8:61) is the thing he lost, and it is the measure the whole book will use. David, for all his terrible sins, never went after another god; Solomon did. Faithfulness in Kings is not sinlessness but belonging to the LORD alone, with a heart that returns to him when it is confronted.

How drift happens. There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD. Each shrine is a courtesy owed to a treaty wife, and each is defensible on its own. That is why the chapter shows us ourselves, and is not just a strange old story. Hearts are rarely turned by one dramatic choice; they are turned by arrangements nobody would call a decision. And it happens when Solomon was old, after Gibeon, the temple and two appearances of God, so no stage of life or spiritual history makes anyone safe in themselves. The safety the Bible offers is in God's keeping, not in our record.

Light makes the sin heavier. God had appeared to Solomon twice and named this very sin in advance (9:6-7). The anger of verse 9 is the anger of a Father who warned his son face to face. Judgment comes through ordinary events: a servant promoted over the forced labour, and two adversaries left over from David's wars, whom God raised up. God governs even the long consequences of old violence, and he is not hurried.

Mercy inside judgment. Every restraint in the sentence (not in your days, not all the kingdom, one tribe kept) is for the sake of David my servant and of the city God chose. The lamp of verse 36 is small but God will not let it go out, and it burns on to the Son of David. That is the gospel shape of the chapter: unworthy people kept on account of another, whose obedience is counted for them (Romans 5:19).

Fighting a word from God. Jeroboam is offered David's own covenant terms, and Solomon answers the prophecy by trying to have him killed, as Saul once tried to kill David. Neither the promise nor the threat of God can be managed by force. The only fitting response to a word from God is to bow to it, and Solomon, who knew more than anyone, is never recorded doing so.

Egypt again. The chapter keeps glancing south. The daughter of Pharaoh heads the list of wives; Hadad grows up in Pharaoh's court; Jeroboam takes refuge with Shishak; and within five years of Solomon's death Shishak will be in Jerusalem carrying off the gold. The road back to Egypt that the law of the king had closed, and that Solomon reopened for horses and marriages, becomes the road by which his enemies are sheltered and his treasures leave. The writer does not point out the connection, but it is there to be seen.

A life filed and closed. The closing summary (vv. 41-43) follows a set pattern that will be repeated for king after king. Solomon's account contains real wisdom, true prayer and a temple God filled with his glory, and it also contains the high places and the assassination order. Scripture does not average the two. It records both and leaves the verdict on his soul with God, while making plain that gifts, learning and a great past do not keep a heart. Only the King who is greater than Solomon does that.
11.examples:
Then: A king who had asked God for an understanding mind, built him a temple, prayed one of the longest prayers in the Old Testament and been visited by God twice in person, spent his old age putting up shrines to other gods on the hill facing that temple, one at a time, for one wife at a time; and when God told him the kingdom would be torn away, he sought to kill the man the prophet had named.

Now: Three things, and they are all uncomfortable. First, the timing: when Solomon was old, after every spiritual advantage a human being has ever had. There is no stage of life at which a person becomes safe in their own strength. Second, the mechanism. There was never a moment when he decided to abandon God, only seven hundred reasonable accommodations, each owed to somebody, until the hill facing the house of God was covered in altars. And third, wholly true: he preached it to a nation and lost it. The question the chapter leaves is not whether your religion is still going on. It is whether anything else shares your heart with God. Where there is, the way back is the one Solomon is never recorded taking: confess it to the God who promised to forgive (1 John 1:9), and rest on the Son of David whose heart was wholly true to his Father in our place. His Spirit, now given to believers, is the one who makes a divided heart whole and keeps it near (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

keyVerse.quote: For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.
keyVerse.note: This verse sums up the tragedy of the wisest king: not a sudden rebellion, but a heart slowly divided, late in life, after every advantage. Solomon had called Israel to be “wholly true” (8:61), and his own heart was not. The verse leaves us longing for the Son of David whose heart was wholly true to his Father to the end, and whose obedience is counted for all who trust him.

11.reflection:
Solomon’s heart was turned not by one great decision but by many small courtesies to his wives’ gods (vv. 4–8). What small concessions could slowly divide your heart, and what helps you notice them early?

Solomon fell “when Solomon was old”, after decades of blessing (v. 4). Why might later life, or a season of success, carry particular dangers? How do the promises of Philippians 1:6 and Jude 24 give hope to someone who fears growing cold?

Even in judgment, God kept one tribe and a lamp in Jerusalem “for the sake of David” (vv. 12–13, 36). How does God’s faithfulness to David point to the way he keeps us for the sake of Christ?

Solomon had more wisdom than anyone, yet his heart turned. Why is knowledge not enough to keep us faithful, and what does the gospel give that knowledge cannot?

12.title: The Kingdom Torn in Two
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.<sup>2</sup>And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt.<sup>3</sup>And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam,<sup>4</sup>"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away.<sup>6</sup>Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?"<sup>7</sup>And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever."<sup>8</sup>But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?"<sup>10</sup>And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs.<sup>11</sup>And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"<sup>12</sup>So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day."<sup>13</sup>And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him,<sup>14</sup>he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."<sup>15</sup>So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>16</sup>And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents.<sup>17</sup>But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah.<sup>18</sup>Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.<sup>20</sup>And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only.<sup>21</sup>When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon.<sup>22</sup>But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God:<sup>23</sup>"Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people,<sup>24</sup>'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel.<sup>26</sup>And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David.<sup>27</sup>If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah."<sup>28</sup>So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."<sup>29</sup>And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.<sup>30</sup>Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one.<sup>31</sup>He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites.<sup>32</sup>And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.<sup>33</sup>He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.
12.overview:
Where we are. Solomon is dead (11:43). Because his heart turned to other gods, the LORD promised to tear ten tribes from his son and give them to Jeroboam, who had fled to Egypt (11:9–40). Now the son, Rehoboam, goes north to be crowned.

The message. Power that will not serve breaks what God has joined, and worship built to keep ourselves safe leads a whole people away from God. Rehoboam will not lighten the yoke, and loses ten tribes; Jeroboam will not trust God’s promise, and invents a religion of his own. Yet through a proud man and a frightened one the LORD keeps his word to the letter.

Why it was said. The exiles who first read Kings had lost both kingdoms and were asking why (see the introduction). This chapter shows where the road began: with a king who would not serve his people, and a king who “made Israel to sin”, the standard every northern king after him would be measured by.

How the chapter makes its case. At Shechem the tribes ask Rehoboam to lighten Solomon’s heavy yoke (vv. 1–5). The old men counsel him to serve; his friends counsel scorn, and he takes their advice, in a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD to fulfil Ahijah’s word (vv. 6–15). Israel answers with an old rebel cry, stones the taskmaster and crowns Jeroboam; when Rehoboam musters for war, God says, “this thing is from me”, and the army goes home (vv. 16–24). Then Jeroboam, afraid his people will return to David’s house, makes two golden calves, with priests and a feast of his own devising (vv. 25–33).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by contrast and by promise. Rehoboam was asked to lighten a yoke and promised scorpions; the Son of David says, “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30), because he “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Jeroboam gave his people a worship nearer home; Jesus, at a well near Shechem, announced worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23), through himself. The breach God decreed here, the prophets promised he would heal under one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:22–24), and Christ died “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

For us. Whoever has charge of others faces Rehoboam’s question: will you serve? We do not do it by nature, but the Servant King gives his Spirit to his people. And when fear tempts us to arrange our approach to God around our own safety and convenience, the cure is to come the way he has given, through his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — My Little Finger Is Thicker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who will not serve loses the people God gave him, and God is at work even in that. All Israel gathers at Shechem, with Jeroboam back from Egypt, and makes one request: lighten the heavy yoke Solomon laid on them, and they will serve Rehoboam (vv. 1–4). The old men who served Solomon advise him to be the people’s servant for one day and win them for ever (vv. 5–7). He prefers the friends he grew up with, who tell him to promise heavier burdens and harsher whips, and he says it to the assembly’s face (vv. 8–14). Then the writer lifts the curtain: this turn of affairs came from the LORD, to fulfil his word through Ahijah (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing ten tribes ask of a new king is relief from the conscripted labour that built the temple and the palace and the chariot cities. Godly rule listens to a just complaint, even one that wounds the ruler's pride.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has charge of others (a parent, an employer, an elder) will one day be asked for relief by people who have carried a load. How we answer in that moment says more about our leadership than any amount of success before it.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt. And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam, "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Shechem, on northern ground, the tribes offer the new king their loyalty on one condition: that he lift the crushing labour his father laid on them. It is not a revolt but a negotiation, and the request is just.

Rehoboam went to Shechem. The coronation is not in Jerusalem. Shechem, in the hill country of Ephraim, is one of the oldest covenant sites in the land: Abraham built an altar there (Genesis 12:6–7), Joshua gathered the tribes there and said, “choose this day whom you will serve” (Joshua 24:15), and Joseph’s bones were buried there (Joshua 24:32). Rehoboam must travel north to be made king on the northern tribes’ ground, and that alone shows how strained the union already is.

Jeroboam returned from Egypt. The reader has met him: the officer over the forced labour of the house of Joseph, to whom Ahijah gave ten pieces of a torn cloak, and who fled to Shishak when Solomon sought to kill him (11:26–40). So the man God has named for ten tribes is in the assembly before Rehoboam has said a word.

Your father made our yoke heavy. The demand is precise. It is not about religion: nobody mentions Solomon’s high places, and Ahijah’s word is quoted at no one. Nor is it separatism: “we will serve you” ends the sentence, and it is an offer. It is about the levy: thirty thousand men sent to Lebanon in monthly shifts, seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters (5:13–15); twenty years of building the temple, the palace and the fortified cities; and twelve districts drawn across the tribal lands, each feeding the court for a month (4:7). The writer has recorded it all since chapter 4 without comment. Here is the comment, from the people who carried it, and their word is “yoke”, what you put on an animal to make it pull.

The other yoke. Keep the word in mind. A thousand years later the Son of David stood among people worn out by their burdens and said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). Rehoboam was asked to lighten a yoke and refused. Christ lifts the heaviest one, and the yoke he lays on us in its place is light, because the one who gives it is gentle.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away. Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?" And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who had served Solomon tell the new king that one day of serving the people will win their loyalty for life. Their advice is not softness but wisdom: authority is held by serving.

Go away for three days. Rehoboam uses the time well at first and consults two sets of advisers. The old men ran Solomon’s government. They administered the levy, and they know what the country thinks of it.

If you will be a servant to this people today. Their counsel is one day against a lifetime: serve them once, when they have asked for something and it costs you, and you will have them for the rest of your life. Both verbs, “be a servant” and “serve them”, come from the ordinary word for a bondman, the word the assembly used in its offer, “we will serve you” (v. 4). You take the servant’s place today; they take it for ever. And “speak good words to them” is not about tone: in the language of treaties, good words are favourable terms.

Not to be served but to serve. When two of the Twelve asked for the chief seats, the Son of David said, “whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:43–45). The correspondence should be stated carefully. The old men offer a king practical advice about what works. Jesus is not offering a technique for keeping power; he is describing what greatness is in his kingdom, grounded in what he came to do, and its cost was not a day of concessions but his life. So the old men’s advice is not the gospel. But it points the same way: even as plain statecraft at Shechem, they had seen that serving is what holds a people.

verseByVerse.quote: But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him. And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?" And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam turns from the experienced to the friends who flatter him, and they tell him to answer a plea for relief with a threat. He did not lack good advice; he went looking for the advice he wanted.

The young men who had grown up with him. Those words are the whole explanation: these are his friends. They grew up in the palace during the richest reign in Israel’s history, among the gold shields and the ivory throne, and never carried a stone. Rehoboam was forty-one (14:21), so they are not boys; the word, the ordinary one for lads, is probably a slighting term for men who had never carried responsibility, something like “the boys”.

What do you advise that we answer this people? Asking twice makes it worse, not better. Note how he frames the question to the second group: what shall “we” answer “this people who have said to me”, quoting their request as a complaint about his father. He has already decided how he feels and is looking for support. That is the ordinary way people get bad advice: asking for counsel while hoping for permission (Proverbs 12:15).

My little finger is thicker than my father’s thighs. The line is crude and meant to be: a boast of force that says, whatever you thought my father was, I am more. He does not deny that his father used whips; he takes Solomon’s record as the baseline he means to exceed. The men asked for a lighter yoke. He promises a heavier one and a crueller instrument.

Why they were so sure. The young advisers are not stupid about tactics; they are certain the north will do as it is told, because in their experience it always has. They watched the gangs go north ten thousand a month and come back. People who have only ever seen power obeyed cannot imagine it refused.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “little finger” occurs only here and in the parallel account (2 Chronicles 10:10); “little finger” is the usual understanding, though some have taken it as a coarser euphemism, which would suit the boast. The “scorpions” are not explained either: probably whips with barbs or pieces of metal worked into the lashes, named for their sting, but the exact instrument is not known. The point is plain either way: something far worse than whips.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament includes a longer, alternative account of these events that makes Rehoboam sixteen, and his son later calls him “young and irresolute” (2 Chronicles 13:7); but most follow the Hebrew, which makes him forty-one (14:21).

verseByVerse.quote: So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day." And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him, he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions." So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam answers the people harshly, and the writer reveals that God was ruling even this foolish choice in order to keep his word. The king is fully responsible, and the LORD is fully in control.

The king answered the people harshly. On the third day the assembly returns as it was told and hears the young men’s speech almost word for word, without the line about the little finger. The word “harshly” is the one used when Joseph “spoke roughly” to his brothers (Genesis 42:7), but here no hidden kindness lies behind it. Twice the writer says that Rehoboam forsook the old men’s counsel (vv. 8, 13): he had both answers in front of him, and chose.

A turn of affairs brought about by the LORD. Here the writer lifts the curtain for one sentence, as at 2 Samuel 17:14, and insists on both halves without explaining how they fit. On the human side everything is accounted for: a vain man, afraid of looking weak in his first week, chose the flatterers; his friends were arrogant because they had never carried anything; the north had a real grievance that nobody in Jerusalem had taken seriously. No one is forced. And the writer says God did it.

Both things together. Samuel and Kings say both things together at the great turning points. Absalom preferred a better speech to Ahithophel’s sound advice, “For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel” (2 Samuel 17:14). Joseph’s brothers meant evil and God meant good, by the same act (Genesis 50:20). Scripture never drops either half: God is not a spectator to whom history happens, and no one in this chapter has an excuse.

That he might fulfill his word. The purpose clause matters. The word spoken “by Ahijah the Shilonite” one chapter earlier, on an empty road with two men present (11:29–39), cannot be stopped by a king’s pride or a nation’s anger. Kings rise and fall; the word of the LORD comes true.

At the cross. The plainest case of all is the cross, where Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and crucified “by the hands of lawless men”, in a single sentence (Acts 2:23). There God’s rule over human sin worked for mercy: the worst thing men ever did became the salvation of the world. The God who turned Rehoboam’s folly to keep his word through Ahijah turned the world’s rejection of his Son to keep every promise he made to David.

Does that make God the author of Rehoboam’s pride? No. God’s providence reaches even to the sins of men, yet the sinfulness comes only from the creature, and God neither causes nor approves it (Westminster Confession 5.4). He did not put folly into Rehoboam; he let a proud man be himself, and steered the outcome to keep his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — To Your Tents, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A grievance left unheard becomes a division that never heals, yet God claims even the breach as his own. Israel answers the king with an old rebel cry and goes home (v. 16). Rehoboam sends the very man who ran the forced labour; the people stone him, and the king flees to Jerusalem (vv. 17–19). The northern tribes make Jeroboam king, and only Judah, with Benjamin, stays with David’s house (vv. 20–21). Rehoboam musters an army to win the north back, but the word of God through Shemaiah forbids war against their brothers, because this thing is from the LORD, and for once everyone obeys (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: A careless word can outlive the one who says it. A slogan shouted by a rebel in David's day becomes, forty years later, the founding cry of a separate kingdom. And behind it lay a quarrel about precedence that nobody troubled to heal. Divisions among God's people seldom start large; they start with pride and are left to grow.
verseByVerse.examples: When trust has broken, sending the very person who embodies the grievance is the surest way to finish it off. Repairing a wrong usually begins by changing what caused it, not by sending its enforcer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents. But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah. Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only. When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon. But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people, 'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The north walks away from David’s house with an old rebel’s slogan, and when Rehoboam tries to win it back by force, God stops him: the division is his doing. Pride has broken the kingdom, and God claims even the breaking as his judgment.

What portion do we have in David? The cry is some forty years old. In David’s day “a worthless man, whose name was Sheba” blew the trumpet and said, “We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!” (2 Samuel 20:1). Sheba had no army and no case, and his revolt was over within a chapter, his head thrown over a wall. His sentence outlived him by decades, and here it founds a kingdom.

Where the crack began. It opened at the Jordan, when Israel and Judah argued over who had the right to bring David home, a quarrel about precedence: “the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel” (2 Samuel 19:43). The very next verse is Sheba’s trumpet. So the line runs: a squabble about who walked beside the king, a slogan handed to humiliated men, a failed revolt, decades of the levy, and a king who would rather sound strong than be obeyed.

Look now to your own house, David. The coldest clause in the verse: go and manage your own family, said to a dynasty God had promised would stand for ever (2 Samuel 7:16).

King Rehoboam sent Adoram. Few decisions in the book are more foolish. Ten tribes have just walked out over the forced labour, and Rehoboam sends them the minister of forced labour, whether to negotiate or to start collecting, the text does not say. Adoram has been in this history a long time: in David’s last list of officials “in charge of the forced labor” (2 Samuel 20:24), in Solomon’s as Adoniram (4:6), running the draft to Lebanon (5:14), named across three reigns without comment. Here is the comment: they stone him to death. And the man who boasted of his little finger is climbing into a chariot as fast as he can.

To this day. The division never healed. The north lasted about two centuries and fell to Assyria; the south went to Babylon nearly a century and a half later. They were never one nation again.

180,000 chosen warriors. Rehoboam musters an army to take the north back by force, and the word through Shemaiah is the second time the chapter says God was behind these events, more strongly than the first. Verse 15 called the refusal a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD; now the breaking of the kingdom David spent his life uniting is God’s own doing, not merely permitted or foreseen: “this thing is from me.” It is his judgment on Solomon’s idolatry, as Ahijah had said (11:31–33).

Your relatives the people of Israel. Literally your brothers: the argument Abner shouted from a hilltop to Joab some eighty years earlier, “How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?” (2 Samuel 2:26).

So they listened to the word of the LORD. A hundred and eighty thousand armed men go home on one sentence from a prophet: the one thing anybody in this chapter does right. Rehoboam would not listen to the old men or to ten tribes standing in front of him, but he listens to Shemaiah. That shows what is wrong with him as well as what is right: he can obey God when a prophet tells him plainly, and he cannot govern people with justice. His religion and his rule never quite met, and he went on fighting Jeroboam for the rest of his life (14:30).

The promise of reunion. The prophets would not let the split be the last word. Ezekiel took two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and held them as one in his hand: “they shall be no longer two nations, and no longer divided into two kingdoms. … My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd” (Ezekiel 37:22, 24). The New Testament sees that promise kept in the Son of David, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep so that “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16), and who died “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52). What Rehoboam’s pride broke, Christ’s death mends, on a scale Ezekiel could only begin to see.

Where is the twelfth tribe? Ahijah’s ten and one (11:31–32) leave one piece unexplained. Benjamin joined Judah (v. 21), and Simeon had long been absorbed within Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1); the “one tribe” is Judah with Benjamin.

Was Jeroboam at the assembly or not? Verses 2–3 put him there, while verse 20 reads as if the tribes sent for him afterwards. Many think verses 2–3 tell his part in advance and verse 20 records the formal summons to make him king. The Greek Old Testament tells his rise in a different order, which shows the story was handed down in more than one form; the events themselves are not in doubt.
verseByVerse.note: From here the kingdom is divided: Israel (ten tribes) in the north, Judah in the south.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–33 — Behold Your Gods, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fear that will not trust God’s promise builds a religion to keep itself safe. Jeroboam fortifies his kingdom and reasons that if his people keep going up to Jerusalem to worship, their hearts will turn back to David’s house and they will kill him (vv. 25–27). So he makes two golden calves, presents them as the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt, and sets them at Bethel and Dan, and it becomes a sin (vv. 28–30). He adds shrines on high places, priests who were not Levites, and a festival a month late, every piece of it devised from his own heart (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: He had been offered David's own covenant on condition of obedience (11:38), and his first act as king is the thing that forfeits it. His stated reasoning is entirely about security: they will kill me. He does it because he is afraid, and fear that will not trust God's promise always finds another way to feel safe.
verseByVerse.examples: Fear is a poor architect of worship. When we arrange our approach to God around what keeps us safe or comfortable rather than around what he has asked, we may keep the forms of religion and lose the God they were meant to serve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel. And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah." So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan. Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one. He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites. And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made. He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afraid of losing his throne, Jeroboam gives Israel a new way to worship the LORD, closer to home and of his own design, and it leads the nation away from God. He does not abandon the LORD’s name; he redesigns his worship, and that becomes the sin that defines the northern kingdom.

Then Jeroboam built Shechem. He fortifies a capital, and Penuel, a crossing east of the Jordan, where Jacob wrestled all night and was named Israel (Genesis 32:28–31).

Jeroboam said in his heart. The reader has met the phrase at a bad moment: “Then David said in his heart, ‘Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul’” (1 Samuel 27:1), and he fled to the Philistines. No priest, no prophet: a man doing his own thinking in a crisis. Jeroboam has more reason not to: a promise from a prophet, in person.

If this people go up to offer sacrifices. Every step of the reasoning is politically sound. Three times a year every male in Israel was to appear before the LORD at the place he chose (Deuteronomy 16:16): the whole adult population of the new kingdom walking into its rival’s capital to worship at a temple built by the dynasty it had just rejected. No new state could survive that.

They will kill me. That is where the reasoning ends, and what drives it: not theology, not even ambition, but fear. Set it beside what God had promised him: “if you will listen to all that I command you … I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you” (11:38). The security he fears for had been guaranteed before he was king, and within a few verses of receiving the kingdom he protects it by means that forfeit the promise. That is the tragedy of the man, and a very ordinary one: he believed the prophecy enough to take the throne, and not enough to trust the God who gave it.

Behold your gods, O Israel. Read it beside Exodus 32. At Sinai Aaron made a golden calf, and the people said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” (Exodus 32:4). Jeroboam says it almost exactly, and makes two. Everybody knew that story, the worst day in the nation’s history: the calf ground to powder and drunk, and three thousand dead (Exodus 32:20, 28). He repeats it deliberately, on a national scale.

Why it worked. He names no foreign god. The sentence is about the God who brought Israel out of Egypt: the right God, identified by the right act. In the surrounding cultures a bull was often the pedestal a god stood on rather than the god itself, and Jeroboam very likely presented his calves as thrones for the invisible LORD, as Aaron had proclaimed, “Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5). So this is the true God worshipped by means he had forbidden, a breach of the second commandment, which forbids images, rather than the first, which forbids other gods (Exodus 20:4–5), and that is why it was so dangerous. Nobody in the north had to decide to abandon the LORD; they only had to accept a more convenient way of approaching him, approved by the state, closer to home. Yet God would not accept the distinction: through Ahijah he calls the calves “other gods and metal images” (14:9). Worship designed to suit us slowly reshapes our picture of God until he is someone else.

He set one in Bethel. The placing is expert. Dan lies at the far north, Bethel on the southern border, about a dozen miles from Jerusalem. Both already had religious history. Bethel, “house of God”, is where Jacob saw the ladder and said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it” (Genesis 28:16). Dan had housed an illegitimate shrine since the judges, with a stolen idol and a hired Levite (Judges 18). Jeroboam invents nothing; he uses ground people already felt religious about.

This thing became a sin. The phrase becomes the writer’s shorthand for the northern kingdom. Until the fall of Samaria, king after king is condemned because he did not depart from “the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin” (2 Kings 10:29; 15:9): two centuries of kings measured against this day.

Priests from among all the people. His second move is as serious as the calves. The priesthood belonged to Aaron’s line within the tribe of Levi, and the Levites had no territory of their own so that they would be spread through the land to teach the law. Chronicles records the result: the northern Levites left their lands and came south, “because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 11:14). He emptied the north of the men whose task was to teach God’s word, and a people without faithful teachers soon forgets what true worship was.

A feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. The Feast of Booths fell on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34), the feast at which Solomon dedicated the temple (8:2); Jeroboam moves it to the eighth. Everything is almost right: almost the same feast, the same date and the same God, at sites with genuine history, with priests and altars, and all of it one month, one tribe and one commandment out. And the king goes up to the altar himself to make offerings, the very thing for which King Uzziah of Judah was later struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

The month that he had devised from his own heart. This is the writer’s verdict on the whole enterprise: not the month God appointed, but the month he thought of. Jeroboam was not irreligious. He was extremely religious, with sanctuaries, clergy, a festival and the king at the altar. But every element of it came out of a man’s own head, for the reason he had stated: “they will kill me.”

The way God has given. Jeroboam’s offer sounds modern: “You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough.” Keep the God, drop the inconvenience. Centuries later, at Jacob’s well near Shechem, where this chapter began, a Samaritan woman asked Jesus which mountain was the right place to worship. He answered that the hour had come when “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23), because the Father had sent his Son to where she was. The long road to God is not cancelled by a king’s convenience; it has been travelled from the other side. The answer to Jeroboam’s calves is not a better shrine nearer home, but the one Mediator God has provided, through whom anyone, anywhere, may come.

Spirituality on your own terms. Many people today want what Jeroboam offered: the comfort of the sacred without its authority, chosen and adjusted by the self. The sociologist Robert Bellah, in Habits of the Heart, described a young nurse who named her faith after herself, “Sheilaism”, a religion of one, steered by her own inner voice. It feels humble and free. But notice what Jeroboam’s religion was for: it was built to keep him safe, and a god designed to serve your security can never call it into question. He is a bodyguard, not a Lord.

Uncertain wording. Verse 30 reads literally, “the people went before the one as far as Dan.” It probably means that the people went all the way to Dan to worship before the calf there; some think a phrase about the other calf, at Bethel, has dropped out of the sentence. The irony is plain either way: the king who said Jerusalem was too far had his people walking to the far north.
verseByVerse.note: Bethel and Dan lay at the southern and northern ends of Jeroboam’s kingdom. The calves echoed Aaron’s golden calf.

12.theology:
Authority is for service. The old men's counsel to Rehoboam is plain statecraft, but it rests on something deeper: a ruler exists for the good of the ruled. Israel's kings were never meant to be masters over their brothers (Deut. 17:20), and the levy had turned the king into a taskmaster. Jesus takes the principle much further, grounding greatness in his own service and his ransoming death (Mark 10:42-45). Rehoboam is the opposite picture: a man who heard the truth from the experienced, preferred the flattery of the comfortable, and turned a just request into an insult. Pride did not merely spoil his reign; it broke the people of God.

Grievances that are heard too late. The writer recorded Solomon's levy for eight chapters without a word of criticism: the thirty thousand to Lebanon, the burden-bearers, the quarrymen, the districts drawn across the tribal lands.
