The comment comes only now, from the people who carried it, and their word is yoke. Glory built on other people's backs can look like blessing for a long time. Scripture does not let us admire the temple and the palaces without hearing, in the end, what they cost the ordinary families of the north. God hears the cry of the burdened even when the court does not, and the stoning of Adoram, the man who had run the levy through three reigns, shows how deep the anger had gone.

Counsel that confirms what we want. Rehoboam did seek advice. He sought two sets of it, framed the question differently to each, and chose the one that agreed with what he already felt. That is the ordinary way wise people make foolish decisions, and it is a warning to anyone who asks for counsel while hoping for permission.

God's rule over human choices. Twice the writer says the breach was God's doing (vv. 15, 24), yet no one is forced and no one is excused. Scripture holds both truths without explaining how they fit: when Absalom rejects Ahithophel's counsel (2 Sam. 17:14), in Joseph's story (Gen. 50:20), and supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23). God's providence does not make him the author of sin; it means that even proud and frightened men cannot stop his word from coming true, and that he can turn the worst human acts toward his good purposes.

Old wounds and long fuses. The cry of verse 16 comes from Sheba's failed revolt, and behind that from a quarrel at the Jordan about which tribes had the first claim on David. Resentments left unhealed in one generation can become the policy of the next. The division itself never healed in Old Testament history, but the prophets promised one people under one Shepherd, and that promise is kept in Christ, who dies to gather God's scattered children into one (John 11:52).

Obedience in one place. When Shemaiah speaks, Rehoboam and his army go home. It is the one good decision in the chapter, and it shows that hearing God's plain word and doing it is possible even for a foolish man. The trouble is that he could obey a prophet and still not govern people with justice. Obedience to God at the moment of crisis is good, and it spared a civil war; but it is meant to flow into the whole of life, including the way we treat those under us. Rehoboam's religion and his rule never quite met.

Fear and the second commandment. Jeroboam had God's promise of a sure house, and he answered it with calculation. His calves did not replace the LORD with another god. They offered the LORD a more convenient worship: closer to home, approved by the state, at places with a religious past, with a priesthood and a festival that were all nearly right. That is why it worked and why it was so deadly. The second commandment guards not only whom we worship but how, because worship devised to suit us slowly reshapes our picture of God. Devised from his own heart is the verdict on all of it.

Teachers driven out. The most lasting damage may have been the least visible. By appointing priests from any tribe, Jeroboam pushed out the Levites, whose task was to teach the law in every part of the land, and Chronicles says they went south (2 Chron. 11:14). A people without faithful teachers soon forgets what true worship was, and two centuries of northern kings would be measured against the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. The way back for any church that has drifted begins with recovering the word of God taught plainly by those he has called.

Almost right is not right. Jeroboam's festival was a month late, his priests from the wrong tribe, his calves a breach of one commandment rather than all ten. Each change could be defended, and together they made a religion that looked familiar and led away from God. The danger for churches is rarely the open denial of Christ; it is the slow redesign of worship to suit our fears and conveniences. The answer is not anxiety about every detail but a glad return to what God has given: his word, his appointed means, and the one Mediator through whom we come.

Two kings who had the answer. Rehoboam had wise counsel, and Jeroboam had a promise from God. Both preferred their own thinking, and between them they broke the kingdom in half. The chapter's hope lies outside both of them, in the Son of David who did not grasp at security but trusted his Father, served instead of being served, and through his obedience gathers a people who will never be divided again.
12.examples:
Then: Ten tribes asked a new king for one thing, that the conscripted labour be lightened, and offered to serve him if it was. The men who had run the government for forty years told him that one day of serving them would buy him their loyalty for life. He asked his friends instead, promised to beat them with something worse than his father had used, and then sent them the minister of forced labour, who was stoned to death in the road.

Now: Three things. The old men's sentence is the one to keep, and its force is that it is not sentiment but arithmetic: a day of genuine service, when somebody has asked for something and it costs you, buys what no authority can command. Anyone who has charge of anybody faces the choice Rehoboam had in those three days. We do not serve that way by nature, and we do not do it perfectly; the one who did, the Son of Man who came to serve and gave his life as a ransom, gives his Spirit to those who follow him, and that is where the strength for it comes from. Second, Rehoboam did not fail to seek counsel: he sought two opinions, chose the one he already wanted, and framed the question differently to each. That is the ordinary way people get bad advice. And third, Jeroboam, whose golden calves were not a turning to another god but a convenience: the right God, correctly named, approached by a method he had devised himself. Worship quietly redesigned to cost less is the danger this chapter is about, and the remedy is to come to God the way he has given, through the one Mediator he has provided.

keyVerse.quote: And they said to him, “If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever.”
keyVerse.note: This is the road not taken, and the whole chapter turns on it. One day of serving would have kept the kingdom; Rehoboam’s refusal broke it, and Jeroboam’s fear completed the damage. The Son of David took the road Rehoboam refused, all the way to the cross, and won a people who will serve him for ever.

12.reflection:
The tribes asked Rehoboam to lighten their yoke, and the old men told him to be a servant to the people for a day (vv. 4–7). Where do you have charge of others, and what would serving them look like when a request costs you something? How does Mark 10:42–45 change the way we think about authority?

Rehoboam asked two sets of advisers and chose the answer he already wanted (vv. 6–11). How can we tell whether we are seeking counsel or seeking permission? Who in your life is free to tell you what you do not want to hear?

The writer says the breach was “a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD” (v. 15), yet holds every person in the story responsible. Where else does Scripture hold these two together, and why is that a comfort when we face the foolish choices of others?

Jeroboam’s calves were not a new god but a more convenient way of worshipping the LORD, built out of fear (vv. 26–33). In what ways are Christians tempted to redesign worship or devotion to suit our comfort, and what does it mean to come to God the way he has given in Christ?

13.title: The Man of God from Judah
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings.<sup>2</sup>And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'"<sup>3</sup>And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'"<sup>4</sup>And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself.<sup>5</sup>The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before.<sup>7</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward."<sup>8</sup>And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place,<sup>9</sup>for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>10</sup>So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.<sup>11</sup>Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king.<sup>12</sup>And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone.<sup>13</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it.<sup>14</sup>And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am."<sup>15</sup>Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread."<sup>16</sup>And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place,<sup>17</sup>for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>18</sup>And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him.<sup>19</sup>So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.<sup>20</sup>And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.<sup>21</sup>And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you,<sup>22</sup>but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'"<sup>23</sup>And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.<sup>24</sup>And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body.<sup>25</sup>And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.<sup>26</sup>And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him."<sup>27</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it.<sup>28</sup>And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.<sup>29</sup>And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him.<sup>30</sup>And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"<sup>31</sup>And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.<sup>32</sup>For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."<sup>33</sup>After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places.<sup>34</sup>And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
13.overview:
Where we are. Jeroboam has just set up his golden calves and invented a festival, and on its first day he stands at his new altar in Bethel to make offerings (12:32–33). Then a stranger walks in from Judah.

The message. The word of the LORD cannot be stopped, bought or revised. It names a king three centuries ahead, splits an altar and heals a hand, and it binds its own messenger: the man of God who let a newer, more impressive word overrule the clear word God had given him dies on the road. God’s word stands, whoever carries or contradicts it, and no sign can soften a heart that will not hear it.

Why it was said. The first readers had seen this word fulfilled in Josiah’s reform (2 Kings 23:15–18), and the north destroyed for Jeroboam’s sin (see the introduction). They had also lived through an age of prophets contradicting prophets, promising peace in the LORD’s name when he had not spoken (Jeremiah 23:16–17): the word to trust is the one that agrees with what God has already said.

How the chapter makes its case. The man of God cries against the altar and names Josiah; the king’s hand withers, the altar splits, the hand is healed at his prayer, and he refuses the king’s table, as God commanded (vv. 1–10). An old prophet of Bethel follows him and, claiming an angel’s word, lies him into coming back to eat (vv. 11–19). At the table God’s true word comes through the liar, a lion kills the man of God on the road, and the old prophet buries him in his own grave, sure that the word against Bethel will stand (vv. 20–32). Jeroboam, having seen it all, changes nothing (vv. 33–34).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God it shows. Even a brave and faithful prophet failed to hold God’s word when he was tired and hungry. Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, held it: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4), and his obedience did not fail, even at the cross. The man of God prayed for the king who struck at him; Christ prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). And the word that waited three hundred years and came true to the letter belongs to the God whose promises all “find their Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Test every voice, however impressive, by what God has already said in Scripture, especially when it releases you from something hard and arrives when you are tired. If you have been led astray, come back: the Lord receives those who return. And do not wait for a bigger sign to move a hard heart; pray for God to open it to his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word against false worship cannot be stopped, and its messenger must obey it in every detail. A man of God from Judah arrives at Bethel as Jeroboam stands at his altar, and cries against the altar itself: a son of David named Josiah will one day burn its priests’ bones on it, and as a sign it will split today (vv. 1–3). The king’s hand, stretched out to seize him, withers; the altar splits; and at the prophet’s prayer the hand is restored (vv. 4–6). Offered a meal and a reward, he refuses, because God has told him to eat and drink nothing there and to go home another way (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology: He names a king three hundred years before the man is born, and it happens (2 Kings 23:15-16). The God who rules history can tell its end from its beginning, and his word against false worship does not lapse with time.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction he has been given is threefold and strange, and it is not explained to him. He does not ask for reasons; he obeys. Some of God's commands we understand only later, and some we are simply asked to keep because he has spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings. And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the very moment Jeroboam stands at his new altar, God sends a prophet to announce its defilement by a king of David’s line, named three centuries before his birth. The false worship has barely begun, and God has already spoken its end.

A man of God came out of Judah. He is never named; the writer simply calls him “the man of God”, as if only his message mattered. He arrives at the exact moment, as Jeroboam stands at the altar he devised, at the festival he moved (12:32–33), and he comes “by the word of the LORD”, a phrase that runs through the chapter, because everything in it turns on what God has said.

O altar, altar. He addresses the altar, not the king, because the altar is where the offence is.

Josiah by name. Prophecies of a coming ruler are common; a personal name given three centuries in advance is not. Isaiah’s naming of Cyrus is the other case (Isaiah 44:28). And the king will be “a son … born to the house of David”: on the day the north turns away from David’s line, God announces that the line will outlast the altar.

The priests of the high places. The sentence falls first on the men who serve at this altar, the priests Jeroboam appointed “from among all the people” (12:31). Burning human bones on an altar defiled it, since touching a human bone or a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16): the altar built to bring Israel near to God would become the most unclean thing in the land.

The fulfilment. It happened. When Josiah destroyed the shrines of the land, the historian stops to point back at this verse: “And as Josiah turned, he saw the tombs there on the mount. And he sent and took the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar and defiled it, according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed, who had predicted these things” (2 Kings 23:16). Human bones were burned on that altar, exactly as this man said, by a king with exactly this name. God’s word may wait three hundred years, but it does not lapse.

Added after the event? Some scholars think the name was added after Josiah’s reform, because a name given so far ahead seems to them impossible. The question is fair, and the answer turns largely on whether God can tell the future. The Bible openly claims that he can, “declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10), and offers this case as a test of that claim, with the fulfilment recorded in a later book.
verseByVerse.note: Josiah fulfilled this prophecy about 300 years later.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'" And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself. The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD. And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God confirms his word at once: the king’s hand withers as he orders the arrest, the altar splits, and the prophet prays for the man who struck at him. Judgment and mercy arrive in the same hour.

This is the sign that the LORD has spoken. The long prophecy needs three hundred years to be verified, so the man of God gives a short one for today: the altar will be torn down and its ashes poured out, and it happens (v. 5).

His hand … dried up. The hand Jeroboam stretches out to have the prophet seized freezes where it is: not struck off, but stuck in the gesture, pointing at the man, where everybody at the festival can see it.

Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God. Look at what the king asks for: not forgiveness, not what he must do, only his hand back. And he calls the LORD “your God”, the prophet’s God, while standing at an altar he built for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

The man of God entreated the LORD. He prays at once and without conditions for the king who tried to arrest him, and the hand is restored on the spot. That is mercy, far more than Jeroboam deserved.

Mercy to the man who struck first. The prophet is a small picture of the One who, with his hands nailed down by those he came to save, prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). And Jeroboam is a warning. He had his hand restored and went on exactly as before (v. 33): a man can take the gift and refuse the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward." And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place, for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'" So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offered a meal and a reward, the man of God refuses, because God has forbidden him to eat, to drink, or to go home the way he came. To sit at Jeroboam’s table would undo the message he has just delivered.

Come home with me, and refresh yourself. This second attack is more dangerous than the first. The soldiers failed; the hospitality is the real threat. A prophet who denounces an altar in the morning and dines with its builder in the evening has unsaid everything he said. Jeroboam would not need to answer the prophecy; he would only need to be seen with the prophet.

I will not eat bread or drink water in this place. In that world, eating and drinking with someone was not merely a meal; it was fellowship and a sign of peace between the parties (see Hospitality). To take bread at Bethel would say there was something here a man of God could sit down with. So the command makes the messenger part of the message: Bethel is under judgment, and God’s servant will not be refreshed by it.

Nor return by the way that you came. The third part is stranger, and it is not explained. Why should the route matter? It looks like an arbitrary instruction attached to a reasonable one, and that is the point: obeying a command whose sense you can see is not much of a test of trust. Faith obeys the one who commands, not only what it understands. It is also the part he will break first, when he turns back.

So he went another way. He obeys all three, at the moment when obeying costs most. Everything about him so far is admirable: he interrupted a state ceremony in a rival kingdom, denounced the altar to its face, faced down an arrest, prayed for the man who ordered it, and refused half the king’s house. He is within reach of being one of the great figures of the Old Testament, and he has very little time left.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — But He Lied to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lie told in God’s name overturns a clear command when the hearer judges by the speaker instead of by God’s word. An old prophet living in Bethel hears what happened, rides after the man of God, and finds him resting under an oak (vv. 11–14). Invited home, the man of God refuses again and repeats the command exactly (vv. 15–17). Then the old man claims equal standing, an angel and the word of the LORD, all of it a lie, and the man of God goes back with him and eats (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The credentials offered are a fellow prophet, an angel, and the phrase by the word of the LORD: exactly what would make the lie convincing. Deception in God's name rarely looks like deception.
verseByVerse.examples: A newer word from a more impressive person does not overrule a clear word we already have. The question to ask is not who is speaking, but whether what they say agrees with what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king. And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone. And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it. And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am." Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread." And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place, for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'" And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him. So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An old prophet of Bethel follows the man of God and, claiming an angel’s message, lies him into disobedience. The man of God had God’s own word, and he let a newer, more impressive voice overrule it.

Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. He is a prophet of the LORD (he receives a genuine word in v. 20), yet he has been living at the centre of Jeroboam’s counterfeit religion, apparently in silence; whatever he is, he has not been crying out against that altar himself. Why he rides after the man of God the text does not say, and the temptation to fill it in should be resisted: admiration, loneliness, or something worse. We are told what he did, not why.

Sitting under an oak. Not walking, but stopped. He has been on his feet since morning, by command with nothing to eat or drink, and has sat down under a tree in the heat. Attacks often come when we are tired and have stopped moving. Even so, he refuses a second time and quotes the command a second time, accurately. He knows exactly what he was told.

I also am a prophet as you are. Then comes the sentence that kills him, and every element of it is chosen. “I also am a prophet as you are” claims equal standing: not a king or a courtier, but someone in the same office, who would know. “An angel spoke to me” claims more than a prophet’s own impression: a messenger from heaven. “By the word of the LORD” is the very formula the man of God has just used twice, so he is answered in his own vocabulary. And the content is plausible. It does not ask him to bless the altar; it revises one practical detail, and it flatters: an angel was sent about you. A better word from a better source, delivered to a tired man under a tree.

But he lied to him. The writer leaves no ambiguity: not mistaken, not a false impression. He lied, deliberately, in the name of God, about an angel.

He had the word himself. This is what the chapter exists to say. God had spoken to him directly, and he had refused a king with that word. Then a man with better credentials brought a newer word that contradicted it, and he did not test it by the one he already had. He judged by who was speaking, not by what was said. The old prophet did not have to argue that God had never spoken; he only had to say that God had said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. That is how it is nearly always done.

The test of every word. Scripture’s rule is consistent. Moses warned that a prophet whose sign comes true, but who leads away from the LORD, is not to be heeded (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Paul includes himself and the angels: “even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). For Christians that clear word is now the written Scripture, complete in Christ, and no voice, dream, impression or impressive teacher may overrule it. We are not left to hold it alone: the Spirit who gave it is given to believers to bring Christ’s words to remembrance (John 14:26).

The true Prophet held the word. Set this beside another hungry man in a lonely place. At the end of forty days without food the Lord Jesus was offered bread by a tempter who would soon be quoting Scripture at him, and he answered with the word God had already given: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). The man of God let the word go when he was tired; the true Prophet held it when he was starving, and later said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). His obedience did not fail at the end of the day, and it is counted for all who, like this prophet, have failed at the end of theirs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word judges even the prophet who carried it, and it comes through the very man who lied. At the table the LORD speaks through the old prophet: because his guest disobeyed, he will not be buried with his fathers (vv. 20–22). On the road a lion kills him and then stands beside the body with the donkey, neither eating nor fleeing, so that all who pass can see it is God’s doing (vv. 23–25). The old prophet recognises the judgment, buries the man in his own grave, mourning him as a brother, and asks to be buried beside him, because the word against Bethel will surely come to pass (vv. 26–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The word of God comes to the liar, at his own table. God's truth does not depend on the character of the one who carries it, and being used by God is no proof of being right with him.
verseByVerse.examples: The old prophet weeps over the man he deceived, calls him my brother, and gives him his own grave. Grief over the harm we have done is real and right, but it cannot undo the harm. That is why the gospel offers not only sorrow but forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you, but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At his own table the liar receives a true word from God: the man of God has disobeyed, and will not be buried with his fathers. God’s truth does not depend on the character of the one who carries it.

The word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. This is the strangest verse in the chapter. The liar is at his own table, eating a meal he obtained by inventing an angel, opposite the man he has deceived, and God speaks through him a true word, fulfilled that same day. The writer does not explain it, but the point is plain: the truth of a message is not guaranteed by the character of the messenger, and usefulness is no proof of integrity. Balaam, a seer hired to curse Israel, prophesied truly (Numbers 23–24), and Caiaphas prophesied truly without knowing it (John 11:51).

You have disobeyed the word of the LORD. The charge is stated with care, and it is laid on the man who had the command; the old prophet’s lie is not mentioned. That is severe, and the severity should be faced rather than argued down.

Deceived, yet responsible. He was lied to. He was tired, hungry and far from home, and most people would have gone. Yet he was responsible, because the word had been given to him and he knew what it said. Being deceived explains what he did but does not excuse it, and Scripture is consistent about this from Eden onward: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Genesis 3:13) was entirely true, and changed nothing.

Your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers. To be laid in the family tomb was the hope of every Israelite, as Jacob asked to be “gathered to my people” and buried with his fathers (Genesis 49:29), and to die far from it was a grief. The sentence does not yet say how he will die, only that he will not go home. He will be buried after all, but in a stranger’s grave in Bethel, the very place he was told not to stay in (vv. 30–31).

verseByVerse.quote: And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back. And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body. And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the road home a lion kills the man of God and then stands guard over his body, so that everyone can see this was God’s judgment, not an accident. The word he disobeyed is carried out exactly, and no further.

He saddled the donkey for the prophet. The old prophet sends him off with every courtesy, as though he were still an honoured guest. No answer to the sentence and no prayer are recorded; the next thing we hear is the lion.

A lion met him on the road and killed him. The writer is deliberate with the details. A lion kills him, and then nothing else happens. The donkey does not bolt, which is the one thing a donkey certainly does near a lion. The lion does not eat the body or attack the donkey, and it does not leave; people walk past it. Lions still lived in the land then, especially in the thickets along the Jordan (Jeremiah 49:19); what nobody had seen was a lion that kills and then stands guard. This was judgment carried out under orders, and it stopped the instant it was done.

Why did the deceived prophet die while the liar lived? The man of God had God’s own word to him directly, and abandoned it for a man’s claim to a revelation. The old prophet’s guilt was real, and God would deal with him in his own way; but the man of God was the one entrusted with the message, and his obedience was part of it. A prophet who told Bethel that God forbade him to eat there, and then ate there, had contradicted his own message in public.

Does God deal this harshly with every believer who is misled? No. The lion was a public, earthly judgment on a prophet whose obedience was itself his message to Bethel. The text passes no sentence on his soul, and the old prophet buries him as “my brother”. Christians who have been led astray by a confident voice should hear the warning, test what they are told by Scripture, and come back. The Lord whose word came to Jonah “the second time” (Jonah 3:1), and who restored Peter beside the lake (John 21:15–17), receives those who return.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him." And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it. And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey. And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him. And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old prophet recognises God’s judgment, carries the body home and buries the man he deceived in his own grave, mourning him as a brother. Scripture leaves this tangled man as he is, and lets him teach us.

It is the man of God who disobeyed. He knows at once what has happened and says so correctly (v. 26), though it was his own lie that caused it. When he arrives, the lion is still there and lets him take the body; the writer repeats that it had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.

Alas, my brother! Here the man becomes hard to read. He lays the body in the grave he had prepared for himself and leads the mourning, and nothing suggests the grief is not real. So we have, in one person, a prophet living quietly in the capital of a false religion; a man who invented an angel; a man through whom God then spoke truly; a man who wept over the result of his own lie; and a man who gave away his own grave. The writer reconciles none of it and does not tell us whether he repented. People are like this, and Scripture declines to tidy them up. It also warns us not to judge a message by its bearer, or a bearer by his gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old prophet asks to be buried beside the man of God, because he is now sure the word against Bethel will come true. His last recorded act is faith in God’s word, and three centuries later it is honoured.

Lay my bones beside his bones. The request is strange and rather moving, and it is not sentimental. He believes the prophecy. He has heard a man name a king three centuries early and watched the same man die within the day for disobedience, and he is convinced that every word was from God. So he makes a practical arrangement about his own bones. If bones are going to be dug up and burned on that altar, the safest grave in the country is beside the man who said so.

Three hundred years later. It worked. At Bethel Josiah asked, “What is that monument that I see?” And the men of the city told him, “It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel.” He answered, “Let him be; let no man move his bones.” So they let his bones alone, “with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria” (2 Kings 23:17–18). The old prophet’s bones were spared because they lay beside the right man’s.

Shall surely come to pass. Spoken by the man who lied, it is still the true conclusion of the story: whatever becomes of the messengers, the word stands.

The cities of Samaria. The phrase uses the name the region later bore, after Omri built the city of Samaria (16:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Signs and mercy cannot by themselves change a heart set against God. In a single day Jeroboam has seen an altar split by a word, his own hand withered and then healed by a prayer, and a prophet killed by a lion for one forbidden meal. Yet he does not turn from his evil way, but goes back to ordaining anyone who wants it as a priest of the high places (v. 33). This becomes the sin that will cut off his house and destroy it from the face of the earth (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: After this thing means after an altar split in front of him, after his own hand withered and was healed by the prayer of the man he had tried to arrest, and after a prophet from Judah named the king who would defile his altar and died on the road for eating a meal. None of it moved him.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam received judgment and mercy in the same hour: a withered hand, and then a healed one. Neither moved him. God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), and the danger is growing used to it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places. And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all he has seen in one day, Jeroboam does not turn back, and his stubbornness becomes the sin that destroys his house. Signs and mercy alone do not change a heart.

After this thing. Count what it includes: an altar split by a word in front of the assembly; the king’s own hand seized up and then healed at the prayer of the man he was arresting; and that same man killed within the day by a lion for one forbidden meal, which proved to everyone that his words were God’s.

Any who would, he ordained. Literally, he filled the hand of anyone who wanted it, the ordinary idiom for installing a priest. The phrase is contemptuous: no tribe, no calling, no qualification, only willingness. He went straight back to the very thing the man of God had denounced.

What signs cannot do. The lesson runs against most people’s instincts: signs do not produce repentance. He saw an altar destroyed by a word and a hand restored by a prayer, and was not moved an inch. The evidence was never the problem.

Neither will they be convinced. Jesus said this in a story about a rich man who wanted someone sent back from the dead to warn his brothers: “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). His own generation watched him heal, feed and raise the dead, and still asked for a sign. In a sense the rich man’s request was granted: a man did rise from the dead. Some believed and many did not. What changes a heart is not a bigger sign but God opening it to his word (Luke 24:45; Acts 16:14), which is why the risen Christ is preached and not merely displayed, and why we pray for those we long to see changed.

This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam. Jeroboam’s dynasty lasts one more generation: his son Nadab reigns two years and is murdered, and Baasha kills every member of the house of Jeroboam, “according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite” (15:29).

Nineteen kings. The verdict outlives the family. Nineteen kings rule the north in its two centuries, and nearly every one after Jeroboam is judged in the same terms: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam. The man who was offered David’s own covenant, “I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David” (11:38), becomes the standing measure of what went wrong with a nation.

13.theology:
God's word stands across centuries. A prophet names Josiah three hundred years ahead, and the later history records the fulfilment with the writer pointing back. The God of Israel is not guessing about history; he rules it. His word against false worship may wait a long time, but it does not lapse.

Mercy to the man who struck first. When Jeroboam's hand froze, the prophet did not gloat or bargain. He prayed at once for the king who had tried to arrest him, and God healed him. Faithfulness to God's word and kindness to its enemies belong together; the prophet is a small picture of the One who prayed for those who crucified him. Jeroboam, for his part, asked only for his hand and called the LORD the prophet's God, which shows how far a man can receive mercy without receiving the Giver.

Obedience when the reason is hidden. The man of God's three commands were not explained, and one of them (the route home) seems arbitrary. That was part of the test. Faith does not obey only what it can see the sense of; it trusts the one who commands. And refusing the king's table mattered: in that world, a shared meal meant fellowship, and a prophet cannot denounce an altar in the morning and dine with its builder at night.

Testing every word by the word already given. The heart of the chapter is the old prophet's lie, dressed in every credential that could make it persuasive: a fellow prophet, an angel, and the very formula by the word of the LORD. The man of God had a clear word and let a newer, more flattering one overrule it. Scripture's rule is consistent: no messenger, however impressive, may contradict what God has plainly said (Deut. 13:1-3; Gal. 1:8). For Christians that clear word is now the written Scripture, and the Spirit who gave it keeps believers in it.

Deceived and still responsible. The judgment on the man of God is severe, and this commentary does not soften it. Being lied to explains his fall but does not excuse it, because the command was given to him. Yet the lion's work was a public judgment on a prophet whose obedience was itself his message; the text does not pass sentence on his soul, and the old prophet mourns him as a brother. Those who have been led astray are called not to despair but to return, and Christ, who held the word when he was starving, has kept it in their place.

God's freedom with flawed messengers. The true word comes through the liar at his own table. God's truth is not guaranteed by the messenger's character, and usefulness is no proof of integrity. The old prophet is a tangle of compromise, deceit, grief and real faith, and Scripture leaves him unresolved. That is honest about people, and it warns us not to judge a message by its bearer or a bearer by his gifts. Even his last act, asking to be buried beside the man of God, is an act of faith in the prophecy, and three centuries later Josiah left both sets of bones alone (2 Kings 23:17-18).

Signs do not change hearts. Jeroboam saw a split altar, a withered and restored hand and a dead prophet in a single day, and went straight back to ordaining any who would. The problem was never a lack of evidence. Only God opening a heart to his word brings repentance, and that is why the church preaches the risen Christ and prays.
13.examples:
Then: A prophet who had faced down a king, watched an altar split at his word, and refused half the king's house because God had told him not to eat or drink in that place, sat down under a tree at the end of a long day. An older prophet told him an angel had said it was all right now, and he went back and ate, and was dead the same day.

Now: Three things. The first is the whole chapter: a newer word from a more impressive person does not overrule a clear word you already have. The lie nearly always has this shape: nobody says God did not say it; they say God has said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. The test is never who is speaking. We are not left to hold the word alone; the Spirit who gave it is given to believers to keep them in it (John 14:26). Second, the severity, which should not be argued down. He was genuinely deceived and genuinely responsible, because the word had been given to him. Being lied to explains his fall but does not excuse it. Yet failure is not the end of the story for those who belong to the Lord: the way back is to return to his word and confess, and he restores. And third, verse 33. Jeroboam saw an altar destroyed by a word and his own hand healed by a prayer, in one day, and changed nothing. If you are waiting for evidence dramatic enough to shift somebody, this chapter says the evidence was never what was missing; pray instead for the God who opens hearts to his word.

keyVerse.quote: And he said to him, “I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, ‘Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.’” But he lied to him.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter and its warning. A lie dressed in every credential, a fellow prophet, an angel and the very formula of a true word from God, overturned a clear command, because the hearer judged by the speaker and not by what God had already said. No messenger, however impressive, may contradict God’s word.

13.reflection:
The man of God refused the king’s table and reward because God had told him to (vv. 7–10). Why did refusing a meal matter so much? Are there places where accepting something would quietly undo what we say we believe?

The old prophet’s lie came with a fellow prophet’s standing, an angel, and the words “by the word of the LORD” (v. 18). What “newer words” compete with Scripture today, and how do we test them? Why are we most open to them when we are tired?

The man of God was deceived and still held responsible (vv. 21–22), yet the old prophet mourned him as a brother. How would you help someone who has been led astray by a confident voice to take the warning seriously without falling into despair?

Jeroboam saw an altar split and his own hand healed, and did not turn (vv. 33–34). Why do signs not change hearts? How should this shape the way we pray for, and speak to, people we love who do not believe?

14.title: Ahijah's Word and Rehoboam's Shields
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick.<sup>2</sup>And Jeroboam said to his wife, "Arise, and disguise yourself, that it not be known that you are the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people.<sup>3</sup>Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child."<sup>4</sup>Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her." When she came, she pretended to be another woman.<sup>6</sup>But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you.<sup>7</sup>Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel<sup>8</sup>and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes,<sup>9</sup>but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back,<sup>10</sup>therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone.<sup>11</sup>Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."'<sup>12</sup>Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die.<sup>13</sup>And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.<sup>14</sup>Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth,<sup>15</sup>the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger.<sup>16</sup>And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin."<sup>17</sup>Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.<sup>18</sup>And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>20</sup>And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.<sup>21</sup>Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.<sup>22</sup>And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done.<sup>23</sup>For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,<sup>24</sup>and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>25</sup>In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made,<sup>27</sup>and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.<sup>28</sup>And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.<sup>29</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>30</sup>And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.<sup>31</sup>And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.
14.overview:
Where we are. Jeroboam has watched an altar split and a prophet die, and changed nothing (13:33–34). Now sickness enters his own house. Then the writer turns back to Rehoboam’s Judah, unseen since 12:24.

The message. Nothing is hidden from God, and nothing substituted fools him. Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise, and a blind prophet greets her by name with judgment on a house that cast God behind its back; yet God notices one boy in whom there is something good. Judah, with the temple and David’s line, is no better, and its gold is carried off to Egypt and replaced with bronze. God sees through costume and substitute alike, and still keeps his promise to David.

Why it was said. The exiles had watched the north carried off beyond the Euphrates, as Ahijah foretold, and the treasures of the temple taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:13; see the introduction). Here both losses begin, in the first generation after Solomon: a north that would not stop sinning, and a south that kept the forms of worship while losing their substance.

How the chapter makes its case. Jeroboam sends his wife, disguised, to ask Ahijah about their sick son, and the blind prophet knows her at the door (vv. 1–6). Jeroboam cast aside the God who raised him, so his house will be swept away; the child alone will be mourned, because God found good in him; and Israel will be uprooted (vv. 7–16). The child dies as she crosses the threshold (vv. 17–20). In Judah the people take up the practices of Canaan, Shishak strips the temple, and bronze shields replace the gold (vv. 21–28). Rehoboam dies at war, and his son reigns (vv. 29–31).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by the need it exposes, by the character of God it shows, and by the promise it keeps. God sees through every disguise, for “no creature is hidden from his sight”, yet in Christ we have a high priest through whom we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:13, 16). The God who noticed something good in a dying boy came in his Son to a child’s deathbed and raised her (Mark 5:41). Where Rehoboam carried bronze in place of gold, the true glory came to dwell among us in the flesh (John 1:14). And the line of a faithless king runs on into the genealogy of Jesus: “Rehoboam the father of Abijah” (Matthew 1:7).

For us. Come to God as you are: he already knows who is at the door, and in Christ he will not cast you out. If you grieve a child, hold on to a God who is not careless of the little ones. And ask which parts of your faith have become bronze, carried with the same ceremony but no longer expecting to meet him, and return to the Lord himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Why Do You Pretend to Be Another?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees through every disguise, and his word against a house that cast him aside comes true to the hour, yet he notices one child in whom there is something good. When his son falls sick, Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah, who knows her by her footsteps because the LORD has told him she is coming (vv. 1–6). The message: God exalted Jeroboam, but he made other gods and cast God behind his back, so his house will be swept away (vv. 7–11). The boy will die as she enters the city, the only one of the family to be mourned and buried, and Israel itself will one day be scattered beyond the Euphrates (vv. 12–16). It happens as she crosses the threshold, and Jeroboam’s reign closes (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The disguise is wasted on a blind man, and it fails anyway, because God tells the prophet who is coming. Nothing is hidden from God, and that is a terror to the one who hides and a comfort to the one who comes openly.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam knew where to go when his child was sick. In a crisis people often reach past the religion they have built for themselves to the God they have neglected. That turning could be the way back to God; the tragedy is to come to him in disguise instead of coming honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick. And Jeroboam said to his wife, "Arise, and disguise yourself, that it not be known that you are the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people. Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his son falls sick, Jeroboam turns not to his calves but to the prophet of the LORD, yet he tries to approach him in disguise. In a crisis he knows where the truth is, and still will not come openly.

Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick. “At that time” means after everything in chapter 13. Jeroboam has two golden calves, sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood he appointed and a festival he devised, and when his child is sick he consults none of it. He sends to Shiloh. He knows perfectly well that the calves cannot help him, and the writer never says a word about it.

Who said of me that I should be king. He chooses the prophet who gave him ten pieces of a torn cloak and the offer of a lasting house like David’s (11:31, 38). Shiloh, in the hill country of Ephraim, was where the tabernacle and the ark had stood in Eli’s day (1 Samuel 1–4), and Ahijah is called the Shilonite after it (11:29). So his wife goes in disguise to the one man in Israel who knows exactly what Jeroboam was promised and what he did with it.

Ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey. The gift is chosen to match the costume: what a village woman would bring a holy man, and what a queen would not.

What we reach for when the child is sick. Jeroboam’s calves served well enough for festivals and national unity, and were useless at a bedside. Most of us run some version of it: lives built on things that work in ordinary weather, a career, money, a reputation. Then the call comes from the hospital, and people who have not prayed in twenty years find themselves praying in the corridor. It is the heart admitting what it knew all along, that the things we serve on good days cannot carry us on bad ones. Jeroboam’s tragedy is that even then he would not come to God himself; he sent his wife in disguise to fetch information.

He came to the bedside. The God Jeroboam had pushed to the edge of his kingdom is the God who, in his Son, walked into a house where a girl lay dead, took her by the hand and said, “Talitha cumi” (Mark 5:41). The calves never came to anyone’s sickbed. He did.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age. And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her." When she came, she pretended to be another woman. But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disguise is wasted on a blind prophet, because God has already told him who is coming. No one can approach God in costume; he knows who is at the door.

Ahijah could not see. The writer places the detail that makes the scene. She has walked some twenty miles in a disguise good enough that nobody on the road knew her, to consult a man who is blind. Jeroboam calculated the deception carefully, the clothes, the gift, the anonymity, and forgot that the man he was deceiving does not get his information by looking.

Come in, wife of Jeroboam. God tells Ahijah before she arrives, even announcing the pretence. He hears her feet in the doorway and greets her by the identity she has spent a day concealing, before she has said a word.

Why do you pretend to be another? It is a real question. The disguise could only ever have fooled a man; it could never touch the thing they actually wanted, which was a word from God. A great deal of religion is like this: approaching God in a costume, presenting a version of ourselves, offering the right sort of gift, when he already knows who is at the door.

I am charged with unbearable news for you. Literally, “I am sent to you with hard things.” The blind old prophet is under orders, and the message is not his to soften. “Hard” is the word used of Rehoboam’s “harsh” answer at Shechem (12:13): the kingdoms that began with a hard word to the people now receive a hard word from God.

No need to pretend. The gospel shows why no pretending is needed. No costume works with God, for “no creature is hidden from his sight” (Hebrews 4:13), and that would be unbearable news if it were all there was. But the same letter goes straight on: we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, so we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy” (Hebrews 4:16). Jeroboam’s wife came disguised and went home with hard things. Anyone who comes to Christ as he really is has his promise: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes, but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back, therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone. Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God charges Jeroboam with throwing away the God who raised him, and sentences his whole house to be swept away. At bottom his sin is contempt for a generous God, and it carries consequences for a whole household.

I exalted you from among the people. The indictment starts where every indictment in Scripture starts, with what God did first. God gave a labour foreman a kingdom. The standard is the one Solomon was measured by, “my servant David”: not sinlessness, since this book knows what David did (15:5), but a heart that never went after another god.

Other gods and metal images. Jeroboam would have said his calves stood for the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt (12:28). God does not accept the distinction: an image made to represent him is counted as another god. What a man worships is settled by what God has revealed of himself, not by the label the worshipper puts on his image.

Cast me behind your back. Thrown over the shoulder: discarded, out of sight, not worth turning round for. And “you have done evil above all who were before you” is a verdict the writer will pass again, on Omri and on Ahab (16:25, 30). Jeroboam is the first.

As a man burns up dung. The judgment is total and the image contemptuous: the dynasty swept out like dung, and its dead left unburied for dogs and birds, the final indignity in that world. It came to pass under Baasha (15:29). Then the word turns to the child.

Is it just for a whole house to be destroyed for a father’s sin? Human courts were forbidden to put children to death for their fathers’ sins (Deuteronomy 24:16). This was God’s own judgment on a royal house that led the nation into idolatry, and its sons carried on the same sins. God as Judge may take any life, and he never punishes the innocent as guilty (Ezekiel 18:20); the one child who was different is singled out for mercy (v. 13).

Uncertain wording. “Both bond and free” renders a pair of Hebrew words that mean something like “shut up and left”, used of a whole family in a few other places (for example 21:21; Deuteronomy 32:36). The exact sense is not known: perhaps slave and free, minor and adult, or those under restraint and those at large. The point is plain: every male, of whatever condition, will be cut off.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die. And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child will die as his mother comes home, but he alone of Jeroboam’s house will be mourned and buried, because God found something good in him. In the middle of judgment God notices and honours one child.

When your feet enter the city, the child shall die. She came to ask whether her son would live. He will die the moment she gets home, and her own arrival will be the signal. She must carry that for twenty miles.

Something pleasing to the LORD. This is one of the most tender verses in Kings, and it is easy to read past in the middle of a judgment oracle. In the family of the man who made the calves and cast God behind his back, God looked, and in one child found something he was pleased with: literally, a good thing toward the LORD was found in him. We are told nothing else about the boy, not his age, not what he did or said. Something in him pleased God, God noticed, and Scripture still records it three thousand years later.

He only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave. Of that whole family, this boy is the one who gets a grave and a nation’s mourning, and he dies first. The writer puts his death right after the sentence about dogs and birds, so that we cannot miss what he is spared. Isaiah says the same in a sentence people find hard until they need it: “the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace” (Isaiah 57:1–2).

Not a general explanation. The verse is not an explanation of why children die, and it must not be turned into one; anybody who has buried a child has been offered enough tidy explanations already. Nor does it make the boy’s death anything other than a grief: his mother walked home to it, and all Israel mourned. Death remains an enemy, even where God is kind within it. What the verse does say is smaller and steadier: that God saw something good in a boy in a house that had turned its back on him, that he said so, and that in taking him before the calamity he was not careless of him.

For grieving parents. There is more to hold than this verse. The Lord Jesus took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), and wept at a friend’s grave though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). With David, who said of his infant son, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23), believing parents may rest their little ones in God’s hands with real hope; and the Christian hope is not only that they are spared, but that they will be raised.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth, the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger. And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahijah looks beyond Jeroboam’s house to the end of the northern kingdom: exile beyond the Euphrates, for the sins Jeroboam taught it. A kingdom built on worship of its own devising has no root.

The LORD will raise up for himself a king. That king is Baasha, who will strike down the whole house of Jeroboam, leaving not one alive, “according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite” (15:29).

Beyond the Euphrates. Israel will be shaken “as a reed is shaken in the water”, bending whichever way the current pushes, with nothing to hold it. Here, in the first generation of the northern kingdom, is its ending. Beyond the Euphrates is Assyria, two hundred years away. The northern tribes were deported in stages, the last when Samaria fell in about 722 BC, and 2 Kings 17 gives the same reasons Ahijah gives here: “The people of Israel walked in all the sins that Jeroboam did” (2 Kings 17:22). And “their Asherim”, the poles of the Canaanite goddess (see the note on vv. 21–28), show where the calves led: once the LORD’s worship had been redesigned, Canaan’s gods followed.

Which he sinned and made Israel to sin. The phrase becomes the writer’s refrain for almost every northern king after him (15:30, 34; 16:26). Jeroboam is judged not only for his own sin but for the sin he taught a nation, and those who lead and teach God’s people still carry that double weight (James 3:1).

Uncertain wording. The words “today. And henceforth” at the end of verse 14 are compressed in the Hebrew and hard to render; they read literally something like “this is the day, and what? even now.” The likely sense is that the judgment is already under way: the king who will carry it out is as good as here.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died. And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child dies the moment his mother reaches home, exactly as God said, and Jeroboam’s reign closes. The word of the LORD comes true to the hour.

As she came to the threshold of the house, the child died. She walks twenty miles knowing what will happen, and it happens as she crosses the threshold. The writer gives her no words, here or anywhere, and no name. All Israel buries and mourns the boy, “according to the word of the LORD”.

The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. Not the biblical book of Chronicles but the royal annals of the northern kingdom, now lost, which the first readers could consult (see the introduction). The writer knew much more than he tells; what he chose to set down was the calves, the altar and the death of this child.

Twenty-two years. Jeroboam’s reign closes with the usual notice, and the son who succeeds him, Nadab, will be murdered within two years (15:25–28).
verseByVerse.note: Tirzah became the capital of the northern kingdom for a time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — He Made Bronze Shields Instead
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah, with the temple and David’s line, is no more faithful than the north, and its glory is carried off. Rehoboam, the son of an Ammonite mother, reigns in the city God chose (v. 21). Judah provokes God to jealousy with high places, pillars and Asherah poles on every hill, doing the very things the Canaanites were driven out for (vv. 22–24). In the fifth year Shishak of Egypt takes the treasures of the temple and the palace, everything, including Solomon’s gold shields. Rehoboam replaces them with bronze, and the guard carries them before the king into the house of the LORD as before (vv. 25–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Five years after Solomon's death an Egyptian army carries away the treasures of his reign, and the writer says he took away everything. Glory that consists in piled-up wealth can be lost in a single season.
verseByVerse.examples: The bronze shields are carried in the same procession as the gold ones were. It is possible to keep every form of worship and lose what it once carried. The remedy is not to abandon the forms but to come back to the Lord they exist to honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done. For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree, and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, with the temple and David’s line, falls into Canaanite worship, and five years after Solomon’s death Egypt carries off its treasures; Rehoboam replaces the gold with bronze and carries on the ceremony. Privilege does not protect, and religious decline usually looks like a cheaper substitute in the same old procession.

The city that the LORD had chosen. Verse 21 sets two things side by side without comment. It takes a whole clause to say that Jerusalem is “the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there”. And the king ruling there is the son of “Naamah the Ammonite”, one of Solomon’s foreign wives, from the people whose god Solomon honoured with a high place on the mountain east of Jerusalem (11:5–7). Since Rehoboam was forty-one when he began to reign and Solomon reigned forty years (11:42), Solomon had married her before he became king. The writer names her again in the chapter’s last verse, so he wants her noticed.

Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Now the south, and the verdict is as bad as anything said of the north. A reader coming out of chapter 12 might think the calves were the whole problem and Judah the faithful remainder. The writer will not allow it: “more than all that their fathers had done”.

They provoked him to jealousy. This is the language of a marriage, and the word God uses of himself in the commandment against images (Exodus 20:5). God is not a landlord who does not mind what his tenants worship; he is a husband who has been wronged. The phrase “on every high hill and under every green tree” becomes the prophets’ standard description of Canaanite worship.

High places and pillars and Asherim. High places were hilltop shrines; pillars were standing stones, often for Baal; Asherah was a Canaanite fertility goddess, Baal’s consort, and an “Asherah” was a wooden pole or carved image set up for her beside the altars.

All the abominations of the nations. The end of verse 24 should stop a reader. God drove the Canaanites out for these very practices, “and the land vomited out its inhabitants” (Leviticus 18:25), and Israel was warned in the same passage that the land would do the same to them (Leviticus 18:28). Judah is now doing what the previous occupants were expelled for, on the same ground, a generation after the temple was dedicated.

Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. Solomon has been dead five years, the temple has stood about thirty-five, and an Egyptian army is at the gates. Shishak is one of the few figures in this history independently documented: he is Sheshonq I, and he left a record of this campaign carved at Karnak, listing the towns he took (see the introduction).
