Jerusalem does not appear in what survives of the list, which fits a city that bought off the invader rather than being stormed. The campaign, about 925 BC, is a fixed point for dating the period. And he is the Pharaoh who had sheltered Jeroboam (11:40).

He took away everything. Four chapters earlier the reader was shown a court where “silver was not considered as anything”, and a fleet came every three years with “gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks” (10:21–22). It lasted five years past its owner. The writer singles out “all the shields of gold that Solomon had made”, two hundred large and three hundred small, hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (10:16–17).

Shields of bronze. Here, in one sentence about a routine, is an exact picture of religious decline. Everything continues. The king still goes up to the house of the LORD; the guard still turns out; the shields are still carried before him in procession and taken back to the guardroom afterwards. The form is intact to the last detail. The metal is not.

As often as the king went into the house of the LORD. Nobody stopped the ceremony or said that gold shields had meant something and bronze ones did not, and within a generation nobody in that guardroom would have remembered that they were ever gold. That is how decline usually goes: not by open rejection or by scandal, but by quietly putting something cheaper in its place while the service goes on unchanged. What in your own practice is bronze now, carried with the same ceremony by someone who no longer expects to meet God in it?

The glory that cannot be carried off. The first readers knew how this story ended: the Babylonians carried off “all the treasures of the house of the LORD” and finally burned it (2 Kings 24:13; 25:9). God’s answer was not a better set of shields. In the fullness of time his glory came to dwell among his people in person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21), which no army could strip, and which he raised three days after it was destroyed.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “male cult prostitutes” means literally “consecrated ones”, men attached to the pagan shrines. Most take it as the ESV does, but some scholars doubt that ritual prostitution was as common as was once thought, and the precise role of these men is uncertain. Either way they belonged to worship God had forbidden (Deuteronomy 23:17).
verseByVerse.note: Shishak is Pharaoh Sheshonq I; he left an inscription listing towns he took in Israel and Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–31 — And There Was War Continually
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A reign that began with God’s word obeyed ends in endless war, and the writer closes it with a quiet reminder of where the trouble began. The rest of Rehoboam’s acts are in the royal records of Judah, and there is war between him and Jeroboam all his days (vv. 29–30). He is buried in the city of David, his Ammonite mother is named a second time, and his son Abijam reigns in his place (v. 31). The line of David goes on, kept not by the faithfulness of its kings but by the promise of God.
verseByVerse.theology: War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually: two kings of one people, whom the prophet had called relatives (12:24), fighting for the rest of their lives. Division among God's people, once begun, is hard to stop.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer names Rehoboam's mother a second time, Naamah the Ammonite, and does not explain why. Sometimes Scripture teaches by placing two facts side by side and trusting us to think.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rehoboam’s reign ends in endless war with the north, and the writer closes it by naming his Ammonite mother a second time. Yet the line of David goes on, kept by God’s promise rather than by its kings.

The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. From here the closing notices alternate between the royal records of Judah and of Israel, as the history of the two kingdoms runs side by side.

What Chronicles adds. Chronicles tells a moment this account leaves out. When Shishak came, Shemaiah told the king and the princes, “You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak”; they humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous”; and God said, “They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them” (2 Chronicles 12:5–7). So Jerusalem was stripped rather than sacked, because of a moment of repentance. The writer of Kings chooses what serves his message, and here he wants us to see the bronze.

There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. The army that went home at Shemaiah’s word (12:24) spent the rest of their lives at war anyway: not the invasion they were forbidden, but border raids, skirmishes and garrison towns, two kings of one people fighting over a frontier that ran through Benjamin, for seventeen years. A man can keep the letter of a command and give his whole life to the thing it was meant to prevent.

Naamah the Ammonite. There she is again, in the last verse, with no comment either time. The writer is quietly finishing a story that began with Solomon’s foreign marriages (3:1; 11:1–8). Solomon loved foreign women; they turned away his heart; he built high places for their gods; and God tore the kingdom in two. The king left in the city God chose, ruling a remnant, doing more evil than his fathers and watching Egypt walk off with the gold, is the son of one of those women. The writer does not state the connection. He writes her name at the top of the reign and at the bottom of it, and leaves it there.

Abijam his son reigned in his place. And yet the line goes on. A faithless king is buried “in the city of David”, and his son takes the throne, because, as the next chapter says, “for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem” (15:4). Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus runs straight through this verse: “Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah” (Matthew 1:7; Abijam is the form of the name in Kings). God kept his promise to David through kings who did not keep faith with him, until the Son of David came whose heart was wholly true.

14.theology:
Coming to God in costume. Jeroboam's own religion is useless to him in a crisis, and he knows it; he sends to the prophet of the LORD. Yet he sends his wife disguised, as if God could be consulted without being faced. The blind prophet who knows her by her footsteps is Scripture's quiet joke on every attempt to get something from God while hiding from him. He sees who is at the door. That is fearful for the one who hides, and it is the ground of hope for the one who comes openly, because the God who sees all has given a High Priest through whom we may approach him as we are.

Grace despised is the heart of sin. Ahijah's indictment begins with what God had given: I exalted you from among the people. Jeroboam's sin is not only that he broke rules but that he threw behind his back the God who had raised him. Sin, at bottom, is ingratitude toward a generous God, and it carries consequences for a whole household and a whole nation.

God's eye for the hidden good. In the worst house in Israel God found something pleasing in one boy, said so, and gave him a grave and a nation's mourning. That is not an explanation of why children die. It is a glimpse of a God who notices what others overlook, who does not lose his own in the crowd of the wicked, and whose kindness can be present even in a death that is truly a grief.

The end seen from the beginning. In the first generation of the northern kingdom, Ahijah already sees its exile beyond the Euphrates, two centuries away, and 2 Kings 17 gives the same reasons when it comes. A nation built on worship of its own devising will be shaken as a reed is shaken in the water: it may stand for a long while, but it has no root, and nothing holds it. The only kingdom that cannot be shaken is the one God himself gives (Hebrews 12:28).

Judah no better. The south has the temple and David's line, and it still does more than all that their fathers had done. Privilege does not protect. God's jealousy is the jealousy of a husband, not a landlord, and Judah's practices are the very ones for which the land had expelled the Canaanites. The kingdom with the right temple can be as unfaithful as the kingdom with the wrong one.

Form without substance. The gold shields go to Egypt, and bronze ones take their place in the same procession. Nothing is renounced; something is quietly substituted. That is how religious decline usually works, and it is a question for churches and for individual believers: whether our routines still carry what they once carried. The cure is not polishing the bronze but returning to the Lord, and Chronicles shows that even in this reign, when the king and princes humbled themselves, God held back the worst (2 Chron. 12:5-7).

Obedience in the letter. Rehoboam obeyed the prophet and did not invade the north, and then fought Jeroboam for the rest of his life. It is possible to keep the letter of a command and pursue the very thing it forbade by other means. God looks for obedience of the heart, and that is what only his grace can give.
14.examples:
Then: A king sent his wife twenty miles in disguise, dressed as a villager and carrying a villager's gift, to get a word from God about their dying son; and the prophet she was deceiving was blind, and greeted her by name from the sound of her feet in the doorway before she had said anything at all.

Now: Three things. Why do you pretend to be another? is the question the chapter leaves standing: the costume could only ever have fooled a man. A great deal of religious practice is like that, and God already knows who is at the door; which is good news, because in Christ we may come as we really are and not be cast out. Second, verse 13, for anybody who has stood at a small grave: it does not explain why children die, and the loss is still a loss. What it does say is that God found something good in a boy whom no one else in that house would have thought to notice, said so, and was not careless of him in his death. And third, the bronze shields. The procession went on, and within a generation nobody remembered they had ever been gold. The question the verse asks without asking it is which parts of your own practice are bronze now. The answer is not to polish the bronze harder but to come back to the Lord himself, who has not changed, and to ask for the Spirit who makes worship living again.

keyVerse.quote: But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you.”
keyVerse.note: Ahijah’s question hangs over the whole chapter. Jeroboam’s wife comes in costume, Judah keeps its ceremonies with bronze in place of gold, and God sees through both. That is unbearable news for anyone who hides, and the beginning of good news for anyone who comes openly, because the God who knows who is at the door has given a high priest through whom we may come as we are.

14.reflection:
In his crisis Jeroboam turned not to his calves but to the prophet of the LORD, yet he sent his wife in disguise (vv. 1–6). Why do people reach for God in a crisis while still trying to keep him at a distance? What would it mean to come to him undisguised, and how does Hebrews 4:13–16 make that possible?

Ahijah’s indictment begins with what God had given Jeroboam: “I exalted you from among the people” (v. 7). How does remembering God’s gifts expose what sin really is? Where are you tempted to cast God “behind your back”?

In the worst house in Israel God found “something pleasing” in one boy (v. 13). What does this verse say, and not say, to parents who have lost a child? Where else does Scripture give them hope?

Rehoboam replaced the gold shields with bronze and kept the ceremony going (vv. 25–28). Which parts of our worship or devotion may have become bronze, and what does returning to the Lord himself look like in practice?

15.title: Abijam, Asa, Nadab and Baasha
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah.<sup>2</sup>He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.<sup>3</sup>And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem,<sup>5</sup>because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.<sup>6</sup>Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life.<sup>7</sup>The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.<sup>8</sup>And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.<sup>9</sup>In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah,<sup>10</sup>and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.<sup>11</sup>And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done.<sup>12</sup>He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.<sup>13</sup>He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron.<sup>14</sup>But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days.<sup>15</sup>And he brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels.<sup>16</sup>And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.<sup>17</sup>Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.<sup>18</sup>Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house and gave them into the hands of his servants. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying,<sup>19</sup>"Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me."<sup>20</sup>And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali.<sup>21</sup>And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah.<sup>22</sup>Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.<sup>23</sup>Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet.<sup>24</sup>And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.<sup>25</sup>Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years.<sup>26</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.<sup>27</sup>Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon.<sup>28</sup>So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.<sup>30</sup>It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>31</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>32</sup>And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.<sup>33</sup>In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years.<sup>34</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 closed the reigns of the first kings of the divided kingdom, Jeroboam in the north and Rehoboam in Judah. From here to the end of 2 Kings the history alternates between the two kingdoms, dating each reign by the other, and weighs every king by one yardstick: whether his heart was “wholly true” to the LORD, the words Solomon preached at the temple’s dedication (8:61) and stopped living by in his old age (11:4).

The message. God keeps his promise for another’s sake, and he looks for a whole heart. Judah’s throne survives an unworthy king only because the LORD keeps “a lamp in Jerusalem” for David’s sake (v. 4). Asa, a flawed king who leaves his work half done, is still said to have a heart wholly true to the LORD (v. 14), because the question is not whether a king was gifted or consistent but whether God had a rival. And in the north a man who carries out God’s judgment on another’s sin walks straight into the same sin.

Why it was said. The exiles who first read Kings had lost David’s throne and were asking whether God’s promise to David still stood (see the introduction). This chapter showed them a lamp that kept burning through bad kings, and the kind of heart God looks for in his people.

How the chapter makes its case. Abijam of Judah walks in his father’s sins, yet for David’s sake the LORD keeps the lamp burning, and even David’s great exception, the matter of Uriah, is named (vv. 1–8). Asa does right, removes the idols and his own grandmother’s Asherah image, leaves the high places standing, and later buys a Syrian alliance with temple silver; yet his heart is wholly true all his days (vv. 9–24). In the north Baasha murders Jeroboam’s son Nadab and wipes out Jeroboam’s house, as Ahijah had said, and then walks in Jeroboam’s way himself (vv. 25–34).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The lamp kept for David’s sake was kept for David’s greater Son: it burned low through many unworthy kings and was still burning when Simeon took a baby in his arms and called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). And the mercy Abijam received, for another man’s sake and not his own, is the shape of the gospel. God deals with sinners for the sake of the one Son of David whose record has no exception in it, and whose obedience is counted as theirs.

For us. God’s verdict on a heart that belongs to him is grace, not grading, and it rests on Christ, not on how much we have finished. That frees us for costly obedience, even at our own table, as Asa’s was. And it warns us against Baasha’s blindness: being right about someone else’s sin is not the same as being free of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps David’s line burning through an unworthy king, for David’s sake and not for the king’s. Abijam reigns three years, walks in all his father’s sins and has a heart not wholly true to the LORD (vv. 1–3). Nevertheless the LORD gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, a son to follow him and a secure city, because David did what was right all his life, with one named exception, the matter of Uriah the Hittite (vv. 4–5). The war between north and south runs on into the second generation, and when Abijam dies his son Asa succeeds him (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: His heart was not wholly true: the verdict passed on Solomon in his old age (11:4) is passed on his grandson in the same words. The writer has found his yardstick, and it asks about the heart before it asks about achievements.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer names David's great sin plainly and does not let it define the whole man. That is how God's people should speak of the failures of those they love and honour: honestly, without hiding them and without reducing a life to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father. Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem, because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life. The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s throne survives a king with a divided heart only because God keeps his promise to David; and the writer, giving that reason, will not pretend David was sinless.

In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam. By dating Judah’s kings from Israel’s and Israel’s from Judah’s, the writer refuses to let either half be read alone. They are one people broken in two, and he keeps making the reader look across the border.

His heart was not wholly true. Solomon used the phrase when he blessed the people (8:61); the writer said at 11:4 that it was no longer true of him; now it is denied to his grandson against the same standard, “as the heart of David his father”. The writer will use this yardstick for three centuries.

Nevertheless, for David’s sake. The dynasty survives a bad king, not because of anything in him. The word “lamp” echoes Ahijah’s prophecy, that David “may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem” (11:36). David’s soldiers had called him “the lamp of Israel” (2 Samuel 21:17), and God uses the word again when Judah deserves destruction: the LORD “was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever” (2 Kings 8:19).

A lamp in Jerusalem. The lamp is David’s line on the throne. A lamp is a small light, and the promise is not that it will blaze, or that the men holding it will be worth much, but that it will not go out. It burns through Abijam, and Ahaz, and Manasseh, down almost to nothing, and it does not go out.

Except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. That David “did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life” is an enormous claim, and a reader fresh from 2 Samuel may want to object. The writer objects for him. First, he makes the exception at all: the worst thing David ever did is named in a verse about why God kept his promise, and the name given is not Bathsheba’s but Uriah’s, whose name closes the list of David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). Second, it is narrow: one matter, named once, with the rest of a seventy-year life on the other side. That is not a whitewash but the test Kings applies everywhere, whether a man belonged to the LORD alone; and God keeping his promise for David’s sake never meant that David was better than he was.

And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. The war is mentioned twice (vv. 6–7): the conflict that began when the kingdom divided is still running in the second generation.

When the figures do not add up. Abijam begins in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year and reigns three years, yet Asa begins in Jeroboam’s twentieth; Nadab reigns “two years” but begins in Asa’s second year and is killed in his third. Ancient scribes usually counted any part of a year as a year, and the two kingdoms seem at times to have counted regnal years differently, so a reign of fourteen months could be written as two years. With these customs most of the numbers fit; a few remain hard, and careful scholars still differ over details.

Abijah in Chronicles. Chronicles calls him Abijah and records a speech and a victory over Jeroboam (2 Chronicles 13). God gave him that victory, though his heart was not wholly true; both books are true. Chronicles also names his mother differently, “Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah” (2 Chronicles 13:2), where Kings has Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. Abishalom is very likely Absalom (2 Chronicles 11:20–21), and “daughter” can mean granddaughter, perhaps through a daughter who married Uriel. The ancient Greek and Syriac translations read Maacah in Chronicles as well, so the spelling there may be a copying slip.

Kept for David’s greater Son. The lamp was still burning when old Simeon took a baby in his arms in the temple and called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). And the mercy shown to Abijam, given for another man’s sake and not his own, is the pattern of every mercy God shows sinners: we too are dealt with for the sake of Another.

One Son of David with no exception. Only one Son of David has no such exception in his record. He was “tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), and for his sake God now keeps his promises to people with an Uriah in their past.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–24 — The Heart of Asa Was Wholly True
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heart wholly true to the LORD is not a perfect record but an undivided loyalty, and Asa shows both. He reigns forty-one years and does right, as David had (vv. 9–11). He clears out the cult prostitutes and idols, and removes his own grandmother Maacah from being queen mother, burning her Asherah image at the Kidron (vv. 12–13). The high places remain, yet his heart is wholly true all his days, and he restores gifts to the temple (vv. 14–15). But when Baasha blockades him at Ramah, he strips the temple treasury to hire Ben-hadad of Syria, and the plan works (vv. 16–22). He dies old, diseased in his feet (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. The words Solomon preached and then failed to live by are said, at last, of someone far less gifted. God weighs the heart's loyalty, not the size of a man's gifts.
verseByVerse.examples: Asa's verdict sits in the same verse as his failure, but the high places were not taken away. A believer can be wholly given to God and still leave something standing that should have come down. That is not a reason for complacency, but neither is it a reason to despair.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah, and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done. He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. And he brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house and gave them into the hands of his servants. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying, "Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me." And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali. And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah. Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet. And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa served the LORD with an undivided heart all his life, though he left the high places standing and in a crisis trusted a pagan king instead of God. Scripture records both, and lets neither cancel the other.

He reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. The longest reign in Judah so far. Since verse 2 named the same woman as Abijam’s mother, Maacah is most likely Asa’s grandmother, “mother” being used of a female ancestor, which also explains why she still holds the office of queen mother into a new reign.

Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. The first good verdict since Solomon’s early years. Asa takes out the idols “his fathers had made”, and that is not small: every one had people who valued it, some were respectable simply from standing a long time, and removing them meant saying that what their fathers did was wrong.

He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother. The queen mother in Judah held a real office, seated at the king’s right hand (compare 2:19), and in a court of many wives she was often the most powerful woman in the kingdom. Asa removes her: his own grandmother, after two reigns in the office. Nor does he simply confiscate her “abominable image for Asherah”. He burns it at the Kidron, below the city, where everybody could see the smoke.

But the high places were not taken away. The writer will attach this qualification to almost every good king from here to the end; only Hezekiah and Josiah finally remove them. They were not simple idolatry: many were local hilltop sanctuaries where the LORD himself was worshipped, convenient and ancient, but not the place God had chosen, and the channel through which Canaanite practice kept seeping in. So Asa cleared out the idols and left the rival places of worship standing, because taking them down would have cost even more than removing his grandmother.

What Chronicles says. Chronicles says that Asa “took away the foreign altars and the high places” (2 Chronicles 14:3), and later that “the high places were not taken out of Israel” (2 Chronicles 15:17). The likeliest reading is that he removed the shrines to foreign gods and some of the high places, but not the local hilltop altars where the LORD himself was worshipped. Both books hold the two facts side by side.

Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. “Wholly true” translates shalem (whole, complete), from the same root as Solomon’s own name. Solomon spoke the words standing before the finished temple with the glory of God inside it: “Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God” (8:61). The writer took them from Solomon (11:4) and denied them to Abijam (v. 3). Here at last they are said of someone.

What a whole heart means. Asa is not a better man than Solomon, and nowhere near as gifted; Chronicles records that he ended badly. A heart “wholly true” is not a measure of achievement or even of consistency. It asks whether the heart has any other god beside the LORD. Solomon had seven hundred marriages and a hill full of altars; Asa had one God and a job half done. The writer records the failure and refuses to let it cancel the verdict, and a reader who can hold only one of them will misread every king in this book.

He brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts. Asa puts treasure back into the temple, which Shishak had stripped in his grandfather Rehoboam’s fifth year (14:25–26).

Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah. Ramah is about five miles north of Jerusalem, on the main road, so fortifying it is a blockade, built “that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah” (v. 17).

Then Asa took all the silver and the gold. He takes the silver and gold out of the house of the LORD, presumably including what he had just put in, and sends it to a foreign king to buy a military favour. (Damascus is the kingdom founded by Rezon, one of the adversaries God raised up against Solomon, 11:23–25.) He pays a pagan king to be treacherous, and says so: “Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel.” It works. The towns Ben-hadad takes (Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah and the district round the Sea of Galilee, here called Chinneroth) lie at Israel’s northern end on the road south from Damascus, so Baasha has to leave his blockade in the south to defend his border in the north. Asa then rebuilds his own frontier at Geba and Mizpah, near Ramah, with Baasha’s own stones.

What God thought of it. Chronicles records God’s verdict, through Hanani the seer: “Because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you. Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand. For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (2 Chronicles 16:7–9). Asa put the seer in the stocks. And “blameless” there is shalem, the very word Kings uses of Asa’s heart, quoted back at him as the thing he had just stopped acting on. The two books make no attempt to smooth the record out. Both are true.

But in his old age he was diseased in his feet. Chronicles supplies what lies behind this afterthought: “In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12). The charge is “he did not seek the LORD”. A man whose heart had been whole toward God for forty years, at the end, in pain, went everywhere except to him. As with the Syrian alliance, he did not turn to another god; he relied on his own resources and did not ask.

A hard number. Chronicles dates Baasha’s move on Ramah to Asa’s thirty-sixth year (2 Chronicles 16:1) and says there was no war until his thirty-fifth (2 Chronicles 15:19); but by the figures in Kings Baasha died in Asa’s twenty-sixth year (16:6, 8), and verse 16 here speaks of war all their days. Perhaps Chronicles counts from the division of the kingdom (about Asa’s sixteenth year), or a numeral was miscopied. Neither can be proved, and nothing in the account depends on the exact year.

A verdict of grace. God’s verdict on a heart that belongs to him is mercy, not a mark for performance. For believers that verdict rests on the one Son of David whose heart never divided for a moment, and whose obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19). He did what Asa failed to do at the end: in his own worst hour he sought his Father “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and trusted him all the way to the cross.

When obedience costs family. The principle beneath verse 13 is one Scripture does not soften: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Most obedience is not costly because a stranger opposes it. It is costly because somebody at the table does. It is a call to first loyalty, not harshness: Asa was a king removing a public idol from a public office, and most family faithfulness looks more like quiet, loving refusal than a bonfire.

What it does not mean: not a rule against doctors. 2 Chronicles 16:12 has been badly used. Isaiah prescribed a poultice of figs for Hezekiah’s boil (2 Kings 20:7), Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke is “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Seeing a doctor and taking medicine are no failure of faith. The fault was not seeking help from physicians but seeking it instead of the LORD: pray, and see the doctor.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “abominable image” (mipletset) appears only in this account and its parallel (2 Chronicles 15:16). It comes from a root meaning to shudder, so it names something horrifying or shocking, but what the object looked like is not known. Some have guessed it was obscene, given Asherah’s link with fertility, but that cannot be proved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — According to the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word against Jeroboam’s house comes true to the letter, but the man who carries it out learns nothing from it. Nadab, Jeroboam’s son, reigns two years in his father’s sin (vv. 25–26). Baasha, an officer from Issachar, murders him during the siege of Gibbethon and wipes out the whole house of Jeroboam, according to the word the LORD spoke by Ahijah, because of Jeroboam’s sins (vv. 27–30). Then Baasha reigns twenty-four years from Tirzah, at war with Asa all his days, and walks in the way of Jeroboam himself (vv. 31–34).
verseByVerse.theology: The word Ahijah gave to a woman in disguise is carried out to the letter: not one that breathed. God's word, spoken quietly in a private house, governs the violent public events that follow.
verseByVerse.examples: The man God used to execute judgment on Jeroboam’s house walked in the way of Jeroboam. Seeing clearly what was wrong with someone else is no protection against doing the same; it may even blind us to ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon. So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place. And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite. It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word against Jeroboam’s house came true to the letter through a conspirator’s ambition, and the man who carried out the judgment walked straight into the same sin.

Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel. Here the set phrase about Jeroboam’s sin (v. 26) appears for the first of many times. From here to the fall of Samaria it is stamped on king after king, each measured against a day at Bethel when Jeroboam set up a calf because he was afraid. “Which he made Israel to sin” is the part that will not go away: he built the sin into the nation’s official worship, so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it.

Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon. Nadab is murdered by one of his own officers in the middle of a siege, and the writer stops to explain. A blind prophet in Shiloh had said that God “will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone” (14:10).

According to the word of the LORD. The word was given in a private house to a woman in disguise, and it is carried out by a soldier of Issachar acting, so far as the text shows, for reasons entirely his own: a conspirator eliminating a rival dynasty, which was standard practice. And the writer says the word of the LORD was fulfilled. It is the same pattern as in 12:15 and 2 Samuel 17:14: a man acting freely, from his own motives, completes something God said. The reason is given plainly (v. 30): the family is cut off for the sins of Jeroboam, not merely because Baasha was ambitious.

He walked in the way of Jeroboam. Baasha was the instrument by which God’s word against the calves was carried out, and the first thing recorded of his own reign is that he “walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.” He wiped out a family for a sin and then committed it. The calves, the priesthood and the festival go on untouched. Baasha changes the dynasty and leaves the religion as he found it, because it made the northern kingdom possible and he needs it as much as Jeroboam did.

Why nothing changes. That is why the judgment fixes nothing. Chapter 16 opens with a prophet bringing Baasha almost word for word the message Ahijah gave Jeroboam, and Baasha’s house is destroyed the same way. Being the instrument of a judgment teaches a man nothing. He can carry out God’s sentence on somebody else’s sin in the morning and take it up himself in the afternoon, and never see the connection.

The judge who did not need judging. The cure for “the sins of Jeroboam” was never a new dynasty but a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), and no conspirator could give it. Only one King executes judgment without needing it himself. Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22), is the one judge who has no share in the sin he condemns, and he took the judgment on himself for those who trust him.

For us. It is easy to be Baasha: right about another person’s sin, zealous against it, and blind to the same thing in ourselves (Romans 2:1). Jesus’ remedy was to start with the log in our own eye (Matthew 7:3–5).

15.theology:
One people, one measure. From here Kings alternates between Judah and Israel and weighs every king by a single question: was his heart wholly true to the LORD, as David's was? It is not a question about talent, success or even consistency. It asks whether God had a rival. That measure explains why a gifted king like Solomon can lose the verdict and a limited king like Asa can receive it.

Mercy for another's sake. Abijam deserved to lose the throne, and God kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem for David's sake. The lamp is small, and it burns through many unworthy kings, but it does not go out, and it leads at last to the Light of the world. That is the shape of the gospel: God deals with sinners for the sake of Another, the Son of David whose record has no exception, and whose obedience is counted as theirs.

Honesty about the saints. Verse 5 praises David without pretending. His worst sin is named, Uriah by name, in a verse about God's faithfulness to him. Scripture never needs to hide the sins of its heroes, because its hope never rested on them. And it does not let one terrible failure erase a life that belonged to God; it holds both together, as it does for every believer who has fallen and been restored.

Costly obedience. Asa's removal of his grandmother shows that faithfulness often costs most at home. The demand Jesus makes, that he be loved above father and mother (Matt. 10:37), is not a call to cruelty but to first loyalty, and Asa shows it can be done with public clarity.

A whole heart and a half-done task. Asa left the high places, bought a Syrian alliance with temple silver, jailed a prophet, and in his last illness did not seek the LORD. Yet Kings says his heart was wholly true all his days. This commentary takes both statements as true together. The verdict is not a grade for performance; it is God's gracious judgment on where the heart belonged. That is encouragement for believers who know how much they leave undone, and also a warning: Asa's later reliance on Syria and on his own competence is the kind of drift that can coexist with real faith and still do real harm. Seeking help from physicians was not his sin; not seeking the LORD was.

The old shrines. The high places Asa left were mostly not shrines to other gods. They were local places where the LORD himself was worshipped, ancient and convenient and loved, like Bethel. Their fault was that they were not where God had chosen to put his name, and they were the channel through which Canaanite practice kept seeping back. Removing a grandmother's obscene image was hard; removing the popular, long-established, half-right places of worship would have been harder still, and Asa did not attempt it. The most stubborn obstacles to faithfulness are often not the open evils but the familiar compromises everybody is used to.

Sin built into a system. The phrase which he made Israel to sin begins here its long run through the book. Jeroboam did not only sin; he built his sin into the institutions of a nation, so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it. Leaders bear a heavier responsibility for this reason (James 3:1), and believers living inside such systems need the word of God to see what everyone around them has stopped noticing.

God rules through people who act freely. Ahijah's word against Jeroboam is fulfilled by Baasha's coup, done for Baasha's own reasons. As at Rehoboam's assembly, God's purpose is accomplished through people acting freely, without making them less responsible or him the author of their sin.

The judge who learns nothing. Baasha destroyed Jeroboam's house for its sin and then walked in that sin himself. Executing judgment does not make anyone righteous, and being right about another's failure does not free us from our own. The only remedy for the sins of Jeroboam is a changed heart, which no new dynasty could give and which God promises in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: A king of Judah stripped his own grandmother of the highest office a woman could hold in the kingdom, cut down the idol she had made, and burned it in the valley below the city where everybody could watch the smoke; and he left the hilltop shrines standing all over the country, because they were popular and old and everybody used them.

Now: Three things. Verse 14 is the one to keep, and it is the most encouraging sentence in the chapter: a heart wholly true is not a score for achievement or even consistency; it asks whether the heart has any other god beside the LORD. Asa left a job half done, hired a pagan army with temple silver, and put a prophet in the stocks, and God's verdict on his heart stands in the same verse as the failure. That is grace, not grading, and for us it rests on the one Son of David whose record has no exception in it. Second, Maacah. Obedience is rarely expensive because strangers object; it is expensive because somebody at your own table does. The Lord who asks for that first loyalty is the one who loved us first, and his Spirit gives the courage it takes. And third, Baasha, the warning nobody expects: he executed God's judgment on another man's sin and then walked straight into it. Being right about somebody else's failure is not the same as being free of it.

keyVerse.quote: But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the chapter’s measure of a king in one sentence: the failure is recorded, and the verdict still stands. A heart “wholly true” is not a perfect record but an undivided loyalty, a heart with no other god beside the LORD. It is grace, not grading, and for us it rests on the Son of David whose heart never divided.

15.reflection:
Abijam kept his throne “for David’s sake” (v. 4), not for anything in himself. How does that help you understand the way God deals with you for Christ’s sake? Where do you still try to earn what he gives for another’s sake?

Asa’s heart was “wholly true” though he left the high places and later trusted Syria rather than God (vv. 14, 18). If a whole heart is not a perfect record, what is it? What are the familiar, half-right compromises in your life that everyone has stopped noticing?

Asa’s costliest obedience was at his own family table (v. 13). How can we put Christ first in our families with both courage and love?

Baasha carried out God’s judgment on Jeroboam’s house and then walked in the same sin (vv. 29, 34). Why is it so easy to condemn in others what we tolerate in ourselves, and how does the gospel free us to look at our own sin first?

16.title: From Baasha to Ahab
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins,<sup>3</sup>behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>4</sup>Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat."<sup>5</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>6</sup>And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it.<sup>8</sup>In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.<sup>9</sup>But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah,<sup>10</sup>Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.<sup>11</sup>When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends.<sup>12</sup>Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,<sup>13</sup>for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols.<sup>14</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>15</sup>In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines,<sup>16</sup>and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.<sup>17</sup>So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.<sup>18</sup>And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died,<sup>19</sup>because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin.<sup>20</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.<sup>22</sup>But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.<sup>23</sup>In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah.<sup>24</sup>He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.<sup>25</sup>Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him.<sup>26</sup>For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols.<sup>27</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>28</sup>And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.<sup>30</sup>And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him.<sup>31</sup>And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.<sup>32</sup>He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.<sup>33</sup>And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.<sup>34</sup>In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 left Baasha on the northern throne, walking in the sins of the man whose family he had wiped out. Chapter 16 runs through five northern kings in under thirty verses, then slows almost to a stop for Ahab, because Elijah is about to arrive.

The message. A people that turns from God’s word does not stand still; it falls, and falls faster. Baasha is given Jeroboam’s sentence word for word, dynasties are cut down by the sword, and each king is worse than the last, until Ahab brings Baal himself into the capital. Through it all one thing does not fail: the word of the LORD, fulfilled against Baasha’s house within a generation (v. 12) and against Jericho’s builder after centuries (v. 34).

Why it was said. The exiles had seen both kingdoms fall and needed to understand why (see the introduction). Here was the north’s long answer to the question of what a people becomes without the king God chose: a throne passed from hand to hand by murder, weighed by a God who keeps his word to the letter.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehu the son of Hanani pronounces on Baasha the sentence Ahijah pronounced on Jeroboam, and adds that Baasha is guilty for destroying Jeroboam’s house; then Zimri murders Baasha’s drunken son Elah and wipes out the family (vv. 1–14). Zimri lasts seven days before the army makes Omri king; after a civil war Omri founds Samaria and does more evil than all before him, and his considerable power gets six verses (vv. 15–28). Then Ahab marries Jezebel, serves Baal and builds him a temple, and in his days Hiel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two sons, as Joshua had said (vv. 29–34).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. Five kings and a rival in one chapter, most of them reaching the throne by the sword, taught the prophets to long for a King who would come not by conspiracy but by God’s appointment, a shepherd like David (Ezekiel 34:23) who would lay down his own life instead of taking other men’s: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Meanwhile the lamp in Jerusalem still burns (15:4). And verse 7, where God fulfils his word through a man who still answers for his crime, finds its greatest instance at the cross, where the worst act in history was the very means God planned to save sinners (Acts 2:23).

For us. God measures by a different scale than the world does, so we need not spend our lives trying to leave a mark; it is enough that our names are written in heaven. And no sin is a light thing (v. 31): drift that is left alone does not stay where it is, but the word that judges is also the word that calls us back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same sin brings the same sentence, and God’s word against Baasha comes true as surely as his word against Jeroboam. Jehu the son of Hanani tells Baasha that God raised him from the dust and made him leader, yet he has walked in Jeroboam’s way, so his house will end like Jeroboam’s, down to the dogs and the birds (vv. 1–4). Baasha dies and his son Elah succeeds him (vv. 5–6). Verse 7 adds that Baasha is guilty both for being like Jeroboam’s house and for destroying it. Then Zimri, a chariot commander, murders Elah while he is drunk and wipes out Baasha’s whole house, as the prophet had said (vv. 8–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Baasha is Ahijah's oracle against Jeroboam with the name changed: the same opening, the same charge, the same sentence. He wiped out one house for its sin and is destroyed for the same sin himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Baasha was the instrument of a judgment, and he is still answerable for how he carried it out (v. 7). It is a warning to anyone tempted to think that serving a good end excuses the means: a manager who removes a dishonest colleague by lying about him, or a campaigner who wins a just cause by cruelty, has not been vindicated by the result.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, "Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins, behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat." Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place. Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it. In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years. But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah, Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place. When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends. Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baasha receives the very sentence he carried out on Jeroboam’s house, and is condemned both for copying Jeroboam and for destroying his family: God used his crime but did not excuse it.

Jehu the son of Hanani. This prophet Jehu is not to be confused with the later king of the same name. His father Hanani is very likely the seer who rebuked Asa about the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chronicles 16:7–10).

Since I exalted you out of the dust. Read verse 2 against 14:7; the writer repeats himself on purpose. Jeroboam heard through Ahijah that God had exalted him and made him leader, and that he had done evil above all before him. Baasha hears the same opening and the same charge, and the same sentence is coming. “Out of the dust” is if anything more pointed: Jeroboam had been a labour foreman; Baasha was an officer of Issachar with a knife and an opportunity. God raised him from nothing.

The dogs shall eat. Verse 4 is almost word for word what Ahijah said about Jeroboam’s house, down to the dogs and the birds (14:11). Baasha stood over the corpses of Jeroboam’s family and knew how and why they died. The oracle that comes to him is the same oracle, and he will have recognised it.

And also because he destroyed it. Verse 7 condemns Baasha on two counts: he was like the house of Jeroboam, and he destroyed it. Yet chapter 15 said that destruction happened “according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite” (15:29). So the same act is both the fulfilment of God’s word and a crime the man must answer for. That is not a contradiction, and the Bible states it in several places. Assyria is the rod of God’s anger against Israel, and God then punishes Assyria for the arrogance with which it struck (Isaiah 10:5–12).

Used, not commissioned. Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned by him. Baasha was not obeying an order; he was a conspirator murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God’s word was fulfilled through what he freely chose to do for his own reasons. The purpose was God’s. The motive was his, and he answers for it.

Drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza. The detail is contemptuous, and meant to be. Notice where Elah is not: his whole army is besieging Gibbethon (v. 15), the siege line where his father murdered Nadab. The king of Israel is at home, in his palace manager’s house, helplessly drunk.

He did not leave him a single male. One generation later it happens again: Baasha wiped out Jeroboam’s house, and Zimri wipes out Baasha’s. The phrase “or his friends” is new; Zimri goes wider than the family. The word is fulfilled exactly, by a man who is about to last a week.

The cross is the great instance. At the cross men did what God’s hand and plan had predestined, and Peter still calls them “lawless men” (Acts 2:23; 4:28). There the worst act in history, done by men who answered for it, was the very means God had planned to save sinners, including some of the men who had called for it (Acts 2:36–41). Baasha’s story shows the rule; Calvary shows it turned to mercy.

For us. Verse 7 answers anyone who thinks a good result justifies the way it was reached. That God brings good out of a wrong never makes the wrong right, nor makes us any less answerable for our motives.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A kingdom without God’s chosen king falls to whoever holds the army, and God measures its strongest man by a different scale. Zimri reigns seven days: the troops at Gibbethon make their commander Omri king and besiege Tirzah, and Zimri burns the palace over himself (vv. 15–20). Israel splits between Tibni and Omri until Tibni dies (vv. 21–22). Omri reigns twelve years, buys the hill of Samaria and builds his capital there, and does more evil than all before him; his might is mentioned only in passing (vv. 23–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Zimri held the throne for a week, and the writer still passes the full verdict on him (v. 19), because a week was long enough to show what he would have done with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Omri was one of the most consequential kings the north ever had, and he gets six verses. A life is not measured here by its reputation, its buildings or its place in other people's records, but by what it did with the God who gave it. That is sobering for the ambitious and a comfort for the obscure.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp. So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah. And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died, because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin. Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri. But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king. In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill. Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zimri’s seven-day reign ends in flames and the army makes Omri king; the most powerful northern king so far is given six verses and a verdict, because God does not measure greatness as the world does.

Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. It is the shortest reign in either book of Kings, and the writer still gives it the full treatment: an opening notice, a verdict, a cause of death and a summary. Seven days was long enough to be judged.

Encamped against Gibbethon. The army is besieging the same Philistine town it was besieging when Baasha murdered Nadab twenty-four years earlier. Two kings have been assassinated while the army sat outside that one town, and it is still not taken.

King over Israel that day in the camp. No prophet, no anointing, no elders, no assembly. The soldiers choose, and the general is king.

Burned the king’s house over him with fire. Whatever drove Zimri (despair, defiance, refusal to be taken alive) is not recorded; the only explanation the writer gives is his sins (v. 19). Scripture records several who took their own lives, among them Saul, Ahithophel and Judas, and commends none of them. If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today: a pastor, a trusted friend, a doctor, or the emergency services if you are in danger now.

Because of his sins that he committed. A week. He cannot have instituted anything or changed any policy. The verdict means that in seven days he did nothing about the calves either, and was going to be exactly what the kings before him were.

So Tibni died, and Omri became king. The writer disposes of a civil war inside the northern kingdom in two verses. He does not say how Tibni died, and the placement leaves little doubt.

He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer. Omri’s one solid achievement is real. Samaria is a superb site, isolated, defensible and commanding the trade roads, and it remained the northern capital until the Assyrians took it after a three-year siege in 722 BC, a considerable testimony to his judgment. The move also gave the new dynasty a fresh start: the palace at Tirzah had been burned with Zimri inside it (v. 18), and Samaria, on a hill Omri bought and built himself, owed nothing to the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha. And he bought it: the writer records the price and the seller’s name. That is a proper transaction, not a seizure.

The dates. They look tangled and are not. Zimri died in Asa’s twenty-seventh year; Omri became sole king in the thirty-first, after four years of rivalry with Tibni; and his twelve years are most naturally counted from the day the army proclaimed him, which brings his death and Ahab’s accession to Asa’s thirty-eighth (v. 29), counting part-years as years as the scribes usually did.

Omri in the wider world. By outside measures he is one of the most significant kings the northern kingdom ever had, one of the few in this book who left a mark on the records of the ancient world. Assyrian royal inscriptions call Israel “the house of Omri” long after his descendants were dead, and the Moabite Stone, set up by King Mesha, names him as the king who subdued Moab. The writer of Kings gives his reign six verses (vv. 23–28) and never mentions the international reputation. That is not ignorance. This historian is not writing about power, and is not impressed by it. He gives chapters to a building and one line to an empire’s foreign policy; he spends thirty-four verses on a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six on the king whose name a superpower used for Israel for a century.

Did more evil than all who were before him. Verse 25 is the entry in the ledger that matters to him. The verdict grows worse with each king, and will grow worse again at verse 30. As for “the might that he showed” (v. 27), the writer knows about it; he simply refers the interested reader to another book.

The anxiety of significance. We tend to read history as the Assyrians did, by who left the biggest mark, and we read our own lives the same way. Much modern ambition is not greed so much as a hunger to matter: to build something, be known for something, leave something that outlasts us. We call it legacy, and it sounds noble. But it is a heavy load, because it can never be finished, and it quietly turns every rival into a threat and every quiet year into a failure. This writer refuses the scale. Omri gets six verses; a widow at Zarephath with a handful of flour will get half a chapter. The reversal runs to the centre of the Bible. The Roman historian Tacitus gave Jesus a single passing sentence, as a man executed under Pontius Pilate; heaven’s record has it the other way round. So Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice in their successes “but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). If your name is written there, you do not have to carve it anywhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Omri founded Samaria as the new capital; Assyrian records long after called Israel “the house of Omri.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab goes beyond every king before him by bringing another god into Israel, and the chapter closes with proof that God’s word does not lapse. Ahab reigns twenty-two years in Samaria and treats Jeroboam’s sins as a light thing: he marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, serves Baal, builds him a temple and altar in Samaria, and makes an Asherah (vv. 29–33). In his days Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho, laying its foundation at the cost of his firstborn and setting up its gates at the cost of his youngest son, as Joshua had said centuries before (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Something new has happened, and the writer marks it. Jeroboam's calves were the wrong worship of the right God; Ahab builds a temple to a different god in the capital, and the friendship with Phoenicia that began under David and Solomon ends, a century later, in a marriage that brings Phoenicia’s god into Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: A man rebuilds Jericho in defiance of Joshua's curse and buries two sons (Josh. 6:26), and the writer puts it in the last verse before Elijah walks in. A land that has turned to the god of rain is about to learn that the LORD's word, not Baal's, governs the sky.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him. And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him. He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria. And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him. In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab goes further than any king before him, bringing Baal himself into Israel’s capital; and the chapter ends with a centuries-old curse fulfilled, to show that God’s word has not lapsed, just before Elijah speaks a new one.

Ahab the son of Omri began to reign. Twenty-two years, and the next six chapters belong to his reign. The writer has covered five kings in twenty-eight verses; from here to chapter 22 he slows almost to a stop, because Elijah is about to arrive.

More than all who were before him. The verdict has been getting worse all through the book. Jeroboam had “done evil above all who were before” him (14:9); Omri did more than all before him; Ahab does more than all of them.

As if it had been a light thing. The calves were not enough for him: sixty years of Jeroboam’s religion was, in Ahab’s estimation, a small matter. Jeroboam’s calves were an offence against the second commandment. He never named another god; he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. It was the wrong worship of the right God. Ahab “went and served Baal and worshiped him”. That is a different commandment and a different sin: not a corrupted approach to the LORD but another god, brought in and installed.

Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians. Jezebel is from Sidon, which is Phoenicia: the same coast, people and gods as Tyre. Hiram of Tyre had loved David, sent him cedar and blessed the LORD by name (5:1, 7). A century later the same alliance brings a Phoenician queen and her god into Israel. Her father carries Baal in his own name (Ethbaal means “with Baal”), and the Jewish historian Josephus records that he was a priest of Astarte before he took the throne. She is not a princess who happens to have brought her own religion. Chapter 18 will say she keeps four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of Asherah at her table, and has been killing the prophets of the LORD.

He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal. Ahab builds a temple for a Canaanite storm god in the city his father founded, puts an altar in it, and makes an Asherah. For the second time in four verses the writer says he exceeded everybody (v. 33).

In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. Go back some five centuries (on the traditional dating of the conquest; rather less on the later dating many scholars prefer). Jericho has fallen, and Joshua puts the city under a curse: “Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates” (Joshua 6:26). Jericho was the first city taken, so, like the first sheaf of a harvest, it was devoted entirely to God, with everything in it destroyed. (The Hebrew word is herem: something given over wholly to God, here by destruction, as his judgment on peoples whose wickedness had run its full course, Genesis 15:16.) It was never to be rebuilt as a fortified city. People did live on the site after Joshua (Judges 3:13), but now a man from Bethel rebuilds it with foundations and gates, the very act Joshua had cursed.

At the cost of Abiram his firstborn. The writer records the price with terrible precision: the firstborn when the foundation went in, “his youngest son Segub” when the gates went up. That most naturally means it took years: he buried his eldest son at the beginning and his youngest at the end, and he kept building. That is what makes the verse unbearable. It was not a single catastrophe he could not have foreseen. The first son died at the foundation, the curse was five centuries old and public, and he went on and finished the gates.
