According to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua. The writer’s only comment. Centuries later, the word was still in force. Ahab appears only as a date, “in his days”, and the verse’s position is the point. The country is worshipping Baal, the god of storm and rain and fertility; his temple is in the capital and his prophets eat at the queen’s table. And on the far side of a verse about a curse that took five hundred years and did not fail, chapter 17 begins with a man walking in from nowhere to say it will not rain again until he says so.

The curse borne. Jericho’s story does not end with Hiel. Elisha healed its water (2 Kings 2:19–22), and centuries later Jesus passed through it, opened blind Bartimaeus’s eyes and brought salvation to the house of Zacchaeus (Mark 10:46–52; Luke 19:1–10), on his way up to Jerusalem to bear the curse himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). God’s word of judgment does not fail, and neither does his word of mercy.

Did Hiel sacrifice his sons? Some think Hiel offered his sons himself as foundation sacrifices; the text does not say so. What it says is that God judged the man who defied his word, and the sons died as the curse had said. That is hard to read, and the writer does not soften it: defiance of God’s word does not stay private, and those nearest to us can bear its cost.
verseByVerse.note: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess from Sidon who promoted the worship of Baal.

16.theology:
Two generations of one family (v. 1). Jehu the son of Hanani brings this word; his father is the seer who rebuked Asa over the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chron. 16:7-10). Father and son told kings on both sides of the border what they did not want to hear, and God kept raising up such voices in a kingdom that would not listen.

The same oracle with the name changed (vv. 2-4). To Jeroboam: because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel... but you have done evil (14:7). To Baasha: since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam. The opening, the charge and the dogs and birds are the same. Baasha had seen the first oracle fulfilled, and he had learned nothing from it.

Used, and answerable (v. 7). Baasha is condemned on two counts: for being like the house of Jeroboam, and for destroying it, though 15:29 called that destruction the fulfilment of God's word through Ahijah. This is not a contradiction. Baasha was not obeying an order but murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God's word was fulfilled through what he freely chose for his own reasons. The purpose was God's; the motive was his. This verse answers anyone who thinks a good result justifies the way it was reached.

Seven days, and a full verdict (vv. 15, 19). The shortest reign in either book still gets an opening notice, a verdict, a death and a summary. A week was long enough to show what Zimri was. And Gibbethon is still not taken: two kings assassinated during sieges of the one town, twenty-four years apart, and the town holds.

The historian's measure is not the world's (vv. 23-28). By external standards Omri is one of the most significant kings the north ever had: a dynasty of four kings, after three ruling houses that lasted fifty years between them, a capital at Samaria, which he bought honestly and which outlived his line by more than a century, and enough weight that Assyrian royal inscriptions called Israel "the house of Omri" for over a hundred years after his family was destroyed. The Moabite Stone names him. His reign gets six verses. The writer knows about the might that he showed and leaves it to another book. He gives four chapters to a building and one line to an empire's foreign policy; thirty-four verses to a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six to this.

As if it had been a light thing (v. 31). Be precise about what is new. Jeroboam never named another god: he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. That was the wrong worship of the right God, a breach of the second commandment. Ahab went and served Baal and worshiped him, and built him a house in the capital. That is a different commandment and a different sin: not a corrupted approach to the LORD but another god installed. The slide took sixty years, and it began with treating the first sin as small.

The Tyrian alliance comes home (v. 31). Sidon is Phoenicia, the same coast, people and gods as Tyre. Hiram loved David, blessed the LORD by name and supplied every beam in the temple; a century later the friendship returns as a marriage that brings Baal to Samaria. What looked like a harmless alliance in one generation carried the seed of idolatry into the next.

Why verse 34 is placed here. Hiel's story has nothing to do with Ahab, who appears only as a date, in his days. The writer puts it last, immediately before a man walks in from nowhere and says there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word. The country is worshipping Baal, the god of storm and rain and fertility, with his temple in the capital and his prophets at the queen's table, and the last thing we are told before Elijah arrives is that a word God spoke centuries ago has just come true, exactly. The reader is meant to know whose word holds.
16.examples:
Then: A man from Bethel rebuilt Jericho against a curse five hundred years old, buried his eldest son when the foundations went in, and went on building for years until the gates were finished, and buried his youngest son when they were hung.

Now: Three things. Verse 7 will not let anybody off: Baasha carried out God's own judgment and is condemned for how he did it. A right outcome does not make right the motive behind it, and being useful to God’s purposes is not the same as being sent. Second, Omri is the quiet rebuke to the world’s ways of measuring a life. He was the most consequential man in that kingdom's history by every measure the world uses, and this historian gives him six verses and one sentence of verdict. And third, Hiel. The first death was the warning, and he finished the gates anyway. Most people who go on with something ruinous are not ignorant of the cost; they have already paid an instalment of it. The way out is not fresh resolve but the mercy Hiel never asked for: the God whose word against Jericho stood for five centuries has a word of pardon that stands as firmly for anyone who stops and confesses (Psalm 32:5; 1 John 1:9), and a Son whose perfect obedience is counted to those who could not finish well.

keyVerse.quote: And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.
keyVerse.note: This verse marks the turning point of the north’s decline: from the wrong worship of the right God to the worship of another god altogether. “As if it had been a light thing” shows how sin works when it is tolerated: what shocked one generation becomes the floor the next builds on. It sets the stage for Elijah and the contest between the LORD and Baal.

16.reflection:
Baasha carried out God’s word against Jeroboam’s house, yet was condemned for doing it (vv. 7, 12). How can God use someone’s wrong actions without excusing them? Where do we see this most clearly at the cross?

Omri, one of the most powerful kings of his age, gets six verses and a verdict (vv. 23–28). How does God’s scale of measurement differ from ours, and how would it change your view of your own work and legacy to rejoice that your name is written in heaven?

Ahab treated Jeroboam’s sins “as if it had been a light thing” (v. 31). How does tolerating one compromise prepare the way for a worse one? Are there sins you have come to treat as light?

Hiel rebuilt Jericho in defiance of God’s word and paid with his sons (v. 34). What does this verse teach about the reliability of God’s word, both in judgment and, through Christ, in mercy?

17.title: Elijah, the Ravens and the Widow
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word."<sup>2</sup>And the word of the LORD came to him:<sup>3</sup>"Depart from here and turn eastward and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.<sup>4</sup>You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there."<sup>5</sup>So he went and did according to the word of the LORD. He went and lived by the brook Cherith that is east of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.<sup>7</sup>And after a while the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to him,<sup>9</sup>"Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you."<sup>10</sup>So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. And he called to her and said, "Bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink."<sup>11</sup>And as she was going to bring it, he called to her and said, "Bring me a morsel of bread in your hand."<sup>12</sup>And she said, "As the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked, only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. And now I am gathering a couple of sticks that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die."<sup>13</sup>And Elijah said to her, "Do not fear; go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake of it and bring it to me, and afterward make something for yourself and your son.<sup>14</sup>For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty, until the day that the LORD sends rain upon the earth.'"<sup>15</sup>And she went and did as Elijah said. And she and he and her household ate for many days.<sup>16</sup>The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah.<sup>17</sup>After this the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. And his illness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.<sup>18</sup>And she said to Elijah, "What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!"<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Give me your son." And he took him from her arms and carried him up into the upper chamber where he lodged, and laid him on his own bed.<sup>20</sup>And he cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?"<sup>21</sup>Then he stretched himself upon the child three times and cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, let this child's life come into him again."<sup>22</sup>And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. And the life of the child came into him again, and he revived.<sup>23</sup>And Elijah took the child and brought him down from the upper chamber into the house and delivered him to his mother. And Elijah said, "See, your son lives."<sup>24</sup>And the woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth."
17.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16 ended with Ahab building a temple for Baal in Samaria, and a curse spoken by Joshua centuries before fulfilled at Jericho: God’s old words are still in force. Now, with no introduction at all, Elijah walks in with a new one, and the book slows down for six chapters of contest between the LORD and Baal.

The message. The LORD lives, and his word rules what Baal was believed to rule: rain, bread and life itself. The same word that shuts the sky over a king who worships Baal keeps a foreign widow’s jar from emptying and calls her dead son back to life. The chapter runs on that word and says so six times (vv. 1, 2, 5, 8, 16, 24), and it ends with a Gentile woman saying what Israel should have been saying: “the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth” (v. 24).

Why it was said. Ahab had made Baal, the storm god thought to send the rain, the state religion of Israel (see the introduction). The first readers, exiles living among other people’s gods, needed to know whether the LORD still lived and ruled outside the land; here he feeds his prophet beyond the Jordan and gives life in Sidon.

How the chapter makes its case. Its three scenes descend in scale and rise in weight: a nation loses its rain, a household its last meal, a mother her only child, and the same word meets each. Elijah announces the drought, then hides by the brook Cherith, fed by ravens until the brook itself dries (vv. 1–7). Sent to Zarephath in Jezebel’s homeland, he asks a starving widow for her last meal, and her flour and oil do not run out (vv. 8–16). When her son dies she thinks God has come to punish her sin; Elijah cries to the LORD, the boy lives, and she confesses that the word of the LORD in his mouth is truth (vv. 17–24).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and promise. Malachi promised that Elijah would come again before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and Jesus said of John the Baptist, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14); the prophet of the wilderness was the pattern for the forerunner who pointed to the King. Jesus himself chose this widow as the sign of God’s grace to the nations (Luke 4:25–26). And at Nain he raised another widow’s son, not by pleading as Elijah did but by his own word, “and Jesus gave him to his mother” (Luke 7:15). He then rose himself, never to die again.

For us. When the brook dries up in the middle of obedience, the word has not run out. God often gives daily bread rather than a full barn, to keep us coming back to him. And when he comes close it is not to collect an old debt: in Christ the bill has been paid, and the empty tomb settles what a lifetime of kind providences could not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — No Rain Except By My Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD, not Baal, is the living God who rules the rain, and he cares for the servant who speaks for him. Elijah appears unannounced before Ahab and swears by the living God of Israel that there will be neither dew nor rain except by his word (v. 1). Then the word of the LORD sends him east of the Jordan to hide by the brook Cherith, where he drinks from the brook and ravens bring him bread and meat morning and evening (vv. 2–6). He obeys exactly. After a while the brook itself dries up, because the drought he announced has reached his own hiding place (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The drought is not a stunt. Deuteronomy 11 says in as many words that if Israel turns to other gods the LORD will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain (Deut. 11:16-17). Ahab has installed the storm god in the capital, and God answers by withholding the very thing Baal was supposed to give: rain.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 carries the weight: the brook fails. The prophet who called the drought down is not exempt from it. God’s provision was real and it came to an end, and its ending was not a sign of God’s displeasure but the way he led Elijah on to the next instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word." And the word of the LORD came to him: "Depart from here and turn eastward and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan. You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there." So he went and did according to the word of the LORD. He went and lived by the brook Cherith that is east of the Jordan. And the ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook. And after a while the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah confronts Ahab in the name of the living God and shuts the sky, the very thing Baal was worshipped to open; then God hides and feeds his servant, and lets even his water run out while he waits for the next word.

Now Elijah the Tishbite. The verse before this one is placed beside it on purpose: a builder from Bethel has just buried two sons rebuilding Jericho, as Joshua said centuries before. Then, with no transition and no introduction, a man is standing in the throne room. Other prophets have their call described: Moses at the burning bush; Isaiah in the temple, his lips touched with a coal; Jeremiah told he was known before he was formed; Amos explaining that he was a herdsman and no prophet’s son. Elijah gets a place name and nothing else: no father, no tribe, no call, no commission.

Of Tishbe in Gilead. Gilead is east of the Jordan: high, rough grazing country, the frontier. He is not a Samaria man. He has walked in from the wrong side of the river, and the court would have heard it in his accent.

Said to Ahab. He speaks in a capital where the queen is the daughter of the king of the Sidonians (16:31), where a temple to Baal has just gone up, where hundreds of prophets of Baal and Asherah eat at the queen’s table (18:19), and where the prophets of the LORD are being hunted and hidden in caves (18:4). The question in the air is whose god this country belongs to, and a man walks in to answer it.

As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives. The usual form of an oath carries extra weight here. In the Canaanite stories Baal dies. He goes down into the throat of Mot, who is death, and while he is there the rains stop and the world goes brown; then he comes back up and the sky opens. That is the shape of the religion Ahab has installed: a god who is dead for part of every year. Elijah stands in the palace of the man who built Baal’s temple, swears by a God who is alive, and shuts the sky.

Before whom I stand. This is court language: to stand before a king is to be his servant, on duty. Elijah stands in front of Ahab and tells him this is not the court he serves in. A man at the mercy of a king with an army claims to be the servant of the real throne, with a message for a lesser one.

There shall be neither dew nor rain. Both, and the first matters more than a modern reader might guess. In that climate the rain stops around May and nothing falls until October, and the land survives the dry months on the heavy dew that comes down at night. Elijah does not merely delay the rain. He takes away the fallback.

What the covenant said. This is not an arbitrary display of power. Moses had put it in writing: “Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit” (Deuteronomy 11:16–17). Ahab has done the first half. God is doing the second, exactly as written.

Aimed at Baal. Baal is the storm. He is drawn with a lightning bolt for a spear and called the rider on the clouds; he is worshipped precisely for rain and grain and calves and children. God does not attack Baal at a weak point. He shuts off the one thing Baal exists to supply, and leaves him three years to produce it.

Except by my word. Then the clause that should stop any reader: not except by the word of the LORD, but by “my word”. God has put the weather of a nation at the disposal of a man’s mouth, and the man says so out loud to the king.

Hide yourself by the brook Cherith. After the most public statement in the kingdom, his first instruction is to hide. He goes east, back over the Jordan into his own home country, out of Ahab’s reach. Chapter 18 will tell us what he was hidden from: Ahab searched every kingdom and nation for him and made them swear they did not have him (18:10).

The ravens brought him bread and meat. A raven is on the list of birds Israel may not eat (Leviticus 11:15); it is a scavenger, a carrion bird. God keeps his prophet alive by a twice-daily delivery from unclean birds, and the food is bread and meat morning and evening: meat twice a day, in a famine, better than most Israelites ate in a good year.

So he went and did according to the word of the LORD. The writer will say this of him again and again. It is the difference between Elijah and every king in the book.

After a while the brook dried up. He prayed the drought down, and the drought came for him. The word did its work on the land, and the land included his ravine. He was not woken one morning to find the brook gone; he watched it narrow to a trickle and the pools go green and then dry, with no word from God about what came next.

In the spirit and power of Elijah. This man from the edge, who called a divided nation to choose its God, became the pattern for another. The angel said that John the Baptist would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17), and John came out of the wilderness by the Jordan, dressed as Elijah had been (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6), to prepare the way for the King himself. Elijah stood before a lesser throne as the servant of the true one; John pointed to the one who sits on it.

Elijah in James. The New Testament keeps hold of “except by my word”. James uses this exact scene to teach ordinary Christians to pray: “Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth” (James 5:17). His point is not that Elijah was a giant, but that he was not. God took an ordinary man into his confidence, and he gives us the same Spirit, who helps us in our weakness when we pray (Romans 8:26).

Not a rebuke. Elijah was exactly where God told him to be, doing exactly what God told him to do, and his supply ran out. That was not a rebuke, and not a sign that he had misheard. God also brings his own provisions to an end. The job that carried you for nine years, the church that fed you, the health that let you serve: these were given at God’s command as truly as the ravens were, and they can dry up while you stand in the middle of his will. A drying brook is not evidence that God has turned against you. Elijah waited, and the next verse begins, “Then the word of the LORD came to him”. The water ran out; the word did not.

Three and a half years. Luke and James give three and a half years of drought (Luke 4:25; James 5:17); “in the third year” (18:1) probably counts from Elijah’s stay with the widow, after a dry season had already begun.

Uncertain wording. “Of Tishbe in Gilead” follows the ancient Greek translation; the Hebrew can also be read “of the settlers of Gilead”. No town called Tishbe in Gilead is known for certain, so the exact meaning of “the Tishbite” is unsure. Either way the point is the same: he comes from the edge.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah means “my God is the LORD.” Baal was worshipped as the god of rain, so a drought struck at his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Jar That Did Not Empty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides for his prophet through the least likely person, and keeps her alive one day at a time. The word sends Elijah to Zarephath in Sidon, Jezebel’s home country, where God has commanded a widow to feed him (vv. 8–9). He finds her gathering sticks to cook a last meal for herself and her son, and asks for water and bread (vv. 10–12). Telling her not to fear, he asks her to make his cake first, with the LORD’s promise that her flour and oil will not run out until the rain comes (vv. 13–14). She does, and the jar and the jug hold out, according to the word of the LORD (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is exactly worded: not filled, not multiplied, but never empty. She is never given more than one day's flour, which is how the manna was given, a day at a time, and it is the petition Jesus put in the middle of the prayer he taught: give us this day our daily bread.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the passage Jesus preached in Nazareth (Luke 4:25-26), and his hearers tried to throw him off a cliff. The offence was that God had gone past Israel to a Sidonian before, and might do it again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to him, "Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you." So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. And he called to her and said, "Bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink." And as she was going to bring it, he called to her and said, "Bring me a morsel of bread in your hand." And she said, "As the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked, only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. And now I am gathering a couple of sticks that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die." And Elijah said to her, "Do not fear; go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake of it and bring it to me, and afterward make something for yourself and your son. For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty, until the day that the LORD sends rain upon the earth.'" And she went and did as Elijah said. And she and he and her household ate for many days. The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends his prophet to a starving foreign widow in Jezebel’s own country, asks her to give first on the strength of his promise, and keeps her alive one day at a time. Here grace reaches outside Israel, and daily bread comes from a jar that is never full and never empty.

Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon. Zarephath belongs to Sidon, which is Phoenicia, where Jezebel comes from (16:31). God’s hiding place for the most wanted man in Israel is in the home territory of the woman who is killing his prophets.

I have commanded a widow there to feed you. It is the same verb used of the ravens. When Elijah arrives, the widow has plainly been told nothing at all; she is gathering firewood for the last meal of her life. God says “I have commanded” of a woman who has received no orders and knows nothing about it, and the arrangement holds anyway.

A widow. Consider the supply line. A widow in that world had no income, no land in her own right and no man to represent her, which is why the law keeps naming her with the orphan and the sojourner. A widow with a child, in a foreign country, in the second year of a famine, is the poorest of the poor. That is the person the LORD chooses to feed his prophet.

Bring me a little water in a vessel. He asks first for water, in a drought, from a stranger, and she goes; then, as she walks away, he adds the bread (vv. 10–11).

As the LORD your God lives. She swears by God’s covenant name, and she says “your”. She knows who this is and whose he is, and she does not claim him. A Sidonian woman at a city gate can identify the God of Israel and does not pretend to belong to him.

Only a handful of flour in a jar. Her inventory is unbearable in its smallness: a handful of flour and a little oil in the bottom of a jug. Two sticks are all the fire one small cake needs, and all the wood she means to gather, because there will not be another meal. “That we may eat it and die” is not said for effect. She has done the arithmetic and reached the end of it, and she tells a stranger so in a level voice.

But first make me a little cake of it. Read on its own, it is one of the most shocking demands in Scripture: a prophet tells a starving woman to bake her last handful of flour for him and feed her child with whatever is left. Two things in the text make it something else. The first is the order of the words. “Do not fear” comes before the demand, and the promise comes straight after it. He is not proposing a transaction in which she loses and he eats; he is telling her what is about to be true and asking her to act on it one meal early. The second is what she is actually asked to risk. She expects to die either way; the choice is not between food and no food, but between eating the last of it alone and staking it on a word from the God she has just named correctly and does not serve.

The jar of flour shall not be spent. The jar is not filled, and the flour is not multiplied into sacks. She is promised only that a nearly empty jar will not become an empty one. So she never has more than one day’s flour in the house. Every morning, for something like two years, she reaches into a jar that ought to be scraped bare, and there is a handful. She is not set free from depending on God day by day; she is kept in it.

She went and did as Elijah said. A Sidonian widow, on the strength of one sentence from a foreign prophet, handed over her son’s last meal. Nobody in Israel does anything like this in the whole book. And see who eats: “she and he and her household”. She fed him and was fed. What she poured out came back to her every morning, which is what the whole Bible keeps saying about giving, and which nobody quite believes until they have tried it.

According to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah. The drought and the flour are the same word doing opposite work: closing the heavens over a king with a temple and hundreds of prophets, and holding open a clay jar for a foreign woman who has nothing.

Jesus preached this at Nazareth. This is the passage Jesus chose in the synagogue at Nazareth, at the start of his ministry. He told his neighbours that “there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow” (Luke 4:25–26). Israelite widows, of God’s own covenant people, were starving in the same famine, and God walked his prophet past all of them to a Gentile. When the congregation heard it they were filled with wrath and tried to throw him off a cliff. They understood him exactly. Here in seed is the gospel going out to the Gentiles (the non-Jewish nations), nine centuries before Paul, and it was already offensive enough to kill for. It is still the good news for every outsider: God’s grace goes looking for people who had no claim on it.

Like the manna. God provided manna the same way: gather each day what you need, and what you hoard overnight breeds worms (Exodus 16:19–20). And it is the petition the Lord Jesus put at the centre of the prayer he taught us: not give us this year our annual bread, but “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

The barn or the jar. Suppose you were offered two arrangements: a full barn, provision secured for years, or the widow’s jar, never empty and never more than a day ahead. Almost everybody wants the barn. And what we want when we want the barn is not really food; it is to be done with needing him. The jar is the better gift, though it does not feel like it, because it keeps you coming back to God each day.

Is “first make me a little cake” a pattern for giving to a minister in order to receive? No. God commanded a particular widow to trust his particular promise through his prophet. It is not a formula for “seed-faith” giving; Christians give out of thanks, not to get (2 Corinthians 9:7).
verseByVerse.note: Zarephath lay on the coast between Tyre and Sidon, in Jezebel’s home territory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who gives bread also gives life, and his word proves true even over death. The widow’s son falls ill until there is no breath left in him, and she turns on Elijah, believing his presence has brought her sin to God’s notice (vv. 17–18). Elijah carries the boy to his upper room and cries to the LORD, asking why he has brought calamity on the widow who sheltered him (vv. 19–20). He stretches himself on the child three times and prays for his life to return, and the LORD listens: the boy revives (vv. 21–22). Elijah gives him back to his mother, and she confesses that the word of the LORD in his mouth is truth (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first raising of the dead in the Bible. Until now every death Scripture records, from Abel to David's infant son, has been final. Here a dead child breathes, and the hope is planted that death need not have the last word: a hope that the empty tomb of Jesus turns into a promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Her confession shows how much it took to convince her. The jar had fed her for months and she still met the crisis by assuming God had come to collect an old debt. Provision, however sustained, had not made her sure of him. A resurrection did.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. And his illness was so severe that there was no breath left in him. And she said to Elijah, "What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!" And he said to her, "Give me your son." And he took him from her arms and carried him up into the upper chamber where he lodged, and laid him on his own bed. And he cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?" Then he stretched himself upon the child three times and cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, let this child's life come into him again." And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. And the life of the child came into him again, and he revived. And Elijah took the child and brought him down from the upper chamber into the house and delivered him to his mother. And Elijah said, "See, your son lives." And the woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When death enters the house God has been feeding, the widow fears that God has come to punish her; Elijah carries her complaint and her son to the LORD, and the first raising of the dead in Scripture proves that the word of the LORD is truth.

After this. After two years of a miracle every morning. The boy does not die during the famine, before help arrives, where we expect death; he dies after God has visibly and repeatedly kept this household alive. She has bread in her hands and a dead son in the next room. “There was no breath left in him” means he died: Elijah speaks of God “killing her son” (v. 20), and his life comes “into him again” (v. 22).

What have you against me, O man of God? What she really believes about God comes out under pressure, as it does with everybody. She believes that having a holy man in the house has drawn God’s attention to her: that while she was an obscure widow in a Phoenician town, whatever she had done was overlooked, and once God came close something old was noticed, and this is the bill. She is not attacking the prophet’s competence. She is saying that God has now looked at her properly, and that when he looks at you properly the news is bad.

Give me your son. The chapter answers her with an event rather than an argument, but its direction is already visible in what Elijah does: not defending himself, not correcting her doctrine, but holding out his hands for the boy. He takes him from her arms, carries him up to his own room and lays him on his own bed.

Have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn? He puts the accusation to God directly, and the verb he chooses is “killing”: have you done this, to her, of all people? The argument he presses is personal: she took me in; she fed me out of an empty jar; this is the household that housed your prophet. The writer records it without a word of rebuke, and the LORD answers it. That tells us what kind of speech God receives from people who are truly his. Elijah is not being irreverent. He does what the psalms do a hundred times over: he takes the complaint to the only One who can do anything about it. Grief that argues with God is still praying. And grief that has run out of words is not shut out either; the Spirit intercedes “with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26).

He stretched himself upon the child three times. He lies down on the body three times, full length, a living man over a dead one. There is no technique here, whatever later readers have found in the number. It is a man putting his own warmth and breath and weight over a child who has none, and asking. Elisha will do the same over another dead boy (2 Kings 4:34). The request itself is the plainest sentence in the chapter: “let this child’s life come into him again.” The word for life is nephesh: the breath, the life, the self.

And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. Everything Scripture has said about death until now runs one way. Abel does not come back. Nor do the generation of the flood, the firstborn of Egypt, Nadab and Abihu, Eli’s sons, or David’s infant: “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23). Through ten books death has been a one-way road. In an upstairs room in a Phoenician town, over the body of a boy whose name we are never told, the door that had only ever opened one way is shown to open both. This is the first raising of the dead anywhere in Scripture, and God gives it to a Gentile child in a widow’s house, in the middle of the worst reign in the book. The chapter that opened with “except by my word” turns on the LORD listening to the same voice. Nobody should build a doctrine of prayer that makes God the servant of a man’s mouth; but neither should anybody read this chapter and assume that what he says to God is heard politely and set aside.

Now I know that you are a man of God. The great confession in this chapter comes from a Sidonian widow, not from Ahab with the whole apparatus of a state religion, nor from anyone in Samaria. Weigh what finally produced it. Two years of daily bread out of nothing did not: she had eaten that miracle for something like seven hundred mornings, and when the crisis came her first instinct was still that God had come to collect an old debt. It took a resurrection, and that is a fair description of what it takes with any of us. Providence, however kind and long sustained, does not by itself convince anybody; the mercies that ought to have settled us are the ones we forget by Thursday. What settles it is a dead thing living.

The word of the LORD in your mouth is truth. Her last phrase is the one the chapter has been leading to since verse 1. That word shut the heavens, sent Elijah east, fed him by carrion birds, moved him to Sidon, kept a jar from emptying, and has now called a child back. The book is about to spend five chapters on a contest between a king with an army and a man with a word, and a widow in a foreign town has already announced the result.

Jesus gave him to his mother. Put this beside a road outside a town called Nain, nearly nine hundred years later. A widow is following the body of her only son out through the gate, and a man stops the procession, touches the bier and says, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” Luke, who knew this chapter and expected his readers to know it, ends the scene on the same note: “Jesus gave him to his mother” (Luke 7:14–15). The crowd said, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” (Luke 7:16). They had Elijah in mind, and they were right as far as they went; but he is far more than a prophet.

The difference is the gospel. Elijah goes upstairs, lies on the body three times, argues, pleads and waits for God to listen. Jesus stops walking, touches the bier and speaks to the dead man. No stretching out, no asking. Elijah had no such power of his own and had to plead for it; the Son of God carries it in his own person, and death hears him as a servant hears his master.

Raised to die again. The boy Elijah raised died again, eventually, as the boy at Nain did, and Lazarus. They were all handed back for a while. Only one man has come out of a grave and not gone back in, and because of him those raisings were signs of the resurrection to come, not merely a delay. The widow got her answer in an upstairs room; we get ours at an empty tomb.

In everyday life. Anyone who has been near a church for long has heard the widow’s fear: a man begins to take God seriously, the diagnosis comes, and the first thing he says is that he was fine while he kept his distance.

Why do we keep God at a distance? Many people keep God at a polite distance and call it intellectual honesty, and sometimes it is. But often, as with this widow, something older is at work: a suspicion that if God came close he would see us properly, and that would be the end of us. The moralist manages that fear by trying to be good enough to survive the inspection; the secular person by deciding that nobody is inspecting. They look like opposites, but both are ways of keeping control of the verdict. The gospel unsettles both, because it agrees with the fear and then overturns it. Yes, God sees everything; nothing is hidden. And in Jesus he came all the way into the house anyway. The religious people of his day complained, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). They meant it as an accusation, and it is the best news there is. When God looks at you properly in Christ, the news is not the bill. It is that the bill has been paid.

17.theology:
The drought is the covenant’s penalty, not a stunt (v. 1). Turn aside to other gods, Moses had written, and the LORD will shut up the heavens (Deut. 11:16-17). And it is precisely aimed: God shuts off the single commodity Baal, the rider on the clouds, exists to supply, and leaves him three years to produce it.

Except by my word (v. 1), and the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah (v. 22). The chapter opens and closes with God binding his action to a man's speech. James takes exactly this scene to teach ordinary Christians to pray, and his emphasis falls on the smallness of the man: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours (Jas. 5:17). The wonder is not the drought. It is that God took a man from Gilead far enough into his confidence to hand him the timing of it.

The brook dries up (v. 7). God ends his own provisions: the brook was his appointed supply, and the brook still dried up. The water ran out and the word did not.

The jar, not the barn (v. 14). Not filled, not multiplied, but never empty: one day's flour for two years, which is manna again (Ex. 16:19-20). God gives the kind of provision that keeps a person at his hand rather than the kind that lets them leave it.

Sent past Israel to Sidon (v. 9). Jesus chose this for his sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:25-26). The Gentile mission is here in seed, and it was offensive the first time.

The first raising of the dead (v. 22). In the ten books before this, no one who dies comes back (2 Sam. 12:23). And when it finally happens, compare the prophet and the Lord. Elijah stretches himself out three times, argues and pleads and waits to be heard; Jesus touches the bier at Nain and speaks to the dead man (Luke 7:14), and Luke closes on this chapter's own note: Jesus gave him to his mother (Luke 7:15; cf. 1 Kings 17:23). The prophet had to plead for the power. The Son has it in himself.
17.examples:
Then: A Sidonian widow gathering two sticks at a city gate, planning her son's last supper out loud to a stranger, handed him the flour instead, and put her hand into a jar that should have been empty every morning for two years.

Now: Three things this chapter presses. First, the brook. Christians are quick to read a failing provision as a verdict on themselves; when something dries up, the better question is not “What did I do wrong?” but “What am I now being told?” Second, the widow's fear in verse 18: that God's nearness has drawn his attention to her sin and this is the bill. That is a real belief and many hold it: “I was safer at a distance.” The chapter does not argue her out of it; it hands her back a living son, and the answer to the fear that God has come to collect is a God who has come to raise. Third, what actually convinced her: not two years of daily bread but a resurrection. Our certainty rests where hers did, on a grave that did not hold.

keyVerse.quote: And the woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth.”
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter runs on the word of the LORD, which shuts the sky, feeds the prophet, keeps the jar from emptying and calls a dead child back. Its climax is a foreign widow confessing what Israel had forgotten: that word is truth. It took a resurrection to convince her, and it is the resurrection of Jesus that settles the same question for us.

17.reflection:
Elijah’s brook dried up while he was exactly where God had sent him (v. 7). Have you known a provision run out in the middle of obedience? How does the next verse, “Then the word of the LORD came to him”, help you wait?

The widow was promised not a full barn but a jar that would not run out, one day at a time (vv. 14–16). Why might God choose to provide this way? How does it shape the way we pray “Give us this day our daily bread”?

When her son died, the widow assumed God had come to punish an old sin (v. 18). Where do you see that fear in yourself or others, and how does the gospel answer it?

Jesus pointed to this Gentile widow at Nazareth (Luke 4:25–26), and at Nain he raised a widow’s son by his own word (Luke 7:14–15). What do these scenes show about who Jesus is and whom his grace reaches?

18.title: Fire on Mount Carmel
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After many days the word of the LORD came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, "Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth."<sup>2</sup>So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria.<sup>3</sup>And Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly,<sup>4</sup>and when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water.)<sup>5</sup>And Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the valleys. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, and not lose some of the animals."<sup>6</sup>So they divided the land between them to pass through it. Ahab went in one direction by himself, and Obadiah went in another direction by himself.<sup>7</sup>And as Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. And Obadiah recognized him and fell on his face and said, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?"<sup>8</sup>And he answered him, "It is I. Go, tell your lord, 'Behold, Elijah is here.'"<sup>9</sup>And he said, "How have I sinned, that you would give your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me?<sup>10</sup>As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. And when they would say, 'He is not here,' he would take an oath of the kingdom or nation, that they had not found you.<sup>11</sup>And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here."'<sup>12</sup>And as soon as I have gone from you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where. And so, when I come and tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me, although I your servant have feared the LORD from my youth.<sup>13</sup>Has it not been told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the LORD, how I hid a hundred men of the LORD's prophets by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water?<sup>14</sup>And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here"'; and he will kill me."<sup>15</sup>And Elijah said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today."<sup>16</sup>So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him. And Ahab went to meet Elijah.<sup>17</sup>When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, "Is it you, you troubler of Israel?"<sup>18</sup>And he answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you have, and your father's house, because you have abandoned the commandments of the LORD and followed the Baals.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah, who eat at Jezebel's table."<sup>20</sup>So Ahab sent to all the people of Israel and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel.<sup>21</sup>And Elijah came near to all the people and said, "How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him." And the people did not answer him a word.<sup>22</sup>Then Elijah said to the people, "I, even I only, am left a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men.<sup>23</sup>Let two bulls be given to us, and let them choose one bull for themselves and cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire to it. And I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood and put no fire to it.<sup>24</sup>And you call upon the name of your god, and I will call upon the name of the LORD, and the God who answers by fire, he is God." And all the people answered, "It is well spoken."<sup>25</sup>Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first, for you are many, and call upon the name of your god, but put no fire to it."<sup>26</sup>And they took the bull that was given them, and they prepared it and called upon the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no voice, and no one answered. And they limped around the altar that they had made.<sup>27</sup>And at noon Elijah mocked them, saying, "Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened."<sup>28</sup>And they cried aloud and cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them.<sup>29</sup>And as midday passed, they raved on until the time of the offering of the oblation, but there was no voice. No one answered; no one paid attention.<sup>30</sup>Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me." And all the people came near to him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been thrown down.<sup>31</sup>Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD came, saying, "Israel shall be your name,"<sup>32</sup>and with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. And he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two seahs of seed.<sup>33</sup>And he put the wood in order and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood. And he said, "Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood."<sup>34</sup>And he said, "Do it a second time." And they did it a second time. And he said, "Do it a third time." And they did it a third time.<sup>35</sup>And the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also with water.<sup>36</sup>And at the time of the offering of the oblation, Elijah the prophet came near and said, "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.<sup>37</sup>Answer me, O LORD, answer me, that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back."<sup>38</sup>Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.<sup>39</sup>And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God."<sup>40</sup>And Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape." And they seized them. And Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slaughtered them there.<sup>41</sup>And Elijah said to Ahab, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is a sound of the rushing of rain."<sup>42</sup>So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Mount Carmel. And he bowed himself down on the earth and put his face between his knees.<sup>43</sup>And he said to his servant, "Go up now, look toward the sea." And he went up and looked and said, "There is nothing." And he said, "Go again," seven times.<sup>44</sup>And at the seventh time he said, "Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea." And he said, "Go up, say to Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you.'"<sup>45</sup>And in a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode and went to Jezreel.<sup>46</sup>And the hand of the LORD was on Elijah, and he gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
18.overview:
Where we are. Elijah has been hidden for three years, by the brook Cherith and in a widow’s house in Sidon, while the drought he announced emptied Israel’s fields (chapter 17). Now the word of the LORD sends him back to Ahab, and the contest between the LORD and Baal comes to its public test on Mount Carmel.

The message. The LORD alone is God, and he will not share his people with another. Israel had not thrown the LORD over but kept him alongside Baal, and on Carmel God makes the choice unavoidable: Baal answers a day of shouting and blood with silence, and the LORD answers a short prayer with fire. Yet the rain was promised before the contest began (v. 1): God is not persuaded into grace, but shows his people who he is so that their hearts may be turned back (v. 37).

Why it was said. Ahab and Jezebel had made Baal, the storm god, the religion of the court, and most of Israel kept both gods (see the introduction). The exiles who first read Kings had lost the land for that same divided worship, and needed to hear why, and that the LORD still answers.

How the chapter makes its case. God promises rain, and on the road Elijah meets Obadiah, Ahab’s chief minister, who has secretly kept a hundred prophets alive (vv. 1–16). Elijah turns the charge of troubling Israel back on the king, gathers the nation to Carmel, asks how long they will limp between two opinions, and sets the test of fire (vv. 17–24). Baal’s prophets shout and gash themselves all day and no one answers; Elijah rebuilds the LORD’s altar, drenches it and prays briefly, the fire falls, the people cry, “The LORD, he is God,” and the prophets of Baal are put to death (vv. 25–40). Then Elijah prays on the summit until a cloud like a man’s hand rises and the rain comes (vv. 41–46).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. On Carmel the fire fell on the sacrifice and not on the people; at the cross the judgment we deserved fell on the Lamb God provided. And Carmel shows that even fire from heaven does not change a heart (19:1–2). Only God can turn hearts back (v. 37), as he does through his Son and Spirit. Jesus asks Elijah’s question in his own words: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

For us. Many of us keep the Lord for Sunday and something else for security, success or comfort. Carmel asks what would have to change if the LORD is God. The God who answers by fire has provided the sacrifice in Christ, so we can stop paying gods that never answer and follow him wholeheartedly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Obadiah in the Cave Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has already promised the rain, and as Elijah goes to face the king, God shows that he has kept faithful servants even inside Ahab’s palace. The word sends Elijah back with the promise of rain (vv. 1–2). The famine is so severe that Ahab and his chief minister Obadiah divide the land between them to search for grass for the horses (vv. 3, 5–6). Obadiah fears the LORD greatly and has hidden and fed a hundred of the LORD’s prophets from Jezebel (vv. 3–4). Meeting Elijah, he is terrified to announce him, afraid the prophet will vanish and Ahab will kill him (vv. 7–14), until Elijah swears by the LORD of hosts that he will show himself today, and Obadiah goes (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Two men serve the same God under the same regime and do it in opposite ways. One stands in the open and tells the king to his face that he is the one troubling Israel; the other keeps his post, keeps his nerve, and keeps a hundred men alive on the palace budget for years. The writer sets them on one road and commends both.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 shows where a ruler's heart lies: three years into a famine, the king's emergency programme is fodder for the chariot horses. What we protect first in a crisis tells us what we really trust.

verseByVerse.quote: After many days the word of the LORD came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, "Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth." So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria. And Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly, and when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water.) And Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the valleys. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, and not lose some of the animals." So they divided the land between them to pass through it. Ahab went in one direction by himself, and Obadiah went in another direction by himself. And as Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. And Obadiah recognized him and fell on his face and said, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" And he answered him, "It is I. Go, tell your lord, 'Behold, Elijah is here.'" And he said, "How have I sinned, that you would give your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me? As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. And when they would say, 'He is not here,' he would take an oath of the kingdom or nation, that they had not found you. And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here."' And as soon as I have gone from you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where. And so, when I come and tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me, although I your servant have feared the LORD from my youth. Has it not been told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the LORD, how I hid a hundred men of the LORD's prophets by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water? And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here"'; and he will kill me." And Elijah said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today." So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him. And Ahab went to meet Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God settles the rain before Carmel begins, and on the road he shows Elijah that he has kept faithful servants even inside Ahab’s palace. Obadiah, the king’s chief minister, has quietly saved a hundred prophets, and the writer commends him, fear and all.

I will send rain upon the earth. Settled in a sentence to one man, before an altar is built or a prophet of Baal opens his mouth. So Carmel is not a bargain struck with heaven, as though fire must persuade God to end the drought. It is a public examination held for the people standing on the mountain, and God has already written its last line.

In the third year. The winter rains have failed twice running; the cisterns cut into the rock are down to silt; the seed grain has been eaten, so even when rain comes there will be nothing to sow; the flocks have been culled and then the breeding stock after them. Where nine people in ten farm, a third year without rain is not hardship. It is the end of the country. (On how “the third year” fits the three and a half years of Luke 4:25 and James 5:17, see the note on 17:1–7.)

Obadiah, who was over the household. Not a butler, but the highest appointment in the kingdom, the chief of the royal administration: the post Arza held when Elah was murdered in his house (16:9), and the post Shebna held in Judah before God gave it to Eliakim with the key of David on his shoulder (Isaiah 22:15–22). (He is not the prophet Obadiah of the short book that bears the name, who lived later.)

Obadiah feared the LORD greatly. So the man who runs the palace where Jezebel keeps eight hundred and fifty prophets is a believer. When Jezebel began killing the LORD’s prophets (the first the reader hears of it, dropped in as though everyone knew), he hid a hundred of them, fifty to a cave, and fed them. In a country with no rain, where the king himself is out looking for grass, someone drew bread and water for a hundred hidden men, month after month, out of the household he ran. If one guard talked, or one supplier counted the sacks, he was dead, and so were they.

The writer’s verdict on Obadiah. Preachers have often been hard on Obadiah, as though a man in a palace must be a compromiser. The writer is not. Before we are told one thing he did, we are told that he “feared the LORD greatly”, and the deeds follow as evidence.

Perhaps we may find grass. Verse 5 condemns Ahab in one sentence. His people are starving, and the king goes out to look for grass for the horses. He is not lazy; he is doing the work himself. He has the wrong priorities. Chariot horses are the army, the army is the throne, and the throne is what he is preserving. The prophets are in a cave, the farmers are burying their children, and the crown’s emergency programme is fodder.

Ahab went in one direction by himself. Each goes alone, perhaps because there was little left to feed attendants on, and it is why the meeting can happen. God empties the road, and then he puts the two of them on it.

Fell on his face. Not the wariness of an official meeting a fugitive, but homage: the second man in the kingdom bows in the road to Elijah. Then hear the two possessives. Obadiah says “my lord Elijah”; Elijah answers, “Go, tell your lord.” Obadiah has said whose man he is, and Elijah reminds him whose service he is in. There is a sting in it, and a fact the chapter does not tidy away: a man can fear the LORD greatly and still have a lord in Samaria who gives him his orders.

How have I sinned? This is the second time in two chapters that someone who fears God meets Elijah and at once hunts for the sin that must be behind it. The widow said it with a dead child in her arms (17:18); Obadiah says it on an open road, at the bare prospect of trouble. It is the reflex of people who take God seriously and have never quite believed he is on their side: bad news arrives, or merely threatens, and before any other thought there is an audit. Elijah answers it in neither chapter, not because it deserves contempt, but because it is the wrong question, and no argument cures it. What cured the widow was a living son in her arms; what settles Obadiah is a promise under oath (v. 15). The fuller answer is the one the gospel gives: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

There is no nation or kingdom. The manhunt has been international: Ahab made neighbouring kingdoms swear that they were not sheltering one man from Gilead. Obadiah also takes it for granted that the Spirit of the LORD moves this man about without notice (v. 12), and that if the king comes and the spot is empty, his own life is forfeit.

I your servant have feared the LORD from my youth. He produces his credentials, not boasting, to a man he fears does not know him: years of secret and costly courage, explained to the one colleague who ought to be glad to see him. And he repeats “Behold, Elijah is here” three times (vv. 8, 11, 14). Frightened men do not argue in straight lines; they circle.

As the LORD of hosts lives. The oath of 17:1 again, with an addition: the LORD of hosts, that is, of armies. Obadiah is afraid of one king with one army, and Elijah swears by the commander of all of them, and the frightened man takes his word. With that Obadiah leaves the story, walking back across a famished country to tell the king where to find the man he had hunted for three years, on nothing but a promise.

Where most Christians stand. Most Christians reading this chapter are not Elijah. They are somewhere in an institution that has gone wrong, doing what good can still be done inside it, unable to fix it, and sure that a braver person would have walked out years ago. The Bible’s word about that person comes in verse 3, before he does anything at all: he feared the LORD greatly. The caves came after. Staying is not the same as going along: Obadiah used his post to defy the queen, and there were things he would not do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — How Long Will You Go Limping
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The real troubler of Israel is the king who abandoned the LORD, and the nation must stop wavering and choose. Ahab greets Elijah as the troubler of Israel; Elijah answers that Ahab and his father’s house have brought the trouble by abandoning God’s commandments and following the Baals (vv. 17–18). At his word the king gathers all Israel and Jezebel’s prophets to Mount Carmel (vv. 19–20). There Elijah asks how long they will limp between two opinions, and the people say nothing (v. 21). So he proposes a test on Baal’s own ground, the God who answers by fire is God, and the people agree (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel was not choosing Baal instead of the LORD but keeping both, and Elijah asks them to stop being two things at once.
verseByVerse.examples: Their silence is the loudest sound in the chapter. It is neither defiance nor repentance; they have no answer because the question is exactly right.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, "Is it you, you troubler of Israel?" And he answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you have, and your father's house, because you have abandoned the commandments of the LORD and followed the Baals. Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah, who eat at Jezebel's table." So Ahab sent to all the people of Israel and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel. And Elijah came near to all the people and said, "How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him." And the people did not answer him a word. Then Elijah said to the people, "I, even I only, am left a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men. Let two bulls be given to us, and let them choose one bull for themselves and cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire to it. And I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood and put no fire to it. And you call upon the name of your god, and I will call upon the name of the LORD, and the God who answers by fire, he is God." And all the people answered, "It is well spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real troubler of Israel is the king who abandoned the LORD, and the people must stop trying to serve both the LORD and Baal. Elijah turns the king’s charge back on him, calls the nation to decide, and sets a test on Baal’s own ground.

Is it you, you troubler of Israel? Ahab’s first sentence after three years of hunting is not a general insult. The Hebrew word behind “troubler” is the one attached to Achan, who took the devoted things at Jericho and brought defeat on the army: “Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today” (Joshua 7:25), which is why the place is called the Valley of Achor, of Trouble. Ahab is calling Elijah an Achan, the one man in the camp whose sin is costing everyone else. It is what a man says when he cannot afford to look at the real cause: the prophet announced the drought, so the prophet must be the drought.

I have not troubled Israel, but you have. This is no personal quarrel: Ahab and his father’s house have “abandoned the commandments of the LORD and followed the Baals”. Moses had said what happens to a nation that turns aside to other gods: the LORD “will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain” (Deuteronomy 11:16–17). Ahab built Baal’s temple, and the closed sky is the result.

Who eat at Jezebel’s table. Eight hundred and fifty men fed daily on the queen’s budget, in the third year of a famine, while the chief minister searches for grass: the clergy of the state religion are the last people in Israel eating well. And a hunted man gives the king an order, and the king obeys it (vv. 19–20).

Why Ahab obeys. Not from repentance. Ahab wants rain, and he will do whatever the prophet says while the prophet is the way to water; when the water comes he will go home to his dinner and his wife and change nothing. It is common enough: doing everything asked, purely out of self-interest, with the heart untouched throughout.

The 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah. From verse 22 onward only Baal’s four hundred and fifty are mentioned. Whether Jezebel kept her own prophets at home or the writer simply leaves them aside, the text does not say, and we should not invent an answer; what it shows is that the contest is fought against the storm god alone. Asherah was a Canaanite fertility goddess, often paired with Baal in the Old Testament; an “Asherah” was also the wooden pole or carved image set up for her worship beside altars.

Gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel. The place is chosen with care: the ridge running down to the sea on the north-west edge of the kingdom, close to Phoenicia, Jezebel’s homeland and Baal’s own territory, with a ruined altar of the LORD on it (v. 30).

How long will you go limping between two different opinions? The verb is posechim, to limp or hobble. Hold on to it, because five verses later the writer uses the same word for Baal’s prophets at their ritual dance: “they limped around the altar that they had made” (v. 26). Elijah’s name for what the nation is doing with its soul is the word for what the false prophets do with their feet.

What he is accusing them of. Not what we usually assume. These people had not renounced the LORD; they had added to him. That was the working arrangement of the northern kingdom: keep the God who brought us out of Egypt for the national story, the oaths and the festivals, and keep Baal for the rain, the barley and the calving, because that was his department. They had not decided to abandon the LORD. They were abandoning him by hedging their bets.

If the LORD is God, follow him. So the demand is not “stop being a pagan” but “stop being two things at once”, and it is put with an almost shocking fairness: “but if Baal, then follow him.” Elijah offers a clean break either way. The Lord Jesus puts the same choice to every hearer: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

The people did not answer him a word. Not an argument, not a jeer, not a confession. You cannot defend the two-opinion life, and almost nobody who lives it ever decided to; it is not a view anyone holds but a way of not deciding. Ask an ordinary divided man to justify himself and he will not fight you. He will go quiet, because the case against him is one he has been carefully not making to himself for years.

The test today. Not “Do you believe in God?” but “Is there anything in your life that would have to change if the LORD is God, which has not changed?” That, and not intellectual doubt, is the limp. And the cure Elijah looks for is not a firmer resolution but the LORD who turns hearts back (v. 37).

I, even I only, am left. It is not true, and Elijah has reason to know it: days before, Obadiah told him that a hundred prophets of the LORD were alive in caves. He is not lying. He has been alone for three years and has begun to believe that he really is the only one. That belief will follow him off this mountain to Horeb, where he says the same words twice (19:10, 14), and where God answers it with a number: seven thousand. It is the great danger for a faithful few, and it is not humility. It is counting without being able to see who else is there.

The God who answers by fire, he is God. Elijah gives away every advantage: they choose the bull and go first, four hundred and fifty men against one, and the test is fire, the lightning Baal is pictured holding: his opponent’s home ground and his opponent’s weapon. Confidence looks like that. A man who thinks his God might not turn up tilts the rules in his own favour.

It is well spoken. That is all the people say between the question of verse 21 and their cry in verse 39. They will not say whether they believe, but they agree that the test is fair. It is a very human place to stand, and it is about to be taken away from them.

Uncertain wording. The word behind “opinions” is rare. It seems to mean branches, or divided thoughts; a related word lies behind “I hate the double-minded” (Psalm 119:113). Some picture a bird hopping from branch to branch, others a man limping at a fork in the road. The sense is clear either way: wavering between two loyalties.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Carmel juts into the Mediterranean near modern Haifa.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The God Who Answers By Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Baal cannot answer and the LORD does, so that the people may know that he is God and that he is turning their hearts back. The prophets of Baal call from morning to evening, limp around their altar and gash themselves under Elijah’s mockery, but no one answers (vv. 25–29). Elijah repairs the LORD’s ruined altar with twelve stones, one for each tribe, and has it soaked three times (vv. 30–35). At the hour of the evening offering he prays a short prayer (vv. 36–37), and the fire of the LORD consumes sacrifice, altar and water. The people fall on their faces confessing, “The LORD, he is God,” and the prophets of Baal are executed at the brook Kishon (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: Fire is what Baal is supposed to command, for he is the lightning, the rider on the clouds. Elijah lets the challenge be decided on the one ground where Baal is supposed to be strongest, gives his opponents the whole day and the first turn, and then floods his own altar so that nothing natural could account for what happens.
verseByVerse.examples: What the crowd shouts in verse 39 is the answer to the question of verse 21, said twice by a nation on its face. Their silence is broken at last, and broken by God's act, not by Elijah's argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first, for you are many, and call upon the name of your god, but put no fire to it." And they took the bull that was given them, and they prepared it and called upon the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no voice, and no one answered. And they limped around the altar that they had made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baal’s prophets are given every advantage and call on him for hours, and there is no answer at all. The men the nation has been limping towards are seen limping round a cold altar.

Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first. They choose the bull, they go first, and they have the numbers and the whole day: “for you are many”. One rule binds both sides: “put no fire to it” (v. 23). Baal was worshipped as the storm god who rode the clouds and hurled the lightning, so a test by fire from heaven is a test on his own ground.

From morning until noon. Some six hours: four hundred and fifty voices on a ridge above the sea, from first light until the sun stood overhead, repeating four words until they stopped meaning anything: “O Baal, answer us!” These men are not frauds putting on a show. They believe it. They have staked their lives, their credibility and the queen’s favour on it, and they are working as hard as men can work.

There was no voice, and no one answered. That is the writer’s finding, and he will repeat it in verse 29. Then the verb of verse 21 comes back: “they limped around the altar.” The nation has been limping between two opinions; here are the men it has been limping towards, hobbling round a cold altar in the noon sun. Elijah’s word for the nation was an exact description, and the writer lets us see it.

verseByVerse.quote: And at noon Elijah mocked them, saying, "Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened." And they cried aloud and cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them. And as midday passed, they raved on until the time of the offering of the oblation, but there was no voice. No one answered; no one paid attention.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah’s mockery exposes a god who can be absent, and the prophets’ answer, their own blood, shows where all man-made religion ends. The LORD who keeps Israel never sleeps, and he asks no blood of his worshippers, because he provides the sacrifice himself.

Elijah mocked them. The mockery is deliberate, sustained and rude, not a lapse of taste. Its suggestions echo the way Baal’s own worshippers pictured him: perhaps he is preoccupied, or relieving himself (the ESV says it as plainly as it deserves), or away on a journey, or asleep and needing to be woken. In the Canaanite stories Baal travels, feasts and fights, and he dies and goes down into the throat of Death and has to be brought back up. Elijah is not simply caricaturing their religion. He is echoing it.

Why the taunt is lethal. That is what makes it lethal rather than merely cruel. A god with a body has a schedule; a god with a schedule can be unavailable; and if he can be unavailable, he can be unavailable today. Set beside it the line Israel sang on the road up to Jerusalem: “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4).

Cut themselves after their custom. Verse 28 is the darkest thing on the mountain. The logic is inescapable once you are inside it. He has not answered, so we have not given enough, so give more. And when six hours of shouting have failed, what is left to give? Your own body. So the swords come out, and the blood runs down four hundred and fifty men in front of a watching nation. That reasoning has no stopping point, and in this religion it did not stop at blood: in time the same worship in the same land was putting children in the fire (2 Kings 17:17; Jeremiah 19:5). A god who never answers can always be told that he was not paid enough, and the price only ever goes one way.

No one answered; no one paid attention. Verse 29 stacks three negatives, no voice, no answer, no attention, from morning until the evening offering, some nine hours in all.

The other altar. On the same hilltop, a few hours later, a bull will burn and not one drop of any worshipper’s blood will be spilled. That is the difference between all man-made religion and the gospel, visible on this hillside before it is ever stated in a doctrine. False religion asks for your blood and keeps asking.
