The true God provides the sacrifice himself: a ram in a thicket, a lamb at Passover, and at last his own Son, so that no blood of yours is asked for.

The gods who are never paid enough. Hardly anyone today cuts himself for Baal, but the logic of verse 28 is alive and well. Make your career the thing that tells you who you are, and it will always want one more late night, one more proof; make it your body or your image, and the standard rises every time you meet it. Even morality works this way when it becomes our saviour: the conscientious person who must be good enough can never stop, because nobody ever tells him he has done enough. A god who is really an extension of our own effort cannot say “enough”; he has nothing of his own to give, and can only take. The God who answered on Carmel works the other way round. He supplied the fire and, in the end, the sacrifice, and on the cross the Son said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). The only altar where the price was ever fully paid is the one where the worshippers did not bleed.

Is such mockery ever right? Isaiah does it at length: a man cuts down a tree, roasts his dinner over half of it and bows down to the other half (Isaiah 44:14–17). But this is contempt poured on an idol, in a public contest whose rules the idol’s own priests have accepted. It is not contempt poured on people, least of all in their grief, and it never licenses that.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew words behind “musing” and “relieving himself” are rare. The first seems to mean lost in thought or busy; the second, literally something like “a going aside”, is taken by many, as by the ESV, as a polite way of saying he has gone to relieve himself, and by others as “he has wandered off”. Either way, Baal is otherwise engaged.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me." And all the people came near to him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been thrown down. Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD came, saying, "Israel shall be your name," and with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. And he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two seahs of seed. And he put the wood in order and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood. And he said, "Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood." And he said, "Do it a second time." And they did it a second time. And he said, "Do it a third time." And they did it a third time. And the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also with water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah rebuilds the LORD’s broken altar as an altar for all twelve tribes, and drenches it so that no one can explain away what is about to happen. Renewal begins by repairing what God had given, in full view of the people.

Come near to me. He brings the people off the ridge and around him, where they can see his hands. Nothing on this altar is going to happen out of sight.

The altar of the LORD that had been thrown down. Quietly devastating: there had been one here. Somebody built it and worshipped at it, and somebody else pulled it apart. Elijah’s first act is not to invent anything. He picks up stones already lying on the hilltop and puts them back where they belong. Reform nearly always begins by repairing what was there, not by inventing something new.

Elijah took twelve stones. Twelve stones, in the northern kingdom, some sixty or seventy years after the split, with Judah a foreign country across a border. It is a political act as much as a religious one, and the writer gives the reason: the name Israel was given by God to Jacob, on a night when he had nothing to recommend him and had just been wrestled to the ground and left limping (Genesis 32:28; 35:10). Ten tribes have walked out and two remain, and Elijah builds an altar that ignores the division. In God’s counting there is one people, and it is named after a limping man, which on a day when the charge is limping is a mercy.

As great as would contain two seahs of seed. The trench is measured not in cubits but in seed. A seah was a dry measure, and two seahs is about fifteen litres of grain, a little under half a bushel. In the third year of a famine, on a hillside full of farmers who have eaten their seed corn, the prophet marks out his altar in the language of a field, and then fills the field with water.

Fill four jars with water. The water could probably be had from a spring on the mountain or from the sea below. In a country where men have been dying over wells, he has twelve jars carried up and poured on the ground, with the people carrying them, so that the extravagance is theirs as well as his. He is removing explanations: when the fire comes, nobody will be able to say that the wood was dry and the sun was hot and these things happen.

Uncertain wording. “As great as would contain two seahs of seed” is literally “like a house of two seahs of seed”. It may give the trench’s size by the ground that much seed would sow, or by how much grain it would hold. Either way it was large.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the time of the offering of the oblation, Elijah the prophet came near and said, "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word. Answer me, O LORD, answer me, that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah’s short prayer asks God to show himself as Israel’s covenant God and to turn his people’s hearts back, because only he can. Its timing ties the north back to the worship God appointed in Jerusalem.

At the time of the offering of the oblation. The evening offering, around the middle of the afternoon, was being made at that moment in the temple in Jerusalem, in the other kingdom, which Ahab does not rule. Standing on a northern mountain before a northern king, Elijah times the most important prayer of his life to the offering on the altar in the city God chose. He is not starting a new religion for the north. He is bringing the north back.

Elijah the prophet came near and said. And how short the prayer is: they shouted all day, and he speaks a few dozen words.

O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. He calls on God by his covenant name and by the fathers he made promises to, and he says “Israel” where one might expect “Jacob”, the name he has just built into the altar (v. 31). This is not one more god being tried after Baal has failed. It is the God of the fathers, asked to keep faith with their children.

That you are God in Israel. He asks three things, in order: that “you are God in Israel”; that “I am your servant”; and that “I have done all these things at your word.” Not one is about winning. He wants it shown that the errand is God’s, and that nothing on this mountain was his idea.

That you have turned their hearts back. Easily read past, and it should not be. He does not pray that the people will turn their hearts back, but that they may know that God has turned them. Even their repentance is asked as God’s own work. Elijah does not for a moment think that fire from heaven will change anybody’s heart unless God changes it. Fire persuades a crowd for an afternoon. Only God turns a heart, and Elijah asks him to.

The heart God promised to turn. God later promised to do this in a new way: “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). He keeps that promise through Christ, by the Spirit. So when we pray for a friend or a child who is limping between two opinions, we pray as Elijah did, asking God to do what no argument and no experience can.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench. And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD answers by fire that consumes everything, and the people confess that he alone is God. The fire fell on the sacrifice, and the people on their faces were spared.

Then the fire of the LORD fell. Count what the fire eats: the offering, which is what fire is for; the wood, which is what fire burns; then the stones, the dust and the water in the trench. It consumes the altar, the ground under it, and the very thing that puts fires out. A day of screaming and blood produced nothing at all; a short prayer produces a fire that eats the mountain.

The LORD, he is God. A man walked in from Gilead with no father named and no call recorded, and a nation on its face gives him the answer he came for, twice.

What the name means. To most of us “the LORD” sounds like a polite word for God. But Baal was only a title, master or owner, which any god could wear. The LORD is a name, the one God gave Moses at the bush: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). He simply is. He does not die with the summer, as Baal was said to, and he cannot be managed. That is what the heart resists: we would rather have a god who is useful, because a useful god can be kept in his department. Yet when the LORD proclaimed his name, he filled it with mercy: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Elijah’s own name means “my God is the LORD”, and here a nation on its face says it with him. See Lord in the Theological Dictionary.

The fire fell on the sacrifice. On Carmel the fire of judgment fell on the sacrifice on the altar, and the people on their faces were spared. That is the shape of the gospel: at the cross the judgment the people deserved fell on the Lamb God provided, and those who trust him are not consumed. And the New Testament puts the name itself on Jesus, who said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and who came to be called on: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).

Call him by name. So when you pray this week, do not speak to a vague “someone up there”. Call on him by name, as the God who has shown you in Christ who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape." And they seized them. And Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slaughtered them there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets of Baal are executed under the law God gave Israel, a judgment for that covenant and that moment which Christ has taken out of his followers’ hands.

Seize the prophets of Baal. Do not hurry past verse 40, explain it away, or pretend it is comfortable. Three things must be said, and all three are needed.

Under a standing law. First, this is a judicial execution under a standing law, not a lynching. Deuteronomy says that the prophet who calls Israel after other gods is to be put to death, and that the community carries it out after inquiry (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 17:2–7). The people seize them, as the law lays down. These are not private enemies; they lead a movement that has been killing the LORD’s prophets (v. 4), and whose worship would go on to burn children.

Under the old covenant. Second, it was a penalty under God’s covenant with one nation, which he had set apart as his own, at a moment when its survival as the people carrying the promise was truly at stake. It is recorded; it is not held up as a pattern to copy.

The sword taken away. Third, and this settles it for a Christian: the New Testament takes the sword out of religion’s hands, with Elijah expressly in view. When a Samaritan village would not receive Jesus, James and John asked, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” “But he turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:54–55). They were recalling Elijah’s fire on the king’s soldiers (2 Kings 1:10–12). They remembered the precedent correctly, but its time had passed, and the Lord did not praise their zeal. “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting” (John 18:36). Nobody may read 1 Kings 18:40 as a warrant for violence in God’s name.

Where Christians differ: should Israel’s penalties for idolatry be applied today? A small number of Christians, called theonomists, hold that Israel’s civil laws, Deuteronomy 13’s penalties included, should be enforced by governments now. This commentary’s view: those laws were given to one nation under the old covenant and are fulfilled and ended in Christ; the moral law remains, but Christ’s kingdom is never advanced by the sword or by coercion.

Textual note. Readers of the King James or New King James will find Luke 9:54–55 longer, with the words “even as Elias did” and the rebuke “ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of”. The oldest manuscripts lack these phrases, but they only say aloud what the scene already means.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–46 — A Little Cloud Like a Man's Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rain God promised comes in answer to persistent prayer, and it begins as something small. While Ahab goes up to eat and drink, Elijah tells him he hears the rain coming, then climbs to the top of Carmel and bows to the ground in prayer (vv. 41–42). Six times his servant looks out to sea and reports nothing; the seventh time a cloud like a man’s hand is rising (vv. 43–44). Soon the sky is black and a great rain falls, and the hand of the LORD is on Elijah as he runs ahead of Ahab’s chariot all the way to Jezreel (vv. 45–46).
verseByVerse.theology: God had already said he would send rain, back in verse 1, before a word was spoken on Carmel. Elijah knows that, and still bows to the ground and sends a man to look seven times. A promise is not the end of praying; it is the only thing that makes praying anything other than shouting at the weather.
verseByVerse.examples: The first sign of the answer to a three-year drought was a smudge on the horizon you could hide behind your palm. That is the usual size of answered prayer when it first appears, and it is why the man who was told to go again six times matters more to most readers than the fire did.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elijah said to Ahab, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is a sound of the rushing of rain." So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Mount Carmel. And he bowed himself down on the earth and put his face between his knees. And he said to his servant, "Go up now, look toward the sea." And he went up and looked and said, "There is nothing." And he said, "Go again," seven times. And at the seventh time he said, "Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea." And he said, "Go up, say to Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you.'" And in a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode and went to Jezreel. And the hand of the LORD was on Elijah, and he gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah prays persistently for the rain God has already promised, and the answer begins as a cloud the size of a man’s hand. The day ends with the prophet at the summit of his life, running before the king in the power of the LORD, and the next page is a message from Jezebel.

There is a sound of the rushing of rain. No rain has fallen, there is not a cloud in the sky, and the sea to the west lies flat and bright to the horizon, yet a man says he can hear it coming. He is not guessing, nor claiming a private premonition. He was told in verse 1: “I will send rain upon the earth.” What he hears is a promise. Faith is very often just this: reporting a sound nobody else can hear yet, because God has said so.

So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Two men come off the same mountain after the same afternoon. Ahab has watched fire fall from heaven, and he goes to his dinner. Elijah climbs higher and folds himself onto the ground with his face between his knees: not a posture of dignity, but of a man in labour or in grief, doubled over.

Promise and prayer together. God had already promised the rain, and Elijah has just announced it to the king; yet he goes up and prays himself double. The promise did not make the praying unnecessary. It made the praying possible. Without it he would only be shouting at the weather; with it he is asking God for what God has undertaken to do, which is the only kind of asking that has firm ground to stand on. James sends plain Christians to this very scene: “he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit” (James 5:18).

There is nothing. Do not rush to the seventh trip. Elijah has just been answered with fire in public. Now he asks for rain, and six times a servant walks up to the lookout and comes back with the same word for a man lying face down in the dirt. If it happened to Elijah on the afternoon of Carmel, it can happen to you, and it is no verdict on your standing. The fire fell in an instant; the rain, though promised, took seven journeys. Jesus taught his disciples “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

A little cloud like a man’s hand. Hold your hand up at arm’s length against the sky: that is the size of the answer to a three-year drought when it first appears, a smudge over the water that a less interested man would not have mentioned. Elijah does not wait for a second cloud; he sends word to the king to harness his chariot before the rain stops him. Faith acts on a hand-sized cloud. Most answers arrive that size, and most people miss them because they are watching for the storm and not for the smudge: the conversation that goes better than expected, the first week of sleep, the small unmistakable loosening of something that has held for years.

He gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab. After three years the sky goes black in an afternoon. Elijah runs some seventeen miles across the plain to Jezreel, in a downpour, on foot, ahead of a chariot, at the end of a day that held a long contest and an execution at the Kishon. And see whom he runs for. To run before a king’s chariot was what a royal escort did to honour the man riding behind. Elijah has called Ahab the troubler of Israel to his face, and now he runs through the storm in front of him like a servant of the crown, bringing the king home. He never wanted Ahab’s throne. He wanted Ahab’s allegiance.

The hand of the LORD was on Elijah. So the chapter closes with the prophet at the highest point of his life: the fire has fallen, the nation has confessed, the rain has come, the prophets of Baal are dead, and the hand of the LORD is on him so that he outruns horses. But the next verse in the book is a message from Jezebel, and within days this man will be sitting alone under a bush far to the south, asking God to take his life. The writer puts the summit and the collapse back to back on purpose, and anyone who has come down off a great day knows why.
verseByVerse.note: Jezreel lay about 17 miles from Carmel.

18.theology:
The verdict precedes the contest (v. 1). God announces the rain before a single altar is built. Carmel is not a way of forcing God’s hand; it is an examination held for Israel's benefit, whose result was written before the candidates arrived. Prayer and public contending are how God's settled purpose comes to pass, not how it gets decided.

Two ways of serving God under a bad king (vv. 3-16). Elijah stands in the open; Obadiah keeps his post and keeps a hundred men alive. The Bible is kinder to the man inside the compromised institution than many of its preachers have been.

Limping between two opinions (v. 21). The people had not chosen to abandon the LORD; they kept Baal as well, to be safe. A divided life like that is not a considered view but a way of not deciding.

I, even I only, am left (v. 22). Untrue, and God will answer it at Horeb with a number (19:18). Feeling alone is the particular danger of a faithful few.

Blood, and whose (v. 28). One religion asks for your blood and keeps asking; the true God provides the sacrifice himself.

The hour and the twelve stones (vv. 31, 36). Twelve stones in a kingdom of ten, and a prayer timed to the evening lamb in Jerusalem. He is not founding a northern religion; he is bringing the north home.

That you have turned their hearts back (v. 37). He does not ask that the people turn. He asks that they may know God turned them. The great public event of his life is prayed over by a man who does not believe spectacle can convert anybody. Malachi took up the same longing when he promised that Elijah would come again to turn the hearts of fathers to their children (Malachi 4:6), and the angel told Zechariah that John the Baptist would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah to do it (Luke 1:17). The turning Elijah prayed for on Carmel is what the gospel of Christ does.

The Kishon, and Luke 9 (v. 40). A judicial execution under a standing covenant law (Deut. 13:1-5; 17:2-7), against the leadership of a movement that had been killing the LORD's prophets. Recorded, not held up as a pattern, and ruled out for the church when Jesus rebuked James and John for wanting Elijah's fire (Luke 9:54-55).
18.examples:
Then: Four hundred and fifty men shouting four words at a clear sky for nine hours, cutting themselves with swords until they were slick with their own blood, hobbling round a cold fireplace in front of a watching nation, and no voice, and no one answering, and no one paying attention.

Now: Three things. First, verse 21 in today’s terms: is there anything in your life that would have to change if the LORD is God, which has not changed? That is the limp, and nobody can defend it. But Elijah did not expect the crowd to cure itself; he asked God to turn their hearts back (v. 37), and God now does that by his Spirit, giving a new heart and causing his people to walk in his ways (Ezek. 36:26-27). Every divided day of ours is covered by the one whose obedience never limped and is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19). Second, Obadiah. A great many Christians are inside an institution that has gone wrong, doing what good can still be done there. Scripture's word over that person is written before any of his deeds: he feared the LORD greatly. Third, the seventh look. The fire fell in an instant and the rain, though promised, took seven journeys. When the answer comes it is usually the size of a hand held up against the sky.

keyVerse.quote: And Elijah came near to all the people and said, “How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” And the people did not answer him a word.
keyVerse.note: Elijah’s question is the question of the whole chapter, and of the book: Israel had not abandoned the LORD outright but was trying to keep him and Baal together. The contest on Carmel exists to make that impossible, and its answer comes in verse 39. Jesus puts the same choice to every hearer: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

18.reflection:
Israel had not rejected the LORD but kept Baal alongside him (v. 21). What “two opinions” do people most often try to hold together today, and where do you see the limp in your own life?

Obadiah served God quietly inside Ahab’s government, while Elijah confronted the king openly (vv. 3–18). What can we learn from each about faithfulness at work or in public life? Where are the lines a believer cannot cross?

Baal’s prophets gave more and more, even their own blood, and no one answered (vv. 26–29). Which modern gods demand ever more from us, and how does the cross, where God provided the sacrifice, set us free from them?

Elijah prayed earnestly for rain God had already promised, and kept praying through six reports of “nothing” (vv. 41–44). How should God’s promises shape the way we pray, and how do we keep going when the answer seems slow?

19.title: Elijah at Horeb
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.<sup>2</sup>Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow."<sup>3</sup>Then he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.<sup>4</sup>But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers."<sup>5</sup>And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat."<sup>6</sup>And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again.<sup>7</sup>And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you."<sup>8</sup>And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God.<sup>9</sup>There he came to a cave and lodged in it. And behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"<sup>10</sup>He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."<sup>11</sup>And he said, "Go out and stand on the mount before the LORD." And behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake.<sup>12</sup>And after the earthquake a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire the sound of a low whisper.<sup>13</sup>And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, there came a voice to him and said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"<sup>14</sup>He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.<sup>16</sup>And Jehu the son of Nimshi you shall anoint to be king over Israel, and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah you shall anoint to be prophet in your place.<sup>17</sup>And the one who escapes from the sword of Hazael shall Jehu put to death, and the one who escapes from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha put to death.<sup>18</sup>Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."<sup>19</sup>So he departed from there and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen in front of him, and he was with the twelfth. Elijah passed by him and cast his cloak upon him.<sup>20</sup>And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you." And he said to him, "Go back again, for what have I done to you?"<sup>21</sup>And he returned from following him and took the yoke of oxen and sacrificed them and boiled their flesh with the yokes of the oxen and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he arose and went after Elijah and assisted him.
19.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 18 ended with Elijah at the height of his life: fire from heaven, a nation on its face, rain after three years, and the prophet running before Ahab’s chariot in the power of the LORD. One message from Jezebel, and within days he is alone in the desert asking to die.

The message. When his servant is spent and sure that everything has come to nothing, the LORD does not cast him off. He restores him gently, with sleep, food and a quiet word; he shows him that his kingdom goes forward by his word, not by spectacle; and he tells him what he could not see: God has kept seven thousand for himself, and the work will go on through others.

Why it was said. The first readers, exiles after the fall of Jerusalem (see the introduction), could easily feel as Elijah did, that God’s cause had failed and the faithful were gone. This chapter tells them that God is still keeping a remnant and his word is still at work.

How the chapter makes its case. Jezebel’s one threat sends Elijah running to the far south, where he asks to die, “for I am no better than my fathers”; God answers with sleep and food, twice, and he walks forty days to Horeb, the mountain of the covenant (vv. 1–8). There he twice answers God’s question by saying that he alone is left; wind, earthquake and fire pass, and the LORD is in none of them, and then comes the sound of a low whisper (vv. 9–14). God sends him back with three commissions, a successor, and the news of seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal (vv. 15–18). It ends in a field, where Elijah’s cloak falls on Elisha, who burns his plough and follows as a servant (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God that Christ reveals. Moses and Elijah, who each met God at Horeb, met Jesus on another mountain and spoke of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). Elijah only felt alone; Jesus truly was left alone, and went to the cross for people whose zeal had run out. The tenderness of God under the broom tree is the tenderness of Christ: “a bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:20).

For us. A great day can be followed by a dark one, and that is not the end of faith. God’s first answer to the exhausted is often rest and bread, then a word, then a task. You are not the only one left, you do not have to be extraordinary, and the work does not depend on you: the Lord keeps his people for himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets his exhausted, despairing servant not with rebuke but with rest, food and gentle care. Ahab tells Jezebel all that Elijah has done, leaving God out of it, and she sends a messenger vowing to kill him within a day (vv. 1–2). Elijah flees to Beersheba, leaves his servant there, and goes on alone into the wilderness, where he sits under a broom tree and asks to die, saying he is no better than his fathers (vv. 3–4). He sleeps; an angel touches him and gives him bread and water, twice, saying the journey is too great for him, and in the strength of that food he walks forty days and nights to Horeb, the mount of God (vv. 5–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Read verse 4 carefully and the despair turns out not to be about Jezebel. His reason is I am no better than my fathers: he has measured himself against what he hoped he was and come up ordinary.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what God does not do. There is no rebuke, no reminder of yesterday's fire, no summons to pull himself together. Care for the body comes first, and the word, when it comes, is kind.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow." Then he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers." And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat." And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet who faced down Baal collapses after his greatest day, less from fear of Jezebel than because the triumph changed nothing; and God meets his despair with sleep, food, a touch and a gentle word, not a rebuke.

Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done. The only report of Carmel from inside the palace has no fire in it. Ahab watched fire fall from heaven and a nation go down on its face, and he goes home and reports a body count: “all that Elijah had done”, not what God did. It is possible to see everything and register none of it, and Ahab is the standing proof.

Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah. See what Jezebel does not do. She has the state at her disposal and Elijah at the gate of her city, and she sends one man with a sentence and a day’s notice. A woman who means to kill a man at dawn does not tell him so the night before. What she wants, it seems, is his absence: a threat will make him run, and a prophet seen running away undoes much of what happened on Carmel. She swears by the gods, too, whose entire clergy died yesterday for failing to produce a spark. Evidence has never yet stopped anyone who did not wish to be stopped.

Then he was afraid. Yesterday he stood alone before the nation and set the terms; today a message arrives and he runs. Say plainly what has happened: the fire fell, the people confessed, the rain came, and none of it has changed the court. Ahab reports it as an atrocity; Jezebel is not even shaken; the nation that shouted “The LORD, he is God” has no voice in Jezreel the next morning. Elijah had prayed that the people might know that God had “turned their hearts back” (18:37), and now he learns for himself what he already believed: fire does not turn hearts. It only lights altars.

He arose and ran for his life. He runs to Beersheba, at the southern edge of the land, some hundred miles away in Judah and out of Ahab’s kingdom, and there he leaves his servant and keeps going. He does not merely flee; he leaves behind the last human being with him. Grief of this kind always wants the room emptied.

Sat down under a broom tree. A desert shrub, a tangle of thin green twigs that gives hardly any shade: simply the only thing standing in that landscape, where a man sat down because he could go no further.

I am no better than my fathers. The prayer is not the one we expect. He does not say, “They are trying to kill me.” His despair is about himself. He had hoped, as every servant of God hopes and few admit, that he might be the one who turned the nation back, not just another prophet in a long line preaching to a country that would not listen. Carmel was his best day, and it changed nothing, and the arithmetic under that bush is: I am ordinary, it made no difference, and I would rather die than go on being ordinary. People do not usually collapse when they fail. They collapse afterwards, when they succeed and find that the success did not deliver what they were really asking of it.

O LORD, take away my life. There is a mercy hidden in the request that he could not have known. He asked the LORD to take his life, and he became one of only two men in Scripture, with Enoch, who were taken without dying (2 Kings 2:11). God’s refusal of the prayer was better than the prayer, and it is not the last time that will be true of somebody.

Arise and eat. Watch the order of what God does. He lets him sleep. Then an angel touches him: a hand on a man who has put a hundred miles between himself and every other human being. Then a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water by his head, ready when he wakes. Then more sleep. There is no rebuke: not a word about Carmel, or the servant left at Beersheba, or the self-pity of verse 4. God does not yet tell him that his theology is faulty or his count wrong. That comes later, on a mountain, after two meals and a great deal of sleep.

The journey is too great for you. The first sentence God addresses to his despair is a diagnosis, and it is astonishingly gentle. He does not call Elijah a coward or say he has let him down. He says, in effect, this is more than you can carry, and I know it. God is the first in the story to say that Elijah’s burden exceeded Elijah’s strength, and he says it as a reason for breakfast.

Forty days and forty nights. The number belongs to Moses on this same mountain (Exodus 24:18; 34:28) and to Israel’s forty years in this same desert. Horeb is Sinai. Elijah is walking back to where the covenant the nation has broken was first made: a prophet who has decided that his ministry has failed goes looking for the place where it all started.

A greater man in the wilderness. Forty days belong later to a greater Man in a wilderness of his own, who was tempted forty days and did not fall: where Israel and her prophets failed, he stood firm, and he did it for them (Matthew 4:1–11). Elijah’s story is echoed in the Gospels in another way too. Many Christians have seen in Herodias, who wanted John the Baptist dead (Mark 6:19), a second Jezebel hunting the second Elijah, and Jesus seems to point that way: “Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him” (Mark 9:13).

Why does success leave us flat? Elijah’s prayer would make sense to many people now. Our culture tells every child they can be anything, and quietly implies that they must be something: not ordinary, not one more in a long line, but the one who made the difference. Every screen lets us measure the gap daily. So we hang our worth on a breakthrough, and when it changes less than we hoped, or never comes, we find ourselves under Elijah’s bush. The trouble is not the ambition but the weight we put on it: we were asking a good day on Carmel to tell us that we matter. God does not answer Elijah by making him extraordinary. He feeds him, lets him sleep, and later tells him there are seven thousand others. The gospel goes deeper still, because it settles our worth before we do anything. The Father said, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11), before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed anyone, and those who belong to him are loved in him. You are free to be ordinary, because you are already loved.

If you are where Elijah was. Hear this plainly. Wanting to die does not put you out of God’s reach: a great prophet prayed for it, God answered with bread, not anger, and James still calls him “a man with a nature like ours” (James 5:17). God used ordinary means first, and still does: rest, food, and a friend who sits with you. Talk to a biblical counsellor or your pastor, and see a doctor for a check-up, because exhaustion and despair often have bodily causes too; medicine, where it is needed, is no failure of faith. Tell someone today. If you are in danger of acting on the thought, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now. Elijah did not have to carry the journey alone, and neither do you.

Uncertain wording. “Then he was afraid” (v. 3) depends on how the Hebrew letters are read, for the same letters can mean “he saw” or “he was afraid”. The ESV and most translations, with the ancient translations, read “afraid”; “he saw” would mean he saw how things stood. Either way, he ran.
verseByVerse.note: Beersheba was the southern edge of Judah; Horeb (Sinai), whose exact site is debated, lay perhaps 200 miles beyond; the journey took forty days.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — A Sound of Thin Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers his discouraged prophet by showing him that he works by his word, not by spectacle. At Horeb, in a cave, the word of the LORD asks Elijah what he is doing there, and Elijah answers that he has been very jealous for the LORD, that Israel has forsaken the covenant, and that he alone is left (vv. 9–10). Then the LORD passes by: a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, but the LORD is in none of them, and after them comes the sound of a low whisper (vv. 11–12). Elijah wraps his face in his cloak and goes out, and to the same question gives the same answer, word for word (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Wind, earthquake and fire are exactly what happened on this mountain when the covenant was cut (Ex. 19:16-18), and they are exactly what happened on Carmel a few weeks ago. God shows him all these displays of power again and says he is not in them. Spectacle is not what turns a nation back to God.
verseByVerse.examples: The second telling is the tenderest part. He says the same words again, unchanged, and God does not argue or withdraw the commission. He answers a repeated complaint with work to do and a fact Elijah did not have.

verseByVerse.quote: There he came to a cave and lodged in it. And behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away." And he said, "Go out and stand on the mount before the LORD." And behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire the sound of a low whisper. And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, there came a voice to him and said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the mountain where the covenant was given, God gently questions his despairing prophet, and shows him that he was not in the wind, earthquake and fire but in a low whisper. The kingdom goes forward not by spectacle but by God’s word.

There he came to a cave. The Hebrew says “the cave”, which has made readers wonder for centuries whether this is the cleft of the rock where God put Moses and covered him with his hand while his glory passed by (Exodus 33:22). The text does not say so, and we should not insist. It does say that the worn-out prophet has come to the mountain where God once passed by Moses and let him see his back.

What are you doing here, Elijah? Not why did you run, but what are you doing here, hundreds of miles from the country you were sent to, in a cave? There is no heat in it. This is the voice that has just fed him twice and let him sleep, asking what a friend asks when he finds you somewhere you had no business getting to. It is meant to be answered.

I have been very jealous for the LORD. Two parts of the answer are true and one is not. His record is true, and God never disputes it. The state of the nation is true: covenant forsaken, altars thrown down (he rebuilt one himself not long before), prophets killed. But “I, even I only, am left”, already said on Carmel (18:22) days after he met Obadiah, and said again in verse 14, has never once been true. Isolation is not a fact he has established; it is a feeling he has lived with so long that he now takes it for a fact.

What it means to be jealous for the LORD. We hear “jealous” as a small, sour word. In Scripture it is first God’s own, the jealousy of a faithful husband for his wife (see on 14:22). To be jealous for the LORD is to share that: to burn when his name is despised and his people are drawn off after other gods. Elijah had it, and God never rebukes it. But zeal drifts easily from God’s honour to our own record, and then it cannot survive failure. While it is about him, a bad year grieves you. Once it is about you, a bad year tells you that you are alone and no better than your fathers.

Wind, earthquake, fire. They are not random. They are what happened the first time on this mountain, when the covenant was given with thunder, lightning, thick cloud, smoke and fire, and “the whole mountain trembled greatly” (Exodus 19:16–18). Elijah is being shown Sinai again. They are also, more sharply, exactly what he has just been through. God answered by fire in front of a nation, and it was magnificent, and it fixed nothing. After each of the three the writer sets the same flat sentence: the LORD was not in it.

The sound of a low whisper. There is a sentimental reading of this that misses the point. God often speaks quietly, and we are poor listeners; but what is answered here is a particular despair in a particular man. Elijah staked everything on the spectacular, and it left the country where it was. God shows him all of it again and says, in effect, I am not in that. Then he speaks in a voice that would not carry across a room, and what it brings is a set of instructions and a number. The kingdom does not come by spectacle. It comes by a word, and by men and women who hear it and go where they are sent.

He wrapped his face in his cloak. As Moses hid his face at the bush (Exodus 3:6), he covers his: he knows that God is present, and that no one may see God and live (Exodus 33:20). Then comes the same question and the same answer, word for word: the same three complaints in the same order, ending in the same untrue sentence, from a man who has just watched God tear a mountain apart and then whisper. There is no exasperation, no “Were you not listening?” Instead God gives him three things to do and one fact he did not have.

Moses and Elijah on another mountain. The two men who met God on this mountain meet again in the Gospels on another, with Jesus. Luke says they “appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). What neither could see at Horeb, the glory of God in a face, they saw there, and what they talked about was the cross. And there was one man whose zeal was wholly for his Father’s name, who really was left alone: “you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me” (John 16:32). His zeal did not end in a cave but on a cross, for people whose zeal had run out, Elijah among them.

When you feel you are the only one. So when you catch yourself thinking, “I’m the only one here who cares,” ask whose honour is really hurt, and pray for the others by name.

Does the low whisper mean God speaks to believers in an inner voice? God was teaching Elijah that his work does not always come in fire and storm, and the whisper carried his spoken word to a prophet. Believers today hear God speak in the Scriptures, complete and sufficient (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17), applied by the Spirit, and quiet impressions must be tested by that word.

Where Christians differ: does God still give new words of revelation today? Many faithful Christians believe that God still gives impressions or prophetic words, to be tested by Scripture. This commentary’s view: the cessationist view, that new revelation ended with the apostles because Scripture is now complete. It is held charitably, and both sides agree that nothing may be set beside the Bible or obeyed against it.

Uncertain wording. “The sound of a low whisper” translates three Hebrew words, qol demamah daqqah, that are hard to put into English. The ESV margin gives “a sound, a thin silence”, something like a sound of fine stillness. The old rendering, “a still small voice”, has stayed in the language because nothing better has been found. What is clear is the contrast with the wind, the earthquake and the fire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Elijah’s despair with work to do, a successor, and the truth that he is not alone. The LORD sends him back to anoint Hazael king of Syria, Jehu king of Israel, and Elisha as prophet in his place (vv. 15–16). Through these three, judgment will fall on Ahab’s house and the Baal worship it brought in, and none will escape (v. 17). Then comes the correction Elijah has needed since Carmel: God will leave seven thousand in Israel whose knees have not bowed to Baal and whose mouths have not kissed him (v. 18). The prophet who thought he was the only one is one of many whom God has kept.
verseByVerse.theology: God does not tell him his sorrow is wrong. He tells him his arithmetic is wrong, and by a factor of seven thousand. And these are not celebrated men; not one of them appears anywhere in the story, which is precisely why Elijah could not count them. God keeps a register the prophet has no access to.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul builds on this verse: I have kept for myself, and so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace (Rom. 11:4-5). The seven thousand did not hold out by their own strength. God held them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria. And Jehu the son of Nimshi you shall anoint to be king over Israel, and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah you shall anoint to be prophet in your place. And the one who escapes from the sword of Hazael shall Jehu put to death, and the one who escapes from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha put to death. Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Elijah’s despair with work to do, a successor to carry the work on, a sure judgment on Ahab’s house, and the news that he has kept seven thousand faithful for himself.

Go, return on your way. The first word to a man who has asked to die is to go back, though not to what he was doing, with three enormous commissions: the reordering of two kingdoms and the appointment of his own successor. God’s answer to “It is enough” is a list of errands. That is not callousness, and it should not be preached as a rebuke. It comes after the sleep, the food and the whisper, in that order, and it is what a man in Elijah’s condition most needs once he has been fed: something to do tomorrow that matters, and someone expecting him to do it.

To be prophet in your place. Read it as the mercy it is. Elijah has twice told God that he is the only one left, and God’s reply includes a young man in a field who will take the office off his hands. He is not indispensable, and being told so is the kindest thing that happens to him on that mountain. The work will go on, and he will not have to be the one carrying it.

Who anoints them. What looks like a loose end is not. Elijah personally anoints none of the three. Elisha he calls with a cloak and no words at all (v. 19). Hazael he never meets; it is Elisha who speaks to him, years later, in Damascus (2 Kings 8:13). Jehu is anointed by one of the prophets Elisha sends, after Elijah has gone (2 Kings 9:1–6). The commission was given to one man and carried out across two men and a generation, and every item on the list was done. You are not obliged to complete the work. You are obliged to start walking back down the mountain.

The one who escapes from the sword of Hazael. A chain of judgment with no gaps in it. Hazael will devastate Israel from outside; Jehu will wipe out Ahab’s house from inside; and Elisha, whose only weapon is a word, finishes what the two swords leave. It is grim, and it is meant to be: the house that installed Baal will be brought down, and there is no exit from the sentence.

Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel. Everything before “yet” has been swords; everything after it is a number. Seven thousand is not a token but a real body of people, in a country Elijah had written off, who have not bowed and have not kissed. Kissing the image was the ordinary gesture of homage before an idol, done in passing at a shrine as easily as touching a doorpost (Hosea 13:2). Seven thousand had quietly declined, for years, with their neighbours watching. None of them is named, and none confronted a king; they were invisible, which is exactly why Elijah could not count them. He was measuring the kingdom of God by the number of people doing what he was doing, the usual mistake of the brave and the exhausted. So God corrects not his feeling but his arithmetic.

A remnant, chosen by grace. Paul makes this verse carry more than it seems to. Arguing that God has not rejected his people, he quotes it with a change of wording that carries his point: “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal” (Romans 11:4). Kings says “I will leave”; Paul says “I have kept for myself”, and draws the line to his own day: “So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5). The seven thousand did not hold out by strength of character. They were held. Their loyalty is God’s achievement and God’s property, which is why it is a comfort and not merely a statistic: a remnant that keeps itself can stop keeping itself at any time, and one that God has kept for himself cannot be lost.

If you are the only one. If you have ever been the only believer in a family, an office, a village or a regiment, this verse is for you, and it says two things. Your count is wrong. And the ones you cannot see are not managing on their own strength any more than you are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s call claims the whole life, and the one who hears it leaves everything gladly to follow. Elijah finds Elisha ploughing with the last of twelve yoke of oxen and throws his cloak over him without a word (v. 19). Elisha runs after him and asks to kiss his parents goodbye, and Elijah leaves the choice with him (v. 20). Elisha slaughters his oxen, cooks them on the wooden yokes, feeds the people in a farewell feast, and goes after Elijah as his servant (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The cloak does all the talking. With no speech, no persuasion and no terms, a garment lands on a young man's shoulders in a field, and the man is called.
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve yoke of oxen is a prosperous farm, and he cooks the team on the ploughing gear: he cannot return to that life, because the animals and gear he farmed with have become the dinner. Jesus had this scene in mind and asked more: his follower may not even go back to say goodbye (Luke 9:61-62).

verseByVerse.quote: So he departed from there and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen in front of him, and he was with the twelfth. Elijah passed by him and cast his cloak upon him. And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you." And he said to him, "Go back again, for what have I done to you?" And he returned from following him and took the yoke of oxen and sacrificed them and boiled their flesh with the yokes of the oxen and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he arose and went after Elijah and assisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah’s cloak falls on Elisha without a word, and the young farmer leaves a prosperous life, burns the means of going back, and follows as a servant. The call is costly and gladly obeyed, and in it God gives the lonely prophet a companion.

Plowing with twelve yoke of oxen. Twelve yoke means twenty-four animals working one field, probably with eleven other ploughmen ahead of him and Elisha bringing up the rear with the last pair. Oxen are expensive, and a family with twelve teams is well off. He is not being rescued from poverty. He is being called out of a good life.

Elijah passed by him and cast his cloak upon him. He says nothing at all; he throws his cloak over the man’s shoulders and keeps going. It is the cloak he wrapped his face in at the mouth of the cave, the cloak that will strike the Jordan so that the water divides, and that will fall from a whirlwind for this same young man to pick up (2 Kings 2:8, 13–14). To put your cloak on a man is to put yourself on him: your office, your name, your obligations.

He left the oxen and ran after Elijah. A weight lands across his shoulders in a field and he knows what it means; he leaves the oxen in the furrow and runs after a stranger going up the road.

Go back again, for what have I done to you? Whatever exactly Elijah means (see the note on the wording below), it is plainly not recruitment. He does not press him, warm to him or sell him the ministry. He puts the decision back into the young man’s hands and walks on.

Boiled their flesh with the yokes of the oxen. He kills the oxen and burns the ploughing gear to cook them. The yokes are the most valuable wooden things on the farm, cut to fit those animals; the team that was breaking the ground an hour ago is the meat; and the people eat it, so that nothing is left. He has made it impossible to go back, and he has done it as a feast rather than a funeral.

And assisted him. The humblest sentence in the chapter. The word means ministered, served, waited on: the word used of Joshua as Moses’ assistant (Exodus 24:13). He did not become a prophet that day; he became a prophet’s servant, and years later people still identify him that way: “Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah” (2 Kings 3:11). The man who gave up his farm signed on to carry the bags.

The plough and the greater call. Set this beside a conversation on a road nine centuries later. A man says to Jesus, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” And Jesus says, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:61–62). He has this scene in mind, and his hearers knew it. Elijah let his man go home to his parents; Jesus does not. The claim is harder because the one making it is greater: a prophet may hand you back your decision, and the Lord of the harvest does not. But the one who calls like that is the one who “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51) and did not look back, for us, and he does not send his followers down the furrow alone.

What this chapter has done. Stand back and look. A man sat under a bush and asked God to end his life because he was no better than his fathers and it had all been for nothing. God gave him sleep, a hot meal, a second hot meal, a mountain, a whisper, three commissions, news of seven thousand faithful people he could not see, and a young man in a field with a cloak on his shoulders. Not one of those was what he asked for. He asked to die, and God gave him a companion, a successor, a country full of hidden brothers and sisters, and in the end a whirlwind instead of a grave.

Uncertain wording. Elijah’s reply, “Go back again, for what have I done to you?”, is compressed, and has long been read two ways. It may mean, “Go on, I have not stopped you; say your goodbyes,” or, “Go back, and think about what I have just done to you before you take another step.” Both readings end in the same place: the decision is Elisha’s, and he makes it.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing a cloak over someone signified calling him to succeed.

19.theology:
Fire does not turn hearts (vv. 1-3). The most spectacular answer to prayer in the Old Testament produced a confession that did not reach the palace, an eyewitness, Ahab, who reports it only as a massacre, and a queen who is not shaken at all. Signs can silence an argument; only God changes a will.

The shape of the despair (v. 4). What wounds Elijah is finding that he is ordinary: even his best day changed nothing. That is why collapse so often follows success rather than failure. Not every despair has this cause; much is illness of body and mind with no reason anyone can find, and God's care in this chapter fits that too.

How God treats a servant who has broken (vv. 5-7). Sleep and food come before any word, and the first word kindly names his trouble: the journey is too great for him. No rebuke is ever issued in this chapter.

Not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire (vv. 11-12). The point is not merely that God speaks softly; it is that spectacular displays of power, like the fire on Carmel, are not what builds his kingdom.

Seven thousand, and whose achievement they are (v. 18). God answers a twice-repeated I only am left by correcting the count. Paul reads it as a remnant, chosen by grace (Rom. 11:4-5), that is, a faithful few: they did not hold out by their own strength; God held them.

The cloak and the plough (vv. 19-21). Elijah calls his successor without a word, with the garment that will one day divide the Jordan. Elisha answers by cooking his oxen over his ploughing gear as a farewell feast, so that he cannot go back. And Jesus, with this scene in mind, asks even more: no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62).
19.examples:
Then: A prophet a hundred miles from anywhere, under a shrub that casts almost no shade, having deliberately sent away the last human being with him, asking God to kill him because he had turned out to be no better than the men who went before him.

Now: Three things. First, the order of God's care. Think of the last person you knew in that condition and recall what you reached for; most of us reach for an argument, a verse, a correction. God reached for sleep and a hot meal, twice, and the first thing he did say was that the journey was too great for the man, not that the man was too small for the journey. Second, the miscount. Anybody who has been the only believer in a family or a workplace keeps a private count of the faithful that is wrong, and wrong in the same direction as Elijah's, because we count the kingdom by the number of people visibly doing what we are doing. Seven thousand people who never once appear in the narrative had not bowed. Third, the repeated complaint. He said the same aggrieved paragraph twice, word for word, after God had shown him wind, earthquake, fire and whisper on Sinai to answer it, and was met with work, a successor and a fact, and never once with impatience.

keyVerse.quote: Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him.
keyVerse.note: Twice Elijah has insisted that he alone is left, and this is God’s answer, not to his feelings but to his count. The faithful are more than he can see, and they are kept by God, which is how Paul reads the verse: “a remnant, chosen by grace” (Romans 11:5). God’s cause has never depended on one heroic servant, but on the Lord who keeps his people for himself.

19.reflection:
Elijah’s collapse came straight after his greatest day (18:46–19:4). Why do you think despair so often follows success or a great effort? What were you hoping your own “Carmel” would give you?

God’s first answer to Elijah was sleep, food and a touch, not a sermon (vv. 5–8). What does this teach us about caring for ourselves and for others who are exhausted or low? When might a doctor or a counsellor be part of God’s care?

The LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but spoke in a low whisper (vv. 11–12). Where are you tempted to look for God only in the dramatic? How does he speak to us now, and how do we listen?

Elijah thought he was the only faithful one left, but God had kept seven thousand (v. 18). How does Paul’s use of this verse in Romans 11:4–5 encourage you? Whom might you thank God for, or seek out, among his “hidden” people?

20.title: Ahab and Ben-hadad
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his army together. Thirty-two kings were with him, and horses and chariots. And he went up and closed in on Samaria and fought against it.<sup>2</sup>And he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel and said to him, "Thus says Ben-hadad:<sup>3</sup>'Your silver and your gold are mine; your best wives and children also are mine.'"<sup>4</sup>And the king of Israel answered, "As you say, my lord, O king, I am yours, and all that I have."<sup>5</sup>The messengers came again and said, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'I sent to you, saying, "Deliver to me your silver and your gold, your wives and your children."<sup>6</sup>Nevertheless I will send my servants to you tomorrow about this time, and they shall search your house and the houses of your servants and lay hands on whatever pleases you and take it away.'"<sup>7</sup>Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land and said, "Mark, now, and see how this man is seeking trouble, for he sent to me for my wives and my children, and for my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him."<sup>8</sup>And all the elders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen or consent."<sup>9</sup>So he said to the messengers of Ben-hadad, "Tell my lord the king, 'All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do.'" And the messengers departed and brought him word again.<sup>10</sup>Ben-hadad sent to him and said, "The gods do so to me and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me."<sup>11</sup>And the king of Israel answered, "Tell him, 'Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off.'"<sup>12</sup>When Ben-hadad heard this message as he was drinking with the kings in the booths, he said to his men, "Take your positions." And they took their positions against the city.<sup>13</sup>And behold, a prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel and said, "Thus says the LORD, Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will give it into your hand this day, and you shall know that I am the LORD."<sup>14</sup>And Ahab said, "By whom?" He said, "Thus says the LORD, By the servants of the governors of the districts." Then he said, "Who shall begin the battle?" He answered, "You."<sup>15</sup>Then he mustered the servants of the governors of the districts, and they were 232. And after them he mustered all the people of Israel, seven thousand.<sup>16</sup>And they went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the thirty-two kings who helped him.<sup>17</sup>The servants of the governors of the districts went out first. And Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, "Men are coming out from Samaria."<sup>18</sup>He said, "If they have come out for peace, take them alive. Or if they have come out for war, take them alive."<sup>19</sup>So these went out of the city, the servants of the governors of the districts and the army that followed them.<sup>20</sup>And each struck down his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen.<sup>21</sup>And the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck the Syrians with a great blow.<sup>22</sup>Then the prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, "Come, strengthen yourself, and consider well what you have to do, for in the spring the king of Syria will come up against you."<sup>23</sup>And the servants of the king of Syria said to him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were stronger than we. But let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they.<sup>24</sup>And do this: remove the kings, each from his post, and put commanders in their places,<sup>25</sup>and muster an army like the army that you have lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot. Then we will fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they." And he listened to their voice and did so.<sup>26</sup>In the spring, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel.<sup>27</sup>And the people of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went against them. The people of Israel encamped before them like two little flocks of goats, but the Syrians filled the country.<sup>28</sup>And a man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because the Syrians have said, "The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys," therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.'"<sup>29</sup>And they encamped opposite one another seven days. Then on the seventh day the battle was joined. And the people of Israel struck down of the Syrians 100,000 foot soldiers in one day.<sup>30</sup>And the rest fled into the city of Aphek, and the wall fell upon 27,000 men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled and entered an inner chamber in the city.<sup>31</sup>And his servants said to him, "Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Let us put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare your life."<sup>32</sup>So they tied sackcloth around their waists and put ropes on their heads and went to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-hadad says, 'Please, let me live.'" And he said, "Does he still live? He is my brother."<sup>33</sup>Now the men were watching for a sign, and they quickly took it up from him and said, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad." Then he said, "Go and bring him." Then Ben-hadad came out to him, and he caused him to come up into the chariot.<sup>34</sup>And Ben-hadad said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will restore, and you may establish bazaars for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." And Ahab said, "I will let you go on these terms." So he made a covenant with him and let him go.<sup>35</sup>And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his fellow at the command of the LORD, "Strike me, please." But the man refused to strike him.<sup>36</sup>Then he said to him, "Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, behold, as soon as you have gone from me, a lion shall strike you down." And as soon as he had departed from him, a lion met him and struck him down.<sup>37</sup>Then he found another man and said, "Strike me, please." And the man struck him—struck him and wounded him.<sup>38</sup>So the prophet departed and waited for the king by the way, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes.<sup>39</sup>And as the king passed, he cried to the king and said, "Your servant went out into the midst of the battle, and behold, a soldier turned and brought a man to me and said, 'Guard this man; if by any means he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.'<sup>40</sup>And as your servant was busy here and there, he was gone." The king of Israel said to him, "So shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it."<sup>41</sup>Then he hurried to take the bandage away from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.<sup>42</sup>And he said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.'"<sup>43</sup>And the king of Israel went to his house vexed and sullen and came to Samaria.
20.overview:
Where we are. At Horeb God told Elijah that judgment on Ahab’s house would come through Hazael of Syria, Jehu and Elisha (19:15–18). Now Elijah steps out of view, nameless prophets carry God’s word, and a war with Syria tests Ahab himself.

The message. The LORD is God everywhere, of the valleys as well as the hills, and he gives a wicked king two victories he has not earned so that he may know it. But God’s help is not a reward to be pocketed: it calls for obedience to his word. A king who receives God’s gifts and then trades away what God has said, for a treaty and a market, has passed sentence on himself.

Why it was said. The exiles lived among nations who believed every god had his territory (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that the LORD has no borders, and shows one more reason the kingdom was lost: kings who enjoyed God’s help and treated his commands as negotiable.

How the chapter makes its case. Ben-hadad besieges Samaria, and Ahab surrenders everything until the elders insist on a line (vv. 1–12). A prophet promises victory “and you shall know that I am the LORD”, and two hundred and thirty-two junior servants rout a drunken coalition at noon (vv. 13–22). The Syrians decide the LORD is only a god of the hills, so God destroys them on the plain at Aphek for his name’s sake; then Ahab calls the captured Ben-hadad “my brother” and lets him go for trading rights (vv. 23–34). A wounded prophet’s story of a lost prisoner makes Ahab pass sentence on himself (vv. 35–43).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God and by the need the chapter exposes. The God who will not be shut into the hills is the God whose risen Son says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). Ahab, like Saul, let go for gain what God had put in his hand; Jesus kept all the Father gave him (John 17:12). And the sentence “your life shall be for his life” is the gospel turned inside out. Here a guilty king forfeits his life for sparing a guilty enemy; at the cross an innocent King gave his life for his enemies, “the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18).

For us. Good things in a life far from God are not God’s approval; they are his kindness calling us to repentance (Romans 2:4). Do not draw borders round his authority, leaving him the Sunday hills while you run the weekday plain. And when we hear our own failures described as someone else’s, and condemn them, the right response is not Ahab’s sulk but to run to the King who bore the sentence we pronounced.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Your Silver and Your Gold Are Mine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An enemy who senses weakness keeps raising the price, and Ahab has nothing inside him to stop it. Ben-hadad of Syria besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings and demands Ahab’s silver, gold, wives and children, and Ahab agrees at once, calling him “my lord” (vv. 1–4). When the demand grows into a search of the palace and the houses of the court, it is the elders and the people who tell the king to refuse (vv. 5–9). Ben-hadad boasts that Samaria’s dust will not fill his soldiers’ hands, and Ahab answers with a proverb against boasting before a battle, which reaches the Syrian king while he is drinking (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahab surrenders his wives, his children and his treasury without a fight and only digs in when the demand becomes a search of his own house. He will give away anything he does not have to watch being taken.
verseByVerse.examples: The courage in this chapter is not the king's. Ordinary people who refuse to be bullied can stiffen a weak leader, and God often keeps a nation from the worst through them.

verseByVerse.quote: Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his army together. Thirty-two kings were with him, and horses and chariots. And he went up and closed in on Samaria and fought against it. And he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel and said to him, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'Your silver and your gold are mine; your best wives and children also are mine.'" And the king of Israel answered, "As you say, my lord, O king, I am yours, and all that I have." The messengers came again and said, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'I sent to you, saying, "Deliver to me your silver and your gold, your wives and your children." Nevertheless I will send my servants to you tomorrow about this time, and they shall search your house and the houses of your servants and lay hands on whatever pleases you and take it away.'" Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land and said, "Mark, now, and see how this man is seeking trouble, for he sent to me for my wives and my children, and for my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him." And all the elders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen or consent." So he said to the messengers of Ben-hadad, "Tell my lord the king, 'All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do.'" And the messengers departed and brought him word again. Ben-hadad sent to him and said, "The gods do so to me and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me." And the king of Israel answered, "Tell him, 'Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off.'" When Ben-hadad heard this message as he was drinking with the kings in the booths, he said to his men, "Take your positions." And they took their positions against the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with a boasting enemy, Ahab gives away everything at the first demand and only draws a line when his people stiffen him; his one good sentence is a proverb against boasting that will one day judge him too.

Ben-hadad the king of Syria. Syria is Aram, with its capital at Damascus, Israel’s chief enemy for the next century. The thirty-two kings are rulers of small dependent city-states, brought along to make it look as if the whole world had come to the gate.

I am yours, and all that I have. Ahab’s answer is as striking as the demand (v. 4). Treasury, queens and royal children are handed over at once, with “my lord” attached. The king of the people God brought out of Egypt calls a foreign besieger his lord and signs away his own children. Words that belong to God alone go to the first strong man who asks.

They shall search your house. The second message (vv. 5–6) is a different kind of demand. The first was tribute, paid at the gate; the second is a search, Syrian soldiers opening chests in the palace and taking “whatever pleases you”, whatever the owner values most. Ben-hadad has raised the price because the first was met so quickly. A man who surrenders everything at the first letter has told you that he will surrender more at the second.

I did not refuse him. Hear what Ahab admits in the middle of his complaint (v. 7). He asks the elders to be outraged on his behalf while telling them, in the same sentence, that he had already given away the wives, the children and the gold without a murmur.

Do not listen or consent. The elders and the people of a starved and idolatrous kingdom are the ones who say no. Even then the king’s refusal keeps “my lord” and “your servant” in it (v. 9): he draws his line where the people told him to draw it, and apologises for it while he draws it.

If the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls. Ben-hadad’s boast (v. 10) is that his army is so large that when Samaria has been pulled down there will not be rubble enough to give every man a fistful as a souvenir. It is the swagger of a man drinking with thirty-two client kings watching.

Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself. Verse 11 is the best sentence Ahab ever speaks, and it is a proverb: do not boast when you buckle your armour on; boast when you take it off, alive, after the battle (compare Proverbs 27:1).
