Remember it, because two chapters later this same man will strap on armour before a battle, in disguise as a common soldier, and an arrow drawn at random will find the join in it (22:30–35). He never takes it off.

As he was drinking with the kings in the booths. Notice where the reply reaches Ben-hadad, because the writer will say it again in four verses: he is drinking, and by the time of the attack he is “drinking himself drunk” (v. 16), the same phrase used of Elah when Zimri killed him (16:9). In this book kings are often found drinking when the decisive thing happens to them.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “booths” (sukkot) is the plural of the word for a temporary shelter, and that is the most natural reading: field shelters in the camp. But it is also the name of the town of Succoth in the Jordan valley, and some scholars read “drinking in Succoth”, Ben-hadad’s base some distance from the siege. Either way, the commander is drinking while the battle is decided.
verseByVerse.note: Ben-hadad was a name, perhaps a dynastic title, borne by several kings of Damascus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — You Shall Know That I Am the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives victory to a king who does not deserve it, in a way that leaves no one else the credit, so that Ahab may know who the LORD is. An unnamed prophet promises the great army into Ahab’s hand and names the unlikely instruments: the young servants of the district governors, with the king leading them (vv. 13–15). They march out at noon while Ben-hadad and his kings are drunk, and his contempt for them costs him the battle; each man strikes down his opponent, and the Syrians run (vv. 16–21). Then the prophet warns that the war is not over: the king of Syria will be back in the spring (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives a victory to a king he has already condemned, not because Ahab deserves it but so that Ahab may know who the LORD is. Paul asks the question this chapter raises: do you presume on the riches of his kindness, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? (Rom. 2:4).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 22 keeps the reader honest about what a deliverance is: the enemy will be back in the spring. A rescue from one temptation or trouble is grace, and it is also a call to watchfulness for the next.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel and said, "Thus says the LORD, Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will give it into your hand this day, and you shall know that I am the LORD." And Ahab said, "By whom?" He said, "Thus says the LORD, By the servants of the governors of the districts." Then he said, "Who shall begin the battle?" He answered, "You." Then he mustered the servants of the governors of the districts, and they were 232. And after them he mustered all the people of Israel, seven thousand. And they went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the thirty-two kings who helped him. The servants of the governors of the districts went out first. And Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, "Men are coming out from Samaria." He said, "If they have come out for peace, take them alive. Or if they have come out for war, take them alive." So these went out of the city, the servants of the governors of the districts and the army that followed them. And each struck down his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen. And the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck the Syrians with a great blow. Then the prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, "Come, strengthen yourself, and consider well what you have to do, for in the spring the king of Syria will come up against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises a wicked king a victory he has not earned, wins it through the least impressive soldiers in the kingdom, and says why: so that Ahab will know that he is the LORD.

Behold, I will give it into your hand this day. Verse 13 raises the question the whole chapter exists to answer. God sends a prophet to Ahab, the man who married Jezebel and built the temple of Baal, and promises him not a warning but a gift.

You shall know that I am the LORD. The reason comes in the same breath, and it will come again at Aphek (v. 28). The victories are not wages and not approval. They are one more attempt to reach a man who watched fire fall on Carmel and learned nothing. God helps first, before Ahab improves, as he still deals with sinners, most fully in this: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

By whom? Ahab asks two questions (v. 14), and both answers leave nobody room to claim the credit. The instrument is not the army but the servants of the district governors, junior men of the provincial administration, as if a nation were defended by the office staff of its local councils. And to “Who shall begin the battle?” the answer is “You”: the king himself goes first, with two hundred and thirty-two men, against a coalition of thirty-three kingdoms. God has done this before with Gideon’s three hundred (Judges 7:2), and he still chooses “what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

All the people of Israel, seven thousand. Ahab’s whole fighting strength is seven thousand, the number God gave Elijah at Horeb (19:18). We should not press the echo, but it is there: the number that looked pitifully small to a prophet who thought he was alone is the number of an army.

They went out at noon. No attempt at surprise: they walk out in the middle of the day, in plain sight of a besieging army, and thirty-three kings are drunk.

If they have come out for peace, take them alive. Ben-hadad gives one order for both possibilities (v. 18). It does not occur to him that it could matter which. That is contempt in its purest form, and it is why he loses.

Each struck down his man. That is the whole account of the battle; the writer has no interest in tactics. Every one of the governors’ servants killed the man in front of him, and the Syrians fled. Ben-hadad got away on a horse, and he will be caught in the next section; what Ahab does with him then is what the chapter is really about.

Come, strengthen yourself. The prophet returns with a warning, not congratulations (v. 22). God’s help today is help for one battle in a campaign still running, and whoever treats a deliverance as the end of the matter has stopped listening too soon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God defends his name against a theology that gave him borders, and Ahab throws away the victory God gave him. The Syrian officers decide that the LORD is a god of the hills, rebuild the army and come back onto the plain at Aphek, where Israel looks like two little flocks of goats beside a host that fills the country (vv. 23–27). Because of what the Syrians said about him, God gives the multitude into Ahab’s hand, and the army is destroyed (vv. 28–30). Ben-hadad’s officers come out in sackcloth to test Israel’s reputation for mercy; Ahab calls him “my brother”, makes a covenant with him for towns and trading rights, and lets him go (vv. 31–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 28 states the motive with unusual bluntness. God does not act because Israel is deserving or even because Israel is desperate. He acts because foreign officers have said in council that the LORD has no power in the valleys.
verseByVerse.examples: What Ahab accepted in exchange for the man God had devoted to destruction was market stalls in Damascus. A soft heart towards what God has condemned, especially when it pays, is not mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servants of the king of Syria said to him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were stronger than we. But let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they. And do this: remove the kings, each from his post, and put commanders in their places, and muster an army like the army that you have lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot. Then we will fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they." And he listened to their voice and did so. In the spring, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. And the people of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went against them. The people of Israel encamped before them like two little flocks of goats, but the Syrians filled the country. And a man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because the Syrians have said, "The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys," therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.'" And they encamped opposite one another seven days. Then on the seventh day the battle was joined. And the people of Israel struck down of the Syrians 100,000 foot soldiers in one day. And the rest fled into the city of Aphek, and the wall fell upon 27,000 men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled and entered an inner chamber in the city. And his servants said to him, "Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Let us put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare your life." So they tied sackcloth around their waists and put ropes on their heads and went to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-hadad says, 'Please, let me live.'" And he said, "Does he still live? He is my brother." Now the men were watching for a sign, and they quickly took it up from him and said, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad." Then he said, "Go and bring him." Then Ben-hadad came out to him, and he caused him to come up into the chariot. And Ben-hadad said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will restore, and you may establish bazaars for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." And Ahab said, "I will let you go on these terms." So he made a covenant with him and let him go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Syrians decide the LORD is only a god of the hills, so God destroys their army on the plain for the sake of his name; then Ahab, given the enemy king, calls him “my brother” and lets him go for a trade deal.

Their gods are gods of the hills. Here is the ancient world’s religion put plainly: gods have territories. Israel’s god is a highland god, strong in the ridges round Samaria; take the fight down onto the flat and his power runs out. It was not a stupid theory but the ordinary assumption of every nation round them, which is why armies chose ground where their own gods were thought strong. What the Syrians cannot conceive of is a god with no borders.

Remove the kings, each from his post. The advice is sound: replace thirty-two amateur allied kings with professional officers, rebuild the army horse for horse and chariot for chariot, and choose your ground. Everything in the plan is competent except the premise underneath it. Aphek is probably the town of that name east of the Sea of Galilee, where the road from Damascus comes down onto level ground, country suited to chariots.

Like two little flocks of goats. The writer’s picture of Israel’s army is exact: two small huddles of animals on a hillside, while the opposing army covers the ground from one horizon to the other.

Because the Syrians have said. Read the reason God gives, because it is not the one we would have supplied (v. 28). Not because Israel is outnumbered, or because Ahab has improved, but because of a sentence spoken in a staff meeting in Damascus about where God’s power stops. He fights this battle for his name, and the writer gives that as the whole of the motive.

For the sake of his name. That ought to reorganise how a Christian prays. The first thing the Lord taught us to ask is not our bread or our forgiveness but “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). God’s concern for his own name is not vanity. It is concern for the truth about the only One worth that much, and every other good thing we want depends on his being the God his name says he is.

Where we draw God’s borders. Hardly anyone today believes in gods of the hills, but most of us still draw maps. God is welcome on certain ground: the Sunday service, the funeral, the crisis. Then there is the level ground where we assume other powers run things: the market, the office, the bedroom, the ballot box, the bank account. But a God who is real cannot be a regional god, any more than gravity can. The sceptic who keeps God out of public life and the believer who keeps him out of the accounts make the Syrians’ mistake: not too much religion, but too small a God.

No place he will not go. Notice why God crossed onto the plain: for his name, on behalf of a king who did not deserve it. The risen Jesus speaks the same borderless language, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me”, and in the same breath, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:18, 20). The God who has no frontier is also the God who has no place he will not go with his people.

The kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Israel’s kings have a reputation abroad for being soft. The Hebrew calls them kings of ḥesed, the word for covenant loyalty and steadfast love. The sackcloth is mourning and the ropes are the posture of men offering their own necks; they walk out dressed as condemned men to see whether the rumour is true.

He is my brother. So says Ahab of the man who a year earlier demanded his wives and children. “Brother” was the word kings used of each other as treaty partners of equal rank. The envoys were watching for a sign, and the moment the word was out they repeated it before he could reconsider (v. 33). Ahab has been read by professionals.

I will let you go on these terms. Look at the price: some border towns, and the right to run Israelite market stalls in Damascus. “So he made a covenant with him” (v. 34). The king who would not keep covenant with the LORD makes one with the enemy the LORD had given into his hand. God had handed him the man, and he sold him for a commercial concession. That is not the mercy Jesus commands toward personal enemies (Matthew 5:44); mercy that costs nothing and pays a dividend is a trade.

A calculation, perhaps. There may have been policy behind it. Assyria was pushing west, and an inscription of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III names Ahab of Israel fighting beside the king of Damascus against him at Qarqar in 853 BC, very probably during the three years of peace that follow (22:1). A spared Damascus may have looked like a useful shield. The writer mentions none of it: whatever the policy, Ahab set it above what God had said about the man (v. 42).

Saul and Agag again. This has happened before in exactly this shape. Saul was sent to devote Amalek to destruction and came back with King Agag alive and the best of the sheep, pleased with himself, and Samuel met him with “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king” (1 Samuel 15:23). Same command, same exception made for a fellow king, same profitable spoil, and eight verses later Ahab hears the same kind of sentence.

Uncertain wording. The “ropes on their heads” (vv. 31–32) are explained nowhere else; they were plainly a sign of surrender, but their exact form and meaning are unknown. “Bazaars” (v. 34) is literally “streets”, most likely a trading quarter for Israelite merchants in Damascus. The numbers in vv. 29–30 are very large, and the Hebrew word behind “thousand” can also mean a military unit, so the true count may be smaller than it reads in English. The point does not depend on the arithmetic: the army that filled the country was destroyed, and its king hid in an inner room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–43 — While Your Servant Was Busy Here and There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brings Ahab to condemn himself by telling him his own story as if it were someone else’s. A son of the prophets asks a colleague, at the LORD’s command, to strike him; the man refuses and a lion kills him, a picture of what it costs to set aside a hard word from God (vv. 35–36). A second man wounds him, and he waits for the king disguised under a bandage (vv. 37–38). He tells of a prisoner he lost while busy here and there, and Ahab pronounces the penalty at once; then the bandage comes off, and the prophet applies the verdict to the king who released the man God had devoted to destruction (vv. 39–42). Ahab goes home vexed and sullen (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The method is Nathan's: get the king to judge a case he cannot see himself in, and then tell him whose case it is (2 Sam. 12:1-7).
verseByVerse.examples: The excuse in the prophet’s story is one that convicts us all: he was not overpowered, only busy with other things.

verseByVerse.quote: And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his fellow at the command of the LORD, "Strike me, please." But the man refused to strike him. Then he said to him, "Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, behold, as soon as you have gone from me, a lion shall strike you down." And as soon as he had departed from him, a lion met him and struck him down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet who refuses a hard command from God is killed, and the incident is placed here on purpose: it is a small mirror of the king who has just set aside God’s hard command about Ben-hadad.

A certain man of the sons of the prophets. The “sons of the prophets” are a company of prophets, mentioned here for the first time and often in Elisha’s ministry afterwards. They live and train together and are sent on errands like this one.

At the command of the LORD. This is hard, and should be read as hard. A man declines to strike a colleague, as any decent person would, and is killed by a lion. But the writer tells us first that the request came “at the command of the LORD”. It was not a strange favour but a word from God through his own prophetic company, and the man decided that his sense of what was reasonable outranked it. Decency is not the standard by which a word from God is measured. The book has told this kind of story before: the man of God from Judah, who knew the LORD’s command and set it aside, was also met by a lion on the road (13:24).

Why the incident is here. It is not an isolated horror. The whole chapter turns on a king who was given a hard command about a captured enemy and did the humane, agreeable, profitable thing instead. Just before the prophet tells his story about it, a man does the humane, agreeable thing instead of what God said, and dies for it. The writer teaches by setting matching cases side by side, and Ahab is about to hear his own case without recognising it.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone today should obey a voice claiming to come from God that calls for harm. This was a direct word to a prophet, for a sign to a king; we have God’s word in Scripture, and it never commands us to hurt the innocent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he found another man and said, "Strike me, please." And the man struck him—struck him and wounded him. So the prophet departed and waited for the king by the way, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes. And as the king passed, he cried to the king and said, "Your servant went out into the midst of the battle, and behold, a soldier turned and brought a man to me and said, 'Guard this man; if by any means he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.' And as your servant was busy here and there, he was gone." The king of Israel said to him, "So shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wounded prophet tells the king a story about a prisoner lost through carelessness, and Ahab, not knowing the story is about him, condemns the man at once.

Disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes. Now we see the reason for the wound. He needs to look like a soldier fresh from the battle, and the bandage across his face keeps the king from recognising a man he would otherwise know. Two chapters later Ahab will wear a disguise himself, and it will not save him (22:30).

Nathan’s method. The method is Nathan’s, and it works as it did on David. Tell the king a case in which he has no personal stake, let his sense of justice do its work, get the sentence out of his own mouth, and then say “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). The penalty in the story, a life or a talent of silver, far more than a soldier could pay, was in effect death.

You yourself have decided it. People will pass a clear and severe judgment on their own conduct all day long, provided somebody else’s name is on the file. Ahab hears of a man entrusted with a prisoner who let him go, and does not hesitate: “So shall your judgment be.” Jesus caught the chief priests the same way with the parable of the tenants (Matthew 21:40–45).

As your servant was busy here and there. There is no claim that the prisoner overpowered him, or that he was outnumbered, ambushed or betrayed. He was busy here and there: occupied with a hundred small legitimate things, none of them wrong, none of them chosen instead of the duty, and at the end of the day the one thing he had actually been given to keep was gone.

How things of value are lost. That is how nearly everything of value is lost: not in a battle or by a decision. No one resolves to lose his children’s affection, or his prayer life, or his marriage, or fifteen years. He is busy here and there, and the thing is gone, and he could not tell you the week it went. But there is a way back: the Son kept perfectly what the Father gave him (John 17:12), and “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “bandage” occurs only here and in v. 41. It was some kind of cloth or band worn over the face; the older translations guessed “ashes”, but a covering for the eyes fits the story best.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he hurried to take the bandage away from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets. And he said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.'" And the king of Israel went to his house vexed and sullen and came to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disguise comes off and God’s verdict falls: because Ahab released the man God had devoted to destruction, his own life and his people will pay; and Ahab goes home in a sulk, not in repentance.

He hurried to take the bandage away from his eyes. The moment the king has passed sentence, the disguise comes off, and the haste matters: Ahab is given no time to soften the verdict he has just pronounced. He knows the man as one of the prophets, perhaps simply by his face, and knows at once that the story was about him.

The man whom I had devoted to destruction. That is the word ḥerem, the ban: a thing placed under God’s sentence and removed from all human use, not to be sold, spared or turned to profit. Jericho was under it, which is why Achan died for taking its silver (Joshua 7), and why Hiel lost two sons when he rebuilt it (16:34). Ben-hadad was under it, and Ahab put him in his chariot and traded him for market stalls.

Your life shall be for his life. The sentence has two halves, and both are carried out. “Your life shall be for his life” is paid at Ramoth-gilead within three years, when an arrow drawn at random finds the seam in Ahab’s armour (22:34). “Your people for his people” is paid over the following century, as Hazael of Damascus grinds the northern kingdom down (2 Kings 10:32–33; 13:7) until Assyria finishes it.

A life for a life, the other way round. The words sound like the gospel turned inside out. Here a guilty king loses his life because he spared a guilty enemy for his own gain. At the cross an innocent King gave his life so that his enemies might be spared justly: “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Ahab traded God’s enemy for profit; Christ paid for God’s enemies with himself, and made them friends.

Vexed and sullen. Hold on to these words, because the writer uses them again four verses later, when Naboth declines to sell a vineyard: “Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen” (21:4), lay on his bed, turned away his face and would eat no food. It is his settled response to being refused anything, by a prophet with a death sentence or a farmer protecting his family’s land: no repentance, no argument, just a mood. The first time it produces nothing. The second time his wife notices and asks what is wrong, and a man is stoned to death for a piece of ground.

When was Ben-hadad devoted to destruction? No earlier command is recorded; v. 42 reveals it. But God had twice said “I will give all this great multitude into your hand” (vv. 13, 28), and the king he gave was God’s to dispose of, not Ahab’s to sell. It was one of God’s unique judgments on persistent wickedness, given by direct command, never a pattern or licence for killing enemies today.
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

20.theology:
Kindness with an aim (vv. 13, 28). God hands victories to the worst king in the book and says why twice: so that he may know who the LORD is. Prosperity in a wicked man's hands is not a verdict of approval on him; it may be the last hand held out before the reckoning. God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

God fights for his name (v. 28). The stated reason for Aphek is not Israel's danger and not Israel's deserving. It is that Syrian officers said in council that his authority stopped at the foothills. He is not a local god whose power covers only one region, and the second battle is fought to show it. This is the first request of the Lord's Prayer acted out on a battlefield: hallowed be your name.

Devoted to destruction, and sold (vv. 34, 42). Ahab exchanged the man God had placed under his ban, that is, sentenced to destruction, for border towns and market stalls. Saul had done precisely this with Agag and lost his kingdom for it (1 Sam. 15:23), and Ahab's sentence is paid in two instalments: his life at Ramoth-gilead (22:34), his people under Hazael in the decades that followed (2 Kgs. 10:32-33).

The lion (vv. 35-36). The man's refusal looks like decency and is disobedience. The penalty is severe and is meant to be, and it stands as a parallel to Ahab's own failure to carry out a hard command.

Self-sentencing (vv. 39-40). Tell a man his own case as if it were someone else's and his sense of justice will convict him without hesitation; he only defends the conduct when he knows it is his. Jesus used the same method on the chief priests with the parable of the tenants: asked what the owner should do to men who killed his son, they passed the sentence themselves, and only then saw that he was speaking about them (Matthew 21:40-45). The Son they rejected is the one the parable was about, and the death they sentenced him to is the death that saves.
20.examples:
Then: Two hundred and thirty-two men from the offices of provincial governors walked out of a besieged city at noon, in full view, against thirty-three kingdoms whose commander was too drunk to care whether they came for peace or for war, and each one killed the man in front of him.

Now: Two things this chapter will not let go. The first is verse 40, your servant was busy here and there. Name what you were given to keep, and then ask honestly how you spent yesterday. Do this not as the price of getting back into God's favour but because there is a way back: the Son kept perfectly what the Father gave him (I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost, John 17:12), his keeping is counted to those who confess what they let slip (1 John 1:9), and the Holy Spirit who dwells in us is given to guard what we were entrusted with (2 Tim. 1:14). The second is Ahab's he is my brother. Mercy that costs nothing and pays a dividend is not mercy; it is a trade, and this one was struck with a man God had put under sentence, for the right to run market stalls in a foreign city.

keyVerse.quote: Because the Syrians have said, “The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys,” therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives both reasons God acts in the chapter: to defend his name against a theology that gave him borders, and to bring an undeserving king to know him. The LORD is not a local god, and his kindness is meant to lead to knowledge and obedience, which Ahab then refuses.

20.reflection:
God gave Ahab two victories “you shall know that I am the LORD” (vv. 13, 28), and Ahab still did not turn. How can good things in our lives be God’s kindness calling us to repentance rather than his approval (Romans 2:4)?

The Syrians thought the LORD was a god of the hills but not of the valleys (v. 23). Where are you tempted to treat God as Lord of some parts of your life but not others?

Ahab called Ben-hadad “my brother” and let him go for trading rights (vv. 32–34). When have you been tempted to set aside something God has said because a compromise looked profitable or kind?

The prophet’s prisoner was lost while he “was busy here and there” (v. 40). What has God given you to keep, and what are the small, ordinary things most likely to crowd it out? How does Jesus’ perfect keeping of his people (John 17:12) give you hope when you have let something slip?

21.title: Naboth's Vineyard
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.<sup>2</sup>And after this Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house, and I will give you a better vineyard for it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money."<sup>3</sup>But Naboth said to Ahab, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers."<sup>4</sup>And Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him, for he had said, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers." And he lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food.<sup>5</sup>But Jezebel his wife came to him and said to him, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?"<sup>6</sup>And he said to her, "Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, 'Give me your vineyard for money, or else, if it please you, I will give you another vineyard for it.' And he answered, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'"<sup>7</sup>And Jezebel his wife said to him, "Do you now govern Israel? Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite."<sup>8</sup>So she wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, and she sent the letters to the elders and the leaders who lived with Naboth in his city.<sup>9</sup>And she wrote in the letters, "Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth at the head of the people.<sup>10</sup>And set two worthless men opposite him, and let them bring a charge against him, saying, 'You have cursed God and the king.' Then take him out and stone him to death."<sup>11</sup>And the men of his city, the elders and the leaders who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had sent word to them. As it was written in the letters that she had sent to them,<sup>12</sup>they proclaimed a fast and set Naboth at the head of the people.<sup>13</sup>And the two worthless men came in and sat opposite him. And the worthless men brought a charge against Naboth in the presence of the people, saying, "Naboth cursed God and the king." So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death with stones.<sup>14</sup>Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, "Naboth has been stoned; he is dead."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, "Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money, for Naboth is not alive, but dead."<sup>16</sup>And as soon as Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab arose to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.<sup>17</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria; behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone to take possession.<sup>19</sup>And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Have you killed and also taken possession?"' And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: "In the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick your own blood."'"<sup>20</sup>Ahab said to Elijah, "Have you found me, O my enemy?" He answered, "I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>Behold, I will bring disaster upon you. I will utterly burn you up, and will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.<sup>22</sup>And I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the anger to which you have provoked me, and because you have made Israel to sin.<sup>23</sup>And of Jezebel the LORD also said, 'The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel.'<sup>24</sup>Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat."<sup>25</sup>(There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited.<sup>26</sup>He acted very abominably in going after idols, as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out before the people of Israel.)<sup>27</sup>And when Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his flesh and fasted and lay in sackcloth and went about dejectedly.<sup>28</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,<sup>29</sup>"Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster in his days; but in his son's days I will bring the disaster upon his house."
21.overview:
Where we are. Ahab has just gone home “vexed and sullen” under a prophet’s death sentence (20:43), and the same words return here (v. 4). The scene moves from the battlefield to a neighbour’s vineyard.

The message. The LORD owns the land and rules over the king, and no one, however powerful, is above his law. He sees the murder done by paperwork and charges it to the man who enjoys the profit: “Have you killed and also taken possession?” (v. 19). Yet the same God who passes the harshest verdict in the book stops to point out a humbled sinner and shows him mercy.

Why it was said. The first readers had lost their land, the inheritance God had given their fathers, and this chapter shows one reason: kings who treated God’s law and their poorer neighbours as obstacles (see the introduction). It also shows them a God who hears even a late and shallow humbling, which was their hope in exile (8:46–50).

How the chapter makes its case. Naboth refuses to sell his family’s inheritance; Ahab sulks and tells Jezebel an edited story (vv. 1–7). Her letters have Naboth stoned by his own neighbours on false testimony, and Ahab takes the vineyard (vv. 8–16). Elijah meets him there with the charge and the sentence on his house and on Jezebel, and the writer adds his own verdict (vv. 17–26). Then Ahab humbles himself, and God defers the disaster to his son’s days (vv. 27–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God. Naboth is an innocent man who would not give up his father’s inheritance, condemned by false witnesses on a charge of blasphemy and killed outside the city so that others could take what was his. Jesus told the story of the tenants who said of the owner’s son, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance” (Matthew 21:38), and then lived it: condemned by false witnesses for blasphemy and suffering “outside the gate” (Mark 14:56–64; Hebrews 13:12). Naboth’s blood cried out for judgment; Jesus’ blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Ahab killed a man to take his inheritance; Jesus let himself be killed to give us his.

For us. God sees what we arrange not to know, and what we leave out when we tell our story. The covetous heart that lies on its bed over one more thing is cured not by wanting less but by receiving more: an inheritance in Christ that no one can take. And if God noticed Ahab’s sackcloth, no one who truly turns to him is too far gone to be welcomed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Inheritance of My Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who will not accept that God’s law limits him is ready for any crime. Ahab offers Naboth a better vineyard or its value in money for the plot beside his palace, and Naboth refuses, because it is the inheritance of his fathers, land God gave his family which the law did not allow him to sell (vv. 1–3). Ahab goes home vexed and sullen, lies on his bed and will not eat (v. 4). When Jezebel asks why, he tells her the refusal with God’s law left out, and she answers with a political theory in a sneering question, “Do you now govern Israel?”, and a promise to get him the vineyard (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Jezebel's question is the collision the whole book has been building towards. In Sidon a king is the law; in Israel the king is under it, and Ahab is the officer charged with enforcing the very statute he is asking Naboth to break.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what he does with Naboth's answer: he drops the inheritance of my fathers when he reports it. How we tell our grievances shapes what others will do about them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. And after this Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house, and I will give you a better vineyard for it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money." But Naboth said to Ahab, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers." And Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him, for he had said, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers." And he lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food. But Jezebel his wife came to him and said to him, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?" And he said to her, "Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, 'Give me your vineyard for money, or else, if it please you, I will give you another vineyard for it.' And he answered, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'" And Jezebel his wife said to him, "Do you now govern Israel? Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naboth refuses to sell the king his family’s land because it belongs to God, and Ahab, who should uphold that law, sulks over a vegetable patch and hands his wife a version of the story with God taken out.

A vineyard in Jezreel. Jezreel is Ahab’s second residence, in the wide fertile valley to the north, where he drove his chariot at the end of chapter 18 with Elijah running ahead of him through the rain. Next to the palace wall is a working vineyard belonging to a man named Naboth.

I will give you a better vineyard for it. Take the offer seriously before condemning it. He does not seize the land. He asks, and offers a choice: a better vineyard in exchange, or its full value in silver. That is more decent than most kings in that part of the world would have troubled to be. Ahab is not being a tyrant here; he is being a neighbour with money.

For a vegetable garden. Only notice what he wants it for: a kitchen plot of herbs and greens close to the house. He intends to pull out a vineyard for salad. A vineyard is not a crop; it is a lifetime. The terraces have to be cut, the stones cleared, the vines planted and staked, and the law would not even let the owner eat the fruit for the first three years, and gave the fourth year’s fruit to God (Leviticus 19:23–25). What grows on that slope was planted by Naboth’s father or grandfather and tended through droughts by people whose graves are in sight of it.

The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers. Everything in the chapter depends on Naboth’s answer (v. 3), and it is easy to hear it as stubbornness, or as a man holding out for a better price. It is neither. When Israel came into the land it was divided by lot under Joshua, tribe by tribe and family by family, and the allotment was not so much a gift of property as a tenancy from God: “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). Land could be leased when a family fell on hard times, but it came back at the Jubilee, every fiftieth year, and an inheritance was not to pass out of the tribe at all (Numbers 36:7).

What Naboth is saying. So Naboth is not haggling. He is explaining that what is asked of him is not in his power. The boundary stones were set when his family drew their lot centuries ago; the owner is God; his sons are the next tenants. “The LORD forbid” is not an exclamation of annoyance but the legal ground stated in one phrase.

Said to Ahab. And consider who hears it. The king of Israel is the one man in the country charged with knowing this law: Deuteronomy requires him to write out his own copy and “read in it all the days of his life”, so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). The man appointed to uphold the covenant has asked a farmer to break it, and the farmer has had to tell him so. The prophets would later condemn exactly this hunger for other people’s land: “They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance” (Micah 2:2).

Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen. These are the words the writer used four verses earlier, when a prophet told Ahab that his life was forfeit (20:43). He reacts to being refused a field exactly as he reacted to a sentence of death. Then the picture, drawn with something close to contempt: the most powerful man between Damascus and Egypt, who has just broken Ben-hadad twice, lies on his bed with his face to the wall and will not eat, because a farmer said no.

The one thing we do not have. It would be comic if it were not so familiar. A man with two palaces, a victorious army and a kingdom, face to the wall over a vegetable patch. A whole economy now runs on producing this feeling: not that we lack necessities, but that the one thing we do not yet have is the thing that would make the rest worth having; and the moment we get it, the feeling moves on. That is how an idol works: whatever is withheld becomes the thing life depends on. The tenth commandment, the one aimed most purely at the heart, is the one Paul said exposed him: “I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7).

An inheritance no one can take. The gospel does not cure covetousness by teaching us to want less, but by giving us more. Ahab killed a man to take his inheritance. Jesus let himself be killed to give us his, “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4). People who know they have that can let their neighbour keep his vineyard.

Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food? Jezebel asks what is wrong. It is a wife’s question, put kindly enough, and she is the only person in the palace who asks it. Everything that follows runs through his answer. A man lying in the dark with a grievance is at his most dangerous when somebody finally asks about it, because the version he gives is the version that will be acted on. Choose carefully who hears your grievance in that condition. Some people will tell you to get up and eat; this one offers to fetch the vineyard.

I will not give you my vineyard. Compare the two accounts. Naboth said “the inheritance of my fathers.” Ahab reports “I will not give you my vineyard.” He has taken out the covenant, God and the law of the land, and left a man refusing to sell a field. He has done this before: coming home from Carmel he told Jezebel all that Elijah had done and left out the fire from heaven (19:1). Twice now he has handed her a version of events with God removed, and both times she answers with violence: a death threat then, a murder now. Whether he did it consciously is beside the point. A man who cannot bear to repeat the religious reason for his defeat to the one person who will do something about it has already decided how he wants the story to end.

Do you now govern Israel? There is the quarrel of the whole book in one sneering question. Jezebel is not merely cruel; she is stating the political theory she was raised in. In Sidon, where her father was king, what the king wants is what happens, and a monarch told no by a subject with a title deed is no monarch. She genuinely cannot see the difficulty. Israel was founded on the opposite principle, one of the most far-reaching ideas in the Old Testament: the king is under the law, not over it. He answers to a covenant he did not write, and a farmer can stand in front of him and say “The LORD forbid”, and be right.

The King who kept the law. Every king of Israel was meant to be the first servant of God’s law. Only one ever was. Jesus, the Son of David, came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), and he used his power not to take what belonged to the weak but to give his life for them (Mark 10:45).

I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite. Jezebel is about to show what her theory costs, and she will do it without breaking a single rule.
verseByVerse.note: Selling ancestral land was against Israel’s law.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Injustice dressed in the forms of law is still murder, and it needs ordinary people to carry it out. Jezebel writes letters in Ahab’s name and under his seal to the elders of Naboth’s town, telling them to proclaim a fast, seat Naboth in the place of honour, set two worthless men to accuse him of cursing God and the king, and stone him (vv. 8–10). His neighbours do exactly as the letters say, and report that he is dead (vv. 11–14). Jezebel tells Ahab to take the vineyard, and he gets up at once and goes down to possess it, asking nothing (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Every step is legally correct: two witnesses (Deut. 17:6), a genuine capital charge (Lev. 24:16), execution outside the city (Lev. 24:14). Jezebel does not break the law's procedures; she uses them. Christians have long seen in Naboth a dark preview of a later trial: a righteous man condemned by false witnesses on a charge of blasphemy and put to death outside the city (Mark 14:56-64; Hebrews 13:12), as Stephen was after him (Acts 6:11-13; 7:58). The difference is that Jesus went knowingly, and the verdict men passed on him in wickedness God had appointed for our pardon.
verseByVerse.examples: It took the neighbours. Not one of the elders of his own town is recorded as objecting. Great wrongs usually need many small consents, and the courage to refuse one is rarely wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: So she wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, and she sent the letters to the elders and the leaders who lived with Naboth in his city. And she wrote in the letters, "Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth at the head of the people. And set two worthless men opposite him, and let them bring a charge against him, saying, 'You have cursed God and the king.' Then take him out and stone him to death." And the men of his city, the elders and the leaders who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had sent word to them. As it was written in the letters that she had sent to them, they proclaimed a fast and set Naboth at the head of the people. And the two worthless men came in and sat opposite him. And the worthless men brought a charge against Naboth in the presence of the people, saying, "Naboth cursed God and the king." So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death with stones. Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, "Naboth has been stoned; he is dead." As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, "Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money, for Naboth is not alive, but dead." And as soon as Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab arose to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jezebel has Naboth judicially murdered by his own neighbours, keeping every form of the law while breaking its whole purpose, and Ahab goes to collect the vineyard without asking a single question.

Sealed them with his seal. The writer does not tell us whether Ahab handed over his seal or Jezebel took it, and there is no point guessing. A royal seal does not go missing without the king knowing. Whatever Ahab did or did not say, he stayed in bed while his seal went out on letters, and he never afterwards asks how the field came free.

Proclaim a fast. Read the instructions with the law open beside them, because the most chilling thing about the plan is that it keeps the forms of the law at every point. A fast is proclaimed, which in a town meant that some trouble was believed to lie on the community and must be searched out. Naboth is seated “at the head of the people”, in the place of honour, because he is a man of standing and because a fall is further from a height. Two witnesses are produced, because the law will not convict on one: “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare 17:6). The charge is a genuine capital offence: blasphemy carried death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16), and cursing the king made it treason as well. And the sentence is carried out outside the city, as the law directs (Leviticus 24:14).

Wickedness with procedures. That is the form wickedness takes wherever a society is orderly enough to have procedures. The crude tyrant sends soldiers; the sophisticated one sends paperwork. Every form was kept, and a man was murdered for a vegetable patch.

Who lived with Naboth in his city. The writer says twice that the elders lived in his city, and the repetition is the accusation. These are not strangers or enforcers sent up from Samaria but his neighbours, who knew his father, watched his sons grow and bought his wine. A letter arrived from the capital, and they convened a solemn assembly, listened to two men they knew were lying, and stoned him on the edge of their own town. An evil like this cannot be done by a queen a day’s journey away. It requires a town.

Naboth cursed God and the king. Not one more word of Naboth’s is recorded. He spoke his one sentence in v. 3, and the chapter never lets him speak again. He sits in the seat of honour and hears two men explain that he has blasphemed, and the last thing he sees is the faces of the men he grew up among.

The blood of his sons. Scripture adds one detail elsewhere, and it should not be withheld. Years later, when Jehu throws a body onto this same ground, he remembers the oracle as concerning “the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons” (2 Kings 9:26). The children were killed too. Of course they were: kill the father and the land passes to the heir; for the ground to fall to the king, the line had to end. A man who would not sell his inheritance lost his sons the same day, and it is the coldest arithmetic in the book of Kings.

Naboth has been stoned; he is dead. The council’s report to the palace is a notice of completion. Jezebel cannot resist adding that this is the vineyard “which he refused to give you for money” (v. 15): even in delivering the prize she reminds him of the humiliation, which tells you a good deal about the marriage.

Ahab arose to go down to the vineyard. He gets up and goes, and asks nothing: not how Naboth died, not who gave evidence, not why a healthy landowner is suddenly dead and his field suddenly free. He had been lying on a bed refusing food, and now he is walking through the vines working out where the beds will go.

Not merely weak. This chapter is often read as though Jezebel were the murderer and Ahab merely a weak man who let her. God’s own assessment, in the next section, does not agree. There is a kind of ignorance a man works to keep. Ahab knew that Naboth would sooner die than sell; then Naboth died, and he did not ask.

The innocent man condemned. Look at Naboth again: a faithful man, condemned by false witnesses on a charge of blasphemy, with the forms of the law kept, and put to death outside the city so that others could have his inheritance. Another would one day stand in that place. Jesus was tried by a council “seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death”, heard false witnesses, then was condemned for blasphemy (Mark 14:55–64) and “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12). He had told the parable himself: the tenants saw the son and said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance” (Matthew 21:38). The difference is that Naboth was taken; Jesus gave himself, and his death was not the end of his inheritance but the way he shares it with us.

Isn’t not knowing a kind of innocence? It is the most modern sin in the chapter. Ahab planned nothing; he simply arranged not to ask. Most of us live inside systems that do some of our dirty work at a distance: the cheap goods whose making we would rather not picture, the company practice nobody examines, the family secret everyone steps round. We tell ourselves that what we did not know cannot be held against us, and we keep the not-knowing carefully maintained. God’s verdict on Ahab says otherwise: the man who enjoys the vineyard and will not ask how it came free is not a bystander. That reaches nearly everyone. But the gospel goes further than the accusation. Over those who condemned Jesus, the scheming and the half-aware alike, he prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). A mercy that can reach even a chosen blindness is the only kind most of us can use.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “cursed” is literally “blessed”, probably a scribal way of avoiding writing “curse God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — Have You Killed and Also Taken Possession?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees the hidden crime, holds the beneficiary guilty, and yet shows mercy to a sinner who humbles himself. The word of the LORD sends Elijah to meet Ahab in the dead man’s vineyard with the charge of killing and taking possession, and a sentence that dogs will lick his blood (vv. 17–19). Ahab calls Elijah his enemy; his whole house is condemned like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and Jezebel with it (vv. 20–24). The writer adds the harshest verdict in the book (vv. 25–26). Then Ahab tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth, and God points it out to Elijah and defers the disaster to his son’s days (vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge names two acts, killing and taking, and lays both on Ahab. He did not write the letters or throw a stone, and the word of the LORD says you have killed.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 29 is the surprise of the chapter. If God answers a repentance that shallow, no reader need wonder what he will give to the real thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, "Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria; behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone to take possession. And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Have you killed and also taken possession?"' And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: "In the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick your own blood."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Elijah to meet Ahab in the stolen vineyard and charges him, not Jezebel or the elders, with both the killing and the taking; the sentence matches the crime.

Arise, go down to meet Ahab. The last time these two men stood together was in the rain on the road to Jezreel, with the prophet running ahead of the chariot (18:46). Elijah has been at Horeb since and out of the story, and the word that brings him back is a murder over a garden. “Who is in Samaria” means the king who reigns from Samaria; he is at this moment in Jezreel.

He is in the vineyard of Naboth. The meeting is arranged with care. Not in the throne room or at the city gate: Ahab is walking between the rows of a dead man’s vines, on ground owned that morning by a family that no longer exists, measuring out where the herbs will go. He looks up, and there is Elijah.

Have you killed and also taken possession? The charge is short, and both acts are laid on Ahab himself. He did not write the letters, give false testimony or throw a stone, and so far as we are told he gave no order, yet the word of the LORD says that he killed. The man who arranged not to know is charged as the man who did it, and the taking of the field is named with the taking of the life, because they were one act. God is the true King of Israel, and his court sits even when the king’s courts have been bought.

Shall dogs lick your own blood. A careful reader will check this verse and find that it does not seem to land where it was aimed. Elijah says the dogs will lick Ahab’s blood where they licked Naboth’s, in Jezreel; 22:38 reports that they licked it at the pool of Samaria. The chapter itself explains this ten verses later, where the sentence is expressly deferred into his son’s days (v. 29). And the Jezreel half is carried out exactly: Jehu has Joram’s body thrown “on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite”, quoting this oracle as he does it (2 Kings 9:25–26). The word did not miss. It was paid in two instalments, and the reason for the delay is written into the text that records it.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahab said to Elijah, "Have you found me, O my enemy?" He answered, "I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the LORD. Behold, I will bring disaster upon you. I will utterly burn you up, and will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel. And I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the anger to which you have provoked me, and because you have made Israel to sin. And of Jezebel the LORD also said, 'The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel.' Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab treats God’s messenger as his enemy, and God answers that Ahab has sold himself to evil: his whole house will be wiped out like the dynasties before it, and Jezebel will lie unburied.

Have you found me, O my enemy? That is what Ahab calls the man who brings him the word of God, and it is the most revealing sentence he ever speaks. Not once in four chapters has he said that Elijah was wrong. When a man has stopped disputing whether the word is true and started resenting the person who carries it, his quarrel is not with the prophet but with God.

You have sold yourself. The reply uses the language of a slave sale: a man putting himself on the block and taking the price. Ahab bought a vegetable garden, and the currency he paid in was himself. Jesus asked the question this verse answers: “For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” (Mark 8:36).

Every male, bond or free. Every last one, from the head of the house down to the slave who sweeps the yard. “Utterly burn you up” is the language already used of Jeroboam’s house (14:10): a house not merely punished but wiped out.

Like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. This sentence has been passed twice already in this book: the houses of Jeroboam and of Baasha were both destroyed, and each time the writer recorded the oracle first and the slaughter afterwards (14:10–11; 15:29; 16:3–4, 11–12). Ahab is told that he is third in the series, in the same words, with the same outcome.

The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel. To be left unburied was the last indignity a body could suffer, and dogs in an ancient city were not pets but half-wild scavengers round the rubbish heaps. Jezebel will be thrown from a window in Jezreel a dozen or so years later, and when men go out to bury her there is almost nothing left to bury (2 Kings 9:30–37).

Uncertain wording. “Bond or free” translates a pair of Hebrew words meaning something like “shut in and left free”. The phrase is used of whole households (14:10; 2 Kings 9:8), and it plainly means “every last one”, but what the two halves originally described is not certain: slave and free, under age and grown, or kept at home and out abroad have all been suggested. “Every male” is literally a coarse expression, “one who urinates against a wall”, a blunt way of saying every man and boy.

verseByVerse.quote: (There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited. He acted very abominably in going after idols, as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out before the people of Israel.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer steps out of the story to give his own verdict: no one ever sold himself to evil as Ahab did, and his worship made Israel’s king like the nations God had driven out.

There was none who sold himself. The narrator rarely comments, and here he does (v. 25), passing the severest verdict he gives on anyone in these two books.

Whom Jezebel his wife incited. This clause is not an excuse offered on Ahab’s behalf; it is part of the charge. Nobody ever sold himself as he did, and he let himself be driven to it by his wife, which is one more thing against him, not a mitigation. Being led into sin by someone close to us explains how it happened; it does not make it someone else’s sin.

As the Amorites had done. The comparison at the end is the sharpest cut. He behaved “as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out”: like the peoples whose wickedness was so complete that God emptied the land of them and gave it to Israel (Genesis 15:16). Israel’s king is now doing the very things those peoples were driven out for, and the reader in exile knows where that road ends: the land God gave can be lost the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his flesh and fasted and lay in sackcloth and went about dejectedly. And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster in his days; but in his son's days I will bring the disaster upon his house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab, under sentence, humbles himself, and God, who sees even a shallow repentance, stops Elijah to point it out and defers the disaster; the judgment is postponed, not cancelled.

When Ahab heard those words. Nobody expects verse 27, and it is put straight after the harshest paragraph in the book so that nobody can miss the contrast.

Put sackcloth on his flesh. The detail is exact: sackcloth next to the skin, not worn over his clothes for show, and he sleeps in it. He tears his robes, stops eating, and goes about the palace like a man at a funeral.

Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? God calls Elijah’s attention to it, as if to make sure he did not look away. The prophet who has just delivered an extermination order is asked to notice that the condemned man is in sackcloth, and to notice it approvingly.

What this repentance is not. Be honest about what this repentance is and is not. It is not saving faith. Nothing is restored: the vineyard is not given back, the perjurers are not prosecuted, the elders of Jezreel are not called to account, Jezebel keeps her prophets and her table, and Naboth’s family is still dead. Before long Ahab will imprison a prophet for telling him the truth and ride to a battle God warned him not to fight (22:26–30). This is a frightened man reacting to a death sentence, not a converted one.

I will not bring the disaster in his days. Yet God answers it, with a real mercy and a real deferral of a real judgment. He does the same at Nineveh, where a pagan city fasts on the strength of one sentence and “God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them” (Jonah 3:10), and he states the principle through Jeremiah: if a nation under sentence turns from its evil, “I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it” (Jeremiah 18:8).

An enormous encouragement. If God pays that much attention to the shabby, self-interested, unfinished humbling of the worst man in the book, enough to stop Elijah and point at it, there is no serious question about what he will do with a repentance that is genuine. The verse exists to stop anyone concluding that he is too far gone to bother turning round. And the mercy that deferred Ahab’s sentence for a few years is small beside the mercy offered in Christ, where the sentence is not postponed but borne, and the one who turns is not given time but forgiven: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

But in his son’s days. The warning is in the last clause. The judgment was postponed, not cancelled, and because it was postponed it fell on people not yet born when the letters went out. Joram will die on Naboth’s plot of ground with Jehu quoting this oracle over the body, and the heads of seventy of Ahab’s sons will be sent to Jezreel in baskets (2 Kings 9:24–26; 10:7). Ahab got what he asked for on both counts: he asked for the vineyard and had it for about three years; he asked, in sackcloth, for time, and he got that too.

Is it just for a whole house to be destroyed for a father’s sin? Human courts were forbidden to punish children for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). This was God’s own judgment on a royal house that led the nation into idolatry, and its sons carried on the same sins (22:52; 2 Kings 3:2–3). God as Judge may take any life, and he never punishes the innocent as guilty (Ezekiel 18:20).

Uncertain wording. “Went about dejectedly” translates a rare Hebrew word meaning something like “softly” or “slowly”. It probably describes the quiet, subdued walk of a mourner; the exact nuance is uncertain, but the sense of a man bowed down is clear.

21.theology:
Why Naboth cannot sell (v. 3). The land allotted under Joshua was held on loan from God, not owned outright: the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev. 25:23), and an inheritance was not to pass out of the family or the tribe (Num. 36:7). The refusal is a legal answer, not a stubborn one, and it is given to the one man in the kingdom required to write out the law in his own hand and read it all his days (Deut. 17:18-20).

Do you now govern Israel? (v. 7). Jezebel's sneer is a whole political philosophy. In Sidon the king is the law; in Israel the king is under it, and a farmer with a title deed can stand in front of him and be right. That single idea, that sovereign power answers to a covenant it did not write, is among the most consequential things the Old Testament gave the world, and this chapter is what happens when a throne rejects it.

Lawful murder (vv. 9-13). On paper every rule was kept. Crude tyranny sends soldiers; developed wickedness sends paperwork, and it needs a town to carry it out. Twice the writer says the men who did it lived in his city.

The version with God taken out (v. 6, cf. 19:1). Ahab reports Naboth’s refusal without its reason, God’s law, as he once reported Carmel without the fire. A man who edits God out of his account of events has already decided how he would like them to end.

Arranged ignorance is not innocence (v. 19). Ahab wrote nothing, swore nothing, threw nothing, and God still says to him: you have killed.

Deferred, not cancelled (v. 29). God points out the sackcloth to Elijah and postpones the sentence, and the repentance is plainly shallow: nothing restored, nobody prosecuted, and a prophet in prison soon after. He answers it anyway, as he answered Nineveh (Jon. 3:10) on the principle he states in Jer. 18:7-8. The encouragement is this: if God honours even that, he will certainly welcome real repentance. The warning is in the last clause: the disaster fell in his son's days, on people not yet born when the letters went out.
21.examples:
Then: The elders and leaders of a small town opened a letter from the capital, proclaimed a solemn fast, seated a neighbour they had known all his life in the place of honour, listened to two men they knew were lying, and stoned him, and the paperwork was in perfect order.

Now: Three things. First, arranged ignorance. Ahab asked no questions because he already knew the answers, and God charges him directly with the murder. Not knowing is a defence only when we did not choose not to know, and most of us can tell the difference in our own case if we are honest. Second, the edited report. Twice he tells his wife what happened with God removed from it. Notice what you leave out when you describe a difficulty to the person most likely to solve it for you. Neither of these is cured by hiding better; the cure is to bring it into the light, where the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), and to ask the Spirit of truth to show us what we would rather not see (John 16:13). Third, verse 29, which is aimed at anybody who believes he has gone too far to turn round. God stopped a prophet in the street to point out the sackcloth on the worst man in the book, and shortened the sentence of a man who never gave the vineyard back. Whatever else that verse means, it rules out the idea that God is reluctant to receive anyone who turns.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, “Have you killed and also taken possession?”
keyVerse.note: God’s charge goes past Jezebel’s letters and the elders’ stones to the man who wanted the field and enjoyed the result. It shows the LORD as the true King of Israel, whose court sees what human courts were bought to hide. The rest of the chapter turns on how Ahab answers this question.

21.reflection:
Naboth refused the king because the land was “the inheritance of my fathers”, held from God (v. 3). What has God entrusted to you that is not yours to trade away, however good the offer?

Ahab lay on his bed over one field he did not have (v. 4). Where do you see the same restless wanting in yourself or in our culture, and how does knowing your inheritance in Christ (1 Peter 1:4) answer it?

Ahab never wrote a letter or threw a stone, yet God said, “Have you killed and also taken possession?” (v. 19). In what areas of life are we tempted to arrange not to know, and what would it look like to bring them into the light?

God noticed even Ahab’s shallow, unfinished humbling (v. 29). What does that tell you about how God will receive anyone who truly turns to him, and how does the cross go further than the mercy Ahab received?

22.title: Micaiah and the Death of Ahab
22.text: <sup>1</sup>For three years Syria and Israel continued without war.<sup>2</sup>But in the third year Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.<sup>3</sup>And the king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, and we keep quiet and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?" And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses."<sup>5</sup>And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD."<sup>6</sup>Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall I go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for the Lord will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>7</sup>But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?"<sup>8</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."<sup>9</sup>Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah."<sup>10</sup>Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.<sup>11</sup>And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"<sup>12</sup>And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>13</sup>And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably."<sup>14</sup>But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak."<sup>15</sup>And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall we refrain?" And he answered him, "Go up and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>16</sup>But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"<sup>17</sup>And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'"<sup>18</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"<sup>19</sup>And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left;<sup>20</sup>and the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another.<sup>21</sup>Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.'<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.'<sup>23</sup>Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; the LORD has declared disaster for you."<sup>24</sup>Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "How did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"<sup>25</sup>And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."<sup>26</sup>And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah, and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,<sup>27</sup>and say, 'Thus says the king, "Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water, until I come in peace."'"<sup>28</sup>And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"<sup>29</sup>So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>30</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle.<sup>31</sup>Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel."<sup>32</sup>And when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is surely the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out.<sup>33</sup>And when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.<sup>34</sup>But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded."<sup>35</sup>And the battle continued that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, until at evening he died. And the blood of the wound flowed into the bottom of the chariot.<sup>36</sup>And about sunset a cry went through the army, "Every man to his city, and every man to his country!"<sup>37</sup>So the king died, and was brought to Samaria. And they buried the king in Samaria.<sup>38</sup>And they washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in it, according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken.<sup>39</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, and the ivory house that he built and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>40</sup>So Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.<sup>41</sup>Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.<sup>42</sup>Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.<sup>43</sup>He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD.
