Yet the high places were not taken away, and the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places.<sup>44</sup>Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.<sup>45</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he warred, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>46</sup>And from the land he exterminated the remnant of the male cult prostitutes who remained in the days of his father Asa.<sup>47</sup>There was no king in Edom; a deputy was king.<sup>48</sup>Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, for the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.<sup>49</sup>Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my servants go with your servants in the ships," but Jehoshaphat was not willing.<sup>50</sup>And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.<sup>51</sup>Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel.<sup>52</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.<sup>53</sup>He served Baal and worshiped him and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger in every way that his father had done.
22.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of 1 Kings and the end of Ahab’s story. He has spared Ben-hadad against God’s sentence (20:42) and taken Naboth’s vineyard by murder, and Elijah has told him that dogs will lick his blood (21:19).

The message. The word of the LORD cannot be outvoted, flattered or dodged. Four hundred prophets can agree, a king can imprison the one man who tells the truth and ride out in disguise, and still an arrow shot at nobody finds him, exactly as God said. And the chapter warns that asking God only for permission, or hearing his word and not obeying it, is the road to ruin, even for a good man.

Why it was said. The first readers had lost land, throne and temple because their kings and people listened to comfortable prophets and silenced the true ones (see the introduction; compare Jeremiah 23:16–17). This chapter shows them where that road ends, and that the word which judged them can be trusted completely, its promises included.

How the chapter makes its case. Jehoshaphat commits himself to Ahab’s war before asking God, and four hundred court prophets approve it (vv. 1–12). Micaiah, the one prophet Ahab hates, speaks only what the LORD gives him: a flock without its shepherd, and a lying spirit sent as judgment, told openly to the king, who answers with prison (vv. 13–28). Ahab goes into battle in disguise, Jehoshaphat is rescued, and a random arrow kills Ahab, whose blood the dogs lick as foretold (vv. 29–40). Then Jehoshaphat’s reign is summed up, and Ahab’s son reigns in his parents’ ways (vv. 41–53).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Micaiah is the faithful prophet who says only what God gives him, and is struck on the face and imprisoned for it; Jesus is the true Prophet who spoke only what the Father gave him to say (John 12:49), and was struck in the face before the high priest (John 18:22). And Israel is left “as sheep that have no shepherd” (v. 17), words Jesus took up when he had compassion on the crowds (Mark 6:34). Ahab is struck down as a false shepherd; Jesus, the good shepherd, “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

For us. Ask God before you promise, not after, and value the one friend who tells you the truth above the many who tell you what you want to hear. No disguise works against God’s word, but those who belong to Christ need none: the providence that found the gap in Ahab’s armour holds every arrow that comes to God’s children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a decision has already been made, asking God becomes a search for permission, and agreement proves nothing. After three years of peace, Ahab proposes a campaign to win back Ramoth-gilead, a just claim but not a commission from God, and Jehoshaphat of Judah pledges his people and horses before he says, “Inquire first for the word of the LORD” (vv. 1–5). Four hundred court prophets give the king the answer he wants (v. 6). Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet of the LORD, and Ahab admits there is one, Micaiah, whom he hates because he never prophesies anything good about him (vv. 7–9). Meanwhile, in the square by the gate, Zedekiah acts out victory with iron horns, and the whole chorus agrees (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in this section asks whether God is sending them into battle. They ask only whether the answer is favourable, and the order of verses 4 and 5 shows why: the commitment came first and the question afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: Here the fact that everyone agrees is a warning, not a proof. Four hundred men say the same thing with a piece of theatre to back it, and one man in a cell turns out to be right.

verseByVerse.quote: For three years Syria and Israel continued without war. But in the third year Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The quiet years run out, and Judah’s king comes north to befriend the house of Ahab, a friendship that will one day bring David’s line within one baby of extinction.

For three years Syria and Israel continued without war. Three years of quiet, and the reader knows what they cost. Ahab bought this peace when he had Ben-hadad in his hands and let him go, taking border towns and market stalls in Damascus for a man God had placed under sentence. A prophet with a bandage over his eyes told him the price: “your life shall be for his life” (20:42). The three years are the interval between the purchase and the bill.

Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down. Since the kingdom tore in two there has been no friendship between Jerusalem and Samaria: this book records war between them again and again (14:30; 15:6, 16), and otherwise silence. Now the king of Judah comes north on a state visit to the house of Ahab.

What Chronicles adds. Chronicles supplies what Kings leaves out, and it changes the colour of everything that follows: “Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab” (2 Chronicles 18:1). His son Jehoram married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18, 26). That woman will one day hear that her son is dead and rise up to destroy all the royal family of the house of David, and for six years the whole line of promise will hang on one baby hidden in a bedroom in the temple (2 Kings 11:1–3).

What the marriage nearly cost. Everything God had sworn to David, the throne, the lasting royal line and the Messiah, comes within one infant of extinction, and the connection that made it possible is formed here, by a good king, over dinner. Yet God kept his word through it: the lamp he had promised to keep burning in Jerusalem for David’s sake (15:4) did not go out.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, and we keep quiet and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?" And he said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?" And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses." And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab has a just grievance, and Jehoshaphat commits his whole kingdom to it before he thinks to ask God, which turns the asking into a search for permission.

Ramoth-gilead belongs to us. Ramoth-gilead is a fortress town east of the Jordan, in the high country Elijah came from, and it is Israelite territory. Ben-hadad had undertaken to hand back the cities his father had taken, as the price of his life (20:34), and three years later he has not done it. Ahab has been cheated by a man he spared, and he says so with feeling: it is ours, and we keep quiet and do nothing.

A just cause, the wrong war. The grievance is legitimate. The war is still the wrong war: having a just cause is not the same as being sent by God, and nobody in this chapter ever asks whether God is sending them.

I am as you are. Read verses 4 and 5 in the order the writer put them, because the order is the point. First comes “I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.” That is not agreement in principle but the total commitment of a kingdom, its army and its cavalry, given without condition to a new ally. Only after everything has been promised does he say, “Inquire first for the word of the LORD.”

How good men come to grief. Jehoshaphat is a genuinely good man (the writer says so plainly in v. 43), and this is exactly how good men come to grief. The decision is made in the warmth of a state visit and a family connection, and seeking God’s mind is added afterwards as a formality, in a room where four hundred employees are waiting to be asked.

In everyday life. Ask honestly how many of the prayers you have offered over a major decision came before the decision was made. Once you have said “my horses as your horses”, you are no longer inquiring; you are looking for permission. Asking first is not a hurdle set by a reluctant God. It is the trust of children who already belong to him, whose Father has promised to lead them by his Spirit and his word (Romans 8:14; Psalm 32:8).
verseByVerse.note: Ramoth-gilead was a fortress east of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall I go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for the Lord will give it into the hand of the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four hundred court prophets give the king the answer he wants, in words vague enough to fit any outcome.

About four hundred men. They are on the payroll and produced on demand, and they give a unanimous answer to a question whose preferred outcome everyone in the room already knew.

The Lord will give it. One small word is worth noticing, because the ESV preserves something of the Hebrew. Where it prints LORD in small capitals it translates the covenant name God gave at the bush; where it prints “Lord” in ordinary letters it translates adonai, which simply means master, and which could be said of any god. Do not make more of it than it will carry: the same men use the covenant name six verses later (v. 12), and one of them claims the Spirit of the LORD to Micaiah’s face (v. 24). They are not prophets of Baal but professional prophets of Israel’s God, or of a version of him tamed to say what the court wants. Yet at the decisive moment, asked the decisive question, they answered with a word that could have meant anybody’s god.

Into the hand of the king. Notice too what the answer leaves unsaid. “The king” is not named: into the hand of the king of Israel, or of the king of Syria who holds the town? Many think the vagueness was deliberate, the kind of oracle that cannot be proved wrong whatever happens. Micaiah will repeat it word for word (v. 15), and then tell the king what it is worth.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so." Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jehoshaphat senses that the four hundred do not speak for God, and Ahab admits there is one man who does, and that he hates him because the truth has never flattered him.

Another prophet of the LORD. Jehoshaphat has sat through four hundred men answering, and he accuses nobody; he simply asks, as politely as the question allows, whether anyone here actually speaks for God. Whatever it was that he heard, he heard it.

There is yet one man. Ahab knows there is a real one. He can name him, he knows where to find him, and he can tell him instantly from the four hundred, which means he also knows exactly what the four hundred are. Ahab is not confused about who tells the truth.

Micaiah the son of Imlah. His name means “Who is like the LORD?”, fitting for the one man in the story who will not make the LORD say what the king wants to hear. Nothing is known of him outside this chapter and its parallel in 2 Chronicles 18: he is sent for, speaks the word, and disappears into a prison cell.

I hate him. Ahab’s objection is not that Micaiah is wrong. In four chapters he has never once said that a word brought to him was false; his complaint is that it is unfavourable. It is the same note as “Have you found me, O my enemy?” (21:20): a man who has stopped arguing with the message and now simply dislikes the messenger.

Let not the king say so. Jehoshaphat’s reply is the measure of him: a mild protest, and then he says nothing more, and goes to the war.

Bring quickly. Having just explained that he hates the man, Ahab sends for him at once, because his guest asked. He is keeping up appearances: he will not act on Micaiah’s word, but he will not be seen refusing to hear it in front of the king of Judah.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them. And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'" And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two kings in their robes watch four hundred prophets stage a public rally for the war, and its leader turns a true word of Scripture into a false promise.

At the threshing floor. A threshing floor is a wide circle of packed earth by the gate, the one flat open space a walled town has, where public business was done. Two thrones have been carried out and set on it; two kings sit in their state robes in the open air, and before them four hundred men prophesy at once, with the whole city watching. It is not a consultation but a rally.

Made for himself horns of iron. Prophets often acted out their message: Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces (11:30), and Jeremiah would later wear a yoke through the streets of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:2). Zedekiah stages the same kind of sign, but notice the words “for himself”: the props, like the message, are of his own making.

With these you shall push the Syrians. The uncomfortable part is that Zedekiah is quoting Scripture. Moses blessed Joseph with this very image: “his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth” (Deuteronomy 33:17). Zedekiah has taken a genuine word of God about the northern tribes and staged it as a promise about tomorrow’s battle. That is how false assurance is usually built: not out of nothing, but out of real verses, correctly quoted, aimed at a situation they were never about.

All the prophets prophesied so. It is comforting when everyone agrees, but it proves nothing. Everyone in that square agreed, every one of them was wrong, and the only man who was right was still walking up the road under escort.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–28 — What the LORD Says to Me, That I Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The true prophet says only what God gives him, whatever it costs. Urged to agree with the majority, Micaiah vows to speak what the LORD says (vv. 13–14). He echoes the four hundred mockingly until Ahab demands the truth (vv. 15–16). Then he gives it: Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, the king dead and the people sent home in peace (vv. 17–18); and a vision of the LORD’s court in heaven, where a spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab’s prophets, a judgment on a king who has refused the truth, now told to him in full (vv. 19–23). Struck by Zedekiah and sent to prison, Micaiah stakes his life on the outcome before all the people (vv. 24–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The vision says something the Bible does not soften: God governs even the deceiving of a man who has refused the truth. But the spirit volunteers, the prophets were already selling favourable answers, and Ahab is told the whole of it: the verse notes below show why this is a sentence passed, not a trick played.
verseByVerse.examples: The deception is described to the man being deceived, in open court, before a horse is saddled. That is a last mercy in the shape of a warning, and Ahab imprisons the man who brought it and rides out anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably." But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressed to fall into line with the majority, Micaiah vows to say only what the LORD gives him to say.

Speak favorably. The messenger thinks he is doing Micaiah a kindness, and his advice shows how the whole court works. He does not claim the four hundred are right, only that they are “favorable”, and that the wise course is to match them. Nobody in this chapter, from the king down to the messenger, judges a prophecy by whether it is true. The only test in use is whether it will please.

As the LORD lives. Micaiah uses the covenant name twice in one short sentence. It is Elijah’s oath, the words that opened this whole part of the book (17:1), and after four hundred men and one small “Lord”, it lands like a door shutting.

What the LORD says to me, that I will speak. He does not promise to bring bad news, or to be brave. He promises to say what he is given to say, which is the only vow a prophet is entitled to make.

The market for agreeable prophets. Ahab’s court is not as far from us as it looks. Much of modern life is built to supply four hundred voices on demand: the feed that learns what we like and serves us more of it, the news that tells our side it was right, the friends we slowly select for agreeing with us. Nobody has to lie outright; the system simply rewards whatever pleases. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, in his essay Live Not by Lies, argued that a lie can rule a whole society only with the small daily cooperation of ordinary people, and that freedom begins when one person quietly refuses to take part. Micaiah is that person.

Why we gather the four hundred. We do not gather them because we are stupid but because we are afraid: the truth about ourselves feels like a death sentence. The gospel does not flatter; it says the four hundred were wrong about us. Yet it is spoken by a Prophet who was struck in the face for telling the truth and then died for the people who struck him, so that the truth no longer has to be hated in order to be survived.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall we refrain?" And he answered him, "Go up and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king." But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah hands Ahab the four hundred’s answer word for word, and Ahab, hearing it from an honest man, knows at once that it is not the truth.

Go up and triumph. Micaiah repeats the four hundred word for word, and the irony must have been audible from the back of the square. It is a mirror held up: Ahab has had a favourable answer four hundred times over, and Micaiah hands him a four hundred and first so that he can hear how it sounds from a man he cannot bully.

Nothing but the truth. The moment Ahab gets the answer he asked for from someone he knows is honest, he demands the truth. All the while four hundred men told him the same thing, he knew he was not being told the truth, and was content.

How many times shall I make you swear? So this is not their first meeting. Ahab has stood here before, demanding the truth under oath and then refusing it when it came (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah’s first vision announces the king’s death in the picture of a flock without its shepherd, and tenderly sends the flock itself home in peace.

I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains. It is a death notice delivered with extraordinary tenderness, not towards the king but past him, towards the people.

As sheep that have no shepherd. The king of Israel is the shepherd; that is the standing image, and it is what God said to David: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2). Sheep on a hillside with nobody gathering them means the shepherd is gone. “These have no master” is God saying, of the king sitting before Micaiah in his robes, that he is as good as dead. The words go back to Moses, who asked God for a successor “that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). The prayer God answered with Joshua, Micaiah now turns into a verdict on Ahab.

Let each return to his home in peace. Then the strangest, kindest clause. God’s instruction concerns the flock: they are to go home safely. The army is not to be destroyed, and the nation is not under sentence today. One man is, and the rest are to be let go.

Like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus took up this picture, and it is one of the tenderest things said about him. Seeing the crowds, “he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (Mark 6:34): the same diagnosis of a country whose leaders had failed it. And on the night he was betrayed he quoted Zechariah over his own disciples: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26:31). The difference is everything. At Ramoth-gilead the shepherd is struck because he is worthless, and the sheep are sent home out of the way. At Calvary the Shepherd is struck for the sheep, and the scattering lasts three days.

Did I not tell you? Ahab has just been told he will die in this battle, and he turns to his guest and says, I told you so. He treats his own death sentence as a point won in an argument, with no thought whether it might be true.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left; and the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.' And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; the LORD has declared disaster for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micaiah’s second vision shows the court of heaven, where the LORD, as judge, lets a lying spirit into the court prophets so that Ahab, who has refused the truth, will go to his death; and Ahab is told all of it.

I saw the LORD sitting on his throne. Nothing in these chapters is harder to accept as it stands. God is seated, and the host of heaven stands on either side of him. Two kings sit on two thrones at the gate of Samaria; Micaiah has been shown the throne that matters.

One said one thing, and another said another. The scene is pictured as a royal council, the court of heaven drawn like the court of an earthly king, as in Job 1–2 and Isaiah 6. Below, at the gate, the council is unanimous; above, it deliberates. The unanimity on earth is the lie, and the decision that counts is taken where Ahab cannot see it, until Micaiah tells him.

Four things held together. Do not soften it: Scripture says in several places that God governs even the deceiving of a man, and uses it as judgment. But four things must be held together, and all four are in the text.

A spirit came forward. First, the spirit volunteers. God asks; a spirit steps forward and proposes the method himself. God does not put a lie into an unwilling mouth, and the Bible never says that he lies: “God is not man, that he should lie” (Numbers 23:19); “he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

In the mouth of all his prophets. Second, look at whose mouths receive it: men who had been selling favourable answers for years before this morning. Nothing new is put into them. They are handed over to what they already were, and left to it.

A strong delusion. Third, Paul describes the same arrangement and gives the reason. Of those who perish “because they refused to love the truth and so be saved”, he writes, “Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). The delusion is not the cause of the ruin but the sentence passed on people who had already made their choice about the truth. Ezekiel says the same of a man who comes to a prophet with idols in his heart (Ezekiel 14:9), and three times in one paragraph of Romans Paul says that God “gave them up” to what they wanted (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

Ahab is told. Fourth, and this settles the fairness of it: the whole proceeding is described to the man it concerns, in public, before a horse has been saddled. He is told that the four hundred are lying, why they are lying, and who arranged it. Nobody was ever deceived with more warning. So it is not a trap but a last mercy in the form of a disclosure, with a way out standing open at every moment: believe the man telling you the truth. Ahab hears it all, has him locked up, and rides out.

A test for today. If the friends who would tell you the truth have gradually been replaced by friends who will not, if the preaching you seek out never leaves a mark, and if the one person who questions you is the one you have decided is difficult, then no lying spirit needs to be sent: the work is already largely done. The remedy is not a stronger will but the mercy that still speaks. God sends his word to people who have stopped listening, as he sent Micaiah, and the Spirit who opens ears is given to all who ask (Luke 11:13).

Does this mean God lies, or makes people sin? The plain reader is right to ask, and the honest answer has two halves. The text does say the LORD put the lying spirit there (v. 23), and Scripture never pretends that God is a bystander to evil: he rules it, sets its limits and turns it to his ends (Job 1:12; Genesis 50:20). It also says he cannot lie (Titus 1:2) and tempts no one (James 1:13), and that the guilt of a lie belongs to the liar. Many read the throne-room scene as a vision given to Micaiah, a picture of what was really happening, not a transcript of heaven’s minutes; on either reading the meaning is the same. Christians have confessed it this way: God’s rule reaches even to sin, yet he is neither its author nor its approver (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 5.4). The plainest proof is the cross, where wicked men did what God’s hand had planned beforehand, and the false charge that Jesus was a blasphemer became the means of our salvation (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). The God who ruled that lie without lying rules this one too.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "How did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?" And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leading court prophet strikes Micaiah in the name of the Spirit, and Micaiah quietly tells him that he will soon be hiding for his life.

Struck Micaiah on the cheek. The man with the iron horns hits him in the face and claims the Spirit of the LORD as he does it. He does not think of himself as a liar. He has told kings what they wanted to hear for so long that he can no longer conceive of God saying anything else.

You shall see on that day. Micaiah’s reply is quiet and exact: there will be a day, and you will spend it in a back room with the door shut. The reader has met that room before. Ben-hadad, after Aphek, “fled and entered an inner chamber in the city” (20:30). The man with the iron horns will end where the defeated king ended, hiding, waiting to hear whether anyone is coming for him.

A shadow of a later trial. Many Christians have seen here a shadow of the day when the one true Prophet stood alone before the religious establishment, and an officer struck him in the face for his answer (John 18:22).

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah, and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son, and say, 'Thus says the king, "Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water, until I come in peace."'" And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab answers the word of God with a prison sentence, and Micaiah stakes his life, before the whole city, on the king not coming home.

Amon the governor of the city. Notice who he is handed to. Amon is the city governor, the civil administrator of Samaria, and Joash is called “the king’s son”, which in these books is often a court title, not a statement about parentage. Micaiah is not sent to a military prison or a dungeon under the palace but signed over to the ordinary authorities as a routine prisoner. The ordinary machinery of government is used to shut away the one voice in it that was telling the truth.

Until I come in peace. Bread and water until I come home safe: Ahab answers the prophecy with an insult, not an argument. “Take him back,” he says, so Micaiah may well have been in custody already. That would explain why he could be produced so quickly, and a good deal about the tone of a man brought from a cell to a rally and told to agree with four hundred well-fed colleagues.

If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me. Micaiah puts his own life at stake, publicly, and knows exactly what he is doing. The law of Moses gives one test for a prophet: “if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken”, and it prescribes death for the prophet who speaks presumptuously (Deuteronomy 18:20–22). So Micaiah stakes his life on a battle he will hear of in a cell, against the unanimous opinion of every professional prophet in the kingdom. If Ahab walks home, Micaiah dies.

Hear, all you peoples! Then he calls the witnesses, in words that are almost the opening line of the prophecy of Micah (Micah 1:2). He wants the crowd on the record: when news comes back from the battle, nobody is to say that this was not said, or that it was said quietly.

Textual note. The Greek translation lacks this last clause, and many think a scribe added it from Micah; nothing in the story depends on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–40 — A Certain Man Drew His Bow at Random
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No disguise can hide a man from the word of God. Both kings go up to Ramoth-gilead, Ahab dressed as a common soldier and Jehoshaphat in his royal robes (vv. 29–30). The Syrian chariots, ordered to fight only the king of Israel, chase Jehoshaphat until he cries out and they turn away (vv. 31–33). Then an arrow drawn at random strikes Ahab at a joint in his armour, and he dies propped up in his chariot at evening (vv. 34–35). The army goes home, just as Micaiah’s vision said, and the dogs lick Ahab’s blood at the pool of Samaria “according to the word of the LORD” (vv. 36–38). His great achievements are filed away in a sentence (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology: Every precaution worked: the robes drew the enemy, the disguise held, the captains turned back. Yet an arrow loosed by a man aiming at nobody found the one man in the field who could not be identified.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who disguises himself against a prophecy has conceded that it is true; he has simply decided to out-manoeuvre it rather than repent.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab rides to the battle he has been told he will not survive, disguised, with his ally in royal robes as a decoy; and good Jehoshaphat goes too, because he has already given away his freedom to refuse.

So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat went up. Verse 29 raises a harder question than Ahab’s stubbornness, because two kings ride out, and one of them is a good man. Ahab’s decision is no surprise: he has spent four chapters hearing the word of God and doing as he pleased, and a man who has already imprisoned the prophet will not be stopped by him.

Jehoshaphat heard it all. But Jehoshaphat was there for all of it. He asked for a prophet of the LORD and got one. He heard the scattered flock and the lying spirit, and watched an honest man struck in the face and led away to bread and water. His last recorded word was “Let not the king say so.” Then he went, put on his robes exactly as asked, and rode north into another man’s war against a word he had personally sent for.

What the alliance cost. This is what the alliance had cost him before a single arrow flew. He did not disbelieve Micaiah; he simply had nothing left with which to refuse, because he had given it all away in verse 4 before he asked God anything. That is how commitments work. They do not usually take your convictions from you. They take away your freedom to act on them.

I will disguise myself. Told in public that he will not come back, Ahab does not cancel the battle or repent. He dresses as an ordinary soldier and asks the ally who said “I am as you are” to ride into the same battle dressed as a king. No innocent reading is available: the enemy’s whole effort goes at the man in the robes, which is what robes are for. Ahab is using his daughter’s father-in-law as a decoy.

What the disguise shows. It shows that he believed Micaiah: not enough to obey him or stay home, but enough to take precautions. Remember what he said about armour three years before, in the best sentence of his life: “Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off” (20:11). He straps this on at dawn. He does not take it off.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel." And when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is surely the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out. And when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Syrian chariots hunt the man in the robes, and when Jehoshaphat cries out, God turns them away: a real rescue, though not an approval of why he was there.

The thirty-two captains of his chariots. Thirty-two captains, where three years before there were thirty-two allied kings: the very reorganisation Ben-hadad’s advisers recommended after his first defeat (20:24). The Syrians learn.

Only with the king of Israel. The order has a single objective: one man. Ben-hadad wants the king of Israel, the man who once took him up into his chariot and called him brother (20:32–33).

And Jehoshaphat cried out. Chronicles tells us what the cry was and what came of it: “Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him” (2 Chronicles 18:31). He is rescued.

An undeserved rescue. That needs saying carefully. God pulls him out of a danger he had no business being near, in an alliance he should never have made, in a war he was never asked to fight. The rescue is real mercy, and it is not an endorsement. When he gets home a prophet meets him (Jehu the son of Hanani, who had rebuked Baasha a generation and more before, 16:1) and asks, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD?” (2 Chronicles 19:2). Being delivered from a foolish decision is not the same as being told it was wise.

verseByVerse.quote: But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded." And the battle continued that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, until at evening he died. And the blood of the wound flowed into the bottom of the chariot. And about sunset a cry went through the army, "Every man to his city, and every man to his country!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
An arrow shot at nobody finds the one disguised king at the one gap in his armour, and he dies at sunset while his army goes home in peace, exactly as Micaiah said.

Drew his bow at random. The Hebrew behind “at random” means “in his innocence”: an unnamed soldier, one of thousands, draws a bowstring at nobody in particular and lets go. The arrow had to find, among thousands, the one man who had removed every mark that identified him, and strike the single seam between the scale armor and the breastplate. Every precaution worked, and none of it mattered.

The lot in the lap. Scripture states the principle in a proverb: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). And another reads as though it were written with this battlefield in view: “No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30–31).

Carry me out of the battle. He asks to be carried out, and he is not. If the king’s chariot leaves the field the army breaks, so they wedge him upright, facing the enemy, and leave him there. He stands until evening in his disguise, held in place, watching a battle he cannot fight, bleeding into the floor of the chariot. It takes him until sunset to die: the most undignified death in the book, and exactly the death of a man who spent his reign propped up by people telling him he was winning.

Every man to his city. Set that beside the oracle: “let each return to his home in peace” (v. 17). At sunset the cry goes down the line, the army disperses, and the flock goes home in peace, exactly as God had said. The man in the cell was right.

No random arrows. There is no such thing as a random arrow, and the doctrine has a second side that most readers need far more than the first. The same providence that made Ahab’s disguise useless means that no arrow has ever reached a child of God without first passing through his hand. Nothing in your life arrives at random either: the diagnosis, the redundancy, the phone call at two in the morning. The God who aimed an arrow at a king in disguise is your Father, and for those who belong to Christ that is not a terror but a reason to sleep in peace. It does not make the arrow painless or the loss small; it means that the hand that allowed it is the hand that holds you, and will not let go.

Uncertain wording. The word the ESV renders “scale armor” is uncommon and seems to mean something like “joinings” or “attachments”; older English versions have “the joints of the harness”. Exactly which pieces of armour are meant is not certain, but the sense is clear: the arrow went in at a joint, where one piece met another.
verseByVerse.note: “At random” is literally “in his innocence” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king died, and was brought to Samaria. And they buried the king in Samaria. And they washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in it, according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab is buried as a king, but the dogs lick his blood from the chariot, just as the LORD had said: the word that was postponed was never cancelled.

They buried the king in Samaria. After Carmel, Naboth, the four hundred and the disguise, Ahab gets a state funeral, and the writer records it without comment, because the comment is in the next verse.

The dogs licked up his blood. They bring the chariot back and wash it out at the public pool, and the dogs come. The pool was evidently a public place where the city’s prostitutes bathed, and the writer records the detail on purpose: the king’s blood goes to the dogs and into their bathwater. Some think these women belonged to the Baal and Asherah worship that Ahab and Jezebel promoted (16:31–33), which would make the shame fitting. Either way, the man who “sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD” (21:25) ends without honour.

According to the word of the LORD that he had spoken. The writer is right to say so, though a reader who remembers chapter 21 will notice that Elijah spoke of the place where dogs licked Naboth’s blood, at Jezreel, and this is Samaria. The reason is in that chapter: because Ahab humbled himself in sackcloth, the disaster on his house was expressly postponed beyond his own days (21:29). The rest is collected from his son, whose body Jehu will throw onto Naboth’s plot while quoting the oracle aloud (2 Kings 9:25–26). The word did not miss. It was paid in two instalments, and the delay was announced in advance.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “prostitutes” normally means exactly that, and nearly all modern translations read it so. Some older interpreters took it differently, and the King James Version has “they washed his armour”. The usual meaning is much the likelier.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, and the ivory house that he built and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahab’s great achievements are filed away in a single sentence, because the writer of Kings measures a king not by his buildings but by how he answered the word of God.

The ivory house that he built. The ivory house was real, and it has been dug up: excavations at Samaria have produced hundreds of pieces of carved ivory panelling, and a century later Amos is still denouncing “the houses of ivory” in that city (Amos 3:15). Ahab was one of the great builders and soldiers of the region; Assyrian records credit him with a large chariot force at the battle of Qarqar, about 853 BC (see the introduction).

Are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles? The writer files all of it in another book, in one sentence, as he did with Omri. He gave four chapters to a temple and a story of its own to a widow’s flour jar, and he gives the ivory house half a line. The historian’s measure is not the world’s, and by now the reader should expect it.

Ahab slept with his fathers. The closing phrase is the gentle one, usually said of kings who died in peace, here applied to a man who bled to death in a chariot in disguise. It is also the last quiet thing anyone will say about the house of Ahab.

Ahaziah his son reigned in his place. The house of Ahab goes on, for now. Ahaziah will reign two years and walk in the way of his father and his mother (vv. 51–53), and his fall opens the next book (2 Kings 1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Every Way That His Father Had Done
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Good kings and bad ones pass, but the story is not over, because the word of the LORD is still at work. Jehoshaphat’s reign is summed up: he did what was right, as his father Asa had, though the high places remained and he made peace with the house of Ahab (vv. 41–45). He cleared out the last cult prostitutes, saw his gold fleet wrecked, and refused a second partnership with Ahab’s son (vv. 46–50). Then Ahaziah takes the northern throne and walks in the way of his father, his mother and Jeroboam, serving Baal (vv. 51–53). The book ends with judgment still pending on the house of Ahab, and the reader waiting for the word to land.
verseByVerse.theology: Ahaziah is the only king in these books whose mother's way is named as a category of its own. Jezebel outlives her husband, and the writer marks it by making her a road that a king can walk in.
verseByVerse.examples: The book stops in the middle of the story. In the Hebrew Bible 1 and 2 Kings are one book, and the break here came in with the Greek translation, probably because the scroll was long.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel. Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. Yet the high places were not taken away, and the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he warred, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And from the land he exterminated the remnant of the male cult prostitutes who remained in the days of his father Asa. There was no king in Edom; a deputy was king. Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, for the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber. Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my servants go with your servants in the ships," but Jehoshaphat was not willing. And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place. Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. He served Baal and worshiped him and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger in every way that his father had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s good king is summed up, faithful but harmed by his ties to Ahab’s house, and Ahab’s son takes Israel’s throne in his parents’ ways: the book ends with judgment pending and the word of the LORD still unfailing.

Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign. The writer turns south and gives the other kingdom its accounting. In Judah the king’s mother is always named, because the queen mother held a real position at court. Twenty-five years is a long and stable reign: while Samaria went through Carmel, a drought, two Syrian wars, a judicial murder and a king bleeding to death in a chariot, Jerusalem had one king throughout.

He walked in all the way of Asa his father. This is a good verdict, one of only a handful in these books, and the writer gives it without qualification before he says anything else.

The high places were not taken away. Then the standing exception. The high places were hilltop shrines where people went on sacrificing to the LORD in the old Canaanite manner, at the wrong altars, outside the temple God had appointed. Almost every good king of Judah gets this footnote, and it is not pedantry: it is the difference between reforming a court and reforming a country. The king could tear down what was in Jerusalem; he could not change what a village did on its own hill on an ordinary evening.

Chronicles on the high places. A reader who checks will find that Chronicles says both that Jehoshaphat “took the high places and the Asherim out of Judah” (2 Chronicles 17:6) and that “the high places, however, were not taken away” (2 Chronicles 20:33). The likeliest answer is that he removed the shrines to other gods and tried early in his reign to remove the rest, but the people’s local altars to the LORD came back and stayed. Chronicles itself gives the reason: “the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their fathers.”

Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel. On this peace (v. 44) the writer offers no opinion, and rightly. On its face it heals a feud of two generations between brothers. What it produced was a battle that nearly killed him, a marriage that put Ahab’s daughter into the house of David, and a generation in which that woman murdered the royal family and reigned six years over Jerusalem. Some decisions cannot be judged in the year they are made: the bill for a peace or an alliance may be presented two generations later to people who had no vote in the matter.

The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat. Once more a reign is filed in another book, and the file holds the finest hour of his life, which Chronicles tells. When a coalition of Moabites and Ammonites came against Judah, the king proclaimed a fast, stood in the temple court and prayed a prayer that ends with words anyone can use: “we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12). The answer came back through a Levite: “the battle is not yours but God’s … You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf” (20:15, 17). And in the morning he put the singers in front of the army.

The same man. At Ramoth-gilead he promised his horses before he asked, and had to cry out for his life in a chariot. Facing that horde he had nothing to promise; he asked first, and stood still.

The remnant of the male cult prostitutes. Real reform, and costly. Cult prostitution had come in with the Canaanite shrines and survived his father’s purge (15:12); Jehoshaphat finished it. Chronicles adds that he sent officials and Levites through the towns of Judah with the Book of the Law, teaching the people (2 Chronicles 17:7–9), the sort of thing that never gets into a chronicle of might and wars and is worth more than either.

There was no king in Edom; a deputy was king. Edom was under Judah’s control, which is why the next verse can speak of a fleet: the port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba lay in Edomite territory.

The ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber. He tried to revive Solomon’s gold route (9:26–28), and the fleet was wrecked in harbour. “Ships of Tarshish” were large ocean-going trading ships, named after Tarshish, a far western port, probably in Spain; Ophir was a source of gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa. Chronicles gives the reason for the wreck, and it belongs with verse 44: he had gone into partnership with Ahaziah of Israel, and a prophet told him, “Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made” (2 Chronicles 20:35–37).

Jehoshaphat was not willing. Asked again, he says no. He allied, lost the ships, and declined the next invitation, which is the honest shape of most people’s obedience. It may be the most encouraging thing in the chapter: a good man, slow and expensive to teach, taught by a God who did not give him up.

Buried with his fathers in the city of David. He is buried in the city of David, where his son’s wife will one day make her attempt on David’s whole line.

He reigned two years over Israel. The son of the man who reigned twenty-two years and built an ivory house gets two, and the writer will spend most of them on a fall through a lattice and a question sent to the wrong god (2 Kings 1).

In the way of his mother. No other king in these books is said to walk in the way of his mother. Beside his father’s way and the way of Jeroboam, the writer opens a third column and puts Jezebel in it: she has become a road, and her son is walking down it. She outlives Ahab by some twelve years and sees two of her sons on the throne, and the sentence Elijah pronounced over her at Naboth’s vineyard is still outstanding.

In every way that his father had done. The last words of the book are “that his father had done”, and nothing is resolved. Elijah has not been heard from since Naboth’s vineyard. Jezebel is queen mother and untouched. Micaiah, so far as we are told, is still in his cell. The sentence on the house of Ahab is pending; Hazael has not been anointed; Jehu is an officer in somebody’s army; and Elisha is serving an old prophet somewhere in the north.

What stands finished. What does stand finished, at the end of these twenty-two chapters, is the thing the book has been about all along. Kings come and go at a bewildering rate: three dynasties fall in two chapters, a temple is built and looted, a kingdom splits, and the great men of the age get half a verse each. Running through it all, never once failing, is the word of the LORD: spoken by Ahijah over a torn cloak, by Joshua over Jericho centuries before Hiel picked up a trowel, by Elijah over a rainless sky, by an unnamed man of God over an altar at Bethel, and by a prisoner in Samaria over an arrow not yet shot. Every one of them landed. Kings are what the book counts; the word is what it trusts.

The Son of David. And the word was not finished with David’s house. It would keep its promise through a hidden baby in the temple, through exile and silence, to the Son of David: the true Shepherd Ahab never was, and the Word made flesh (John 1:14).

Why do the reign lengths and synchronisms not seem to add up? Israel and Judah counted regnal years differently at different times: one counted the year a king came to the throne as his first year, the other did not; and sons often reigned alongside their fathers as co-regents, with the overlapping years counted to both. When these practices are allowed for, the dates largely fit together, as Edwin Thiele showed, and match Assyrian records at key points (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. Verse 47 is compressed, and its exact sense is not certain. Most take it to mean that Edom had no king of its own and was governed by a deputy, probably appointed from Judah, which explains how Jehoshaphat could use an Edomite port. Either way Edom was not independent; a generation later it “revolted from the rule of Judah and set up a king of their own” (2 Kings 8:20).

22.theology:
The order of verses 4 and 5. A genuinely good man commits everything and afterwards asks God about it. Once the promise is made, the inquiry is no longer an inquiry but a search for permission.

One small word at verse 6. Where the ESV prints LORD in small capitals it renders the covenant name; where it prints Lord it renders adonai, master, which any nation could say of any god. The four hundred answer the decisive question with the ordinary word. It should not be pressed far, since the same men use the covenant name at v. 12, but Jehoshaphat at once asked for a prophet of the LORD, and Micaiah opens with as the LORD lives (v. 14). The reader is meant to hear the difference.

A just cause is not a commission (v. 3). Ahab has a rightful claim to the city, but God has not sent him to fight for it. The only test anyone applies to a prophecy here is whether it is favorable (v. 13).

The lying spirit (vv. 19-23). The spirit volunteers, and God never lies. The mouths that receive it had been selling favourable answers for years, and they are handed over to what they already were, as Paul says of those who refused to love the truth (2 Thess. 2:10-11). And Ahab is told, in public, before he saddles a horse. It is not a trap but a last warning, with the way out standing open.

Sheep without a shepherd (v. 17). The prophecy announces the king’s death, yet it is spoken tenderly towards the people, his flock, and at sunset the flock goes home. Jesus took up the same words over the crowds (Mark 6:34), and at Calvary the Shepherd was struck for the sheep (Matt. 26:31).

No random arrow (v. 34). Every precaution Ahab took worked perfectly and was irrelevant, because the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov. 21:31). The same providence means no arrow has ever reached a child of God except through his Father's hand.
22.examples:
Then: A king, told in open court that he would not come home, dressed as a private soldier, put the visiting king in the royal robes, hid in his own army, and was held upright in his chariot until the sun went down.

Now: Three things. First, verse 5: after my horses as your horses, what looks like seeking guidance is shopping for approval. Second, the lying spirit is less exotic than it looks: surround yourself with agreeable voices and its work is largely done already. Third, the disguise: believing the word enough to take precautions and not enough to obey it, admitting that God is right and then trying to dodge the consequences. That is the posture a respectable reader is most likely to be standing in. The way out is not more resolve but the mercy Ahab refused: God still speaks to those who have stopped listening, the Son of David obeyed his Father where every king of Israel failed, and those who come to him in confession are forgiven and given his Spirit to walk in the truth (1 John 1:9; Galatians 5:16).

keyVerse.quote: But Micaiah said, “As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak.”
keyVerse.note: Micaiah’s vow is the hinge of the chapter. Against four hundred agreeable voices, a messenger’s friendly advice and a king’s hatred, he will say only what God gives him, and everything that follows proves that word true. It presses the chapter’s question on every reader: do we want God’s word, or only a favourable one? And it points to Jesus, the Prophet who spoke only what the Father gave him and was struck for it.

22.reflection:
Jehoshaphat promised “my horses as your horses” before he said “Inquire first for the word of the LORD” (vv. 4–5). Think of a significant decision you have made: when did you really begin to ask God about it? What helps us to ask before we commit, not after?

Ahab hated Micaiah “for he never prophesies good concerning me” (v. 8), and surrounded himself with four hundred agreeable voices. Who in your life tells you the truth, and how do you treat them? How can we be that kind of friend to one another?

Ahab believed Micaiah enough to disguise himself but not enough to stay at home (v. 30). Where are we tempted to take precautions against God’s word instead of obeying it?

An arrow drawn “at random” found the king (v. 34). How does God’s rule over every detail comfort those who belong to Christ, the Shepherd who was struck for his sheep, especially when hard things come?
